cards.question: In the _____ of 29 August 2026, a narrow majority on a turnout above 82 per cent rejected resuming accession talks that a eurosceptic government had paused in 2013.
cards.answerDate: Applied17 July 2009Talks pausedspring 2013Voted29 August 2026
cards.abstract:
The Iceland referendum of 29 August 2026 was an advisory vote, held under the Elections Act, on one question: whether Iceland should resume accession negotiations with the European Union. It was not a vote on joining, because if talks resumed and ended in a deal, a second referendum would decide on membership itself. Iceland had applied on 17 July 2009, at the height of its financial crisis, and in June 2010 the European Council unanimously agreed to open negotiations and grant it candidate status. By early 2013 the two sides had closed 11 of the 33 negotiating chapters, but the election of May 2013 swung Iceland back towards Euroscepticism and brought in a government that declared a pause. In March 2015 the foreign minister wrote to the Council presidency that Iceland should not be considered a candidate, although Iceland’s ministry says the application was never formally withdrawn.

The coalition formed after the elections of late 2024 had promised a vote, and on 6 March 2026 it asked parliament to hold it on 29 August. The National Electoral Commission’s count of 30 August showed 118,040 votes against resuming talks and 105,339 for, or 52.8 per cent to 47.2, on a turnout of 82.6 per cent. Opponents stressed sovereignty and fishing grounds, while supporters, led by the prime minister, pointed to economic stability, lower interest rates and security amid the war in Ukraine. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said membership would stay off the agenda for the rest of her term, which ends in 2028, and the Commission said it respected the choice. Iceland stays outside the Union but inside the European Economic Area and the Schengen area, and the government was expected to ask parliament whether to withdraw the application formally.

cards.question: Estonia’s prime minister from January 2021 until July 2024, _____ was then appointed by the European Council as High Representative for a term running to 31 October 2029.
cards.answerDate: Estonian PM26 January 2021 – July 2024HR/VPfrom 1 December 2024
cards.abstract:
Kaja Kallas is the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, the European Union’s top diplomat, and since 1 December 2024 she has also been a Vice-President of the European Commission. Under Article 18 of the Treaty on European Union the holder conducts the common foreign and security policy as mandated by the Council, presides over the Foreign Affairs Council and ensures the consistency of the Union’s external action. The European Council appointed her on 24 July 2024, with the agreement of the Commission President-elect, for a term running to 31 October 2029. A lawyer by training, she worked as an attorney and law-firm partner for more than a decade before entering politics in 2011. She sat in the Estonian parliament in 2011–2014 and 2019–2021, in the European Parliament from 2014 to 2018, and led the Reform Party from 2018 to 2024.

She became prime minister on 26 January 2021, the first woman to lead Estonia’s government since independence, and stood down in July 2024 to take the Brussels post. Her premiership was marked by a firm line on Russia, including her opposition in 2021 to inviting President Putin to an EU summit. On 9 March 2026 she told the EU Ambassadors Conference that current trends point to a new world order of competition and coercive power politics, with military powers seeking to establish and secure spheres of influence, and that rules and institutions built over 80 years are weakening. She named three priorities: supporting Ukraine and strengthening defence, stabilising the neighbourhood, including through faster enlargement, and pursuing economic partnerships and trade agreements. Euronews reported in June 2026 that critics faulted her remarks on China and her push to use immobilised Russian assets, while diplomats said the limits are structural, since foreign policy needs unanimity, so one no can derail a decision, and the Commission has taken a larger geopolitical role.

cards.question: Under a secret protocol to the pact of 23 August 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union fixed a boundary between their _____ across the Baltic states and Poland.
cards.abstract:
Spheres of influence are regions where a great power claims a privileged, usually exclusive, say over the politics, security or economy of weaker states and expects rivals to keep out. The idea is older than the term: in 1494 Spain and Portugal divided newly discovered lands between themselves, and in the 19th century the concept became tied to imperial rivalry. In December 1823 President James Monroe told Congress that the American continents were no longer to be considered subjects for future colonisation by any European power. The General Act of the Berlin Conference of 26 February 1885 required any power taking territory on the coasts of Africa to notify the other signatories, so that they could press claims of their own. The best-known written case is the secret protocol to the German–Soviet pact of 23 August 1939, which fixed a boundary between German and Soviet spheres of influence across the Baltic states and Poland and was to be kept strictly secret.

On 9 March 2026 the High Representative, Kaja Kallas, told EU ambassadors that trends point to a new world order of competition and coercive power politics, with 'military powers who aim to establish and secure spheres of influence'. She added that the norms, rules and institutions the world has built over 80 years were already weakening. The Union’s founding treaty sets a different principle, guiding it by the UN Charter, international law, the Helsinki Final Act and the aims of the Charter of Paris. The Helsinki Final Act of 1975 lists sovereign equality first among its principles and records each state’s right to be or not to be a party to treaties of alliance and its right to neutrality. Scholars note that the term is mostly used against rivals, that powers rarely admit to a sphere because it would restrict their room for manoeuvre, and that spheres are not a separate kind of order but practices of control and exclusion found within any hierarchy.

cards.question: Under the Treaty of Lisbon, the Union’s _____ is one heading that covers foreign and security policy, trade, development aid, sanctions and international agreements, guided by the principles of Article 21.
cards.answerDate: Lisbon signed13 December 2007Lisbon in force1 December 2009
cards.abstract:
External action is the treaty term for the European Union’s action on the international scene, from foreign and security policy to trade, development aid, sanctions and international agreements. Title V of the Treaty on European Union sets out the general provisions on external action, and its Article 21 says the Union’s action abroad is to be guided by democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for international law. Article 21 lists objectives such as safeguarding the Union’s values, security and integrity, preserving peace, fostering sustainable development in poorer countries and promoting multilateral cooperation. Part Five of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union carries the detail, covering the common commercial policy, development cooperation, humanitarian aid, restrictive measures, international agreements, delegations and the solidarity clause. The common foreign and security policy sits in a separate chapter of Title V under its own rules, so external action is wider than foreign policy in the narrow sense.

The Treaty of Lisbon, which entered into force on 1 December 2009, created the post of High Representative, a Commission Vice-President charged with ensuring the consistency of external action, and the External Action Service. One analyst notes that Lisbon merged the objectives of the external policies, from security to development, trade and environment, in Article 21, which in theory allows a more integrated approach. Article 21(3) requires the Union to ensure consistency between the different areas of its external action and between these and its other policies, a task shared by the Council and the Commission, assisted by the High Representative. Consistency is hard because the areas follow different rules: foreign and security policy decisions need unanimity and exclude legislative acts, whereas the common commercial policy is an exclusive Union competence in which the Commission negotiates under directives from the Council. The Commission made the same point in 2006, warning that unsatisfactory coordination between actors and policies costs the Union potential leverage, politically and economically.

cards.question: The Treaty of Lisbon leaves national diplomacies in place beside the Union’s own powers, so what the Union does abroad is sometimes described as a _____ built from several parts.
cards.abstract:
Composite foreign policy describes how the European Union deals with the outside world: no single government or institution makes it, because it is put together from the member states’ foreign policies, the common foreign and security policy and the Commission’s external powers. The treaties say the common foreign and security policy is put into effect by the High Representative and by the member states, using national and Union resources. A declaration annexed to the Treaty of Lisbon adds that these provisions, the High Representative’s office and the External Action Service leave the member states responsible for formulating and conducting their own foreign policy, diplomatic services and seats in international organisations. The Union has competences of its own: the common commercial policy is exclusive, while in development cooperation and humanitarian aid it conducts a common policy without preventing the member states from exercising theirs. Researchers describe the result as a complex fusion of intergovernmental, transgovernmental and supranational forms, for which one study prefers the label multilevel governance.

The High Representative sits in both camps, presiding over the Foreign Affairs Council, where the member states meet, and serving as a Vice-President of the Commission. The Commission’s 2006 paper said that external action depends first on political agreement among the member states, then on instruments and resources, and then on the roles of the institutions. It urged closer cooperation between the institutions and the member states, including shared diplomatic training and clear, single messages to partners from Commission delegations and national embassies. The composite design also lets any member state block a decision, since decisions on the common foreign and security policy are taken by the European Council and the Council acting unanimously, except where the treaties provide otherwise. Researchers who study the whole field add that it includes the external side of internal policies and action by groups of member states outside formal procedures, which no single theory of integration has yet fully captured.

cards.question: The Commission’s 2006 paper Europe in the World described the _____ of internal policies such as energy, environment, agriculture and migration, which it said shape the Union’s influence abroad.
cards.abstract:
The external dimension of an EU policy is the part that works beyond the Union’s borders or bears on its relations with other countries, as with the internal market, agriculture, energy or migration. The Treaty on European Union recognises this directly: Article 21(3) requires the Union to pursue its external objectives in 'the external aspects of its other policies' as well as in its dedicated external action. The treaties also give the Union exclusive competence over the customs union and the common commercial policy, so only the Union may legislate in them unless it empowers the member states. Trade agreements are negotiated by the Commission, in consultation with a special committee of the Council and within directives the Council issues. The Commission’s 2006 paper Europe in the World said that internal policies play a vital part in the Union’s external influence, and called internal and external policies inextricably linked, since the internal market could not exist without a common customs regime and trade policy.

It said the Union had led the international response to climate change, health pandemics and the governance of genetically modified products, drawing on expertise from its internal policies. It also noted that energy and justice and home affairs had developed fast, and that managing migration was increasingly important for good relations with neighbours. It warned that, even with sufficient political will, the Union’s impact falls short when its policies lack coherence. A later study defines internal sectors as those whose effects fall mainly inside the Union, such as agriculture, justice and home affairs, competition, energy, environment and single-market regulation, and finds that the integrated approach to conflict, which stresses diplomacy, defence and development, neglects them in practice. Another study from the same project defines European foreign and security policy broadly, as all the external dimensions of policies, internal ones included, plus action by member states outside the formal procedures.

cards.question: In July 2013 the Commission wrote that Europe’s responsibility for its own security requires a certain degree of _____: the ability to decide and act without depending on third parties’ capabilities.
cards.answerDate: Commission paper24 July 2013European Council19 – 20 December 2013Global StrategyJune 2016
cards.abstract:
Strategic autonomy, in the words of the European Parliament’s research service, is the capacity of the EU to act autonomously, without depending on other countries, in strategically important policy areas. The idea began in defence: one study traces it to the Saint-Malo Declaration of 1998, where 'autonomy' was chosen over 'independence', although official EU documents did not use it until 2013. In July 2013 the Commission wrote that Europe must be able to assume responsibility for its own security, which needed a certain degree of strategic autonomy: to decide and act without depending on the capabilities of third parties. The European Council of December 2013, in its first thematic debate on defence since Lisbon, said a stronger defence industry could also enhance the Union’s strategic autonomy and its ability to act with partners. The 2016 Global Strategy gave the idea centre stage, saying that an appropriate level of ambition and strategic autonomy was important for Europe’s ability to foster peace and safeguard security.

The research service divides the debate into phases: security and defence in 2013–2016, defending European interests amid Brexit, the Trump presidency and China’s assertiveness in 2017–2019, and the pandemic’s focus on supply chains in 2020. Since 2021 the idea has spread across nearly every policy area, including values, and terms such as 'open strategic autonomy' and 'strategic sovereignty' are often used instead. After Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Strategic Compass said it would enhance the Union’s strategic autonomy and its ability to work with partners. Michaels and Sus found no common understanding: France saw strategic autonomy as a long-term goal of independence from the United States, while others, especially in Central and Northern Europe, judged that reading illusory and harmful, and the vagueness let all pay lip service. The research service adds that the concept stays blurred by shifting terminology and can be limited by member states, non-EU countries and international organisations.

cards.question: A well-known 1993 argument blamed the gap between expectations and performance on limited ability to agree, sparse resources and missing instruments, which together restrict the Union’s _____ in world affairs.
cards.abstract:
Capacity to act is the Union’s ability to agree on a course of action together and to carry it out effectively in the world. The classic statement is the 'capability–expectations gap' of 1993, which Christopher Hill used to explain the distance between what was expected of the Union abroad and what it could deliver. Hill ascribed the gap to the Union’s limited ability to agree on policy, its sparse resources and the lack of instruments at its disposal. The treaties give the common security and defence policy 'an operational capacity drawing on civilian and military assets', but say that its tasks are performed using capabilities provided by the member states. Foreign and security decisions are taken by the European Council and the Council acting unanimously, and the exceptions that allow qualified majority voting do not apply to decisions with military or defence implications.

The Commission’s July 2013 paper linked capacity to industry, calling the defence industrial base a key element of Europe’s capacity to ensure the security of its citizens. It added that a credible partner must be able to decide and to act without depending on the capabilities of third parties. The European Parliament’s research service defines EU strategic autonomy as the capacity of the EU to act autonomously, so capacity to act is the core of that debate. One study lists 'capacity to act' with open strategic autonomy, strategic sovereignty and resilience among related terms that became increasingly prominent, and notes that the many terms blurred the notion. To strengthen its capacity to act, the 2022 Strategic Compass promised an EU Rapid Deployment Capacity able to deploy up to 5,000 troops and faster, more flexible decision-making, while calling itself no silver bullet.

cards.question: Political scientists call a relatively short period when constraints on actors relax and their choices can set a long-lasting path a _____, one of the main ideas of historical institutionalism.
cards.abstract:
A critical juncture is a relatively short period in which the usual constraints on political actors loosen, so that their choices become unusually likely to shape the outcome of interest. Historical institutionalists use the idea to explain why institutions and policies follow one path, because choices made in such a period close off alternatives and set off self-reinforcing processes that are very hard to alter. The concept grew out of macrohistorical work such as Lipset and Rokkan on European party systems and Collier and Collier on how Latin American states incorporated organised labour. Capoccia and Kelemen defined a critical juncture in 2007 as a relatively short period in which there is a substantially heightened probability that agents' choices will affect the outcome of interest. 'Short' is judged against the path-dependent process that follows, so a decade can be a juncture for an outcome a century later but not for one a year later.

They stressed that contingency, not change, defines a juncture, so a near miss in which reform was seriously considered and narrowly rejected still counts. Their own EU example is the preliminary ruling procedure of the Treaty of Rome, which they call a significant critical juncture for EU law, while the Court of Justice's later doctrines of supremacy and direct effect show a far lower degree of criticalness. In international relations Drezner treats critical junctures as events that trigger a discontinuous shift in key variables, and he argued in 2020 that the COVID-19 pandemic was unlikely to be one. The Strategic Compass of 2022 called Russia's war a 'tectonic shift in European history', and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops found no critical juncture in security and defence or in enlargement, because no constitutional-level change had followed and the changes remained reversible. Schwarz reached a different verdict by a different route, judging that enlargement is undergoing a significant critical juncture but has not reached a turning point, which he defines as a lasting, irreversible departure from the old path.
questions: Whether Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 amounted to a _____ for EU defence and enlargement policy depends on whether the changes it prompted reached constitutional level.
Even a near miss, in which change was seriously considered and narrowly rejected, can count as a _____, because what defines one is heightened contingency rather than a change of outcome.

cards.question: The 2007 World Politics article by _____ defined a critical juncture as a relatively short period of heightened probability that agents' choices matter, and showed how to study one.
cards.answerDate: PublishedApril 2007
cards.abstract:
Capoccia and Kelemen are the political scientists Giovanni Capoccia and R. Daniel Kelemen, whose article 'The Study of Critical Junctures' appeared in World Politics in April 2007. It won the American Political Science Association's 2008 award for the best journal article in qualitative and multi-method research. Their starting point was that critical junctures were often invoked casually, as bookends in stories of institutional development, with far less conceptual care than the path-dependent processes that follow. They defined critical junctures as relatively short periods of time during which there is a substantially heightened probability that agents' choices will affect the outcome of interest, and Capoccia later restated that definition in a handbook chapter. Because a moment critical for one institution may leave others untouched, they asked scholars to name the unit of analysis, such as a party system, a policy or a regime, for which a juncture is said to be critical.

Their central claim is that contingency, not change, defines a juncture, so a near miss in which change was seriously considered and narrowly rejected still counts, and leaving such cases out would add selection bias to comparisons. The same stress on open options led them to favour counterfactual analysis and theory-guided narrative, which study what happened in the context of what could have happened. Their first example is Turner's study of the thirty days before Hitler became chancellor in January 1933, a juncture of one month for a regime that lasted twelve years. Their second is the preliminary ruling procedure written into the Treaty of Rome, which they judged a significant critical juncture for the constitutionalisation of EU law, unlike the later doctrines of supremacy and direct effect. Later work on the EU borrows their definition, among them Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops on the war in Ukraine, and Schwarz on whether enlargement has reached a turning point.

Arguing that a juncture need not end in change, and that ignoring near misses builds selection bias into comparisons, _____ criticised scholars who equated critical junctures with moments of change.

cards.question: Having served from 2016 to 2022 as NATO's assistant secretary general for defence investment, _____ later wrote a policy brief arguing that Europeans must prepare to defend the continent with less American help.
cards.answerDate: NATO post2016 – 2022ECFR brief3 July 2024ASD postfrom 1 September 2025
cards.abstract:
Camille Grand is a French defence and security expert who has worked in government, at a think tank, at NATO and at an industry association. From 2008 to 2016 he directed the Fondation pour la recherche stratégique, a leading French think tank on defence and security. In October 2016 he became NATO's Assistant Secretary General for Defence Investment, and he held the post until 2022. In that post he piloted NATO's work on capability delivery, missile defence, and armament and technology cooperation. He joined the European Council on Foreign Relations in November 2022 as a distinguished policy fellow, and since 1 September 2025 he has led ASD, the Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe.

His policy brief of 3 July 2024 argues that Europeans must prepare to defend the continent with less American help whoever wins the US election, because US troops in Europe have fallen since the Cold War and Washington is turning to the Pacific. He recalls that European states averaged over 3% of GDP on defence in the Cold War and cut it afterwards, and that it was still only 50% above its 2000 level in 2024 despite the Wales pledge of 2014, made after the annexation of Crimea, to move towards 2%. He calls many armies 'bonsai armies' and cites three American experts who say Europe should provide at least half of the forces needed against a major-power aggressor, a baseline he thinks Europe may need to exceed if US support declines. He proposes a joint plan for Ukraine, a ten-year plan to close gaps in strategic enablers supplied by the US by 2035, and EU funding of tens of billions a year instead of the €1.5 billion planned for 2025 to 2027. He writes that the EU 'has morphed into a defence player' and proposes a commissioner for the defence industry to coordinate research, industrial policy and procurement support, but not an EU defence minister, which would require treaty change.

cards.question: A July 2024 policy brief from the European Council on Foreign Relations, titled _____, warned that a second Trump presidency could sharply reduce US support and urged a decade-long plan for European defence.
cards.answerDate: Published3 July 2024
cards.abstract:
Defending Europe with Less America is a policy brief by Camille Grand, a former NATO assistant secretary general, published by the European Council on Foreign Relations on 3 July 2024. The 2024 report on EU competitiveness makes a related point, noting 12 types of battle tank in Europe against one made in the United States. Its premise is that Russia's war on Ukraine exposed the poor state of European militaries and defence industries after decades of 'peace dividends', and its deep reliance on the United States. It argues that Europe has money but not mass, since European states outspent Russia four to one in 2023 yet many armies are 'bonsai armies', 12 European countries have no tanks and 14 no fighter aircraft. It recalls the Wales Summit pledge of 2014 to move towards spending 2% of GDP on defence, which 23 allies met by 2024 against three in 2014.

It warns that a second Trump presidency could sharply cut US support, but argues for planning on less American help whoever wins, since the US is turning to the Pacific and its troops in Europe fell from 248,000 in 1989 to 64,000 in 2021. Its answer is a 'full force package', including combat support and strategic enablers now supplied mainly by the US, and a sustained decade-long plan to close the main shortfalls by 2035 through joint acquisition. It asks for a joint emergency plan for aid to Ukraine, and for EU funding of tens of billions of euros a year instead of the €1.5 billion planned for 2025 to 2027. On institutions, it says the EU 'has morphed into a defence player' and proposes a defence-industry commissioner rather than an EU defence minister. NATO reports that European allies and Canada raised defence spending from 1.4% of combined GDP in 2014 to 2.3% in 2025, and at The Hague in June 2025 allies agreed to invest 5% of GDP annually by 2035.

cards.question: After the Cold War, many European governments cut military budgets and spent the savings elsewhere, a so-called _____ that left armies short of capacity when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
cards.abstract:
The peace dividend is the benefit a state gains when it spends less on its military because threats have receded, freeing money and resources for other purposes. In 1995 an International Monetary Fund working paper estimated a substantial long-run peace dividend, in the form of higher capacity output, from the markedly lower military spending most regions had achieved in the late 1980s. In Europe the term points to the years after the Cold War, when governments cut defence budgets under the American security umbrella and used the money for other goals. European states averaged more than 3% of GDP on defence during the Cold War, according to a 2024 policy brief, which adds that spending dropped significantly afterwards and that new NATO allies also cut when they joined. The 2024 report on EU competitiveness uses the phrase in the same sense, saying that stable geopolitics under US hegemony let the Union separate economic policy from security and use the 'peace dividend' from lower defence spending for domestic goals.

Its second volume adds that EU military spending declined for fifty years, thanks to a prolonged period of peace and the US security umbrella, and that the decline reversed from 2014 and rose strongly after 2022. The policy brief says decades of peace dividends and neglect atrophied European forces and defence industries, which made their help to Ukraine complicated and slow. At the Wales Summit in 2014, after Russia annexed Crimea, NATO leaders agreed to reverse the trend of declining defence budgets and to move towards spending 2% of GDP on defence within a decade. NATO figures put European allies and Canada at 1.4% of their combined GDP in 2014 and at 2.3% in 2025, when their combined spending rose by nearly 20% in real terms. At The Hague in June 2025 allies went further, committing to invest 5% of GDP annually by 2035, with at least 3.5% on core defence requirements and up to 1.5% on related security spending.

cards.question: Commissioned by Ursula von der Leyen in September 2023 from a former European Central Bank president, the _____ of September 2024 warned of an 'existential challenge' to Europe's growth and values.
cards.answerDate: RequestedSeptember 2023Published9 September 2024
cards.abstract:
The Draghi report is the common name of The Future of European Competitiveness, a study published by the European Commission on 9 September 2024 in two parts. Ursula von der Leyen asked Mario Draghi, the former president of the European Central Bank, to prepare it in September 2023, and the report states that it should not be taken as the Commission's official position. Part A sets out a competitiveness strategy for Europe, and Part B gives the in-depth analysis and recommendations by sector, including a chapter on defence. Its foreword says a wide gap in GDP has opened between the EU and the US, driven mainly by weaker productivity growth, and calls the combination of slow growth and rising needs an 'existential challenge'. The investment share of GDP would have to rise by around 5 percentage points, the foreword says, against 1 to 2% of GDP a year for the Marshall Plan, and commentators put the sum at about €800 billion a year.

It names three areas for action: closing the innovation gap with the US and China, a joint plan for decarbonisation and competitiveness, and increasing security and reducing dependencies. In the third area it calls for a genuine EU 'foreign economic policy', or statecraft, that coordinates trade agreements and direct investment with resource-rich nations, stockpiles in critical areas and industrial partnerships. On defence it says fragmentation and a lack of standardisation weaken Europe's ability to act as a cohesive power, with 12 types of battle tank operated in Europe against one produced by the US. It blames slow decisions too, as a failure to coordinate where it matters: issue-by-issue rules with multiple veto players mean that new laws take 19 months on average from proposal to signature. Josep Borrell largely agreed with its defence diagnosis but doubted some recommendations, Philip McCann called its sectoral, space-blind perspective a weakness, and the Commission's competitiveness compass of January 2025 builds on its analysis.

cards.question: In the _____ of 22 August 2025, a former central bank president told an Italian audience that the illusion that 450 million consumers would bring geopolitical power had evaporated.
cards.answerDate: Delivered22 August 2025
cards.abstract:
The Rimini speech is the address that Mario Draghi, a former Italian prime minister and president of the European Central Bank, gave on 22 August 2025 at the Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples in Rimini. He began by saying that the EU had long believed its 450 million consumers would bring geopolitical power and leverage in trade, and that this year would be remembered as the year that illusion evaporated. His evidence was US tariffs that Europe had to accept, American pressure to spend more on defence, a marginal European role in Ukraine peace talks, China's use of rare earths, and Europe standing by as Iranian nuclear sites were bombed and, in his words, the massacre in Gaza intensified. On 21 August the EU and US had published a joint statement setting an all-in US tariff rate of 15% on most EU goods and an EU plan to buy more US military equipment. He argued that scepticism of the Union was aimed not at its values but at its ability to defend them, because models of political organisation emerge to solve the problems of their time and must change with them.

Europe, he said, was ill-equipped for a world in which geo-economics, security and the stability of supply sources rather than efficiency shape trade, and economic strength was necessary but not sufficient for geopolitical strength. The Union had to turn from a spectator, or at best a supporting actor, into a protagonist, and its political organisation had to change. He pointed to €2 trillion of additional defence spending planned to 2031 and to internal barriers equal to a 64% tariff on machinery and a 95% tariff on metals. He called for common debt for large European projects in defence research, energy networks and disruptive technologies, because investments made in isolation cannot reach the scale needed. The speech built on the competitiveness report of 2024, which had already warned of 'geo-economic fragmentation' and called for a 'foreign economic policy'.

cards.question: Defined by one strategist in 1990 as the logic of conflict expressed in the grammar of commerce, _____ treats trade, investment and sanctions as instruments of geopolitical power.
cards.abstract:
Geoeconomics, also written geo-economics, is the use of economic instruments such as trade, investment, sanctions and finance to achieve geopolitical goals. The word is usually credited to a 1990 essay by the strategist Edward Luttwak, who called it a neologism for the 'admixture of the logic of conflict with the methods of commerce'. It is older than that essay, since German writers used it from the early 20th century and Arthur Dix published a book on it in 1925, so a genealogy of the term calls the claim that Luttwak coined it mistaken. Robert Blackwill and Jennifer Harris described geoeconomics in 2016 as the statecraft of using economic instruments for geopolitical goals, and argued that the United States too often reached for the gun over the purse. Scholars of the EU sort its tools into defensive ones, which protect against other states' leverage, and offensive ones, which build chokepoints, and into inducements and sanctions.

The Union came late to this thinking, because its trade policy was long shaped by neoliberal ideas and because member states hold competence over national security. The shift began in 2017, when Jean-Claude Juncker said Europeans were 'not naïve free traders', and produced the investment screening regulation of 2019, the Foreign Subsidies Regulation and International Procurement Instrument of 2022 and the Anti-Coercion Instrument agreed in 2023. Bauerle Danzman and Meunier call this 'reluctant geopoliticization' because the Union favoured defensive tools, and its economic security strategy of 20 June 2023 named four kinds of risk, including weaponised economic dependencies. The Draghi report of 2024 warned that Europe's dependencies could become vulnerabilities if trade fragments along geopolitical lines, and that the EU needed a genuine 'foreign economic policy', or statecraft. In his Rimini speech of 22 August 2025 Mario Draghi said Europe was ill-equipped for a world in which geo-economics, security and stable supply rather than efficiency shape trade, and that the United States and China use control of strategic resources and technologies to extract concessions.

cards.question: Proposed by René Pleven in October 1950 to allow a German contribution without a German army, the _____ treaty was signed in Paris in May 1952 and never came into force.
cards.answerDate: Proposed24 October 1950Signed27 May 1952Rejected30 August 1954
cards.abstract:
The European Defence Community was a planned supranational army for six western European states, whose treaty was signed in Paris on 27 May 1952. It began as a statement by the French prime minister René Pleven to the National Assembly on 24 October 1950, which proposed a European army tied to the political institutions of a united Europe. His aim was to let Germany contribute to the defence of western Europe without a German army, since French leaders feared that German divisions and a German ministry of defence would revive militarism. The national contingents were to be merged at the level of the smallest possible unit, under a European minister of defence answerable to an assembly, and paid for from a common budget. The European forces were to serve under the unified Atlantic command, and a European Political Community was drafted alongside the treaty.

By August 1954 four of the six signatories, Belgium, West Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, had ratified the treaty, and Italy seemed about to follow. On 30 August 1954 the French National Assembly instead adopted a preliminary motion that removed the treaty from its agenda without a debate on its text, by 319 votes to 264 in the count Anthony Teasdale gives. Teasdale lists the causes as stronger Gaullist and continued Communist hostility, divisions among Socialists and Radicals, the fall of Dien Bien Phu, and the refusal of the prime minister Pierre Mendès France to make ratification a question of confidence. Within two months the London and Paris conferences produced the modified Brussels Treaty and Western European Union, and West Germany joined the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in May 1955, so that German rearmament went ahead without a European army. The same account says that the failure ended political integration in defence, and Teasdale adds that the Treaty of Rome of 1957 was careful to avoid the unfinished political business the community had left open.

cards.question: Tabled by France in November 1961 and January 1962, the two _____ proposed a union of states with unanimous decisions that Dutch and Belgian ministers refused to sign before Britain joined.
cards.answerDate: First draft2 November 1961Second draft18 January 1962Talks ended17 April 1962
cards.abstract:
The Fouchet Plans were two French draft treaties, tabled on 2 November 1961 and 18 January 1962, for a union of states coordinating the foreign policy, defence and culture of the six members of the European Communities. They are named after Christian Fouchet, the French ambassador who chaired the committee of the Six set up at the Paris summit of February 1961. President Charles de Gaulle wanted a Europe of sovereign states, so the first draft gave a council of governments unanimous decisions, with one or two abstentions not blocking a decision. That draft promised a common defence policy in cooperation with other free nations, a nod to the Atlantic Alliance that the second draft dropped while adding economics. West Germany, Italy and Luxembourg were ready to negotiate on the French text, but the Netherlands called it unacceptable and Belgium moved into opposition.

The Dutch and Belgian governments feared that unanimity would give France a veto, that the union would weaken the supranational Communities, and that a European foreign policy would loosen the Atlantic Alliance. The second draft, changed in de Gaulle's own hand, hardened these points, and in February 1962 the other five states answered with a counter-draft keeping defence within the Atlantic Alliance and giving the Court of Justice a role. The talks ended in Paris on 17 April 1962, when the Dutch and Belgian ministers said they would sign no treaty until Britain had joined the Communities, and they were never resumed. Georges-Henri Soutou argues that the plan was also de Gaulle's bid to reform the Atlantic Alliance, with strategic and nuclear questions as the main cause of its failure. European Political Cooperation became the substitute from 1970, and Anthony Teasdale notes that an intergovernmental pillar of comparable shape came only with the Maastricht Treaty.

cards.question: Created in October 1954 by amending the Brussels Treaty to admit West Germany and Italy, the _____ offered an alternative to the failed European Defence Community while relying on NATO military staffs.
cards.answerDate: Signed23 October 1954ReactivatedOctober 1984Closed30 June 2011
cards.abstract:
The Western European Union was the defence organisation created in 1954 by modifying the Brussels Treaty of 1948 to admit West Germany and Italy. The Protocol signed in Paris on 23 October 1954 renamed its Council the Council of Western European Union and had it establish an Agency for the Control of Armaments. The Paris Accords that created it were seen as an alternative to the failed European Defence Community, and they ended the occupation of West Germany while banning German atomic, biological and chemical weapons. A new Article IV recognised the undesirability of duplicating NATO military staffs and made the Council and its Agency rely on NATO's military authorities for information and advice on military matters. Beside the Council of foreign ministers the organisation had a consultative parliamentary Assembly, and its core commitment was mutual defence under Article V.

Its work stayed closely linked to NATO, and after a dormant period ministers reactivated it by the Rome Declaration of October 1984. The Council's report of June 1984 called it the only European organisation empowered by treaty to discuss defence and security, and said that reactivation should contribute to the cohesion of the Atlantic Alliance and not substitute for it. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 had the Union request the organisation, as an integral part of its development, to elaborate and implement Union decisions with defence implications, and nine members declared it the defence component of the Union. In June 1992 it defined the Petersberg tasks of humanitarian or rescue missions, peacekeeping and crisis management, which the European Union later took over, and its remaining functions moved to the Union from 2000. In March 2010 ten states said that, with the mutual assistance clause of the Treaty of Lisbon, the organisation had accomplished its historical role, and it ceased to exist as a treaty-based organisation on 30 June 2011.

cards.question: Under Article 5 of the treaty signed in Washington on 4 April 1949, an armed attack on one member is an attack on all, which made _____ the heart of western defence.
cards.answerDate: Signed4 April 1949
cards.abstract:
NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, is the military alliance founded by the North Atlantic Treaty, signed in Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve states. They were the United States, Canada and ten western European states, among them Belgium, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. Under Article 5 an armed attack against one or more members in Europe or North America is an attack against them all, and each will take such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force. The treaty followed the Brussels Treaty of March 1948 and a resolution proposed in the United States Senate in May 1948 that opened the way to negotiations. By October 1950 the allies had agreed that all forces in Europe, whatever their nationality, would serve under a single command, as René Pleven told the French National Assembly.

That arrangement shaped later European schemes, since Pleven's own defence community was to place its forces at the disposal of the unified Atlantic command, and the North Atlantic Council had twice declared it of paramount importance. When that project failed, the modified Brussels Treaty of 1954 required its members to work in close cooperation with NATO and to rely on its military authorities, recognising the undesirability of duplicating NATO staffs. The Single European Act of 1986 left room for security cooperation within the Western European Union or the Atlantic Alliance, and the Maastricht Treaty of 1992 required the Union's policy to respect certain members' obligations under the North Atlantic Treaty. The Treaty of Lisbon says that commitments and cooperation in defence shall be consistent with commitments under NATO, which, for the states that belong to it, remains the foundation of their collective defence and the forum for its implementation. Michaels and Sus report that Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 confirmed NATO as the driver of European security, with a division of labour between the Union and the alliance.

cards.question: Set up after The Hague summit of December 1969 on the basis of the Davignon Report, _____ let foreign ministers consult at least every six months without a treaty basis.
cards.answerDate: Initiated1 – 2 December 1969Established27 October 1970Treaty basis1 July 1987Replaced1993
cards.abstract:
European Political Cooperation was the system by which the member states of the European Communities consulted one another and coordinated their foreign policies from 1970, at first without a treaty basis. It began at The Hague summit of 1 and 2 December 1969, where the heads of state or government told their foreign ministers to study how to advance political unification as the Communities enlarged, and to report by the end of July 1970. A committee of the heads of political departments, chaired by Étienne Davignon of Belgium, drafted a report that the foreign ministers adopted in definitive form at Luxembourg on 27 October 1970. The Davignon Report set two aims, mutual understanding through regular information and consultation, and solidarity through harmonised views and joint action where feasible. Foreign ministers were to meet at least once every six months and a Political Committee of the heads of political departments at least four times a year.

Beyond that, the Commission was consulted only if the activities of the Communities were affected, Parliament met ministers informally twice a year, and the report did not mention security or defence. The European Parliament's fact sheet calls it the substitute for the political community that the Fouchet negotiations failed to create, and Anthony Teasdale counts its codification in a treaty in 1987 among the steps that the stalemate delayed. Later reports at Copenhagen in 1973 and London in 1981 and the Solemn Declaration on European Union of 1983 refined its practice, and the Single European Act of 1986 confirmed and supplemented them. Title III of the Act gave it a treaty basis from 1 July 1987, with duties to consult, a secretariat in Brussels and closer coordination on the political and economic aspects of security. Article 31 kept the Court of Justice out of Title III, and the Maastricht Treaty of 1992 repealed that title when it created the common foreign and security policy.

cards.question: Signed in Luxembourg and The Hague in February 1986, the _____ revived the single market project and, in Title III, gave foreign policy cooperation a treaty basis for the first time.
cards.answerDate: Signed17 February 1986In force1 July 1987
cards.abstract:
The Single European Act was the first substantial amendment of the Treaty of Rome, signed at Luxembourg on 17 February 1986 and at The Hague on 28 February 1986, and in force from 1 July 1987. Nine member states signed on 17 February, Denmark, Italy and Greece followed on 28 February, and an appeal to the Irish courts by a private citizen delayed entry into force by six months. Its main purpose was the internal market, to be fully operational by 1 January 1993, through a six-year programme to remove the national regulations that still obstructed trade. It replaced unanimity with qualified majority voting in several areas, including the internal market, and introduced the cooperation procedure that gave the European Parliament real, if limited, legislative powers. It also gave the Communities new powers over cohesion, research and the environment, and brought cooperation in foreign policy into the treaties.

For foreign policy, Title III wrote European Political Cooperation into a treaty for the first time, with the parties undertaking in Article 30 to endeavour jointly to formulate and implement a European foreign policy. They agreed to inform and consult each other on foreign policy matters of general interest, to consult before deciding their final positions, and to take full account of the positions of their partners. The Presidency was made responsible for initiating action and representing the member states to third countries, a secretariat in Brussels was to assist it, and the parties were to coordinate more closely on the political and economic aspects of security. Article 31 withheld the powers of the Court of Justice from Title III, and the Act left room for closer security cooperation within the Western European Union or the Atlantic Alliance. Anthony Teasdale counts the codification of foreign policy in 1987 among the steps that the Fouchet stalemate had delayed, and the Maastricht Treaty repealed Title III when it created the common foreign and security policy.

cards.question: Signed on 7 February 1992 by twelve states, the _____ created the European Union, founded on the Communities and supplemented by a common foreign and security policy and cooperation in justice and home affairs.
cards.answerDate: Signed7 February 1992In force1 November 1993
cards.abstract:
The Maastricht Treaty, the Treaty on European Union, was signed at Maastricht on 7 February 1992 by the twelve member states of the European Communities and entered into force on 1 November 1993. It created the European Union, which Article A said was founded on the European Communities, supplemented by the policies and forms of cooperation the treaty established. Commentators describe the result as three pillars, the Communities, the common foreign and security policy in Title V and justice and home affairs in Title VI, although the treaty does not use that word for them. The first pillar was changed to prepare economic and monetary union, ultimately including a single currency, and the treaty created citizenship of the Union. Titles V and VI used the common institutions but worked by intergovernmental methods, with few supranational features such as involving the Commission and consulting Parliament.

For external action, Title V set up the common foreign and security policy, in which the Council could define common positions and decide on joint action, with unanimity as the general rule. Article J.4 added that the policy would include the eventual framing of a common defence policy, which might in time lead to a common defence, and asked the Western European Union to implement defence decisions. Article L kept the Court of Justice out of these titles, and Simon Duke notes that, although limited qualified majority voting was possible, practice remained unanimity. Danish voters rejected the treaty in June 1992, a solution including the Edinburgh decision followed in December, and a second referendum in 1993 had a positive outcome, after which a German Constitutional Court ruling of 12 October 1993 cleared the way for entry into force. Finn Laursen judged in 1992 that the common foreign and security policy was one of the treaty's more disappointing aspects, whereas Anthony Teasdale sees its intergovernmental design as the settlement of a dilemma left open since the Fouchet talks.

cards.question: Title V of the 1992 Treaty on European Union set up the _____, in which the Council defined common positions and adopted joint actions, generally by unanimity, outside the Court of Justice's jurisdiction.
cards.answerDate: Signed7 February 1992In force1 November 1993
cards.abstract:
The Common Foreign and Security Policy is the Union's policy for foreign and security affairs, established by Title V of the Treaty on European Union signed at Maastricht on 7 February 1992. The treaty gave the Union and its member states the task of defining and implementing a policy covering all areas of foreign and security policy, including safeguarding the Union's common values, fundamental interests and independence. The policy took over from European Political Cooperation, whose Title III in the Single European Act the treaty repealed, and formed a second pillar beside the European Communities and justice and home affairs. Titles V and VI used the common institutions but worked by intergovernmental methods, a design Anthony Teasdale links to the Fouchet Plans, with few supranational features such as involving the Commission. The European Council set the guidelines, the Council took the decisions and the Presidency represented the Union.

There were two instruments, a common position, to which national policies had to conform, and a joint action, which committed the member states in the positions they adopted. The Council acted unanimously except on procedural questions, though it could define matters for qualified majority voting when adopting a joint action, and constructive abstention, listed in the lecturer's slides among the 1990s instruments, came only with the Treaty of Amsterdam. Sanctions followed such a decision: where a common position or joint action provided for it, the Council interrupted or reduced economic relations with a third country under Article 228a, by qualified majority on a Commission proposal. Defence was left open, since Article J.4 provided for the eventual framing of a common defence policy and asked the Western European Union to implement defence decisions, while Article L excluded the Court of Justice. Finn Laursen called the policy one of the treaty's more disappointing aspects in 1992, and Simon Duke counts about 430 declarations against about 50 common positions and joint actions since 1993.

cards.question: Described in the early 1970s as long on economic power and short on armed force, the Community was cast as a _____, one that would bring contractual politics to relations between states.
cards.answerDate: Introduced1972 – 1973Critique1982Extended1990
cards.abstract:
Civilian power is the idea that an international actor can be influential through economic and diplomatic means and legal agreements, without relying on armed force. In the early 1970s François Duchêne applied it to the European Community, arguing that a nuclear stalemate in Europe would devalue military power and open space for 'civilian forms of influence and action'. In his 1973 formulation the Community was 'long on economic power and relatively short on armed force', and its interest lay in domesticating relations between states through 'structures of contractual politics'. Ian Manners reads the definitions given by Twitchett and Maull as containing three features: the centrality of economic power, the primacy of diplomatic cooperation, and willingness to use legally binding supranational institutions. Hanns Maull extended the label beyond Europe in a 1990 article in Foreign Affairs titled 'Germany and Japan: The New Civilian Powers'.

Hedley Bull attacked the idea in 1982, arguing that the influence of civilian actors such as the Community was conditional on a strategic environment supplied by the military power of states, which they did not control. The French national assembly’s rejection of a European Defence Community in 1954 left a military role for the Community taboo until the Treaty on European Union was agreed in 1991. The common European security and defence policy agreed at Cologne in 1999 led some writers to speak of a 'military power Europe', while others argued that its tasks still fell within civilian power. Richard Whitman concluded in 2002 that the notion kept its empirical and theoretical purchase, and Kristian Nielsen later noted that it describes the means of power, not its ends. Article 42 of the Treaty on European Union says the common security and defence policy provides 'an operational capacity drawing on civilian and military assets', and the foreword to the 2016 Global Strategy said an exclusively 'civilian power' does not do justice to an evolving reality, adding that soft and hard power go hand in hand.

cards.question: Born in London in 1927 to a Swiss father and a French mother, _____ worked for Jean Monnet at the Coal and Steel Community and directed a strategic studies institute from 1969.
cards.answerDate: Born17 February 1927Key essays1972 and 1973Died12 July 2005
cards.abstract:
François Duchêne was a writer and analyst of European affairs who was born in London on 17 February 1927, died in Brighton on 12 July 2005, and is best known for the idea that the European Community was a civilian power. The son of a French-speaking Swiss father and a French mother, he took a double first at the London School of Economics and wrote leaders for the Manchester Guardian from 1949. Jean Monnet read his articles on the challenges facing a ruined continent and invited him, at 25, to join the planning of a new Europe. He was information officer at the High Authority of the European Coal and Steel Community from 1952 and directed Monnet’s private office at the Action Committee for the United States of Europe from 1958. He directed the International Institute for Strategic Studies from 1969, led the new Centre for European Research at Sussex University from 1974, and wrote a 1994 biography of Monnet that his obituarist called definitive.

Richard Whitman traces the notion of a 'civilian power Europe' to two Duchêne essays, 'Europe’s Role in World Peace' of 1972 and 'The European Community and the Uncertainties of Interdependence' of 1973. Whitman calls it an exercise in futurology: a nuclear and superpower stalemate would devalue military power and let Europe turn 'war and indirect violence' into 'civilised politics'. In 1973 Duchêne described a Community 'long on economic power and relatively short on armed force' whose interest was to domesticate relations between states through 'structures of contractual politics'. Whitman, citing Stavridis, treats this as both an empirical observation about the Community’s means and a normative assertion about how relations between states ought to be domesticated. Ian Manners recalls that Hedley Bull’s 1982 attack on civilian power answered writers such as Duchêne, with whom Bull nonetheless shared a focus on the state system and direct physical power.

cards.question: Defined as obtaining preferred outcomes through attraction and persuasion rather than coercion or payment, _____ was named in a 1990 book that challenged the belief in American decline.
cards.answerDate: Coined1990Full account2004
cards.abstract:
Soft power is the ability to obtain preferred outcomes through attraction and persuasion rather than through coercion or payment. Joseph Nye coined the term in his 1990 book Bound to Lead, which challenged the belief that American power was in decline, holding that if you can get others to want what you want you can economise on sticks and carrots. In a 1990 article in Foreign Policy he set 'co-optive or soft power', which gets others to want what you want, against the 'hard or command power' of ordering them to do what you want. He linked it to intangible resources such as culture, ideology and institutions, and in his 2004 book named a country's culture, political values and foreign policies as its three sources. Nye stressed that soft power is not a normative concept, since 'bad' people can exercise it, and that combining it skilfully with hard power amounts to 'smart power'.

Nye notes that European leaders increasingly invoked the Union’s soft power, and the foreword to its 2016 Global Strategy says the Union has always prided itself on it while adding that soft and hard power 'go hand in hand'. Heather Grabbe concluded that the Union’s long-term influence on the post-communist candidates worked primarily through soft power and voluntary rather than coercive means. Kristian Nielsen finds the Union’s sources of attraction mainly in its narrative of peaceful integration, its enlargement policy and its stated commitment to democracy and human rights, rather than in culture. He argues that soft power alone does little to close the gap between what the Union is expected to do and what it can do, and that it differs from civilian power, which concerns means, and from normative power, which concerns what the Union is. Critics call the concept confusing and ethnocentric, since attraction does not automatically become influence over policy, and note a liberal bias that overlooks the conservative values attracting followers to Russia.

cards.question: A Rhodes Scholar who joined Harvard’s faculty in 1964, _____ was dean of the Kennedy School from 1995 to 2004 and an assistant secretary of defense under President Clinton.
cards.answerDate: Born1937Term coined1990Died6 May 2025
cards.abstract:
Joseph Nye was an American political scientist and public official who was born in 1937, joined the Harvard faculty in 1964, and died on 6 May 2025 at the age of 88. He studied at Princeton, was a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford and took his doctorate at Harvard, and his first book was a study of Pan-Africanism and East African integration. With his longtime collaborator Robert Keohane he wrote the 1977 book Power and Interdependence, which developed the concept of complex interdependence and was often treated as a foundation of neoliberalism, a label Nye resisted. In the Carter administration he was a deputy under secretary of state from 1977 to 1979, and under President Clinton he chaired the National Intelligence Council in 1993 and 1994 and was assistant secretary of defense for international security affairs in 1994 and 1995. He was dean of the Kennedy School of Government from 1995 to 2004, and by his death he had published 14 books and more than 200 journal articles.

Nye coined 'soft power' in his 1990 book Bound to Lead, which answered the belief in American decline by adding to military and economic power the ability to affect others by attraction and persuasion. In the autumn 1990 issue of Foreign Policy he contrasted this co-optive power, resting on culture, ideology and institutions, with the hard power of command. He returned to the idea in his 2004 book Soft Power, which named culture, political values and foreign policies as its sources, and he later described the skilful combination of hard and soft power as 'smart power'. He observed that the concept took on a political life of its own, in China from 2007 and in Europe, where more leaders began to refer to the Union’s soft power. The Kennedy School’s obituary reports that in his last years he warned that American soft power was being squandered, while he remained optimistic about its long-run resilience.

cards.question: Defined by an ability to shape what passes for normal in world politics through ideas and principles rather than force, _____ was proposed for the Union in a 2002 journal article.
cards.answerDate: Key article2002Policy brief2009
cards.abstract:
Normative power is the ability to shape what counts as normal in world politics through norms and ideas rather than force, and Ian Manners proposed in 2002 that the European Union be understood this way. His article began from Hedley Bull’s 1982 attack on 'civilian power' and argued for looking beyond civilian and military power to the ideational impact of the Union’s international identity. Manners traced the Union’s 'normative difference' to its post-war historical context, its hybrid polity and its political-legal constitution. From treaties, declarations and the Copenhagen membership criteria of 1993 he drew five core norms, peace, liberty, democracy, the rule of law and human rights, and four minor ones, including sustainable development and good governance. The Treaty on European Union now says that the Union is founded on the values of human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights, and that its action abroad is guided by the principles behind its creation.

In a 2009 policy brief Manners described normative power in its purest form as ideational rather than material, legitimate in its principles, persuasive in its actions and socialising in its impact. Persuasion in this sense involves argumentation and the conferral of prestige or shame, from public declarations of support to symbolic sanctions. He tested the idea on the Union’s pursuit of the international abolition of the death penalty, a norm it seeks to make normal in world politics. Kristian Nielsen notes that normative power concerns what kind of power the Union is, since for Manners it acts by what it is rather than by what it says or does. Tanja Börzel and Thomas Risse ask how far the Union diffuses distinctively European ideas, since human rights, democracy and multilateralism are also part of a wider order promoted by 'Western' countries.

cards.question: Writing at the University of Kent in 2002, _____ answered a critique of the Community’s civilian role by arguing that its ability to shape what counts as normal deserved much greater attention.
cards.answerDate: Key article2002Revisited2024
cards.abstract:
Ian Manners is a scholar of the European Union who is listed on Lund University’s staff page as a professor in its Department of Political Science, and he is best known for the idea of 'normative power Europe'. He published 'Normative Power Europe: A Contradiction in Terms?' in the Journal of Common Market Studies in 2002, while he was at the University of Kent at Canterbury. The article began from Hedley Bull’s 1982 attack on the Community’s 'civilian power' and from the claim of writers such as François Duchêne that civilian means had replaced military power. Its core proposal is that, alongside the Union’s civilian and military capabilities, its ability to shape what passes for 'normal' in world politics needs much greater attention. It argues that the Union’s normative basis consists of five core norms, peace, liberty, democracy, the rule of law and human rights, and that six factors diffuse them, from contagion to the cultural filter.

Manners later headed the European Union research unit at the Danish Institute for International Studies and, by his own account, directed EU studies research programmes in Britain and Denmark. In 2024 he wrote that the 2002 article had been voted one of the five most important academic EU works of the 2000s and remained the most cited article published in the journal. The 2024 article, which led a symposium marking 20 years of the approach, redefined normative power as empowering actions in concert that reshape conceptions of normal for the planetary good. Kristian Nielsen notes that Thomas Diez argued in 2005 that the approach is an attempt at identity construction and that Manners’s claim, that the Union acts by what it is, is bolder than the claims made for soft power. Tanja Börzel and Thomas Risse cite his 2002 article among the works on how the export of ideas has helped to construct a distinct foreign policy identity for the Union.

cards.question: The process through which norms, understood as shared expectations about appropriate behaviour, spread across time and space is called _____, which researchers attribute to coercion, incentives, socialisation, persuasion or emulation.
cards.answerDate: EU typology2002
cards.abstract:
Norm diffusion is the process through which norms, understood as collectively shared expectations about appropriate behaviour, spread across time and space. Researchers distinguish several mechanisms of diffusion: coercion, the manipulation of utility calculations through incentives, socialisation, persuasion and emulation. Ian Manners argued in 2002 that a normative basis does not by itself make the Union a normative power, so one must ask how its norms are diffused, and he named six factors. Contagion is the unintentional spread of ideas from the Union, as in Mercosur’s attempts at regional integration, informational diffusion works through policy initiatives and declarations, and procedural diffusion through institutionalised relationships such as agreements or enlargement. Transference works through trade, aid and technical assistance, overt diffusion through the Union’s physical presence in delegations and monitoring missions, and the cultural filter decides whether third states learn, adapt or reject a norm.

In a 2009 brief Manners wrote that normative power works through persuasion, argumentation and the conferral of prestige or shame and aims at socialisation, partnership and ownership. He noted that conditionality facilitates both procedural and transference diffusion, since it is required in all agreements with third countries. Frank Schimmelfennig and Ulrich Sedelmeier found that in eastern enlargement the transfer of EU rules was best explained by reinforcement by reward, with success depending on the credibility of conditionality and the domestic costs of adoption. Kristian Nielsen points out that conditionality is essentially coercive, although Manners rejects the assumption that normative power requires a willingness to use force. Tobias Lenz found that policy-makers in Mercosur and the Southern African Development Community increasingly adopted EU-style institutions through spurred emulation, while Tanja Börzel and Thomas Risse stress that diffusion meets resistance and has not produced homogeneity.

The adoption of EU-style institutions in Mercosur and the Southern African Development Community is analysed as spurred emulation, one route by which _____ from the Union reaches other regions.

cards.question: The prospect of membership, tied to the Copenhagen conditions of 1993 and policed through gate-keeping, benchmarking, models, money and advice, gave the Union a _____ over the candidates’ laws and institutions.
cards.answerDate: Copenhagen21 – 22 June 1993Period studied1989 – 2004Book2006
cards.abstract:
Transformative power is the Union’s capacity to change other countries by transferring its policies and institutions to them, and it is the title of Heather Grabbe’s 2006 study of the Central and East European candidates. Her book examines how the Union’s conditions for membership transformed Central and Eastern Europe between 1989 and 2004. Grabbe found that the Union had enormous potential power over domestic politics, because every candidate government claimed membership as its first foreign policy priority, but that it used that power at only a few key points. At the Copenhagen European Council of 21 and 22 June 1993 the Union agreed that associated countries that so desired would become members once they met conditions that included stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law and human rights. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union now lets any European state that respects the Union’s values and is committed to promoting them apply, taking into account the conditions of eligibility agreed by the European Council.

Grabbe identified five routes of influence in the accession process: gate-keeping, benchmarking, models, money and advice. Frank Schimmelfennig and Ulrich Sedelmeier explain rule transfer by an external incentives model of reinforcement by reward, whose success varies with the credibility of conditionality and the domestic costs of adopting rules. Tanja Börzel and Thomas Risse add that in the accession process the Union relied mostly on external incentives and capacity-building, while socialisation, persuasion and emulation have received little attention in the literature. In 2018 the Commission wrote that a credible accession perspective is 'the key driver of transformation' in the Western Balkans. Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier’s 2019 reassessment found that the credibility of incentives is the crucial condition, and that doubts about lasting change arise from democratic backsliding in some new member states and slow progress in the Western Balkans.

cards.question: A senior adviser on the Balkans and Turkey to the Commissioner for enlargement from 2004 to 2009, _____ also directed the Open Society European Policy Institute in Brussels before joining Bruegel.
cards.answerDate: Working paper1999Adviser to Rehn2004 – 2009Book2006
cards.abstract:
Heather Grabbe is a policy analyst and researcher who has written on EU enlargement, advised on it inside the European Commission and commented on it from think tanks. She holds a PhD from the University of Birmingham, where she was at the Institute for German Studies when she wrote a 1999 working paper on the conditions of EU membership. She was deputy director of the Centre for European Reform, a London think tank, and from 2004 to 2009 senior adviser on the Balkans and Turkey to Olli Rehn, then Commissioner for Enlargement. She has also directed the Open Society European Policy Institute in Brussels, and she is now a senior fellow at Bruegel and a visiting professor at University College London. Her book The EU's Transformative Power: Europeanization through Conditionality in Central and Eastern Europe was published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2006.

The book shows how the Union's conditions for membership transformed Central and East Europe between 1989 and 2004, with free movement of persons and the Schengen rules as its detailed cases. According to the publisher's summary, the Union had enormous potential power over the whole range of domestic politics in the candidate countries but could use it at only a few key points before accession. The same summary says that its long-term influence worked mainly through soft power and voluntary rather than coercive means, as Central and East Europeans took on the Union's norms and methods under the Commission's guidance. Her 1999 paper had traced how the conditions for membership grew from trade and aid to the heart of domestic policy making, making the Union the key external driver of policy reform for the five applicants then in negotiations. Sedelmeier counts the book among the studies of the Union's impact on Central and Eastern Europe that made the Europeanisation of applicant states a distinct and increasingly sophisticated research area.

cards.question: The EU's capacity to harness the whole and the parts in pursuit of shared goals during crises is analysed as _____, built on leadership, coordinated institutions and a policy toolkit.
cards.answerDate: Schapiro Lecture20 June 2022
cards.abstract:
Collective power is the idea that the EU, though it lacks a government, a deep public purse and robust coercive power, can amass resources and instruments and affect outcomes by harnessing the whole and the parts in pursuit of shared goals. Brigid Laffan set out the idea as Collective Power Europe in her 2022 Schapiro Lecture in Dublin, and she places it on the 'power to' side of the distinction between power over and power to. She presents it as going beyond market power Europe, which sees the EU exercising power by externalising its market-related policies and regulation, and beyond normative power Europe, which underplayed the harder dimensions of power. Collective power has an affinity with protean power, which Katzenstein and Seybert define as the effect of improvisational and innovative responses to uncertainty. It is about creating capacity by mobilising and applying resources, including finance, knowledge, human capital and an innovative policy toolkit.

Her framework has three elements of capacity creation: leadership in framing challenges and finding consensus, the mobilisation and coordination of EU institutions, and a policy toolkit for shared challenges. She argues that without agreement on what the problem is, and unity, the EU struggles to act, and she points to its quick framing of Brexit in statements on 24 June 2016, the day after the referendum. She finds the European Council at the centre of the institutional response in all three crises, Brexit, the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, framing it and tasking other institutions with work. On the toolkit, she says the reflex is to adapt existing instruments before inventing new ones, and she calls the July 2020 recovery package, financed by borrowing, a display of collective power under duress that broke a long-standing taboo. Others are more cautious: Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops found no constitutional-level change in security, defence or enlargement after 2022, and Helwig judges the Union's geopolitics accidental rather than intentional.

Unlike market power Europe and normative power Europe, which rest on the single market and on values, _____ is described as the power to get things done through shared leadership and shared tools.

cards.question: Appointed in 2013 to direct the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies in Florence, _____ retired from the European University Institute in 2021 and later became Chancellor of the University of Limerick.
cards.answerDate: Centre directorfrom 2013RetiredAugust 2021Schapiro Lecture20 June 2022
cards.abstract:
Brigid Laffan is a professor of European politics who built her career at University College Dublin and the European University Institute in Florence. At University College Dublin she was founding director of the Dublin European Institute from 1999 and vice-president of the university from 2004 to 2011. In 2013 the European University Institute recruited her as director of its Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies, and she retired from the Institute in August 2021. She is now an emeritus professor of the Institute and, since November 2023, Chancellor of the University of Limerick, which she entered as one of its founding students in 1972. Her 2022 Schapiro Lecture, given at the Royal Irish Academy in Dublin on 20 June 2022, appeared in Government and Opposition in 2023.

In it she argues that the EU has emerged as a collective power in response to the crises since 2008, and that Collective Power Europe is a promising lens for analysing the 21st-century Union. She builds the concept on the distinction between 'power over' and 'power to': the EU is a power not in the traditional sense of command power but in the power to amass resources and instruments and affect outcomes. Her framework has three elements of capacity creation: leadership and framing, the mobilisation and coordination of institutions, and the policy toolkit. She tests them on the EU's responses to Brexit, the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, and concludes that these differed in speed and breadth from its earlier responses to the euro and refugee crises, a step change rather than muddling through. She says her article leaves aside the constraints on the EU's collective power, and studies of the period after 2022 are more cautious, finding no constitutional-level change in security, defence or enlargement and calling the Union's geopolitics accidental.

Drawing on the distinction between 'power over' and 'power to', _____ built a concept of the EU's capacity to harness the whole and the parts in pursuit of shared goals.
