cards.question: Defined as the ability of an actor to constrain the choices available to another in a non-trivial way, _____ is a relational idea, in contrast to an actor's capacity to act.
cards.abstract:
Power over is the ability of an actor or a set of actors to constrain the choices available to another actor or set of actors in a non-trivial way, in the definition that Amy Allen gave in 1999. It is a relational concept and a form of social power, and so it is the usual contrast to 'power to', which is a form of outcome power, the power to act and exercise agency. Its classic statement is Robert Dahl's of 1957, that A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something that B would not otherwise do. Max Weber's definition of power as the probability of carrying out one's will despite resistance, and Steven Lukes's account of A affecting B contrary to B's interests, belong to the same family. The idea is not always judged negatively, since Dahl's definition is non-evaluative, though some writers use power over as a synonym for domination.

In international relations, Barnett and Duvall observe that discussion tends to privilege one form of power, an actor controlling another, and they call its direct form compulsory power. Their example is the United States using its military power to compel others to change their foreign policies. Laffan argues that the EU, seen against a nation state, lacks a government, strong state capacity, a deep public purse and robust coercive power, so that it is a power 'not in the traditional sense of power over, command power'. The Union's superior bargaining power, resulting from asymmetrical interdependence in its favour, was the precondition for its ability to withhold rewards from candidates that had not met its conditions. On one account of Central and Eastern Europe, the Union had enormous potential power over the whole range of domestic politics in the candidate countries, but was able to use it only at a few key points before accession.

cards.question: Treated as capacity, potential or wherewithal rather than control over other people, _____ is power understood as the ability to act and bring about outcomes.
cards.abstract:
Power to is the ability of an actor to act and bring about outcomes, power understood as capacity, potential, ability or wherewithal rather than as the control of other people. Thomas Hobbes took power to be a person's present means to obtain some future apparent good, and Hannah Arendt called it the human ability not just to act but to act in concert. Pansardi traces the split to Hanna Pitkin and Peter Morriss, who held that power should be defined by what agents can do rather than by the consequences of their actions for others. Keith Dowding calls it 'outcome power', the ability of an actor to bring about or help to bring about outcomes, and treats it as the more basic notion, since power over always presupposes some power to. In international relations, Barnett and Duvall argue that power must be studied both as one actor's control of another and through the structures and processes that enable and constrain actors' ability to shape their fates.

Laffan cites Talcott Parsons, who in 1963 called power the ability 'to get things done' and argued that a focus only on its distributive aspects underplayed collective power. She builds on it her concept of Collective Power Europe, a power not in the traditional sense of power over but the power to amass resources and instruments and affect outcomes. In her view, probing the Union's power to get things done is a useful antidote to the focus on incompleteness and weakness that pervades much analysis of it. The lecturer's slides call power to close to strategic autonomy, which the Parliament's research service defines as the capacity of the EU to act autonomously, without depending on other countries, in strategically important policy areas. The quest for strategic autonomy in security and defence has been described as a maturation in two phases, the second running since late 2013.

cards.question: In November 2019 the incoming Commission President promised a geopolitical Commission, and analysts have asked whether the EU can be a true _____ without the means or consensus to act as one.
cards.answerDate: Speech to MEPs27 November 2019
cards.abstract:
Geopolitical power is the capacity to win influence in great power rivalry, generally understood as a zero-sum contest for control of territorial and increasingly virtual spaces in which economic, political and even military tools are not kept apart. Four schools of geopolitical thought tie power to geography, to military strength, to norms and narratives, and to economic leverage. On one assessment, the Union has not raised its conventional and nuclear capabilities enough to act independently, though it has made its economic toolbox more geostrategic and since 2022 has used the European Peace Facility to send lethal military aid to Ukraine. From late 2013, as turbulence grew at its doorstep, the Union began to stress the need to become a more capable geopolitical power. Laffan adds that the earlier image of the Union as a normative power underplayed the harder dimensions of power and is inadequate in a world of hard geopolitics.

On 27 November 2019, presenting her team to the European Parliament, the Commission President-elect, Ursula von der Leyen, said: "This is the geopolitical Commission that I have in mind, and that Europe urgently needs." She described a world in which too many powers speak only the language of confrontation, and said that her Commission would speak the language of confidence, in the European way, while engaging as a responsible power. The political guidelines she had set out as a candidate asked the Union to be ambitious, strategic and assertive in the way it acts in the world, but they did not use the word geopolitical. Håkansson finds that the Commission took on a larger geopolitical role than many expected, most clearly in trade and industrial policy, and used Russia's invasion of Ukraine to widen its mandate in security, defence and sanctions. Helwig judges the Union's geopolitics accidental rather than intentional, because its institutions and members lack a consensus on how far the geopolitical role should go.

cards.question: At his confirmation hearing on 7 October 2019, the incoming High Representative said the Union, with tools like a powerful trade policy, had to learn to use the _____ to be more strategic.
cards.answerDate: Hearing7 October 2019Remarks9 December 2019Interview29 October 2020
cards.abstract:
The language of power is the phrase with which Josep Borrell, a former Spanish foreign minister, said in 2019 that the European Union must learn to act as a power. He used it on 7 October 2019 at his confirmation hearing before the foreign affairs committee of the European Parliament, where he sought the post of High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and Vice-President of the Commission. Asked how the Union could become more strategic and coherent, he pointed to tools such as a powerful common trade policy and diplomatic power and said it had to learn to use the language of power. He took up the post in December 2019, and on 9 December he explained that learning the language of power means being able to react using all the tools the Union has at its disposal. In October 2020 he repeated that Europe must learn quickly to speak the language of power and not rely only on the soft power it used to wield.

He stressed that this was not a call for military force, saying that the Union's might is not the military component and that it was built against the very idea of power politics. What he meant was to capitalise on trade and investment policy, financial power, diplomatic presence and rule-making capacity, combined so as to maximise their geopolitical impact. He located the weakness in will rather than means, saying that Europe's problem is a lack of political will to combine its powers, and he noted that foreign policy is decided by unanimity, so every country has a veto. Laffan cites the remark in arguing that the idea of normative power underplayed the harder dimensions of power and is inadequate in a world of hard geopolitics. Helwig calls geopolitics one of the buzzwords of the Union's 2019 to 2024 institutional cycle, in which the High Representative chimed in with a call to relearn the language of power.
questions: Not a call for military force, the _____ meant, in the High Representative's own gloss, combining trade, investment, finance, diplomatic presence and rule-making so as to maximise the Union's geopolitical impact.
Learning the _____ became shorthand for a more geopolitical Union after the 2019 hearing, though the High Representative said in 2020 that Europe lacked political will rather than power.

cards.question: Adopted in Bonn on 19 June 1992 by the Western European Union, the _____ listed humanitarian and rescue work, peacekeeping and combat-force tasks in crisis management as missions its members' units could undertake.
cards.answerDate: Declared19 June 1992Treaty signed2 October 1997Treaty in force1 May 1999
cards.abstract:
The Petersberg tasks are the crisis-management missions listed in the Petersberg Declaration, which the Council of Ministers of the Western European Union adopted in Bonn on 19 June 1992. Apart from common defence, which stayed under the Washington and Brussels treaties, its member states' units could be used for humanitarian and rescue tasks, peacekeeping tasks and tasks of combat forces in crisis management, including peacemaking. It followed the Maastricht decision of December 1991 to develop the Western European Union as the defence component of the European Union and a stronger European pillar of the Atlantic Alliance. Decisions to use units belonged to the organisation's Council, but joining any operation stayed a sovereign decision for each member state. The historian André Dumoulin notes that the organisation defined these tasks in 1992 on top of its common-defence role, and that the Union took them over at the cost of dropping the idea of including common defence.

The European Union took the list into the Treaty of Amsterdam, signed on 2 October 1997 and in force from 1 May 1999, which repeated the three kinds of task. The same article gave the Union access to an operational capability through the Western European Union, which Fabrizio Pagani reads as absorbing part of its heritage without merging the two. Moravcsik and Nicolaïdis argue that a Swedish-Finnish proposal sought a stronger Union role in peacekeeping, and that the tasks were the most British and neutral governments would accept, made acceptable by constructive abstention and a veto. At Cologne in June 1999 the European Council said the Council must be able to decide on the full range of Petersberg tasks and began work to include the Western European Union functions needed for them. The Lisbon Treaty widened the list in what is now Article 43 of the Treaty on European Union, adding joint disarmament operations, military advice and assistance and post-conflict stabilisation, and saying all tasks may help the fight against terrorism.

cards.question: Signed on 2 October 1997 and in force from 1 May 1999, the _____ gave the Council's Secretary-General the added function of High Representative for the common foreign and security policy.
cards.answerDate: Signed2 October 1997In force1 May 1999Solana started18 October 1999
cards.abstract:
The Treaty of Amsterdam amended the Treaty on European Union and the treaties establishing the European Communities, and it was signed on 2 October 1997 and entered into force on 1 May 1999. It updated and clarified the Maastricht Treaty, deleted or amended over 50 obsolete articles and renumbered the rest, partly to prepare the Union for enlargement. Visas, asylum and immigration moved from intergovernmental cooperation into normal decision-making, and co-decision with the European Parliament was extended to most policy areas. In foreign policy the treaty added common strategies to joint actions and common positions, kept unanimity as the general rule and allowed qualified majority voting only for decisions based on a common strategy or implementing a joint action or common position. Its security article repeated the Petersberg tasks and gave the Union access to an operational capability through the Western European Union, which Fabrizio Pagani describes as taking over part of its heritage without merging the two.

The treaty created the post of High Representative for the common foreign and security policy and gave it to the Secretary-General of the Council rather than to a separate figure. Andrew Moravcsik and Kalypso Nicolaïdis report that France championed a more visible 'Mr CFSP' and other governments opposed it, leaving a Council official assisted by a new policy planning and early warning unit in the General Secretariat. The European Council designated Javier Solana at Cologne in June 1999, and he took up the post on 18 October 1999, saying that a unit for planning and early warning had just been created. A Council member could qualify its abstention by a formal declaration, not applying the decision but accepting that it bound the Union and avoiding conflicting action; the decision fell only if abstainers held over a third of weighted votes. Jolyon Howorth noted in 2000 that the High Representative relied on about twenty advisers and that the post's relationship with the Commissioner for External Relations remained unspecified and sensitive.

cards.question: Issued by Tony Blair and Jacques Chirac after a Franco-British summit in December 1998, the _____ said the Union must have a capacity for autonomous action backed up by credible military forces.
cards.answerDate: Summit3 – 4 December 1998
cards.abstract:
The Saint-Malo Declaration is the joint declaration on European defence issued by Tony Blair and Jacques Chirac at their summit at Saint-Malo on 3 and 4 December 1998. It said that the Union must have the capacity for autonomous action, backed up by credible military forces, the means to decide to use them and a readiness to do so, in order to respond to international crises. It tied this to making a reality of the Treaty of Amsterdam, with the Council taking decisions on an intergovernmental basis across the common foreign and security policy. It kept NATO in place: the collective defence commitments of the Washington and Brussels treaties must be maintained, and the Union would act where the Alliance as a whole was not engaged. It also called for structures to analyse situations and plan strategically, and for strengthened armed forces supported by a strong and competitive European defence industry.

Maartje Rutten, who compiled the period's core documents, describes a sea change in British attitudes lifting decades-long objections to an autonomous Union military capacity, and notes that Saint-Malo is widely seen as the start of European defence. Jean-Yves Haine and Burkard Schmitt read it as a meeting point of a British reconsideration of its veto and a French shift towards NATO, so that 'autonomy' was a compromise. Jolyon Howorth calls it the strategic gamble Tony Blair took, because strengthening the Western European Union or borrowing NATO assets had proved unsatisfactory and the Union needed capacity of its own. At the joint press conference on 4 December Blair said Europe needs capabilities and political leadership of its own, especially when the United States will not engage, and cited Kosovo, where he said they had not been able to act as he wished for Europe. The wording was repeated at Cologne in June 1999, and Michaels and Sus report an interviewee's account that 'autonomy' was carefully chosen over 'independence' in the Saint-Malo negotiations.

cards.question: Meeting in December 1999 under the Finnish presidency, the _____ set a military headline goal for 2003, to be met by voluntary national contributions without a European army.
cards.answerDate: Met10 – 11 December 1999Goal deadline2003
cards.abstract:
The Helsinki European Council was the meeting of the Union's heads of state or government held in Helsinki on 10 and 11 December 1999 under the Finnish presidency. On enlargement it decided to open accession negotiations in February 2000 with Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Romania and Slovakia, judging each candidate on its own merits. It recognised Turkey as a candidate state 'destined to join the Union' on the same criteria as the others, with a pre-accession strategy to follow. It also committed the Union to completing the intergovernmental conference on institutional reform by December 2000. Its security and defence section built on the Cologne European Council of June 1999, which declared that the Union must have the capacity for autonomous action and asked the Finnish presidency to carry the work forward.

Helsinki underlined the determination to develop an autonomous capacity to take decisions and, where NATO as a whole is not engaged, to launch and conduct EU-led military operations, a process that did not imply creating a European army. The headline goal asked member states, cooperating voluntarily, to be able by 2003 to deploy within 60 days and sustain for at least a year forces of up to 50,000 to 60,000 persons capable of the full range of Petersberg tasks. It also agreed new political and military bodies in the Council, interim ones from March 2000, and a non-military crisis management mechanism, and said the Union would work on conflict prevention with the United Nations and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe. Burkard Schmitt stresses that the goal created a pool of national units rather than a standing force, and that the civilian priority areas of police, rule of law, civilian administration and civil protection were set at Feira in June 2000. Jolyon Howorth reckoned that rotating such a force would need a pool approaching 200,000 troops, and Eva Michaels and Monika Sus add that the goal, never formally abandoned, soon became unrealistic.

cards.question: Signed in February 2001 and in force from 1 February 2003, the _____ prepared the institutions for a Union of 27 and allowed enhanced cooperation in foreign policy, though not in defence.
cards.answerDate: Signed26 February 2001In force1 February 2003
cards.abstract:
The Treaty of Nice amended the Treaty on European Union and the treaties establishing the European Communities, and was signed at Nice on 26 February 2001 and entered into force on 1 February 2003. Its aim was to reform the institutions for an enlarged Union of 27 members, something the Amsterdam Treaty had been meant to do but had failed to. It reshaped the Commission, moving from two commissioners for the larger states and one for the others to a maximum of 27, designated by rotation on a strictly equal basis. It also rebalanced the weighting of Council votes and raised the qualified majority threshold to 73.9% of the votes from 71.3%, with a majority of states representing at least 62% of the population if one asks. Enhanced cooperation became easier, needing a minimum of eight states rather than a majority, and was extended to the common foreign and security policy, excluding defence.

For foreign policy, the new Article 27b of the Treaty on European Union limited enhanced cooperation to implementing a joint action or common position and said it 'shall not relate to matters having military or defence implications'. The treaty also rewrote Article 25 to give the Political and Security Committee political control and strategic direction of crisis management operations, under the Council's responsibility. Antonio Missiroli notes that the Military Committee and Military Staff, unlike that committee, were left out of the treaty, mainly because some non-allied states were reluctant to see them in it. Ireland's constitution requires a referendum, and its voters rejected the treaty in June 2001 by 53.87% to 46.13% and accepted it on 19 October 2002 after a Seville declaration on neutrality, making Ireland the last of 15 states to ratify. Dan Felsenthal and Moshé Machover analysed the voting rules in the treaty's final form and found one for the existing 15 members an improvement, but two for an enlarged Union to have extremely undesirable features.

cards.question: Established by a Council joint action of 12 July 2004, with headquarters in Brussels and the High Representative as its head, the _____ works on defence capabilities, armaments cooperation and research.
cards.answerDate: Established12 July 2004Current statute12 October 2015
cards.abstract:
The European Defence Agency is the Union's agency for defence capabilities development, research, acquisition and armaments, established by Council Joint Action 2004/551/CFSP, adopted at Brussels on 12 July 2004. The Thessaloniki European Council of June 2003 had asked for such an intergovernmental agency during 2004, and the European Security Strategy called it an important step towards more flexible and efficient military resources. It acts from Brussels under the Council's authority in support of the common foreign and security policy, without prejudice to national defence competences, and its Steering Board of defence ministers or their representatives decides. Its head is the Union's senior foreign-policy official, the Secretary-General and High Representative in 2004, who was to be the essential link to the Council, while a chief executive runs the daily work. The Joint Action gave it four fields: defence capabilities for crisis management, armaments cooperation, the defence industrial base and equipment market, and defence research and technology.

Article 45 of the Treaty on European Union gives the agency a treaty basis and lists tasks from checking national capability commitments to proposing multilateral projects and supporting defence technology research. It lets the Council set the statute by qualified majority, and the present statute, Council Decision 2015/1835 of 12 October 2015, continues the agency as established in 2004. Burkard Schmitt records that a European armaments agency had been on the defence agenda for over ten years, with two armaments bodies created outside the Union in the mid-1990s as possible precursors. The Parliament's fact sheet describes it today as helping armed forces work more closely together, running joint training and coordinating joint military priorities and projects, with the High Representative at its head. Carlos Martí Sempere wrote in 2008 that harmonising operational needs was highly complex because of doctrinal, operational and industrial differences and that deeply rooted protectionism made effective procurement hard to impose, while Eva Michaels and Monika Sus report that the rift over Iraq hampered its early efforts.

cards.question: Deployed to Bunia in the Democratic Republic of Congo in June 2003, the _____ was the first EU-led military operation conducted without relying on NATO assets or capabilities.
cards.answerDate: UN mandate30 May 2003Launched12 June 2003Mandate ended1 September 2003
cards.abstract:
Operation Artemis was a European Union military operation in Bunia, the capital of the Ituri district of north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, mounted under a Council joint action of 5 June 2003, with a mandate to 1 September 2003. It was the Union's first military deployment outside Europe and the first without NATO assistance, whereas the earlier Concordia operation in Macedonia had used NATO assets through the Berlin Plus arrangement. Ugandan troops left Bunia in May 2003 as Hema and Lendu militias fought, and Human Rights Watch reported hundreds of civilians killed there in early May and tens of thousands forced to flee. The small United Nations mission there could not protect those who sheltered near its compound. After the UN Secretary-General asked for a multinational force under a lead state, France offered to lead it, and on 30 May 2003 the Security Council authorised it in Resolution 1484.

The Council adopted Joint Action 2003/423/CFSP on 5 June 2003, naming the operation Artemis, with France as framework nation, Major General Neveux as operation commander and a headquarters in Paris, and launched it on 12 June 2003. Gustav Lindstrom puts the deployment at about 2,000 troops, roughly 1,700 of them French and about 70 Swedish, with a force headquarters in Entebbe, and its mandate covered the airport, displaced people in the camps and, if required, civilians. The troops declared Bunia and a zone around it weapons-free without disarming the militias, began handing over to a larger UN force on 1 September, and left by 7 September, while violence went on in the countryside. Simon Duke argues that normative entrapment played a significant role, modified by awareness that one larger state would carry the bulk of the burden, while János Tomolya calls the test limited because strategic lift and a strategic reserve were lacking. Eva Michaels and Monika Sus add that France saw an opportunity for emancipation from NATO and that the Battlegroup concept drew on Artemis.

cards.question: Signed in December 2007 and in force from 1 December 2009, the _____ established a High Representative who is also a Commission Vice-President and who chairs the Foreign Affairs Council.
cards.answerDate: Signed13 December 2007In force1 December 2009
cards.abstract:
The Treaty of Lisbon amended the Treaty on European Union and the Treaty establishing the European Community, was signed in Lisbon on 13 December 2007 and took effect on 1 December 2009. It began as a constitutional project after the Laeken Declaration of 2001, and after French and Dutch voters rejected the Constitutional Treaty in 2005 a conference moved its content into amendments of the existing treaties. The treaty merged the three pillars, gave the Union a single legal personality and replaced the rotating presidency of the European Council with a long-term President. Foreign policy kept its own rules: decisions on the common foreign and security policy remain largely intergovernmental and need unanimity, the Court of Justice has limited jurisdiction, and enhanced cooperation needs unanimous agreement. The treaty introduced the common security and defence policy as an integral part of that policy, giving the Union an operational capacity drawing on civilian and military assets for missions abroad.

The High Representative is appointed by the European Council by qualified majority with the Commission President's agreement, conducts the common foreign and security policy, chairs the Foreign Affairs Council and is a Commission Vice-President. Antonio Missiroli described this double-hatting in 2004 as a personal union of two roles drafted in the Convention, which also proposed the External Action Service that now assists the High Representative. Article 42(7) added an obligation of aid and assistance by all means for a state suffering armed aggression on its territory, consistent with NATO commitments and the specific character of some states' policies. France invoked that clause for the first time after the Paris attacks of 13 November 2015, and ministers said that no formal decision by the Council was legally required to activate it. Article 42(6) allows permanent structured cooperation among states with higher military capabilities, begun in 2017, and Steven Blockmans and Ramses Wessel doubted in 2009 that the institutional changes would greatly improve decision-making, leadership or crisis management.

cards.question: Renamed from the European Security and Defence Policy by the Treaty of Lisbon in 2009, the _____ covers the Union’s military and civilian crisis-management missions, from Operation Artemis onwards.
cards.answerDate: New start1998First missions2003Renamed2009
cards.abstract:
The Common Security and Defence Policy gives the Union an operational capacity drawing on civilian and military assets, for missions outside the Union that keep the peace, prevent conflict and strengthen international security. Article 43 of the Treaty on European Union lists its tasks, from disarmament operations, humanitarian and rescue tasks and military advice to peace-keeping and combat forces in crisis management. Its origin is the Franco-British summit at Saint-Malo in December 1998, which declared that the Union needs the capacity for autonomous action backed by credible military forces, and the slides call this its new start. The Cologne and Helsinki European Councils of 1999 followed, and Helsinki set a goal of deploying 50,000 to 60,000 people within 60 days and planned a non-military crisis management mechanism. The slides say the Treaty of Lisbon of 2009 renamed the European Security and Defence Policy, and Parliament’s fact sheet agrees that this treaty introduced the present policy.

The first missions came in 2003: Artemis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which the slides call the first autonomous EU-led military operation, Concordia in Macedonia and a police mission in Bosnia. Lindstrom adds that Artemis began in June 2003 at the request of the United Nations with about 2,000 personnel, Michaels and Sus tie it to an Anglo-French consensus, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops count four military operations by 2008. The slides state that defence and military decisions are always taken by unanimity, and Article 42(4) has the Council act unanimously on a proposal from the High Representative or a member state. Parliament’s fact sheet notes that decisions on the European Defence Agency and on Permanent Structured Cooperation use qualified majority voting, and the slides list the latter, at Articles 42(6) and 46, with coalitions of the willing at Article 44. The slides make the High Representative responsible for the operational conduct of missions, whereas Article 43 gives the post the task of coordinating their civilian and military aspects.

In 2003 the Union launched its first missions under the _____: Artemis in the Congo, Concordia in Macedonia and a police mission in Bosnia, with Artemis the first autonomous EU-led military operation.

cards.question: Presented in 2003 by the Union’s first High Representative, the _____ called Russia a strategic partner and was the first strategy of its kind that the Union had ever produced.
cards.answerDate: Presented2003Document dated12 December 2003Updated2008
cards.abstract:
The European Security Strategy is the short document A Secure Europe in a Better World, dated Brussels, 12 December 2003, which set out the Union’s view of its threats and objectives. Bailes records that Javier Solana unveiled a first version on 16 June 2003, that the Thessaloniki European Council welcomed it on 20 June, and that the European Council adopted a revised text on 12 December. Anthony, Grand and Lewis describe a document of about 15 pages, drafted after the divisions over the war in Iraq, that covers five threats: terrorism, weapons of mass destruction, regional conflicts, state failure and organised crime. The strategy names three objectives: addressing the threats, building security in the neighbourhood and an international order based on effective multilateralism. It also calls for a ‘strategic culture that fosters early, rapid, and when necessary, robust intervention’.

The lecture slides list it first among the key developments in defining the common interest, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops credit Solana, the first High Representative, with presenting the Union’s first ever such strategy. On Russia the text says the Union should work for closer relations and that common values will reinforce progress towards a strategic partnership, whereas Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops summarise it as calling Russia a ‘strategic partner’. Anthony, Grand and Lewis place its drafting when the defence policy was in its infancy, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops count four military operations between 2003 and 2008. Michaels and Sus note that, apart from a vague reference to the ‘decision-making autonomy’ of the Union and NATO, the strategy made no mention of strategic autonomy. They call the update of 2008 unimpressive, with its truism that the Union must be ‘still more capable, more coherent and more active’, and Gordon adds that it kept the old threats and added cyber threats, energy security and climate change.

cards.question: Issued in June 2016 under the High Representative and Vice-President, the _____ added military and defence dimensions to the common foreign policy and declared that soft and hard power go hand in hand.
cards.answerDate: AdoptedJune 2016CompassMarch 2022
cards.abstract:
The EU Global Strategy is the document Shared Vision, Common Action: A Stronger Europe, which High Representative Federica Mogherini presented to EU leaders at the summit of 28 June 2016. The European Council had asked her to prepare it in June 2015, and the European Union Institute for Security Studies records consultations with member states, institutions and civil society in the year between. The strategy sets five priorities for external action, which Parliament’s fact sheet also records, and the first, the security of the Union, calls for an appropriate level of ambition and strategic autonomy. In her foreword Mogherini writes that the Union takes pride in its soft power, but that an exclusively ‘civilian power’ does not do justice to an evolving reality, since the Union deploys seventeen military and civilian operations. She adds that soft and hard power go hand in hand, and the text states that in this fragile world soft power is not enough.

The slides say the strategy adds ‘hard’ power to ‘soft’ by bringing military and defence dimensions into the Common Foreign and Security Policy, and that it seeks strategic autonomy. They give three objectives for it, stability, the spread of EU standards and the promotion of EU values, citing Michel 2020, whereas the strategy itself sets five priorities. The slides add that it asks the Union to respond to external conflicts and crises, build the capacity of partners and protect the Union and its citizens, tasks the Council’s Implementation Plan of November 2016 repeats. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that hard power intentions were pronounced in the strategy, but that the years to February 2022 brought no fundamental shift, because strategy stayed far ahead of policy realities. Michaels and Sus add that when strategic autonomy took centre stage in the strategy it mostly referred to the Common Security and Defence Policy, and that it achieved buzzword status.

cards.question: Adopted in 2016 to implement the Union’s global strategy, the _____ brought together a coordinated annual review on defence, a military planning capability and a stronger rapid response toolbox.
cards.answer: Implementation Plan on Security and Defence
cards.answerDate: Plan2016PESCO2017Planning unitJune 2017EPFMarch 2021
cards.abstract:
The Implementation Plan on Security and Defence is the note in which High Representative Mogherini, who also heads the European Defence Agency, proposed how to put the EU Global Strategy into practice in security and defence. The Council note is dated 14 November 2016 and was meant for the Foreign Affairs Council that month and the European Council in December. It rests on a new level of ambition with three tasks drawn from the strategy: responding to external conflicts and crises, building partners’ capacities and protecting the Union and its citizens. Its thirteen proposals include a Coordinated Annual Review on Defence, a strategic-level capability within the European External Action Service for non-executive military missions, a stronger rapid response toolbox with the EU Battlegroups, and an inclusive Permanent Structured Cooperation. The Global Strategy had already floated an annual coordinated review of military spending plans, and the draft Council conclusions of 14 November 2016 welcome the plan as a proposal and set the level of ambition from it.

The slides call the plan a white paper, whereas the Council’s document presents it as a proposal from the High Representative. They list under it the annual review, Permanent Structured Cooperation established in 2017, a military planning capability established in June 2017 and a rapid response toolbox with EU battlegroups and civilian capabilities. They also show the European Peace Facility, established in March 2021, in this chain, though the plan itself asked for a review of the Athena financing mechanism and the Facility came later. Michaels and Sus say that new security instruments developed rapidly from the plan’s adoption, making defence the fastest-growing field of European cooperation, but that until February 2022 implementation was cumbersome, with insufficient national funding. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops likewise call 2016 to February 2022 a period of many initiatives but no fundamental shift, because strategy stayed far ahead of policy realities.

cards.question: Listed among the measures of the 2016 implementation plan to enhance defence cooperation, the _____ offers an overview of military defence capabilities in Europe.
cards.answerDate: Plan2016Slow untilFebruary 2022
cards.abstract:
The Coordinated Annual Review on Defence, known as CARD, is a process in which the European Defence Agency and the EU Military Staff review member states’ defence plans and propose collaborative opportunities in capability development. The agency says it was launched in 2017 as part of implementing the EU Global Strategy and runs in a two-year cycle synchronised with Permanent Structured Cooperation and NATO’s defence planning process. Its stated reason is that defence ministries had traditionally done their planning and procurement in isolation, without much coordination among themselves. The Global Strategy had floated the idea of an annual coordinated review at EU level to discuss member states’ military spending plans and bring greater coherence to defence planning. The draft Council conclusions of 14 November 2016 ask the High Representative for proposals by spring 2017 on a member-states-driven review, voluntary in nature, to deepen cooperation and make defence spending more coherent.

The slides list it among the measures of the Implementation Plan on Security and Defence of 2016 that enhance defence cooperation, and the Session 3 slides call it an overview of military defence capabilities in Europe. Those slides place it with Permanent Structured Cooperation, the European Defence Fund and the Military Planning and Conduct Capability among the developing EU security and defence initiatives. Michaels and Sus say the European Defence Fund and the annual review improved defence-industrial cooperation, though until February 2022 implementation was cumbersome because member states differed on long-term objectives and national funding was insufficient. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops list the review among the innovations of 2016 to February 2022 that brought no major shift, because strategy stayed far ahead of policy realities. The agency’s 2024 report, approved by defence ministers on 19 November 2024, projects spending of €326 billion, up more than 30% on 2021, yet says national efforts will not suffice and more cooperation is needed.

cards.question: Established in March 2021, the _____ was first set up for non-lethal military aid only, excluded the transfer of weapons and had a ceiling of 5 billion euros for its six-year cycle.
cards.answerDate: EstablishedMarch 2021AdaptedMarch 2022Ukraine fundMarch 2024
cards.abstract:
The European Peace Facility is a fund outside the EU budget, set up by a Council decision of 22 March 2021. It has two pillars, one financing the common costs of EU military operations and one for assistance measures for the benefit of third countries. Mogherini proposed it in 2018 to merge and expand the funding of Athena and of African Union peace support operations, with a budget for 2021 to 2027 of €5.69 billion, or €5 billion at 2018 prices. Member states pay in proportion to their gross national income, and Article 31 of the Treaty on European Union lets a state abstain with a formal declaration, so that it need not apply a decision but accepts that it commits the Union. Maślanka adds that the Facility already envisaged reimbursing lethal weapons offered by member states, but that this was seen as the most controversial form of military support.

The slides list the Facility among the ways of implementing the Global Strategy and show it as established in March 2021. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that it was at first set up only for non-lethal military aid, excluded weapons transfers and had a ceiling of €5 billion for its six-year cycle. Bilquin records that on 28 February 2022 the Council adopted a €450 million measure for lethal equipment, the first such use of an EU tool for a third country, and Michaels and Sus call this an overnight transformation into a powerful instrument. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops add that the March 2022 adaptation crossed red lines of national law such as Germany’s armament export laws, and that Austria, Malta and Ireland saw it as a step too far but invoked Article 31 rather than stop it. In March 2024 the Council added a Ukraine Assistance Fund of €5 billion, taking the ceiling above €17 billion, and Soler reports that members can now draw on it for much of the cost of training and deployment.

Austria, Malta and Ireland invoked Article 31 of the Treaty on European Union over changes to the _____, which in March 2024 gained a Ukraine Assistance Fund of 5 billion euros.

cards.question: Established in June 2017 as a permanent command and control structure inside the EU Military Staff, the _____ is so far the only permanent military strategic headquarters of the Union.
cards.answerDate: EstablishedJune 2017Compass goal2025Exercise HQ2024MILEX26June 2026
cards.abstract:
The Military Planning and Conduct Capability is a permanent command and control structure at the military strategic level, set up inside the EU Military Staff in Brussels to plan and conduct the Union’s non-executive military missions. Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/971 of 8 June 2017 gave the Director of the Capability, who is also Director General of the EU Military Staff, responsibility for that planning and conduct. The decision records the Council’s agreement of 6 March 2017 to create it as a short-term objective, to work alongside the Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability. Michaels and Sus note that the Union set up its civilian counterpart in 2007, but that the United Kingdom vetoed initiatives for a military Operational Headquarters. It first commanded the training missions in Somalia, Mali and the Central African Republic, and the European External Action Service now lists those in Somalia, the Central African Republic, Ukraine and Mozambique.

The slides list it among the ways of implementing the Global Strategy, show it as established in June 2017 and call it so far the only EU military permanent strategic headquarters. The slides quote the Strategic Compass goal that by 2025 it would plan and conduct all non-executive military missions and either two small-scale or one medium-scale executive operation, a wording the Council’s own note repeats. That note plans staffing of up to 115 cost-shared seconded national experts by 2024, a different count from the slides’ figure of about 200 personnel taken from a 2026 ELIAMEP paper. The slides say it reached its declared full operational capability in 2025 and acted as Operation Headquarters for the MILEX exercise of 2024, in which the exercise report notes that 33 member-state personnel augmented it. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that its director coordinates the training mission for Ukraine, which might advance it towards executive operations, and Soler reports that it is the designated operational headquarters of the Rapid Deployment Capacity and that its director commanded MILEX26 in June 2026.

cards.question: Adopted in March 2022 as a concrete roadmap for the Union as a security provider, the _____ rested on a common threat assessment between the 27 member states, which was unprecedented.
cards.answerDate: AdoptedMarch 2022Planning goal2025
cards.abstract:
The Strategic Compass is the Union’s security and defence strategy of 2022, which the first session’s slides call a concrete roadmap for the Union as a security provider. Member states adopted it in March 2022 as a plan to strengthen security and defence policy by 2030, built on four pillars: act, secure, invest and partner. Its first chapter rests on the first comprehensive EU Threat Analysis, conducted in 2020, to be revisited at least every 3 years. Its measures include a stronger Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity, a Hybrid Toolbox with rapid response teams and a Rapid Deployment Capacity of up to 5,000 troops, which reached full operational capability in May 2025. Scazzieri noted that, unlike the Global Strategy of 2016, member states formally endorsed it, and that its military ambition was modest, since it dropped the 60,000 troops of the Helsinki goals of 1999.

The second session’s slides end their overview of policy evolution with it, paired with the question ‘Defence union?’, and a Session 3 slide says the European External Action Service coordinated its preparation. Michaels and Sus date it to March 2022 and call it the most detailed yet the most operational security strategy document the Union has ever had, where member states made significant progress in defining ambitions and instruments. The slides call it unprecedented, because it meant conducting a common threat assessment between the 27 member states, and a report of 2026 names that common assessment among its key successes. The slides quote a critique of 2022 that its preparation was a ‘long and arduous bureaucratic process’ that eliminated the original big ideas, ask whether it was written in lowest common denominator mode, yet add that it listed many concrete new projects. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that after 2022 the Union changed its discourse to identify Russia as a clear threat to European security, and they refer to the Compass in support.

An EU Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity, hybrid rapid response teams and a cyber diplomacy toolbox are measures of the _____, in which the Union after 2022 identified Russia as a clear threat.

cards.question: Published in 2019 as an example of a separate and specific strategy for one part of the world, the _____ is linked with the phrase ‘the systemic rival’.
cards.answerDate: Outlook2019Autonomy phase2019–2022
cards.abstract:
The EU–China Strategic Outlook is a joint communication of the Commission and the High Representative, issued on 12 March 2019 as a contribution to the European Council. It reviewed relations with China and set out 10 concrete actions for discussion and endorsement by the European Council. It built on the Strategy on China of 2016, which it called the cornerstone of EU engagement, and argued that the balance of challenges and opportunities had shifted. Its best-known passage says that China is, in different policy areas, a cooperation partner, a negotiating partner, an economic competitor in the pursuit of technological leadership and a systemic rival promoting alternative models of governance. Brattberg and Le Corre call the use of ‘systemic rival’ unprecedented in an EU document, link it to frustration over market access, and report that the European Council quickly endorsed the ten actions.

The lecture slides give the Outlook as their example of a separate and specific strategy for one part of the world and attach to it the phrase ‘the systemic rival’, though the document itself calls the Strategy on China of 2016 the cornerstone. The slides place it on a ‘unified’ approach slide, after the Global Strategy of 2016 and the Security Union Strategy of 2020 and before the Strategic Compass of 2022. The Compass repeats the formula, saying that China is a partner for cooperation, an economic competitor and a systemic rival. A fifth-session slide speaks of enlargement governance challenged by the Chinese ‘systemic rival’ in the Balkans, and the first session’s slides date a phase of strategic autonomy, from 2019 to 2022, to a wish to reduce dependence on China in key supply chains. Chimits, Ghiretti and Stec wrote in 2023 that this threefold approach brought cohesion to the EU’s position, but that member states and institutions diverged in applying some of the 10 actions, while a Parliament briefing of 2020 saw China acting as a systemic rival on a growing number of issues.

cards.question: Beginning with travel bans and asset freezes after Crimea’s annexation in 2014, the Union’s _____ were at first considered too soft, as member states were reluctant to accept the economic consequences.
cards.answerDate: Crimea response2014Packages from23 February 202217 packages by20 May 2025
cards.abstract:
The sanctions against Russia are the Union’s packages of sanctions since the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and, on a far larger scale, since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the slides count 21 packages of them. Portela and Kluge describe a regime first established in March 2014 and expanded in three waves that year, with asset freezes and travel bans on individuals and economic and financial restrictions. After the downing of flight MH17 in July 2014, it restricted capital-market access for some Russian banks and banned trade in arms and dual-use goods. Article 215 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union lets the Council adopt such economic measures by qualified majority on a joint proposal of the High Representative and the Commission. The Commission’s list counts the first package of the 2022 series on 23 February 2022 and the 21st on 23 July 2026.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops count 17 packages between 23 February 2022 and 20 May 2025, so their count stops at a fixed date, while the slides’ count of 21 matches the Commission’s list of July 2026. They write that the response of 2014 was mostly statements and sanctions on companies and individuals, limited by member states’ reluctance to accept the economic consequences, so it was considered too ‘soft’ to deter or punish Russia. The 17 packages of 2022 to 2025 were more far-reaching, covering energy, oil and gas and disinvestments, yet the authors call the development incremental, because it built on the response of 2014. The slides list sanctions among the instruments of the Common Foreign and Security Policy in the 1990s, taken by unanimity, with individual sanctions contested by some member states. They add that the Commission prepared sanctions in December 2021 and took charge of them, that the Court of Justice is competent as an exception, as Article 275 allows for measures on individuals, and that Switzerland took over parts of the 16th and 18th packages in 2025.

cards.question: The former Lithuanian prime minister _____ holds the new Commissioner portfolio for Defence and Space in the second von der Leyen Commission, a post that cannot gain full defence competence without treaty change.
cards.answerDate: Force proposed2026
cards.abstract:
Andrius Kubilius is the European Union Commissioner for Defence and Space in the second von der Leyen Commission, and the slides list him among the recent developments of 2024 to 2026, adding the word industry to the title. The Commission’s biography lists him as Prime Minister of Lithuania in 1999–2000 and 2008–2012 and an MEP from 2019. His mission letter of 1 December 2024 asks him to bring defence work together under a true European Defence Union, working closely with the High Representative, and to present a White Paper on the Future of European Defence within 100 days. The same letter says that member states will always be responsible for their armed forces, from doctrine to deployment, and that Europe must spend more, spend better and spend European. Article 42 of the Treaty on European Union explains the limit, because a common defence arises only when the European Council, acting unanimously, so decides and member states adopt that decision under their constitutional requirements.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops call the creation of the Commissioner for Defence and Space a significant institutional innovation, though the portfolio will not gain full competence over security and defence any time soon, because that would require treaty change. They add that the post goes beyond discourse and rhetoric, but that, being below the constitutional level, the changes are not irreversible and have not fully solved the persistent problems of an intergovernmental Common Foreign and Security Policy. The Commission and the High Representative presented the White Paper for European Defence – Readiness 2030 on 19 March 2025, expecting up to €800 billion of additional defence expenditure, depending on what member states mobilise. Soler reports that in 2026 he argued that a standing European military force deserves renewed consideration as Washington’s security commitments become more uncertain. She adds that he has proposed a standing pan-European force of at least 100,000 troops, separate from national armies and designed to complement US forces stationed in Europe.

cards.question: Presented as a joint communication of the Commission and the High Representative on 5 March 2024, the _____ aims to strengthen the readiness of the European defence technological and industrial base.
cards.answerDate: Communication5 March 2024Ukraine fundMarch 2024
cards.abstract:
The European Defence Industrial Strategy, known as EDIS, is the strategy of 2024 that the slides, under the name European Union Defence Industry Strategy, list among the recent developments of 2024 to 2026 in which the Union seeks organisational solutions. Formally it is a joint communication of the Commission and the High Representative of 5 March 2024, which the mission letter tasks the Defence Commissioner with overseeing. It says that the Union must swiftly enhance its defence readiness after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It invites member states to procure at least 40% of defence equipment collaboratively by 2030 and at least 50% of defence investments within the EU by 2030, after noting that nearly 80% went to non-EU suppliers since 2022, against about 60% before. Article 346 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union lets a member state take the measures it considers necessary to protect its security interests in arms, munitions and war material.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops, quoting a 2024 description, say it aims to strengthen the readiness of the European defence technological and industrial base to respond to the geopolitical security environment created by Russia’s invasion. They note that the Ukraine Assistance Fund of March 2024 is linked to a ‘buy European’ clause, in line with the strategy, which nudges member states to speed up developing their own industrial base. The strategy proposes an Innovation Office in Kyiv, and Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley add an ambition to integrate Ukraine’s defence industry through joint drone production. They report that the heads of MBDA and Saab argued in 2024 for including UK firms, while France and others argued for ‘buy European’ and Sweden, Germany and Poland lobbied for UK firms to receive EU-mobilised defence funding. The Court of Auditors adds in 2026 that EU funding instruments require products to be sourced predominantly within the EU or associated countries, but that strict sourcing can delay procurement and raise costs.

cards.question: A 2026 review by the _____ warned that the lack of effective EU-wide top-down defence planning could lead to fragmented investments, duplication of efforts or capability shortages.
cards.answerDate: Review cited2026
cards.abstract:
The European Court of Auditors is the Union’s external auditor, which Article 285 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union charges with carrying out the Union’s audit, with one national of each member state as a member. Article 287 has it examine the accounts of all Union revenue and expenditure, check that money was received and spent lawfully and that financial management was sound, and publish an annual report. It may also submit observations at any time, especially special reports on specific questions, and give opinions when another institution asks for one. Its review 01/2026, ‘EU defence policy in the spotlight’, was adopted on 14 July 2026, covers developments from 2020 to mid-2026 and is, in the Court’s words, not an audit report but a review based mainly on public information. The Court adds that its mandate pertains specifically to EU funds and that it has no audit mandate for all the bodies and instruments involved in defence.

The slides put the Court on a page headed ‘Defence planning still disjointed’, which quotes a 2026 review linked under the reference NEWS-RV-2026-01. They quote it as saying that the lack of effective EU-wide top-down planning, with insufficient coordination between European and national funding streams, could lead to fragmented investments, duplication of efforts or capability shortages. The review itself speaks of ongoing capability gaps, and explains that EU capability planning, unlike NATO’s top-down process, is neither cyclical nor linear but largely bottom-up, with member states identifying their own needs. Egmont had written in 2021 that defence planning remained stuck at the national level, and the European Defence Agency runs the Coordinated Annual Review on Defence, set up to end planning in isolation without significant coordination. The slides add that if additional funding is not used correctly it could cause implementation risks and bottlenecks in materials, key components or skilled personnel, a risk the review also names for funds that industry struggles to absorb.

cards.question: Decisions on defence and military matters in the Union’s foreign and security policy are always taken by _____ in the Council, so the agreement of all 27 member states is needed.
cards.abstract:
Unanimity is the rule that Article 31(1) of the Treaty on European Union makes general for the common foreign and security policy, whose decisions the European Council and Council take unanimously unless the chapter provides otherwise. Article 31(4) keeps decisions with military or defence implications outside the majority exceptions, so on defence the agreement of all 27 member states is always needed. Blockmans writes that the general rule often holds the EU back, because governments with different interests tend to settle on the lowest common denominator. Koenig lists cases from 2016 to 2019 in which single governments, such as Hungary, Greece and Italy, blocked or delayed EU statements and sanctions. Soler reports that sending the Union’s Rapid Deployment Capacity into action still requires the unanimous approval of all 27 member states in the Council, which leaves the force vulnerable to political deadlock.

The slides give unanimity for the common foreign and security policy, except under the enabling clause, and for the common security and defence policy, with proposals coming from the High Representative or a member state. They define veto players, quoting Tsebelis in 2002, as actors whose agreement is necessary for a change in the status quo, and cite Scharpf’s joint decision trap, where member states dominating decisions under unanimity get stalemate, the lowest common denominator or deals. As consequences they name issue linkage, meaning a strategically used vote, the delay in sanctions against Belarus after the 2020 presidential election because of Cyprus, and the delay in starting negotiations with North Macedonia. Fiott and Tercovich date the Belarus case: on 21 September 2020 Cyprus refused to sign off the sanctions, linking them to measures against Turkey over gas drilling, and it agreed on 2 October 2020. For enlargement the slides say decisions are unanimous at each main step, from candidate status to the accession treaty, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops find that unanimity in security and defence still prevailed after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
questions: The delay in adopting sanctions against Belarus after its 2020 presidential election, caused by the position of Cyprus, shows how one government can hold up foreign policy under _____ in the Council.
Where member states dominate decision-making under _____, the result can be stalemate, the lowest common denominator or deals, which is the diagnosis behind the joint decision trap.

cards.question: Under Article 31(2) of the Treaty on European Union the Council acts by _____ when it adopts a decision implementing a decision defining a Union action or position, or appoints a special representative.
cards.answerDate: EP resolutionJune 2022Group of FriendsMay 2023EPRS report28 August 2023
cards.abstract:
Qualified majority voting, or QMV, lets the Council adopt a decision without every government’s consent, and Article 16(3) of the Treaty on European Union makes it the Council’s default. Since 1 November 2014 a qualified majority means at least 55% of the Council’s members, covering at least 15 of them and at least 65% of the Union’s population, and a blocking minority needs at least four members. The Commission’s 2018 factsheet says the EU has moved from unanimity to QMV many times in its history and that QMV is now the standard voting rule, unlike in the common foreign and security policy. Article 31(2) of the treaty lists four foreign policy cases for QMV, but an emergency brake lets a member oppose a majority decision for vital and stated reasons of national policy. Paragraph 3 lets the European Council extend QMV by a unanimous decision, but paragraph 4 excludes decisions with military or defence implications.

The slides give QMV as the rule for the parts of external action run by the Community method, such as trade policy, neighbourhood policy and humanitarian aid. For the common foreign and security policy they list four QMV cases, summing up one as implementing a decision already made by the European Council, where the treaty says any decision implementing a decision defining a Union action or position. The slides add that defence and military matters are always unanimous, a slide on a 2023 research service report calls the cases non-exhaustive, and the Session 4 slides call QMV through different pathways possible but limited. Their reform ideas move sanctions, human rights and civilian missions to QMV, with military aspects excluded, the three areas the Commission proposed in 2018, and a 2023 study found unanimity had obstructed action in them. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report that Parliament’s resolution of June 2022 proposed switching from unanimity to QMV, and nine member states launched a Group of Friends on QMV on 4 May 2023.

cards.question: In the _____ the Commission proposes, the Council of Ministers votes by qualified majority or unanimity and the European Parliament co-decides in two readings, with a trilogue if the two disagree.
cards.answerDate: EPC established1970Maastricht CFSP1992
cards.abstract:
The Community method is, in the Commission’s White Paper on European Governance of 2001, the way of working in which the Commission alone makes the legislative and policy proposals that the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament adopt. The White Paper adds that qualified majority voting in the Council is essential to the method, that the Court of Justice guarantees the rule of law, and that interests pass through two filters, the Commission’s general interest and democratic representation. Article 294 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union sets out the ordinary legislative procedure: a Commission proposal, up to two readings by Parliament and Council, and a Conciliation Committee if they still disagree. Trilogue talks of Parliament, Council and Commission remain the preferred route to agreement, and 86% of proposals in Parliament’s 2019 to 2024 term were adopted at first reading. Woolcock explains that Lisbon gave Parliament joint powers with the Council over trade legislation and a consent role in trade agreements.

The slides call the method the EU’s ordinary decision-making procedure and show co-decision as two readings with a trilogue if Council and Parliament disagree, where the treaty names the Conciliation Committee. Their table of decision-making in external action, sourced to Schuette in 2019, puts trade, neighbourhood policy and humanitarian aid under the method with qualified majority voting, and lists energy, environment, migration and refugee policy as external dimensions of internal policies. The slides list trade policy, enlargement, democracy promotion, neighbourhood policy, development cooperation and humanitarian assistance as the Commission’s community areas. The common foreign and security policy stands against this: Article 24 of the Treaty on European Union has the European Council and Council define it unanimously and excludes legislative acts, and Blockmans calls intergovernmentalism its governance mode par excellence. The slides say Parliament has no formal co-decision powers in that policy but approves its budget, and the Session 2 slides call European Political Cooperation of 1970 intergovernmental as opposed to the community method.

cards.question: Introduced by the Treaty of Amsterdam in 1997, _____ means that one member state can abstain from a common foreign and security policy action and let the others go ahead with it.
cards.answerDate: Introduced1997InvokedFebruary 2022EPF changedMarch 2022
cards.abstract:
Constructive abstention lets a member of the Council abstain in a foreign policy vote and add a formal declaration, so that it need not apply the decision but accepts that the decision commits the Union. In a spirit of mutual solidarity it must refrain from any action likely to conflict with or impede Union action based on the decision, and the other member states must respect its position. If the members making such declarations represent at least one third of the member states and one third of the Union’s population, the decision is not adopted. Moravcsik and Nicolaïdis report that in the Amsterdam negotiations of 1997 the Petersberg tasks were made acceptable to all by an opt-out on demand, through constructive abstention, and a veto. Blockmans calls the device unique in the treaties, but notes that by 2017 it had been used only once, when Cyprus abstained in February 2008 on the decision creating the EULEX Kosovo mission.

The Session 2 slides credit the Treaty of Amsterdam of 1997 with introducing it and list it among the 1990s instruments as the way of opting out of a joint action, which needs unanimity. The Session 3 slides state that member states decide by unanimity and can abstain, naming this constructive abstention, and their table of options and breaks places it at Article 31(1) TEU. Fiott and Tercovich add that Greece, Romania, Slovakia and Spain, which also did not recognise Kosovo, agreed to the Kosovo mission without abstaining, so Cyprus used the device alone. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops show it at work in February 2022, when Austria, Malta and Ireland invoked Article 31 TEU to voice reservations about lethal-equipment support under the European Peace Facility and let the changes go ahead. Bartoloni explains that under the 2021 decision on the Facility such a state pays none of the costs, but argues that for sanctions the duty not to obstruct makes the device hard to use.

cards.question: Under _____, the Council acts by qualified majority when it adopts any decision implementing a decision defining a Union action or position, or when it appoints a special representative.
cards.answerDate: EPRS report28 August 2023
cards.abstract:
Article 31(2) TEU, in the Treaty on European Union, lists the cases in which the Council acts by qualified majority in the common foreign and security policy, by derogation from the unanimity rule of paragraph 1. The first two cases are a decision defining a Union action or position on the basis of a European Council decision on strategic interests and objectives, and one on a High Representative proposal made after a specific European Council request. The third is any decision implementing a decision defining a Union action or position, and the fourth is the appointment of a special representative in accordance with Article 33. An emergency brake stands beside them: if a member of the Council opposes a majority decision for vital and stated reasons of national policy, no vote is taken and the matter can go to the European Council for a unanimous decision. Paragraph 4 keeps decisions with military or defence implications out of the reach of paragraphs 2 and 3.

The slides take the list from a 2023 report of the European Parliament’s research service and label Article 31(2) TEU the enabling clause in their table of treaty options. That label is not the treaty’s, but Koenig uses it for the provision that lets the Council decide by qualified majority in predefined cases. The slides’ voting table gives unanimity for the policy except under the enabling clause, and a separate slide says the article allows for veto if vital national interests are affected, while defence and military decisions stay unanimous. Blockmans found that by 2017 none of the four exceptions had been used, and in 2018 the Commission suggested exploring the article, which Koenig says it wanted used for amending sanctions listings. Duval argued in May 2026 that the article gives ministers broad scope to decide by qualified majority, particularly on sanctions, but that most member states had opposed using it for fear of losing their veto.

cards.question: Listed at Article 31(3) TEU in a table of treaty options for the common foreign and security policy, the _____ sits beside constructive abstention, the enabling clause and enhanced cooperation.
cards.answerDate: EP resolutionJune 2022
cards.abstract:
The passerelle clause is a treaty provision that lets the European Council, acting unanimously, authorise the Council to decide by qualified majority where the treaties require unanimity. Its general form, Article 48(7) of the Treaty on European Union, applies to Title V of that treaty, which holds the foreign and security rules, and to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, but not to decisions with military implications or in defence. The European Council needs the consent of the European Parliament, and a single national parliament can stop the decision by making known its opposition within six months of being notified. The common foreign and security policy has its own clause in Article 31(3), under which the European Council may unanimously decide that the Council acts by qualified majority in cases beyond those listed in Article 31(2). Article 31(4) keeps military and defence decisions out of its reach, and the Parliament’s research service reported in 2023 that the clause had never been activated.

In the slides’ table of options and breaks under the treaties the clause stands at Article 31(3) TEU, after constructive abstention and the enabling clause and before enhanced cooperation, and the slides give it by name and article number only. In 2018 the Commission invited the European Council to use Article 31(3) for three areas: positions on human rights in international bodies, sanctions regimes and civilian missions. Koenig calls it the more controversial clause because it allows a permanent passage to qualified majority, and her survey of diplomats in late 2019 found six member states in favour of extension and ten opposed. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report that the European Parliament’s resolution of June 2022, adopted by 355 votes to 154, asked for treaty revision, with proposals that included use of the Lisbon passerelle clauses. They add that in security and defence some constitutional-level rules could change without treaty revision through certain Lisbon provisions, but that even these remain unused.

cards.question: The Treaty of Nice of 2001, in force from 2003, made _____ possible in the Union’s common foreign and security policy, a treaty option now listed at Article 20 TEU.
cards.answerDate: Treaty of Nice2001Nice in force2003PESCO2017
cards.abstract:
Enhanced cooperation lets member states that wish to go further together use the Union’s institutions within its non-exclusive competences, as Article 20 of the Treaty on European Union provides. The Council authorises it only as a last resort, once the Union as a whole cannot attain the objectives within a reasonable period, and at least nine member states must take part. It stays open to every member state at any time, only participating states vote in the Council, and its acts bind only them and are not part of the acquis that candidates must accept. For the common foreign and security policy Article 329(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires opinions from the High Representative and the Commission and a unanimous Council decision to authorise it. The Treaty of Nice opened this field to it through an inserted Article 27b, which limits it to implementing a joint action or common position and rules out matters with military or defence implications.

The lecture slides list it as one of four treaty options for the common foreign and security policy, at Article 20 TEU and Articles 326 to 333 TFEU, though Article 20 refers to Articles 326 to 334. The Session 2 slides list the Treaty of Nice of 2001, in force from 2003, as making enhanced cooperation possible, which matches the record of Article 27b. In the slides’ table it stands under the common foreign and security policy, while Permanent Structured Cooperation stands under the common security and defence policy. The Session 4 slides use the same heading for security and defence initiatives, starting with Permanent Structured Cooperation of 2017, which they base on Articles 42(6) and 46 TEU and Protocol 10 and call member states driven and project based. Blockmans adds that Lisbon extended enhanced cooperation to the whole common foreign and security policy, yet by 2017 it had not been used there in practice.

cards.question: Labelled the solidarity clause in a table of treaty options for the common security and defence policy, Article 42(7) TEU is the _____, listed beside Permanent Structured Cooperation and coalitions of the willing.
cards.abstract:
The mutual assistance clause is Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union: a member state that suffers armed aggression on its territory is owed aid and assistance by all the means in the other member states’ power. The aid must accord with Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, and the clause does not prejudice the specific character of the security and defence policy of certain member states. Commitments in this area must also be consistent with those under NATO, which remains the foundation of collective defence for its members. The Council’s Legal Service records that the Treaty of Lisbon introduced the clause, that its wording matches the Constitutional Treaty’s, which never entered into force, and that it resembles Article V of the modified Brussels Treaty. The Legal Service calls it a distinct and autonomous provision, applicable to all member states, whose language and purpose are not identical to those of Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty.

The lecture slides list Article 42(7) beside Permanent Structured Cooperation at Articles 42(6) and 46 and coalitions of the willing at Article 44 as the three treaty options for the common security and defence policy. The slides label it the “solidarity clause” and say no more of it, but that name belongs to Article 222 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which covers a terrorist attack or a natural or man-made disaster. France invoked Article 42(7) for the first time on 17 November 2015, after the Paris attacks, and the ministers of all member states pledged unanimous and full support. Fazio notes that France chose it over the solidarity clause because it involves only member states, needs no unanimous Council decision and has no formal procedure. She argues that its obligations are automatic, unlike those under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, but not unconditional, because of the clause on the specific character of some states’ policies and the NATO clause.

cards.question: Listed at Article 44 TEU among the options for the common security and defence policy, _____ appear beside the solidarity clause and Permanent Structured Cooperation in a table of treaty options.
cards.answerDate: Emphasis seen2025
cards.abstract:
Coalitions of the willing are the groups of member states to which Article 44 of the Treaty on European Union lets the Council entrust a task, if they are willing and have the necessary capability. The task must come within the decisions the Council adopts under Article 43, the expanded Petersberg tasks, so the Article creates no new category of operation. Thierry Tardy traced the wording to the draft constitutional treaty of 2003, when documents urged more flexibility in crisis management and so some sort of ‘coalition of the willing’ inside the Union. The High Representative’s report for the December 2013 European Council saw benefits in flexibility and speed of action and named France’s Operation Serval in Mali as a case in point. Luigi Scazzieri added in 2022 that such an operation would fly the EU flag and draw on EU funding for common costs, but would still need unanimity, so states set on acting quickly would keep to ad hoc groupings.

The lecture slides list coalitions of the willing at Article 44 TEU in their table of treaty options for the common security and defence policy, beside the solidarity clause and Permanent Structured Cooperation. They also list them among four pathways out of the joint decision trap, as informal groupings of member states with the Friends of Libya as an example. A European Parliament committee noted in 2023 that Article 44 had never been used, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops observe in 2025 an emphasis on creating such coalitions, away from the constraining rules of a policy where unanimity still prevails. In March 2025 the High Representative said she would apply the formula to military support for Ukraine ‘so that one country cannot block everybody else’, a reference to the Hungarian veto. Christoph Meyer of King’s College London argues, as Soler reports, that if NATO cannot be reformed policymakers must consider another institutional design and until then, he said, “we’re stuck with coalitions of the willing”.
