cards.question: Article 31(2) TEU allows for veto if vital national interests are affected, a safeguard on qualified majority decisions that can be called the _____ in foreign policy voting.
cards.abstract:
The emergency brake is the name a 2023 study for the European Parliament’s research service gives to the safeguard in Article 31(2) of the Treaty on European Union. Article 31(1) makes unanimity the rule for decisions in the common foreign and security policy and lets an abstaining member qualify its abstention, so that it need not apply the decision. Article 31(2) lets the Council act by qualified majority in four cases, among them a decision proposed by the High Representative at a specific request of the European Council and the appointment of a special representative. The same paragraph says that if a member of the Council declares that, for ‘vital and stated reasons of national policy’, it intends to oppose a decision to be taken by qualified majority, a vote shall not be taken. The High Representative then seeks a solution acceptable to that state, and failing that the Council may, by qualified majority, ask for a unanimous decision of the European Council.

The lecture slides state that Article 31(2) TEU allows for veto if vital national interests are affected, and they do not use the phrase emergency brake. The treaty speaks instead of ‘vital and stated reasons of national policy’ and of a vote not being taken, and the slides’ wording is looser than the text. The same slide adds that defence and military decisions are always taken by unanimity, which matches Article 31(4), since paragraphs 2 and 3 do not apply to decisions with military or defence implications. George Tsebelis argued in 2013 that the paragraph is meant to turn a qualified majority decision into a unanimous one, because the High Representative bases talks with the dissenting state on the majority position. A 2018 Commission factsheet cited the failure in June 2017 to adopt an EU statement on China at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and the 2023 study notes that the passerelle clause of Article 31(3) has never been activated.

cards.question: Appearing beside the Commission, the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament in the diagram of the Community method, the _____ is also credited with competence over sanctions as an exception in foreign policy.
cards.answer: Court of Justice of the EU
cards.answerDate: Single Act1986Opinion soughtJanuary 2026
cards.abstract:
The Court of Justice of the EU is one of the Union’s seven institutions and consists of two courts, the Court of Justice and the General Court. It hears actions against member states, actions to annul EU acts and, in preliminary rulings, questions from national courts on the interpretation or validity of EU law. Under Article 218(11) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Parliament can ask it whether an envisaged agreement is compatible with the Treaties, and an adverse opinion bars the agreement unless it is amended. In the common foreign and security policy its role is limited, because Article 24(1) of the Treaty on European Union gives it no jurisdiction, except to monitor compliance with Article 40 and to review certain decisions under Article 275 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Luigi Lonardo explains that this exception covers Council decisions imposing restrictive measures on natural or legal persons, and calls the Court’s Rosneft judgment of 28 March 2017, the first preliminary ruling requested on such an act, a landmark decision.

The lecture slides show the CJEU in their diagram of the Community method beside the Commission, the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament. Their list of rules for foreign and security policy decision-making includes CJEU competence over sanctions, marked as an exception, as the treaty provisions are. The Session 2 slides say that the Single European Act of 1986 included European Political Cooperation in the treaties, but without ECJ jurisdiction. The Session 6 slides report that in January 2026 the European Parliament voted to ask the CJEU for an opinion on whether the EU–Mercosur agreements are compatible with the treaties, which effectively paused its consent procedure, and the press release gives the vote as 334 to 324. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops name a landmark decision of the CJEU, besides treaty amendment, as a way in which constitutional-level rules can change when higher-level constraints make policy change difficult.

cards.question: Individual or collective actors whose agreement is necessary for a change in the status quo are known as _____, whose preferences and configuration both matter when foreign policy is decided under unanimity.
cards.abstract:
Veto players are, in the words of George Tsebelis, actors whose agreement is necessary for a change of the status quo, so a country able to block a unanimity decision counts as one. His book Veto Players: How Political Institutions Work of 2002 argues that political systems differ most in how much veto power they give political actors over policy choices. It holds that more veto players, or a greater ideological distance between them, make policy more stable and impede significant departures from the status quo. It tests the theory on data from advanced industrialised countries and on EU legislation, and has a chapter on the Union’s institutions. In a working paper of 2013 Tsebelis added that changes by unanimity are very difficult to make and that unanimity is the default in foreign policy.

The lecture slides place the concept under the difficulties of decision-making under unanimity and credit its definition to Tsebelis’s book of 2002, adding that both the preferences of veto players and their configuration are important. They add that using one’s veto may be more likely in conditions of power asymmetry, and that Article 31(2) TEU allows for a veto if vital national interests are affected, where the treaty speaks of ‘vital and stated reasons of national policy’. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that rational institutionalist approaches highlight veto players and, following Tsebelis, that a policy can remain in deadlock until the preference configuration or the decision-making rules change, and so see a high threshold for change in security and defence and in enlargement. With numerous veto players and unanimity, they expect sustainable change to need both informal and formal alterations of institutional rules, and on enlargement they conclude that institutional change is still obstructed by veto players. Hungary’s veto stopped an EU declaration on Hong Kong on 10 May 2021, and in 2018 one state held up a civilian mission in the Sahel until another dropped its reservations on a mission to Iraq.

cards.question: The 2002 book on how political institutions work, published by Princeton University Press, was written by _____, whose findings on deadlock are applied in a 2026 article to the EU's security and defence policy.
cards.answerDate: Book2002
cards.abstract:
George Tsebelis is a political scientist who in 2013 held the Anatol Rapoport Collegiate Professorship at the University of Michigan. He wrote the book Veto Players: How Political Institutions Work, published in 2002 by Princeton University Press. The book argues that political systems are best told apart by how much veto power they give political actors, and that more veto players, or a greater ideological distance between them, make policy more stable. His working paper of 2013 traces the Union’s bridging of qualified majority and unanimity from the Luxembourg Compromise of 1966 to the Lisbon Treaty and analyses Article 31(2) TEU. He notes that under unanimity every country able to block a decision is a veto player, and a 2023 study for the European Parliament’s research service records Hungary’s veto of an EU declaration on Hong Kong on 10 May 2021.

The lecture slides list the book among their additional references and take from it their definition of veto players as individual or collective actors whose agreement is necessary for a change in the status quo. The slides place the definition under the difficulties of decision-making under unanimity, where both the preferences of veto players and their configuration are important. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write in a 2026 article in West European Politics that Tsebelis has shown that when decision-making involves multiple veto players, a policy can remain in deadlock until the preference configuration or the decision-making rules change. They list the book among the institutionalist works on which they build their stages of change, and use his result to point to a high threshold for change in security and defence and in enlargement, both subject to unanimity. Tsebelis reads Article 31(2) TEU, under which a vote is not taken when a member invokes ‘vital and stated reasons of national policy’, as a device that turns a qualified majority decision into a unanimous one.

cards.question: When member states dominate decision-making under unanimity and decisions end in stalemate or lowest common denominator deals, the _____ is said to be at work in the Union's foreign policy.
cards.abstract:
The joint decision trap is the concept with which Fritz Scharpf explained a paradox of European integration, ‘frustration without disintegration and resilience without progress’. In 1988 he compared joint decision-making in German federalism with that of the European Community, where member governments take part directly in central decisions and unanimity is required in effect. Such conditions, he argued, systematically generate sub-optimal policy unless a problem-solving style replaces bargaining, and bargaining had prevailed. He explained the trap by the interests of member governments, for whom present arrangements look like a local optimum compared with more centralisation or with disintegration. A reference entry adds that any actor harmed by a change can block it unless compensated, and in 2006 Scharpf judged his analysis basically valid but simplified, needing a complement on the non-political policy-making of the European Central Bank and the Court of Justice.

The slides present the trap through Scharpf’s work of 1988 and 2006: when member states dominate decision-making under unanimity, decisions result in a stalemate or lowest common denominator deals. They list issue linkage, a delay in adopting sanctions against Belarus and a delay in starting negotiations with North Macedonia as consequences, and a 2023 study traces the Belarus delay of 21 September 2020 to a dispute over parallel sanctions on Turkey. On divergence between member states they list geographical position, historical ties, different threat perceptions and domestic regimes, and add that external crises can upgrade the common interest. Their pathways out of the trap are a common strategic culture, crisis and external pressure, technical level decisions and coalitions of the willing, and they quote Borrell in 2020 saying that the more Europeans agree on how they see the world, the more they agree on what to do. Soler reports that sending the Rapid Deployment Capacity into action still requires the unanimous approval of all 27 member states as threat perceptions differ, and the Session 6 slides list the trap among the exam concepts to explain in five lines.

cards.question: Work from 1988 and 2006 by _____ holds that when member states dominate decision-making under unanimity, decisions result in stalemate or lowest common denominator deals.
cards.answerDate: Cited work1988Article2006
cards.abstract:
Fritz Scharpf is the German scholar who identified the joint decision trap in the early 1980s, first in German federalism and then in the policy-making of the European Union. The Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies lists him as Director Emeritus and publishes his essays on the multilevel European polity as Community and Autonomy, which includes the 1988 essay on the trap and the revisit of 2006. His article of 1988 in Public Administration compared joint decision-making in German federalism with that of the European Community, where member governments take part directly in central decisions and unanimity is required in effect. He argued that this systematically generates sub-optimal policy unless a problem-solving style replaces bargaining, and that bargaining had prevailed in both systems. In his article of 2006 in the Journal of Common Market Studies he judged the original analysis basically valid but simplified, in need of a complement on the non-political policy-making of the European Central Bank and the Court of Justice.

The lecture slides cite Scharpf for the joint decision trap, naming his work of 1988 and 2006, and list him as F. Scharpf in their references. According to that slide, when member states dominate decision-making under conditions of unanimity, decisions result in a stalemate or lowest common denominator deals. The slides’ additional references give his 2006 article, The joint-decision trap revisited, in volume 44, issue 4 of the journal, pages 845 to 864. A reference entry states the two conditions as agreement of the constituent governments being needed and being unanimous or nearly so, so that any actor harmed by a change can block it unless compensated. The pattern shows in foreign policy, where the Commission recorded that in June 2017 no EU statement on China could be adopted at the United Nations Human Rights Council, and a 2023 study traces the Belarus sanctions delay of 21 September 2020 to a dispute over parallel sanctions on Turkey.

cards.question: Disengagement from the commonly agreed consensus attitude, as when a member state vetoes a decision or threatens to veto without justification or previous discussion, is called _____ in a 2023 research service report.
cards.abstract:
Norm contestation is the name of a body of research on challenges to shared norms, and Heidi Maurer and Nicholas Wright draw on it to study challenges to EU foreign policy cooperation from member states. They build on a distinction between direct contestation, which is openly voiced, and indirect contestation, a hidden kind that shows up in implementation. Their own term is systemic contestation, in two forms: passive contestation, when member states disengage from initiatives and their implementation, and tacit contestation, when they fail to act to safeguard the system. Article 31(1) of the Treaty on European Union makes unanimity the rule in this policy, so one refusal can block a decision. They illustrate it with several member states that in 2018 withdrew from the United Nations Global Compact for Migration without first informing their counterparts or seeking a prior discussion in Brussels.

The lecture slides define norm contestation as disengagement from a commonly agreed consensus attitude, as when a member state vetoes a decision, or threatens to veto, without justification or without previous discussion. They credit this to Dyduch and Müller in a 2023 report by the European Parliament’s research service, at page 19, and place it on the same slide as the joint decision trap. The next slide lists issue linkage, a delay in adopting sanctions against Belarus and a delay in starting negotiations with North Macedonia as consequences of voting under unanimity, without saying whether they are cases of norm contestation. A 2023 study for the research service describes Hungary’s veto of an EU declaration on Hong Kong on 10 May 2021 and the delay of the Belarus sanctions on 21 September 2020 by a dispute over parallel sanctions on Turkey. On 6 March 2025 Hungary opposed European Council conclusions on Ukraine for the first time since 2022, so 26 states delivered separate conclusions, and the slides add that using one’s veto may be more likely in conditions of power asymmetry.

cards.question: A strategically used vote under unanimity in foreign policy or related areas is known as _____, one of the consequences of foreign policy voting under unanimity.
cards.abstract:
Issue linkage makes agreement on one question depend on a concession on another, and Müller and Slominski describe hostage-taking as a veto combined with such tactical linkage to win concessions in an unrelated policy area. In foreign policy every government holds a veto, because Article 24(1) of the Treaty on European Union requires the European Council and the Council to act unanimously, except where the Treaties provide otherwise. Article 31 lists the exceptions, such as decisions that implement an earlier decision and the appointment of special representatives, which the Council may take by qualified majority. The Centre for European Reform counted 45 vetoes between 2011 and 2025, including blocked statements, and wrote that unanimity had been “hijacked by bilateral disputes” and used to win concessions on unrelated issues. Müller and Slominski describe a “soft” form that hides the link, and argue that the timing of Hungary’s vetoes on Ukraine decisions during its rule-of-law dispute points to it.

The lecture slides list issue linkage first among the consequences of foreign policy voting under unanimity. They describe it as a strategically used vote under unanimity in foreign policy or related areas. Beside it the slides list a delay in adopting sanctions against Belarus after the 2020 presidential election, due to the position of Cyprus, and a delay in starting negotiations with North Macedonia, but they do not say whether either was a case of issue linkage. On Belarus, Borrell said on 21 September 2020 that the required unanimity was not reached, and the Centre for European Reform later wrote that Cyprus blocked the sanctions to pressure the EU in its dispute with Turkey. The North Macedonia delay was a Bulgarian veto on the negotiating framework that lasted from 2020 until Bulgaria and North Macedonia accepted a French compromise in June and July 2022, after Borrell had pointed to the failure of the unanimity rule.

cards.question: Following the protests after the 2020 presidential election, the position of Cyprus is blamed for the _____, an example of a cost of foreign policy voting under unanimity.
cards.answerDate: Election2020
cards.abstract:
The delay of sanctions against Belarus in autumn 2020 was a case of the EU failing for several weeks to adopt restrictive measures that its own leaders had announced. Belarus held a presidential election on 9 August 2020, which the Council found inconsistent with international standards and marred by the repression of independent candidates and a brutal crackdown on peaceful protesters. On 11 August 2020 the High Representative declared on behalf of the Union that the elections were neither free nor fair, and stated that measures could be taken against those responsible for violence, unjustified arrests and falsification of the results. Such restrictive measures are decisions in the common foreign and security policy, which the European Council and the Council take unanimously unless the Treaty provides otherwise. When the foreign ministers met on 21 September 2020, High Representative Borrell said that there was a clear will to adopt the sanctions but that the required unanimity was not reached, because one country was not part of the consensus.

The slides give the delay of sanctions against Belarus as an example of the consequences of foreign policy voting under unanimity. They say the sanctions concerned human rights violations following the protests after the 2020 presidential election, and put the delay down to the position of Cyprus. The slides do not use the word veto and do not set out that position, which the Centre for European Reform describes as blocking the sanctions to pressure the EU in its dispute with Turkey. The Council added 40 people to the list on 2 October 2020 on a proposal from the High Representative, a decision that followed the European Council conclusions of 1 October 2020. A Session 2 slide on strategies and outcomes says of Belarus that the EU failed to affect violent repression in 2020 and that sanctions continue.

cards.question: National officials' socialisation leading to a common _____ is listed as one pathway out of stalemate under unanimity, together with crisis and external pressure, technical level decisions and informal groupings of member states.
cards.abstract:
A strategic culture is the set of beliefs, values, norms and practices that shapes how a political community understands threats, judges the legitimacy of military force and chooses partners. The research service of the European Parliament described the idea in 2021 as a shared perception of threats and a common strategic vision, and added that experts find the concept largely elusive. The 2003 European Security Strategy had already called for “a strategic culture that fosters early, rapid, and when necessary, robust intervention”. The Strategic Compass, the EU’s security and defence strategy adopted in March 2022, aims to advance towards a common forward-looking strategic culture. In a speech of 25 May 2020 Borrell told German ambassadors that the Union lacked a common strategic culture, and that too often member states clung to national viewpoints instead of seeing a broader common interest.

The slides name the creation of a common strategic culture as one pathway out of the stalemate under unanimity, beside crisis and external pressure, technical level decisions and informal groupings of member states. They describe it as the socialisation of national officials leading to a common strategic culture, and cite Müller, 2016, page 362. The slides quote Borrell, in 2020, saying that the more Europeans agree on how they see the world and its problems, the more they will agree on what to do about them. They trace divergence between member states to geographical position, historical ties and alliances, cultural affinity, different threat perceptions, domestic political regimes and pressure from other states, and add that external crises can upgrade the common interest. Michaels and Sus report, from a 2024 article based on interviews in seven member states, that strategic cultures and threat perceptions among the 27 continue to differ and were not fundamentally changed by the war, and a 2026 paper by the Finnish Institute of International Affairs finds that threat perceptions, approaches to the use of force and alliance preferences still differ.

cards.question: Bringing together heads of state and government, the _____ provides strategic objectives and policy guidelines through the conclusions of its summits, including on enlargement, and appoints the High Representative by qualified majority.
cards.answerDate: Defence summitDecember 2013Versailles10 – 11 March 2022Candidacy23 June 2022
cards.abstract:
The European Council consists of the heads of state or government, its President and the President of the Commission, and the High Representative takes part in its work. Article 15 of the Treaty on European Union gives it the task of providing the Union with impetus and defining its general political directions and priorities, without legislative functions. Under Article 26 it identifies the Union’s strategic interests and defines general guidelines for foreign policy, and it decides by consensus unless the Treaties provide otherwise, meeting formally about four times a year. Michaels and Sus say that its conclusions on defence of December 2013 heralded the second phase of the EU’s maturation as an autonomous security and defence actor. An informal European Council at Versailles on 10 and 11 March 2022 called Russia’s war of aggression a tectonic shift in European history, and on 23 June 2022 it granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova.

The slides describe it as the body of heads of state and government that adopts the common strategy, principles and guidelines and, through the conclusions of its summits, sets strategic objectives and policy guidelines, also for enlargement. They show it appointing the High Representative and Vice-President with qualified majority, and member states in the Council or the European Council deciding foreign and security policy by unanimity, and they quote Article 31(2) TEU. The slides quote Maurer and Wright, 2021, describing it as engaged in policy making like never before, a more active top player in the hierarchy and the place where sensitive, controversial issues go directly, and they note a disengagement with foreign ministers. Maurer and Wright base these words on diplomats’ interviews, while another quoted passage says the European Council deals with security issues in a haphazard manner and should become more operational and structured. The slides looking towards the final exam list the European Council among the concepts that may come up in its concepts part.

cards.question: Chaired by the High Representative except when it discusses trade, the _____ meets once a month and brings together foreign ministers and, when appropriate, defence, development, European integration or trade ministers.
cards.abstract:
The Foreign Affairs Council is the Council configuration that elaborates the Union’s external action on the basis of strategic guidelines from the European Council and ensures that the action is consistent. The Council’s Rules of Procedure of 2009 make it responsible for the whole of external action, namely the common foreign and security policy, the common security and defence policy, common commercial policy, development cooperation and humanitarian aid. Article 18 of the Treaty on European Union says that the High Representative presides over it, and the Rules of Procedure let the High Representative ask the presidency minister to stand in where necessary. The Council has 10 configurations, and the Foreign Affairs Council alone has a permanent chair, whereas the presidency country’s minister chairs the others. Maurer and Wright call the High Representative’s appointment as permanent chair Lisbon’s key procedural innovation for the Political and Security Committee, because it gives the office crucial agenda-setting power.

The slides call the Foreign Affairs Council the main decision-making body on foreign policy and defence within the Council of Ministers, adding the words “but see Maurer and Wright 2021”. They say it consists of the ministers of foreign affairs and, when appropriate, of defence, development, European integration and trade, meets once a month and is chaired by the High Representative, except when it discusses trade issues. The slides list its responsibility for external action as foreign policy, defence and security, trade, development cooperation and humanitarian aid, which matches the Rules of Procedure. Maurer and Wright, drawing on diplomats’ interviews, describe a gradual eclipsing of the Council as the primary venue for foreign affairs decisions as the European Council became the strategic policy-setter, although its monthly meetings continue. On the slide on the European Council the slides quote the same authors saying that sensitive, controversial issues go directly to the European Council, and they note a disengagement with foreign ministers.

cards.question: Permanent and based in Brussels, the _____ is an ambassador-level body of the Council that monitors the international situation in areas covered by the common foreign and security policy and contributes to policy formulation.
cards.answerDate: AgreedDecember 2000In placefrom 2001MEP meetingsfrom 2010
cards.abstract:
The Political and Security Committee monitors the international situation in the areas covered by the common foreign and security policy and delivers opinions to the Council, on request or on its own initiative. Article 38 of the Treaty on European Union gives it, under the responsibility of the Council and the High Representative, the political control and strategic direction of crisis management operations. The Helsinki European Council agreed in principle to set it up, an interim committee was set up in February 2000, and the Nice European Council agreed on the permanent one in December 2000. A Council decision of 22 January 2001 established it, and its annex calls it the linchpin of the common foreign and security policy. The Council’s Rules of Procedure provide that a representative of the High Representative chairs it, a post Maurer and Wright place in the European External Action Service.

The slides describe it as a permanent, Brussels-based Council body at ambassador level, under the Council and the High Representative, and point to Maurer and Wright, 2021, for arguments about different levels of activism. They say it monitors the international situation, contributes to policy formulation and directs crisis management operations, and the Session 2 slides date it from 2001 after the Nice European Council of December 2000. The slides call it a venue for consultation and socialisation, citing Juncos and Pomorska, 2006, who found that diplomats in the working groups feeding into it follow consensus-building codes out of strategic calculation. They quote Maurer and Wright, 2021, saying that it has been central to the institutionalisation of EU foreign and security policy making and that its ambassadors are only as powerful as their compromises, because if they cannot agree there may well not be an EU position. The slides cite page 862 for relations with the EEAS as the most significant component of day-to-day negotiations, and add that since 2010 designated members of the European Parliament have met the Committee on civilian CSDP missions.

cards.question: Made up of the chiefs of defence and in place since 2001, the _____ is the highest military body within the Council and advises the Political and Security Committee.
cards.answerDate: AgreedDecember 2000In place since2001
cards.abstract:
The EU Military Committee is composed of the chiefs of defence of the member states, who are regularly represented by their permanent military representatives. It is the highest military body established within the Council, and based on consensus it gives military advice and makes recommendations to the Political and Security Committee. The Nice European Council of 7 to 11 December 2000 agreed on its establishment, and a Council decision of 22 January 2001 set it up. Its chairman is appointed by the Council on the recommendation of the committee meeting at the level of the chiefs of defence, for three years unless the Council decides otherwise. The chairman attends Council meetings when decisions with defence implications are taken, and the committee gives military direction to the EU Military Staff, which a decision of the same day placed in the Council’s General Secretariat.

The slides describe the committee as a body of chiefs of defence that is the highest military body within the Council since 2001, and say that it advises the Political and Security Committee. The slides on the Council’s further bodies call it the “European Military Committee”, while the slides on the Union’s institutional evolution use the name EU Military Committee, shortened to EUMC. The latter slides list it among the bodies agreed by the Nice European Council in December 2000, together with the Political and Security Committee, the EU Military Staff and the European Defence Agency. The slides give 2004 as the year of the Defence Agency, which fits the Joint Action of 12 July 2004 that created it after the Thessaloniki European Council of June 2003 called for such an agency. In The Parliament Magazine of 29 June 2026, Paula Soler names General Seán Clancy as chairman of the committee and quotes him saying “It is ultimately a political question” about the Rapid Deployment Capacity, which he says was established with “a very clear statement in terms of level of ambition”.

cards.question: Known by the abbreviation CIVCOM, the _____ is one of the Council’s further bodies and advises the Political and Security Committee, which is an ambassador-level body based in Brussels.
cards.answer: Committee for Civilian Aspects of Crisis Management
cards.answerDate: Helsinki Council1999Compact signed2018
cards.abstract:
The Committee for Civilian Aspects of Crisis Management, known as CIVCOM, was set up by a Council decision of 22 May 2000 and consists of representatives of the member states. It operates as a Council working party that reports to the Permanent Representatives Committee and advises the Political and Security Committee on civilian aspects of crisis management. The decision followed the Helsinki European Council of December 1999, which asked for work on such a committee, and the Lisbon European Council of March 2000, which asked for it to be set up by or at the Feira summit. The annex to the 2001 decision on the Political and Security Committee says that it receives information, recommendations and opinions from CIVCOM and sends it guidelines. Juncos and Pomorska place CIVCOM and its military counterpart between the bodies above them, the second formation of the Permanent Representatives Committee and the Political and Security Committee, and the Council working groups below.

The slides, which abbreviate the name to CIVCOM, list it among the Council’s further bodies as advising the Political and Security Committee, the ambassador-level body based in Brussels, on civilian aspects. It stands beside the Political and security group, which deals with preparing the Committee’s meetings, implementation and the partnership with NATO, and beside the committee of chiefs of defence. The slide on civilian CSDP names the committee and then lists four priority areas, which are policing, rule of law, civilian administration and civic protection. The slide on the emergence of the CSDP, covering the Helsinki European Council of 1999, gives the civilian dimension in nearly the same terms, whereas the 2023 Civilian CSDP Compact speaks of “the Feira priorities” of police, rule of law and civil administration. The slides add that a Civilian CSDP Compact, signed under the Finnish presidency in 2018, aimed to make civilian CSDP more capable, more effective and more joined-up, while the EEAS dates the first Compact to 2018 and the second to May 2023.

cards.question: Appointed by the European Council with a qualified majority, the _____ chairs the Foreign Affairs Council except on trade, leads the Union’s diplomatic network and also belongs to the Commission.
cards.answerDate: Post created1997Upgraded2009First strategy2003
cards.abstract:
The High Representative and Vice-President, shortened to HR/VP, is the Union’s senior foreign policy official, appointed by the European Council by qualified majority with the agreement of the Commission President. Article 18 of the Treaty on European Union makes the holder one of the Commission’s Vice-Presidents and gives the holder the chair of the Foreign Affairs Council. Article 27 adds that the holder proposes policy, ensures that Council decisions are carried out and conducts political dialogue with third parties for the Union. The Parliament’s research service noted in 2012 that the job is often called triple-hatted, for its Commission, Council and policy roles, and that the Lisbon treaty provides no deputy. The post grew out of the High Representative created by the Treaty of Amsterdam, which took effect in 1999 although the slides give 1997, and Javier Solana held it from 1999 to 2009 before Catherine Ashton began the Lisbon version in December 2009.

The lecture slides give the HR/VP the overall steering of the common foreign and security policy and the common security and defence policy, with building consensus among the member states. They add the operational conduct of EU missions, consistency of external action and political dialogues, and show proposals coming from the HR/VP, from the HR/VP with the Commission, or from a member state. The slides say the holder leads the Union’s diplomatic network, heads the European Defence Agency and the EU institute for security studies, and chairs the Foreign Affairs Council except on trade. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops call Javier Solana the EU’s first High Representative, who pushed the CSDP at a remarkable pace and presented the first European Security Strategy in 2003. In the slides’ 2026 material Kaja Kallas, in office since 1 December 2024, argues that a strong shared network of 145 delegations is more valuable than duplicated national diplomatic services.

cards.question: Established in 2010 to overcome the artificial separation of external economic and foreign policy relations, the _____ took over all civilian and military crisis management structures from the Council Secretariat.
cards.answerDate: Lisbon treaty2009Established2010German proposalSeptember 2026
cards.abstract:
The European External Action Service, the EEAS, is the Union’s diplomatic service, a functionally autonomous body separate from the Council Secretariat and the Commission, under the authority of the High Representative. Article 27(3) of the Treaty on European Union provided for it, saying it comprises officials from the Council Secretariat and the Commission together with staff seconded from national diplomatic services. The Council set it up by a decision of 26 July 2010, after the European Parliament adopted its resolution on 8 July by 549 votes to 78, with 17 abstentions. Staff and departments moved over from the Council Secretariat and the Commission on 1 January 2011, and the EEAS says it has carried out the common foreign and security policy since 2011. The decision places the crisis management and planning directorate, the Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability, the EU Military Staff and the Situation Centre under the direct authority of the High Representative.

The slides date the EEAS to 2010 and name three problems it was to overcome: the artificial separation of external economic and foreign policy relations, coordination problems between the Commission and the Council secretariat, and discontinuity between Council presidencies. They say it took over all civilian and military crisis management structures, supports the High Representative, heads the EU Delegations and chairs the Political and Security Committee, although the decision has the High Representative designate that chair. The ‘Dancing partners’ slide cites Maurer and Wright 2021 for relations with that committee as the most significant component of day-to-day CFSP negotiations, with cooperation almost daily. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine is run by the EEAS’s Military Planning and Conduct Capability, and the Session 4 slides place EastStratCom within the service. The slides quote Andrew Sherriff that blaming the EEAS alone for a slow and fragmented EU would be grossly unfair, and report a German proposal of September 2026 to merge it into the Commission.

cards.question: Cooperating with the embassies of the member states and reporting weekly, the _____ form a global network that the EEAS heads and represent the Union around the world.
cards.abstract:
The EU Delegations are the Union’s diplomatic missions in third countries and at international organisations, and Article 221 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union says that they represent the Union. The same article places them under the High Representative’s authority and requires close cooperation with the diplomatic and consular missions of the member states. Until the Lisbon treaty took effect in December 2009 they were Delegations of the European Commission, and Novotná writes that the upgrade made them houses representing the whole Union rather than one institution. The 2010 decision on the EEAS gives each delegation a Head of Delegation, who has authority over all its staff and is accountable to the High Representative. The Commission’s enlargement site counts some 144 delegations and offices worldwide, and its Global Gateway release of 2021 gave them a key role in coordinating projects in partner countries.

The slides say the EEAS heads the EU Delegations and the Union’s representation around the world, citing Article 221 of the Treaty on European Union, although that article belongs to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. They add that the delegations cooperate with the embassies of the member states and report weekly, which they describe, citing Maurer and Wright 2021, as a global network to rely on. The slide on the High Representative says the post leads the EU’s diplomatic network without naming the delegations, while the decision has heads of delegation take instructions from the High Representative. In the slides’ 2026 material Kaja Kallas argues that a strong shared network of 145 delegations is more valuable than duplicating national diplomatic services, a view sourced to Politico. The slides on the Parliament’s consultations list an exchange of views with heads of mission and heads of EU delegations, next to meetings since 2010 between a designated group of MEPs and counterparts from the Political and Security Committee, the EEAS and the Commission on civilian missions.

cards.question: Listed among the security and defence related bodies of the European External Action Service, the _____ is described as the Union’s autonomous information gathering.
cards.abstract:
The Intelligence and Situation Centre, abbreviated INTCEN, is the Union’s civilian intelligence analysis body, a directorate of the European External Action Service reporting directly to the High Representative. It began in 2002 as the EU Situation Centre in the Council Secretariat, attached to the office of the High Representative Javier Solana, with intelligence staff seconded from member states. In 2007 it agreed the Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity with the Intelligence Directorate of the EU Military Staff, so that all assessments issued to member states are joint products. The Situation Centre transferred to the EEAS on 1 January 2011 under the 2010 decision, which names it beside the crisis management and planning directorate, the Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability and the EU Military Staff. The EEAS dates the rename to March 2012 and expands INTCEN as EU Intelligence Analysis Centre, whereas Bossong dates it to 2011 and the slides use Intelligence and Situation Centre.

The slide on EEAS security and defence related bodies lists the Situation Centre, later the EU intelligence and situation centre INTCEN, with the Security and Defence directorate, the Integrated approach for Security and Peace Directorate and both planning and conduct capabilities. It adds the phrase autonomous information gathering after the centre’s name and says no more about how the centre works. The record is narrower, since the EEAS fact sheet says the centre is not an operational agency and has no collection capability, and Bossong writes that member states voluntarily transmit finished intelligence reports. The slides on the Strategic Compass of 2022 list an EU Single Intelligence Analysis Capacity among its measures, and the Compass itself calls it the single entry point for strategic intelligence from member states and promises to strengthen it by 2025. A Session 1 slide on the limits to the Union’s capacity to act names intelligence among the weaknesses in defence that cannot be quickly overturned, and Bossong put the centre in 2018 at around 100 employees.

cards.question: Established in 2007 and listed among the security and defence related bodies of the EEAS, the _____ has since overseen all civilian operations of the Union.
cards.answerDate: Established2007MPCC created2017
cards.abstract:
The Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability, the CPCC, is the headquarters in the European External Action Service for the Union’s civilian CSDP missions. Its Managing Director is the Civilian Operation Commander for each such mission, appointed by the High Representative for a fixed term to ensure periodic rotation. The idea came from a letter of 13 June 2006 proposing a Civilian Operation Commander for a clearer chain of command, and the Council approved guidelines for that structure on 17 and 18 June 2007. The 2010 decision on the EEAS placed the CPCC under the direct authority of the High Representative, and its staff transferred from the Council Secretariat on 1 January 2011. In March 2025 the EEAS announced a new Civilian Operations Headquarters for 13 civilian missions, with some 120 experts, which the Centre of Excellence for Civilian Crisis Management says replaced the CPCC.

The slides list the CPCC among the EEAS security and defence related bodies, directly before the Military Planning and Conduct Capability. Michaels and Sus write that the EU established it in 2007 and that it has since overseen all civilian operations. They set its creation in the mid-2000s, when the Franco-British consensus had weakened, the CSDP had become increasingly leaderless and enthusiasm for security and defence cooperation had waned, and add that the EU adopted the Civilian Headline Goal 2010 that year. Similar progress was not possible on military operational planning, they write, because the UK vetoed initiatives to set up an Operational Headquarters. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the Military Planning and Conduct Capability was created in 2017 as a permanent operational headquarters for EU CSDP operations.

cards.question: Adding the Global Gateway and the Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime, von der Leyen’s first Commission is described as a _____ that took a more strategic approach to trade.
cards.answerDate: Sanctions workDecember 2021Defence strategy2024
cards.abstract:
The Geopolitical Commission was the label Ursula von der Leyen gave her first Commission in November 2019. Baracani and Kassim argue that this was a considerable risk, since she took office without the lead-candidate mandate, by a narrow majority and with little EU-level experience, and that the Commission’s powers in foreign policy, defence and security are limited and often indirect. The Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime was set up by a Council decision of 7 December 2020 under Article 29 of the Treaty on European Union, on a proposal from the High Representative. The Global Gateway strategy, launched by the Commission and the High Representative on 1 December 2021, aims to mobilise up to €300 billion in investments between 2021 and 2027. Håkansson judges that the Commission took on a larger geopolitical role than many expected, though it has at times strained relations with other institutions.

The slides use the label for von der Leyen’s first Commission, which added elements such as the Global Gateway and the Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime after the Juncker Commission had taken some important steps, and took a more strategic approach to trade. They list sanctions that the Commission prepared already in December 2021 before taking charge of them, citing Baracani and Kassim 2024, and the first response to Ukraine’s candidacy for enlargement, which the Commission formulated. A second slide names the anti-coercion instrument, the investment screening framework and the Critical Raw Materials regulation, and the slides judge the Commission very successful in extending its influence in security, defence and economic protection. They name Andrius Kubilius as Commissioner for Defence and Space, which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops call a significant institutional innovation that will not give full competence over security and defence soon, since that would need treaty change. Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley report that the Defence Industrial Strategy of 2024 proposed an unprecedented Commission role in defence production, but argue that its centralised defence-industrial network has reinforced the network’s contested nature.

Measures such as the anti-coercion instrument, the investment screening framework and the Critical Raw Materials regulation show how the _____ has extended its influence in security, defence and economic protection.

cards.question: Abbreviated _____, the Commission’s directorate-general for European Neighbourhood and enlargement negotiations is listed among the Commission’s departments with strong external aspects.
cards.abstract:
DG NEAR is the slides’ label for the Commission’s directorate-general for European Neighbourhood and enlargement negotiations, whereas the Commission’s website now names its enlargement department DG ENEST, the Directorate-General for Enlargement and the Eastern Neighbourhood. That page says the department takes forward enlargement and eastern neighbourhood policy, works closely with the European External Action Service and supports accession negotiations as required by the Council. It manages the bulk of the Union’s financial and technical assistance to candidate countries through instruments such as the Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union has an applicant state address the Council, which acts unanimously after consulting the Commission and receiving the consent of the European Parliament. The Commission screens each policy chapter with the candidate and reports to the member states, and no chapter is closed until every government is satisfied with progress as analysed by the Commission.

The slides list DG NEAR among the directorates-general with strong external aspects, next to DG Trade, DG Competition, a new directorate-general for defence industry and space and the service department for Foreign Policy Instruments under the High Representative. They place enlargement and neighbourhood policy among the Commission’s competences under community areas, and the 2010 decision on the EEAS names the neighbourhood instrument but not the pre-accession one among those the High Representative coordinates. On enlargement negotiations the Session 5 slides list the Commission, with DG Near and various other directorates-general, among the institutions involved, beside the Council, the European Parliament and the member states. They add that the Commission leads the process and is also a gatekeeper, in the slides’ phrase a friend who tells the truth, while decision-making is intergovernmental and by unanimity. The steps the slides give to the Commission are an opinion on an application, a questionnaire screening readiness, a draft negotiating framework and a brief opinion on the Treaty of Accession, but each step is named for the Commission and not for DG Near.

cards.question: Handling operational expenditures in crucial areas of EU external action, the _____ is a Commission service department that sits under the High Representative.
cards.abstract:
The Service for Foreign Policy Instruments, FPI, is the Commission department that puts EU foreign policy into action, designing and managing projects with the European External Action Service and other Commission departments. Article 9(6) of the 2010 decision on the EEAS makes actions under the common foreign and security policy budget, public diplomacy and election observation missions the responsibility of the High Representative and the EEAS. It adds that the Commission is responsible for their financial implementation under the High Representative’s authority as Vice-President, through a department co-located with the EEAS. Article 41 of the Treaty on European Union charges the operating expenditure of the common foreign and security policy to the Union budget, except for operations with military or defence implications. The Commission says that the service prepares the budget for each operation, ensures the funding on the basis of the Council legal act and monitors implementation, while the EEAS is responsible for operational planning and policy direction.

The slides describe the service as handling operational expenditures in crucial areas of EU external action. They list it among the parts of the Commission that matter in the common foreign and security policy, next to the President and the directorates-general. On the slide on the Commission’s areas and competences it appears as a service department under the High Representative, in the list of departments with strong external aspects that also names DG NEAR, DG Trade and DG Competition. The Commission’s page lists the High Representative and Vice-President above the service’s Director and Head of Service, and says the service manages funding instruments such as the European Peace Facility. The slides add that the High Representative is also Vice President of the Commission and chairs a monthly meeting of all Commissioners with international issues in their portfolio.

cards.question: Despite having no formal co-decision powers in CFSP, the European Parliament approves association and trade agreements through the _____ and shares co-decision on trade decision-making.
cards.answerDate: Mercosur dealDecember 2024Request to CJEUJanuary 2026
cards.abstract:
The assent procedure is the lecture slides’ name for the European Parliament’s approval of association and trade agreements, which Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union calls consent. Article 218(6) makes the Council’s conclusion of an agreement depend on that consent in listed cases, among them association agreements. Parliament can approve or refuse the negotiated text but cannot amend it, and its consent is sought only at the last stage. Where an agreement relates exclusively to the common foreign and security policy, known as CFSP, Parliament is neither asked for consent nor consulted, although it must be kept informed at every stage. Parliament may also ask the Court of Justice whether an envisaged agreement is compatible with the Treaties, and after an adverse opinion the agreement may not enter into force unless it is amended or the Treaties are revised.

The lecture slides list assent among the Parliament’s powers in external action, beside CFSP budget approval, co-decision in trade, non-legislative resolutions and debates, and the Sakharov Prize. They stress that the Parliament has no formal co-decision powers in CFSP, where the High Representative is to consult it regularly and debates are held twice a year. In enlargement, the slides put the Parliament’s assent after the Commission’s brief opinion and before the Council’s unanimous approval, as Parliament’s own fact sheet does. On the deal with the South American trade bloc Mercosur, concluded in December 2024, the slides give the route as consent by the Parliament and a qualified majority in the Council, and the agreement has since been split into two, signed on 16 January 2026, that each need that consent. On 21 January 2026 the Parliament voted by 334 to 324 to ask the Court of Justice whether the agreements conform with the Treaties, which the slides say effectively paused its consent procedure.

cards.question: Together with the Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime, the _____ is one of the geopolitical elements that the first von der Leyen Commission added to the steps already taken under Juncker.
cards.abstract:
The Global Gateway is the strategy launched on 1 December 2021 by the Commission and the High Representative to boost digital, energy and transport links and strengthen health, education and research systems worldwide. It aims to mobilise up to €300 billion in investment between 2021 and 2027 through a Team Europe approach joining the EU, member states and the European Investment Bank. Its financing was to combine up to €135 billion of guaranteed investment, up to €18 billion in EU grants and up to €145 billion of planned investment by European financial institutions. The Parliament’s research service writes that since 2015 the EU had tried to narrow the global investment gap, not least to counter China’s Belt and Road Initiative, but that experts found its assistance fragmented. Heldt argues that member states agreed on the strategy because of competition with China as an infrastructure lender in Africa, a shift to private investment in development finance and the Commission’s entrepreneurial leadership.

The lecture slides name the Global Gateway as one of the geopolitical elements added by the first von der Leyen Commission, together with the Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime. They present these additions under the label “Geopolitical Commission” and note that the Juncker Commission, which had claimed to lead a ‘political Commission’, had already taken some important steps. The slides list further signs of the Commission’s geopolitical role: a more strategic approach to trade, preparing sanctions on Russia already in December 2021 and formulating the first response to Ukraine’s candidacy for enlargement. The slides say nothing of what the Global Gateway does, so the account of its content above rests on the Commission’s launch text. A later Parliament research paper calls the Global Gateway partly geopolitically motivated despite its development framing, and Parliament’s fact sheet adds that a 2026 resolution urged pursuing it as an alternative to the Belt and Road Initiative.

cards.question: Described as a European Magnitsky act for individual sanctions and passed in 2020, the _____ is counted among the geopolitical elements added by the first von der Leyen Commission.
cards.answerDate: Magnitsky act2020
cards.abstract:
The Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime is a framework adopted by the Council on 7 December 2020 for targeted restrictive measures against serious human rights violations and abuses worldwide. It covers genocide, crimes against humanity and other serious violations such as torture and enforced disappearance, and it can list persons and entities including state and non-state actors. Listed persons face an asset freeze and, if they are individuals, a travel ban, and the Council establishes and amends the list acting by unanimity on a proposal from a member state or the High Representative. Eckes notes that the regime is modelled on the United States Global Magnitsky Act of 2016 and that the Netherlands originally tabled the initiative, in November 2018 according to Portela and her co-authors. In April 2025 the list held 149 entries, 116 individuals and 33 entities.

The lecture slides name the regime as one of the geopolitical elements added by the first von der Leyen Commission, together with the Global Gateway, under the label “Geopolitical Commission”. A slide on strategies and outcomes lists a European Magnitsky act for individual sanctions, passed in 2020, which this card takes to be the regime although the slide does not name it, and notes that some member states contested such sanctions. The slides present the regime as a Commission addition, yet the record shows that the Council adopted it, under the unanimity rule of the common foreign and security policy. The slides blame the delay in adopting sanctions on Belarus after the 2020 protests on voting under unanimity, and the Parliament’s research service confirms that Cyprus threatened a veto on 21 September 2020 over its own proposal on Turkey, agreeing on 2 October. In their reform ideas the slides list sanctions and human rights among decisions proposed for qualified majority voting, and in July 2021 the Parliament, by 584 votes to 73, regretted the Council’s choice of unanimity for this regime.

cards.question: Listed among the trade measures of the Geopolitical Commission, the _____ appears next to the Anti-Coercion Instrument and a corporate sustainability due diligence directive that aims to exclude forced labour.
cards.abstract:
The International Procurement Instrument is Regulation (EU) 2022/1031 of 23 June 2022, which lets the Commission restrict third-country firms’ access to the EU’s public procurement and concession markets. The Commission may open an investigation on its own initiative or on a complaint from a member state or an EU interested party, and must invite the third country to consult. Where a third-country practice seriously impairs the access of EU firms and consultations fail, the Commission may adopt a restrictive measure by implementing act, either a score adjustment on tenders or their exclusion. A measure applies only above thresholds of €15 million for works and concessions and €5 million for goods and services, and expires after five years unless extended. The Commission first proposed such an instrument in March 2012, arguing that more than half of the world’s procurement market was closed through protectionist measures, and Parliament adopted the final text on 9 June 2022.

The lecture slides name the instrument as an example of the trade measures of the Geopolitical Commission, alongside the Anti-Coercion Instrument and a corporate sustainability due diligence directive meant to exclude forced labour. They list a more strategic approach to trade among the signs of that role, and class investment screening as trade defence and the critical raw materials regulation as a measure for open strategic autonomy. In the slides’ table, trade policy follows the Community method of joint decision by Commission, Parliament and Council, and the instrument fits because it rests on Article 207(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and passed the ordinary legislative procedure. The slides say the directive aims to exclude forced labour, whereas Directive (EU) 2024/1760 requires companies to address adverse human rights impacts in their chains of activities, among them forced labour. The ban on products made with forced labour is a separate measure, Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, which applies from 14 December 2027.

cards.question: Next to the International Procurement Instrument and a corporate sustainability due diligence directive, the _____ is listed among the trade measures of the Geopolitical Commission.
cards.abstract:
The Anti-Coercion Instrument is Regulation (EU) 2023/2675 of 22 November 2023, which lets the Union respond when a third country uses trade or investment measures to pressure the EU or a member state. It defines economic coercion as such a measure, applied or threatened to force or stop a particular act by the Union or a member state and so interfere in its sovereign choices. The Commission first examines a case, normally within four months, and then proposes that the Council determine that coercion exists, which the Council does by implementing act, acting by qualified majority. Then the Commission seeks an end to the coercion through consultations and, as a last resort, may adopt response measures such as limits on trade, investment or public procurement. The Commission proposed the instrument on 8 December 2021, describing economic coercion as a practice that undermines the EU’s open strategic autonomy, and the regulation entered into force on 27 December 2023.

The lecture slides name the instrument as one of the trade measures of the Geopolitical Commission, together with the International Procurement Instrument and a corporate sustainability due diligence directive meant to exclude forced labour. The same slide says the Commission has been very successful in expanding EU competence in security, defence and the protection of the EU’s economic interests. The slides list the investment screening framework separately, as a trade defence measure, and the Commission’s page says Regulation (EU) 2019/452 on it has applied fully since 11 October 2020. In the slides’ table, trade policy follows the Community method and qualified majority voting, unlike the unanimity of the common foreign and security policy, known as CFSP, and the instrument fits because it rests on Article 207(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Parliament adopted its first-reading position on 3 October 2023 by 578 votes to 24, as co-legislator with the Council, a role the slides say it lacks in foreign and security policy.

Trade policy follows the Community method and qualified majority voting, and the Commission’s geopolitical trade measures include the _____ and the International Procurement Instrument.

cards.question: Presented as a measure to strengthen the Union’s open strategic autonomy, the _____ is one of the Commission’s geopolitical measures, listed beside trade measures and investment screening.
cards.abstract:
The Critical Raw Materials Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of 11 April 2024, which sets a framework for a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials to the EU. The Commission proposed it on 16 March 2023, noting that the EU relies almost exclusively on imports for many of these materials and that it sourced 97 % of its magnesium in China. Annex I lists 17 strategic raw materials, which the regulation includes in a wider list of critical raw materials that the Commission puts at 34 in 2023, up from 14 in 2011. By 2030 it sets benchmarks of extracting at least 10 %, processing 40 % and recycling 25 % of the EU’s annual consumption of strategic raw materials, with no third country supplying more than 65 % of any one. Its legal basis is Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union on the internal market, and Parliament adopted the text on 12 December 2023 by 549 votes to 43, with 24 abstentions.

The lecture slides list the critical raw materials regulation as a measure to strengthen the EU’s open strategic autonomy, under the heading of the Geopolitical Commission. The regulation’s recitals use the same words, saying that a common framework should safeguard the Union’s economic resilience and open strategic autonomy. The slides class the international procurement and anti-coercion instruments as trade measures and investment screening as trade defence, so the raw materials regulation is the item on that list tied to open strategic autonomy. Elsewhere the slides describe strategic autonomy from 2019 to 2022 as a way to reduce dependence on China in key supply chains, and Michaels and Sus write that from 2020 EU actors added the qualifier open. They add that the Spanish Council Presidency of 2023 took the lead in reviving open strategic autonomy and called for greater EU capacity in energy, digital technology, health and food.

cards.question: Besides non-legislative resolutions and debates, the European Parliament’s activities in external action include the _____, listed beside its approval of the CFSP budget.
cards.abstract:
The Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought is the European Parliament’s annual award to individuals and organisations that defend human rights and fundamental freedoms, given since 1988. It is named for Andrei Sakharov, the Soviet nuclear physicist and dissident who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975. Political groups or at least 40 Members nominate candidates each September, a shortlist of three follows in October and the Conference of Presidents selects the winner. The winner receives €50,000 at a plenary session at the end of the year, when the Parliament usually calls for the release of jailed laureates. The 2025 prize went to the imprisoned journalists Andrzej Poczobut of Belarus and Mzia Amaglobeli of Georgia, and earlier laureates include Nelson Mandela and Alexei Navalny.

The lecture slides list the Sakharov Prize among the Parliament’s activities in external action, with approval of the budget of the common foreign and security policy, known as CFSP, co-decision in trade, assent to association and trade agreements, and resolutions and debates. The slide starts from the point that the Parliament has no formal co-decision powers in CFSP, where the High Representative is to consult it regularly and debates are held twice a year, a contrast with trade, where it adopts framework measures jointly with the Council under Article 207(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Article 36 of the Treaty on European Union supports that description and lets the Parliament put questions and make recommendations to the Council or the High Representative, and its research service adds that it must still be informed of agreements relating exclusively to CFSP. Parliament’s fact sheet adds that it approves the annual CFSP budget except military expenditure under the off-budget European Peace Facility, and that despite its limited formal role it scrutinises the policy and gives strategic input. The human rights fact sheet places the prize beside Parliament’s resolutions, its monthly debates on violations and the Sakharov Prize Network, which supports laureates.

cards.question: Subtitled “The _____”, a research service report of the European Parliament dated 28 August 2023 examined qualified majority voting in the Union’s common foreign and security policy.
cards.answer: Costs of Non-Europe in foreign policy
cards.answerDate: Report28 August 2023Group of FriendsMay 2023
cards.abstract:
The Costs of Non-Europe in foreign policy is the slides’ subtitle for a European Parliamentary Research Service study of 28 August 2023, titled ‘Qualified majority voting in common foreign and security policy: a cost of non-Europe report’. Its authors are Cecilia Navarra and Lenka Jančová of the European Added Value Unit, with Isabelle Ioannides. Cost of non-Europe reports examine where deeper EU integration could bring benefits, and this one looks at decision-making rules rather than at competences. It identifies a ‘cost of unanimity’, meaning the extent to which unanimity contributes to the policy’s challenges, and draws on four case studies on Hong Kong, Belarus, Russia and Kosovo. It assesses 15 alternatives to unanimity, ranging from options within the existing Treaties to Treaty change and a shift to a supranational mode.

The slides list the 2023 report as an additional reference, head a list of qualified majority possibilities with it, calling the list non-exhaustive, and they give reform ideas for moving sanctions, human rights and civilian missions to qualified majority voting, excluding military aspects. The report’s own non-exhaustive box of qualified majority possibilities names Articles 31(2), 41(3) and 46(2) of the Treaty on European Union. Article 31(2) lets the Council act by qualified majority on a decision based on a European Council decision on strategic interests, on a High Representative proposal following a specific European Council request, on a decision implementing an earlier one and on appointing a special representative. Article 41(3) covers the start-up fund for urgent financing of defence initiatives, and Article 46(2) the decision establishing permanent structured cooperation, taken after consulting the High Representative. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops cite the study as Navarra and colleagues, saying it clarified the possibilities of proceeding with less unanimity, next to the Group of Friends on Qualified Majority Voting, launched by nine member states on 4 May 2023 to speed up foreign-policy decision-making.

cards.question: A German proposal in September 2026 to make the External Action Service part of the Commission puts _____ on the table, because it may end the service’s separate existence.
cards.answerDate: Established2010German proposalSeptember 2026Politico report11 September 2026
cards.abstract:
The EEAS reform debate concerns the European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic service, which the slides say was established in 2010. Article 27(3) of the Treaty on European Union provides that the High Representative is assisted by a service of officials from the Council’s General Secretariat and the Commission and of staff seconded from national diplomatic services. Its organisation is left to a Council decision acting on a proposal from the High Representative, after consulting the European Parliament and obtaining the Commission’s consent. Council Decision 2010/427/EU of 26 July 2010 made it a functionally autonomous body under the High Representative’s authority, and the service’s own site dates its work from 2011. Article 13(3) of that decision required a review by mid-2013, after which a report from three research institutes set out options from tidying the text to more ambitious amendment.

According to the slides, it was set up to overcome the artificial separation between the EU’s external economic and foreign policy relations, coordination problems between the Commission and the Council secretariat, and the discontinuity between Council presidencies. They add that all civilian and military crisis management structures were transferred to it from the Council Secretariat, and that it now supports the High Representative, heads the EU delegations and chairs the Political and Security Committee. They say a German proposal in September 2026 to make it part of the Commission may end its separate existence, and they cite Politico of 11 September 2026. Euronews reported on 31 August 2026 a joint Franco-German plan, not a German one alone, that would amend the 2010 decision, while Deyl writes that a qualified majority suffices legally but unanimity is politically advisable. The slides report Kallas defending a shared network of 145 delegations over duplicated national services and quote Andrew Sherriff on unfair blame, while Lehne argued in March 2026 for merging the service into the Commission.

cards.question: Launched in 2017 for member states that want to go further in defence, _____ rests on Articles 42(6) and 46 of the Treaty on European Union and is member state driven and project based.
cards.answerDate: Lisbon Treaty2009Launched2017Project list2018IRIS assessment2026
cards.abstract:
Permanent Structured Cooperation, or PESCO, was established in 2017 as a route for member states that want to go further in defence. Article 42(6) of the Treaty on European Union provides for it among states with higher military capabilities and more binding commitments to one another for the most demanding missions, a possibility that the Lisbon Treaty introduced. The slides say it rests on Articles 42(6) and 46 of the Treaty and on Protocol No. 10, and that it is member state driven and project based. Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2315 of 11 December 2017 established it after notifications from 23 member states on 13 November and two more on 7 December, which made 25 participants. Its annex lists 20 commitments, among them a medium-term rise of defence investment expenditure to 20 per cent of total defence spending as a collective benchmark.

The slides give 25 member states, an initial list of 17 projects adopted in 2018 and more than 70 ongoing projects, while the European Defence Agency reported in May 2025 that all member states except Malta take part and that 75 of 83 projects since 2018 are ongoing. The slides list commitments such as making strategically deployable formations available, overcoming capability shortfalls under the Capability Development Plan and contributing to at least one capability project. They add that the capability targets serve both EU and NATO requirements, and give the EuroDRONE project of France, Germany, Italy and Spain and the airborne electronic attack project as examples. A slide on critical assessments asks whether PESCO delivers at the necessary scale, and reports that the French institute IRIS found in 2026 that of 83 projects only 3 have reached their objectives, while the European Defence Agency counts 66 projects of which almost 50 per cent are in the execution phase. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that progress in substance was much weaker than at the rhetorical level, and Leuprecht and Hofer conclude in 2026 that PESCO still faces significant institutional hurdles.

cards.question: Listed among the EU’s security and defence initiatives beside PESCO, the Coordinated Annual Review on Defence and the Military Planning and Conduct Capability, the _____ is described as the Commission’s own.
cards.abstract:
The European Defence Fund, or EDF, is an EU programme that co-funds collaborative defence research and development, set up by Regulation (EU) 2021/697 of 29 April 2021. The Commission proposed it in June 2018 as one fund that brings together the Preparatory Action on Defence Research and the European Defence Industrial Development Programme. Its general objective is to foster the competitiveness and innovation capacity of the European defence industry, and its development actions aim to reduce duplication and fragmentation. The regulation set the envelope for 2021 to 2027 at €7.953 billion, of which €2.651 billion is for research and €5.302 billion for development, while the Commission now gives nearly €7.3 billion. A project needs a consortium of at least three eligible entities in three different member states or associated countries, and a development action within a PESCO project may receive a funding rate 10 percentage points higher.

The lecture slides list it among the EU’s security and defence initiatives, beside Permanent Structured Cooperation, the Coordinated Annual Review on Defence and the Military Planning and Conduct Capability. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops name it among the innovations between the Global Strategy of 2016 and February 2022, but say these did not amount to a fundamental shift because strategy stayed far ahead of policy realities. Michaels and Sus write that the Fund and the Coordinated Annual Review improved defence-industrial cooperation, but that until February 2022 implementation was rather cumbersome, with insufficient national defence funding a main challenge. Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley call it the Commission’s Fund, say its innovation objectives resemble those of the NATO Innovation Fund, and note that Norway is the only non-member state to take part, though the Commission’s page also names Ukraine as associated. Soler reports Javi López, a vice president of the European Parliament, saying that the nearly €8 billion Fund and the €1.5 billion European Defence Industrial Programme narrow the capability gap, but that investment remains modest relative to the challenge.
