cards.question: Coordinated by Spain, the PESCO project on _____ covers the design, development and testing of a multi-jamming capability, including stand-off, stand-in and escort jamming.
cards.abstract:
Airborne Electronic Attack, or AEA, is one of the two Permanent Structured Cooperation projects that the slides give as examples, the other being EuroDRONE, and the slides say it is coordinated by Spain. In this project electronic attack means jamming, and an EDF fact sheet quoted by Defense News says the system is meant to jam any signals used for targeting European aircraft while disabling adversary electronic-warfare emitters. Defense News describes stand-in jamming as close to hostile air-defence systems, stand-off jamming as long-range jamming outside the weapons-engagement zone, and escort jamming as protecting one’s own forces from enemy air defences. Permanent Structured Cooperation was established by Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2315 of 11 December 2017, and Council Decision (CFSP) 2019/1909 of 12 November 2019 added 13 projects, bringing the list to 47. The 2019 list gives it as number 42 with Spain, France and Sweden as members, and a Commission fact sheet links it to REACT, a design study costing about €14.8 million, coordinated by the Spanish firm Indra.

The slides cite the project’s own description: it is meant to let European and NATO air forces operate safely within EU territories and to be interoperable with the existing and planned assets of the member states and in cross-domain operations. The project covers the design, development and testing of a multi-jamming capability, including stand-off, stand-in and escort jamming, based on existing technological cores at the level of European industries. The slides add that the capability targets of Permanent Structured Cooperation serve both EU and NATO requirements. Withington wrote in 2024 that the project is led by Spain and that the architecture could be fitted inside a combat aircraft or carried in a pod that can be swapped between crewed aircraft and drones. Defense News reported in 2025 that the second phase of REACT received €40 million in EU funding on a total budget of €69.7 million, and that Europe largely depends on the United States for airborne electromagnetic warfare.

cards.question: In a table of actors promoting Russian influence in Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine, the _____ is listed first, with one centre in Belarus, four in Moldova and eleven in Ukraine.
cards.abstract:
The Russkiy Mir Foundation, whose name means ‘Russian World’, was created by a decree of President Vladimir Putin of 21 June 2007. Its founders are the Russian ministries of foreign affairs and of education, and since 2021 its management has been appointed directly by presidential decree. It supports Russian-language teaching, Russian-language media and cultural projects abroad through grants and through its Russian Centres, which numbered 104 in 52 countries at the beginning of 2022. Lutsevych describes the ‘Russian World’ as a flexible tool, first meaning the Russian speakers of the post-Soviet region and the diaspora, and later everyone who feels an affinity with what Russia stands for. The European Parliament’s resolution of 23 November 2016 listed the Foundation among the Russian government’s think tanks and special foundations, next to the agency Rossotrudnichestvo and the television channel RT.

The lecture slides list the Foundation first in a table of actors and channels promoting Russian influence in Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine. The table counts its centres as one in Belarus, four in Moldova and eleven in Ukraine, and the slides add no description of the Foundation itself. Lutsevych found the same weighting, since almost half of the Russian Centres in the Commonwealth of Independent States were in Ukraine, where the Foundation spent about $1 million a year. Further rows of the table list the Rossotrudnichestvo Centre for Science and Culture, students studying in Russia, coordinating councils of Russian compatriots, and Orthodox and youth organisations, under the heading Channels of Russian influence. Lachowicz argues that after 2014 the idea of the Russian world, as the Foundation represents it, became the base of a broadly irredentist foreign policy.

cards.question: In Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine alike, the _____ Centre for Science and Culture is listed among the actors and channels promoting Russian influence, in the row after the Russkiy Mir Foundation centres.
cards.abstract:
Rossotrudnichestvo is the Russian federal agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, compatriots living abroad and international humanitarian cooperation, established in 2008. Lutsevych describes it as an umbrella organisation for a network of Russian compatriots that funds ‘public diplomacy’ projects and runs 60 Russian Centres of Science and Culture and 25 offices in Russian embassies. In 2014 it was officially given a flagship role in developing Russia’s soft power, and its budget rose by 50 per cent to 3 billion roubles, or $95.5 million. A Ukrainian study of 2022 counts at least 97 ‘Russian Houses’ worldwide, says the agency reports directly to the Russian foreign ministry, and names cultural exchange, work with compatriots and humanitarian aid as its three main fields. Moldova’s government says the Russian Cultural Center there, set up in 2009 and funded by Rossotrudnichestvo, served as cover for activities undermining the country’s sovereignty, and in November 2025 its cabinet approved a draft law to denounce the agreement of 1998 behind it.

The lecture slides list the Rossotrudnichestvo Centre for Science and Culture in the column of each of Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine in their table of actors and channels promoting Russian influence. The row sits below the row for the Russkiy Mir Foundation centres, which counts one centre in Belarus, four in Moldova and eleven in Ukraine, whereas the Rossotrudnichestvo row gives no number. The slides print the name as Rosstrudnichestvo and give no description of what the Centre does. After this row the table goes on to list students studying in Russia, coordinating councils of Russian compatriots, and Orthodox and youth organisations. The European Parliament’s resolution of 2016 named Rossotrudnichestvo as a special authority of the Russian government, and Lachowicz calls the Russian Houses it runs the main pillar of Russian-language expansion.

cards.question: A row of the table of actors promoting Russian influence names the _____ in Belarus, in Moldova and, as an All-Ukraine body of organisations, in Ukraine.
cards.abstract:
The Coordinating Councils of Russian Compatriots are country-level bodies for ‘compatriots’, a group that a Ukrainian study defines broadly and rather vaguely as Russian speakers and Russians living outside Russia. Lachowicz dates the turn from an inconsistent diaspora policy to the First World Congress of Russian Compatriots Living Abroad in 2001, attended by President Putin. In 2009 a World Coordinating Council of Russian Compatriots Living Abroad was established, uniting scattered local councils from different countries and formalising their relations with Russian diplomatic missions. Lachowicz lists these councils with Rossotrudnichestvo, Russian cultural centres and the Russkiy Mir Foundation as one network of institutions that work closely with the Federation Council. Lutsevych places associations of compatriots in the second tier of the Kremlin’s system, made up of trusted partners funded by state foundations, presidential grants or loyal companies.

The slides’ table has a row for these councils in each country column, naming a Coordinating Council of Russian Compatriots in Belarus, one in Moldova and, for Ukraine, an All-Ukraine Coordinating Council of Russian Compatriot Organizations. The row comes after the row on students studying in Russia, nearly 25,000 from Belarus, nearly 25,000 from Moldova and nearly 13,000 from Ukraine, and before the row on Orthodox and youth organisations. Lutsevych reports that members of a Coordination Committee of Russian Compatriots in Ukraine were among the main recipients of Russkiy Mir Foundation grants, whose only criterion was that projects be in Russian. Lachowicz records that the Fund to Support and Protect the Rights of Compatriots Living Abroad, called Pravfond, was founded in 2012 by the Russian foreign ministry and Rossotrudnichestvo, and the EU listed it in April 2026 as a core instrument of Russian foreign influence and propaganda. The slides do not use the phrase compatriot policy, and they give no description of what the councils do.

Alongside the Russkiy Mir Foundation centres and the Rossotrudnichestvo Centre for Science and Culture, the table of Russian influence also lists the _____ for each of the three countries.

cards.question: Among the measures listed under the EU’s response, the European Commission’s 2018 _____ follows the Communication on tackling hybrid threats from the High Representative and the EEAS.
cards.answerDate: Action plan2018Council callsOctober 2018
cards.abstract:
The Action Plan against Disinformation is a Joint Communication of the European Commission and the High Representative, adopted on 5 December 2018. It defines disinformation as verifiably false or misleading information spread for economic gain or to deceive the public intentionally, and that may cause public harm. It answers the European Council’s call of 18 October 2018 for measures to “protect the Union’s democratic systems and combat disinformation, including in the context of the upcoming European elections”. Its response rests on four pillars: better detection and exposure by the Union’s institutions, coordinated and joint responses, mobilising the private sector, and raising awareness and societal resilience. It builds on the East StratCom Task Force, set up after the European Council of March 2015 asked for an action plan on strategic communication, and it expected the strategic communication budget to rise from €1.9 million in 2018 to €5 million in 2019.

The lecture slides list it under the heading European Commission, dated 2018, in their account of the EU’s response, after the Communication on tackling hybrid threats and before the East StratCom Task Force. The slides open that list with the European Council’s conclusions of October 2018, which they quote as calling for “measures to protect the Union’s democratic system and combat disinformation”, in the singular where the plan’s own quotation has ‘systems’. The slides list it as a Commission measure, but the plan itself sets out actions for the Commission and the High Representative, with the assistance of the EEAS. The recap at the start of Session 5 says that propaganda and disinformation play an increasing role in forming perceptions, and the Session 2 slides list an EU toolbox against foreign information manipulation and interference among the Strategic Compass measures. The Court of Auditors judged in 2021 that the plan was relevant but incomplete, and Pamment notes that the Rapid Alert System it created is not currently used to its full potential.

cards.question: Part of the EEAS, the _____ is named in the EU’s response beside the hashtag #EUvsDisinfo, after the European Commission’s 2018 Action Plan against Disinformation.
cards.abstract:
The East StratCom Task Force is a unit of the EEAS, the EU’s diplomatic service, set up to address Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns. It followed the European Council meeting of 19 and 20 March 2015, which invited the High Representative to develop an action plan on strategic communication to address Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns. Under the action plan on strategic communication of 22 June 2015, its mandate has three strands: promoting EU policies in the Eastern neighbourhood, strengthening the media environment there, and improving the Union’s capacity to forecast, address and respond to Russian disinformation. At the start it had no resources of its own and was paid from the administrative expenditure of the EEAS and of the Commission’s Service for Foreign Policy Instruments. By December 2018 it had catalogued over 4,500 examples of Russian disinformation, and it received €1.1 million in 2018 and €4 million in 2020.

The lecture slides list the Task Force, which they also call the East Strategic Communication Task Force or EastStratCom, as part of the EEAS in their account of the EU’s response. The slides write the hashtag #EUvsDisinfo beside it, and the next slide is titled EUvsDisinfo, the name of the Task Force’s public campaign and database. It comes last in a list that opens with the European Council’s conclusions of October 2018 and includes the Communication on tackling hybrid threats and the Commission’s Action plan against disinformation, and the slides give it no date and no description of its work. The European Parliament’s resolution of 23 November 2016 called for reinforcing the Strategic Communication Task Force, under the Twitter username @EUvsDisInfo, as an online space with tools for identifying disinformation. The Court of Auditors found in 2021 that the task forces had improved the EU’s capacity to respond to disinformation but were not adequately resourced or evaluated, and Pamment notes that the Task Force attributes pro-Kremlin media with a disclaimer that this does not represent EU policy.

cards.question: Written as a hashtag beside the East Strategic Communication Task Force, _____ is the last name in the list of the EU’s response and then gets a slide to itself.
cards.abstract:
EUvsDisinfo is the flagship project of the East StratCom Task Force of the EEAS, established in 2015 to better forecast, address and respond to Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns. Its core objective is to raise public awareness of the Kremlin’s disinformation operations, using data analysis and media monitoring in 15 languages. Its searchable database held more than 9,700 cases on 1 October 2020 and more than 11,000 in the spring of 2021. Its publications state that they do not represent an official EU position, and a case listed does not necessarily mean that an outlet is linked to the Kremlin. The European Parliament’s resolution of 23 November 2016 called for reinforcing the Strategic Communication Task Force, under the Twitter username @EUvsDisInfo, as an online space with tools for identifying disinformation.

EUvsDisinfo appears in the lecture slides as the hashtag #EUvsDisinfo, written after the East Strategic Communication Task Force, or EastStratCom, which the slides describe as part of the EEAS. Both close the slides’ list of the EU’s response, which also names the European Council’s conclusions of October 2018, the Communication on tackling hybrid threats and the Commission’s Action plan against disinformation of 2018. The slides then give EUvsDisinfo a slide of its own, and the text of that slide is the title alone. The recap at the start of Session 5 lists, as its policy point, that propaganda and disinformation play an increasing role in forming perceptions. The Court of Auditors found in 2021 that EUvsDisinfo had been instrumental in raising awareness of Russian disinformation, but that its hosting by the EEAS raised questions about its independence, since it could be perceived as representing the EU’s official position.

cards.question: Issued by the High Representative and the EEAS, the _____ is listed among the EU’s responses, between the European Council’s October 2018 conclusions and the Commission’s action plan against disinformation.
cards.abstract:
The Communication on tackling hybrid threats is the Joint Communication of 6 April 2016 titled Joint Framework on countering hybrid threats: a European Union response. It describes hybrid threats as a mixture of coercive and subversive activity, with conventional and unconventional methods, that state or non-state actors can pursue while staying below the threshold of formally declared warfare. It followed an invitation from the Foreign Affairs Council of 18 May 2015 to the High Representative to present a joint framework, after the EEAS circulated a food-for-thought paper on the subject that month. It sets out 22 actions, among them an EU Hybrid Fusion Cell inside the EU Intelligence and Situation Centre of the EEAS and a Centre of Excellence for countering hybrid threats. It states that the primary responsibility for countering hybrid threats related to national security and defence lies with the member states, while common threats can be met better by a coordinated EU response.

The lecture slides list the Communication as a measure of the High Representative and the EEAS in their account of the EU’s response, whereas the text itself is a joint document of the Commission and the High Representative. The same list names the European Council’s conclusions of October 2018, the European Commission’s Action plan against disinformation of 2018, and the East Strategic Communication Task Force, part of the EEAS. The slides name the Communication without giving a date or describing its contents. The Session 2 slides on the Strategic Compass of 2022 list EU hybrid rapid response teams to support member states, CSDP missions and partner countries, and say that in the early 1990s border conflicts were expected rather than threats to member states or conventional or hybrid warfare. The Action Plan of 2018 says the Communication set up the Hybrid Fusion Cell and led to the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, and Parliament in November 2016 welcomed it and urged its implementation without delay.

cards.question: Listed as a project of Permanent Structured Cooperation, _____ is a Medium Altitude Long Endurance project of France, Germany, Italy and Spain.
cards.abstract:
EuroDRONE is the slides’ name for the project that the Council’s decisions call European MALE RPAS, or Eurodrone, where MALE stands for Medium Altitude Long Endurance and RPAS for remotely piloted aircraft system. The Council added the project to the list of Permanent Structured Cooperation projects on 19 November 2018, as project 24, with Germany, Czechia, Spain, France and Italy as its members. Permanent Structured Cooperation itself was established by a Council decision of 11 December 2017 among 25 member states, and its governance leaves projects to groups of participating states that agree to undertake them. A Commission fact sheet of 2021 records a direct award under the European Defence Industrial Development Programme for an 18-month design phase costing about €290 million, of which the EU would pay at most about €98 million. On 24 February 2022 the armaments agency OCCAR signed for Germany, France, Italy and Spain a contract with Airbus for the development and manufacture of 20 systems and five years of initial in-service support.

The Session 3 slides give EuroDRONE as one of two examples of Permanent Structured Cooperation projects, a Medium Altitude Long Endurance project of France, Germany, Italy and Spain, beside Airborne electronic attack, coordinated by Spain. The Session 4 slides repeat it as their example of a project, describe it as slow to get going, and place beside it a remark attributed to a French defence committee, “Drone of yesterday we might have tomorrow”. The record fits the slow start, since the industrial contract came more than three years after the Council added the project. The slides name the four states that buy the aircraft through OCCAR, but the Council lists Czechia as a fifth member, and the German defence ministry says the project covers the operation of the system after it enters service. The Session 4 slides call the participating member states driven and project based, and both sets of slides say its capability targets serve EU and NATO requirements alike.

cards.question: Of 83 projects, only 3 have reached their objectives, according to the _____, a 2026 critical look at whether Permanent Structured Cooperation delivers capability increases at the necessary scale.
cards.answerDate: Assessment2026
cards.abstract:
The IRIS assessment of PESCO is, in the lecture slides, a critical assessment of Permanent Structured Cooperation by the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, credited to Maxime Cordet and dated 2026. Permanent Structured Cooperation, known as PESCO, is a framework in which willing member states make binding defence commitments to one another, and Article 46 of the Treaty on European Union governs it. Under Article 46 a state that wishes to take part notifies the Council, which sets up the cooperation and lists the participants by qualified majority, and other decisions are taken by unanimity of the participating states. PESCO was initiated in 2017 and 26 of the 27 member states now take part, Malta having stayed out because of its constitutional neutrality, and the commitments are legally binding. Projects are its working units, and the Parliament’s fact sheet of March 2026 counts 74 under seven headings.

The slides give the IRIS finding as follows: of 83 projects only 3 have reached their objectives, which they set under the question whether PESCO delivers capability increases at the necessary scale. Beside it they place the European Defence Agency’s finding that out of 66 projects almost 50 per cent are in the execution phase, and the Agency’s report of October 2025 adds that some projects should be retired or moved elsewhere. The two figures do not measure the same thing, since one counts projects that have reached their objectives out of 83 and the other projects in the execution phase out of 66, and the slides do not reconcile them. Other counts differ again, since the Session 3 slides give 17 projects in 2018 and more than 70 now, the Agency’s 2026 report covers 74, and a Martens Centre brief of February 2026 assesses 83. The High Representative’s report to the Council in 2024 gave a positive outlook for ongoing projects but said that only half of the 26 meant to deliver results by 2025 were expected to do so.

cards.question: Under the heading TV news, the outline of the channels of Russian influence names the TV news outlet _____ after the items on narratives targeting EaP states and on actors and linkages.
cards.abstract:
RT, which has also been called Russia Today, is a Russian international television network whose first international channel launched in 2005, and it describes itself as publicly financed from the budget of the Russian Federation. Elswah and Howard, who interviewed 23 current and former staff, call it the best-funded formal news organisation working for the Kremlin and, citing earlier reports, put its budget at about $30 million at the start and above $300 million by 2011. They found that Russian senior editors control political content and that the channel’s line turned towards an anti-Western focus after the 2008 conflict in Georgia. In 2017 EUvsDisinfo, the flagship project of the European External Action Service against Kremlin information operations, called RT the Russian authorities’ most expensive international prestige project. Among the sanctions that the Commission lists as adopted following Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine is a prohibition on broadcasting certain Russian state-owned media outlets in the EU, though the overview does not name the outlets.

The slides name RT under the heading TV news, the third item of the outline slide headed Channels of Russian influence. The other two items of that outline are narratives targeting EaP states, and actors and linkages, and the slides give no description of RT beyond its name. The table of actors and channels promoting Russian influence in Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine follows the outline and does not list RT. A 2017 EU-STRAT working paper by Dimitrova and colleagues on Russian soft power in the Eastern Partnership countries notes growing interest in state-owned outlets such as Russia Today and Sputnik, but adds that national and local news reporting may matter just as much. Its monitoring of television news in Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine found that, apart from Russian channels, Russia did not have a more positive image than the EU, which is close to the slides’ report that, not counting Russian channels, TV news in Moldova and Belarus are balanced.

cards.sub: Lecture 4 · The Brussels effect and perceptions

cards.question: Resting on EU market size, the _____ has a de jure aspect, the adoption of EU style regulations by foreign governments, and a de facto aspect, the adoption of standards by companies.
cards.abstract:
The Brussels effect is the European Union’s ability to set rules for global markets on its own, a term that the legal scholar Anu Bradford introduced in a 2012 article. That article argued that the EU can issue regulations that take root in developed and developing markets alike without help from international institutions or other states. Bradford later explained that the power rests on a large, fairly uniform consumer market that companies find hard to avoid, and that being a regulatory power is a conscious state choice. Her 2020 book names five conditions, which are market size, regulatory capacity, stringent standards, inelastic targets and non-divisibility, and one reviewer found it compelling but not entirely robust or scientific. Bendiek and Stuerzer add that exporting norms needs agreement among the member states at home.

The Session 2 slides include the Brussels effect among the labels in their diagram of the evolution of different kinds of EU power. The Session 4 slides base the effect on the size of the EU market and cite Bradford 2020, page 2, for two aspects, the de jure one being the adoption of EU style regulations by foreign governments and the de facto one being the adoption of standards by companies whose incentives EU regulation has changed. For the effect to occur the slides name a large economy with a large market, regulatory capacity and activity, and an institutional architecture linking market size with regulatory influence, and they add that not all areas are subject to it. Under the limits of the effect the slides quote Bradford 2024 on a weakly enforced EU model letting tech companies continue to rule the world, and they list cross issue bargaining, in which EU weakness in defence has led to a less robust response to the Trump administration’s push against regulating big tech in Europe. A CSIS analysis of March 2026 describes Washington as trying to contain the spread of EU digital rules through clauses in its trade agreements.
questions: A large market, regulatory capacity and an institutional architecture linking market size with regulatory influence are conditions for the _____ to occur, though not all areas are subject to it.
Weak enforcement of the EU model and a US push against regulating big tech in Europe are among the limits of the _____, which rests on market size.

cards.sub: Lecture 4 · The Brussels effect and perceptions

cards.question: The Brussels effect’s two aspects, de jure and de facto, are cited to a 2020 work by _____, who is also cited on digital regulation.
cards.abstract:
Anu Bradford is a Finnish-American legal scholar and the Henry L. Moses Professor of Law and International Organization at Columbia Law School. She took degrees at the University of Helsinki and at Harvard Law School, where she earned a doctorate of juridical science in 2007, and she joined the Columbia faculty in 2012. Her fields are European Union law, digital regulation, international trade law and comparative antitrust law. In 2012 she published the article “The Brussels Effect” in the Northwestern University Law Review, arguing that the EU can set rules that reach well beyond its borders, and the term has since spread through academic and political debate. Her book of the same name followed in 2020 and was named one of the best books of that year by Foreign Affairs, and her book Digital Empires followed in 2023.

The Session 4 slides cite Bradford in three places, on the Brussels effect, on digital regulation and in a quotation about enforcement, and they give only her surname. They cite Bradford 2020, page 2, for their statement that the Brussels effect is based on the size of the EU market and has a de jure aspect among foreign governments and a de facto aspect among foreign companies. The slides say that her work on digital regulation identifies three models, those of the US, the EU and China, under the heading of different worlds of regulation, and they name no book for it. Her book Digital Empires compares a market-driven American, a rights-driven European and a state-driven Chinese approach to regulating technology, the same three jurisdictions as in the slides. On the limits of the Brussels effect the slides quote Bradford 2024 as saying that a weakly enforced EU model means that tech companies continue to rule the world, and in a December 2023 interview she said the EU must prove that it can enforce its rules because its record so far leaves much to be desired.

cards.sub: Lecture 4 · The Brussels effect and perceptions

cards.question: Based on the size of the EU market, the _____ is the adoption of EU style regulations by foreign governments, and it is paired with a second, de facto aspect that concerns companies.
cards.abstract:
The de jure Brussels effect occurs when foreign governments adopt EU style regulations, whereas the de facto effect concerns the voluntary choices of companies. Anu Bradford describes it as complementing the de facto effect, in which EU standards spread through market forces alone. In her book, as a reviewer summarises it, companies that have already adjusted to EU rules can press their own governments to adopt the same level of regulation so that they stay competitive at home. The book treats data protection as a case where the de facto effect was followed by a de jure one, food safety as a case where it was not, and aviation emissions as a case where foreign governments changed their laws without companies adapting first. Examples of adoption include China’s Personal Information Protection Law of 2021, which gives GDPR-like protections against private companies, and the Eurasian Economic Union’s adoption of 5,830 product standards identical to those of the EU, according to the cep study of 2026.

The lecture slides define the de jure Brussels effect as the first of two aspects of the Brussels effect, the adoption of EU style regulations by foreign governments. They base the whole effect on the size of the EU market and cite Bradford 2020, page 2, for a two-part account, in which the other aspect is that EU regulation changes the incentives of foreign companies. For the effect to occur at all, the slides name a large economy with a large market, regulatory capacity and activity, and an institutional architecture that links market size with regulatory influence. They add that not all areas are subject to the effect, which also needs stringent standards, inelastic targets for regulation and indivisibility. A CSIS analysis of March 2026 describes Washington as trying to contain the spread of EU digital rules abroad, with Brazil’s digital markets bill of September 2025 among the targets of its pressure.
questions: Where foreign governments adopt EU style regulations, the result is the _____, which differs from the aspect in which foreign companies adopt standards because EU regulation has changed their incentives.
Of the two aspects of the Brussels effect, the _____ is the one in which foreign governments, rather than foreign companies, adopt EU style regulations.

cards.sub: Lecture 4 · The Brussels effect and perceptions

cards.question: Based on the size of the EU market, the _____ is the aspect in which EU regulation changes the incentives of foreign companies and leads to the adoption of standards by companies.
cards.abstract:
The de facto Brussels effect occurs when companies voluntarily comply with EU rules outside the EU, without the countries concerned requiring it. Anu Bradford explains that firms often find it easier to design to EU standards, which are often the strictest in the world, than to run different production for different markets. Siegmann and Anderljung describe the choice as two decisions, whether to stay in the EU market and, if so, whether to offer EU-compliant products everywhere or two different products. Bradford gives the General Data Protection Regulation, the EU’s data protection law, as an example, because its ‘privacy by design’ principle increasingly ensures that products are built to a single standard. A 2026 survey by the Centre for European Policy found that over two-thirds of companies apply EU product standards in third countries, yet it also found that 70 per cent consider the effect a disadvantage because of higher costs and less flexibility.

The lecture slides define the de facto Brussels effect as the aspect in which EU regulation changes the incentives of foreign companies and leads to the adoption of standards by companies. They base the effect as a whole on the size of the EU market and cite Bradford 2020, page 2, for an account in which the other aspect, the de jure one, is the adoption of EU style regulations by foreign governments. Among the things needed for the effect to occur the slides list a large economy with a large market, regulatory capacity and activity, and an institutional architecture that links market size with regulatory influence. They add that inelastic targets for regulation are needed, with consumer markets rather than capital as the example, and that indivisibility is needed too. Under the limits of the effect the slides quote Bradford 2024 as saying that a weakly enforced EU model means that tech companies continue to rule the world, and in 2023 Bradford said that the EU must prove it can enforce its rules.

Of the two aspects of the Brussels effect, the _____ is the one carried out by foreign companies rather than foreign governments, which adopt EU style regulations in the de jure aspect.

cards.sub: Lecture 4 · The Brussels effect and perceptions

cards.question: Even where _____ and activity exist alongside a large market, not all areas are subject to the Brussels effect, which also needs stringent standards, inelastic targets for regulation and indivisibility.
cards.abstract:
Regulatory capacity is a jurisdiction’s expertise and ability to produce well-crafted legislation, ideally earlier than others, and to sanction those who do not comply. Anu Bradford stresses that being a regulatory power is a conscious choice by a state, not something that follows from the size of its market. A 2026 study by the Centre for European Policy attributes the EU’s capacity to extensive regulatory powers gained through treaty changes and the case law of the Court of Justice, and to specialised institutions with the expertise to regulate complex products. The same study adds that capacity is not only the making of rules but also their enforcement, and it notes that breaches of the General Data Protection Regulation can bring fines of up to €20 million or 4 per cent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Siegmann and Anderljung add that capacity includes coherence between the relevant institutions, and that being the first jurisdiction to regulate an issue gives a further advantage.

The lecture slides list regulatory capacity, which they phrase as regulatory capacity and activity, second among the things needed for the Brussels effect to occur. They place it between a large economy with a large market and an institutional architecture that links market size with regulatory influence. The slides add that not all areas are subject to the effect, which also needs stringent standards, inelastic targets for regulation and indivisibility. They cite Bradford 2020, page 2, for their account of a Brussels effect based on the size of the EU market, with a de jure aspect among foreign governments and a de facto aspect among foreign companies, and they do not explain what the capacity consists of. Bendiek and Stuerzer argue that the EU’s capacity also has an internal basis, since political capital built up in consensus-based deliberation makes its positions credible abroad, while Bradford said in 2023 that the EU’s enforcement record leaves much to be desired.
questions: The conditions for the Brussels effect begin with a large economy with a large market, then _____ and activity, and then an institutional architecture linking market size with regulatory influence.

Foreign governments adopting EU style regulations and foreign companies adopting standards are the two aspects of the Brussels effect, which needs, among other things, _____ and activity alongside a large market.

cards.sub: Lecture 4 · The Brussels effect and perceptions

cards.question: Among the conditions for the Brussels effect is the presence of _____ for regulation, with consumer markets, not capital, given as the example.
cards.abstract:
Inelastic targets are one of the five conditions that Anu Bradford sets for the Brussels effect, together with market size, regulatory capacity, stringent standards and non-divisibility. Bradford argues that a jurisdiction can regulate unilaterally only targets that are inelastic, meaning that they cannot move away from its rules. Consumers are her main example, because they are not mobile and companies must follow the rules of the market where they sell. Capital is the contrast, since a reviewer notes that her argument leaves out capital markets, where companies can choose which jurisdiction applies to them, unlike consumer markets. A 2026 study by the Centre for European Policy gives product safety and consumer protection as areas where access to the internal market depends on compliance with EU rules, and company law and tax law as areas where companies have alternatives.

The lecture slides list inelastic targets for regulation among the conditions for the Brussels effect and specify consumer markets, not capital. They first name a large economy with a large market, regulatory capacity and activity, and an institutional architecture that links market size with regulatory influence. They then say that not all areas are subject to the effect, which also needs stringent standards, inelastic targets for regulation and indivisibility. Siegmann and Anderljung treat inelasticity as a feature of demand and supply both inside and outside the EU, so that the market does not shrink when new rules change prices, costs or quality. The slides base the effect on the size of the EU market, with a de jure aspect among foreign governments and a de facto aspect among foreign companies, and they do not define inelastic targets beyond the example of consumer markets.

cards.question: Of the conditions for the Brussels effect, _____ comes last, after stringent standards and inelastic targets for regulation such as consumer markets.
cards.abstract:
Indivisibility, which Anu Bradford calls ‘non-divisibility’, means that a company’s production or conduct cannot be divided between markets, so that it adopts one standard for all of them. Bradford states the test as a comparison: the benefits of adhering to a single standard must exceed the benefits of taking advantage of laxer standards in other markets. She first set out the conditions in a 2012 article, and her 2020 book treats this one under three headings, legal, technical and economic non-divisibility. Patrin’s review adds that Bradford finds it often explains where the effect occurs, as in competition policy, data protection and chemical safety, while in food safety diverging consumer preferences often make products divisible. Siegmann and Anderljung, who apply the framework to artificial intelligence, make the criterion more precise by defining it as the difference in cost between selling one product everywhere and selling a different one in each market.

The lecture slides give indivisibility as the last item on their list of what is needed for the Brussels effect to occur. They place it after stringent standards and inelastic targets for regulation, which they illustrate with consumer markets rather than capital. Bradford’s chapter keeps the same order, with inelastic targets such as consumer markets coming before non-divisibility, because consumers, unlike capital, cannot flee to less regulated jurisdictions. The slides introduce these three conditions with the point that not all areas are subject to the Brussels effect, and they name indivisibility without defining it or giving an example. They base the effect on the size of the EU market, with a de jure aspect among foreign governments and a de facto aspect among foreign companies, and they cite Bradford 2020, page 2, for this account.

cards.question: Work cited under the heading of different worlds of regulation identifies _____, namely the US model, the EU model and the China model.
cards.abstract:
Three models of digital regulation are what Anu Bradford’s book Digital Empires sets out for the United States, China and the European Union. Oxford University Press published it in 2023, and its first part gives one chapter to each model, the American market-driven, the Chinese state-driven and the European rights-driven. Bradford says in an interview that the US model is predominantly market-driven, emphasising free speech and innovation with minimal government interference. She adds that China’s state-driven model uses technology as a tool for political control, while the EU takes a rights-driven approach that puts individual rights and democratic values first, which Finger’s review summarises as regulation that upholds the fundamental rights of individuals. Bendiek and Stuerzer contrast the Brussels effect with the ‘Beijing effect’ of Chinese data governance, which they say works mainly on weaker and dependent actors, and they note that US companies updated their terms of service after the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation.

The lecture slides say that Bradford’s work on digital regulation identifies three models, those of the US, the EU and China, and they place this under the heading of different worlds of regulation. Under the same heading they list the role of values, for example belief in privacy and discomfort with the excessive power of tech giants. Bradford herself names the right to privacy as an example of the values involved and speaks of growing discomfort with the harms linked to the large technology companies. The slides also list diversity inside the EU and among the member states, trade offs in tech regulation and challenges in regulating AI, and they give no detail about the content of the three models. On the limits of the Brussels effect they quote Bradford 2024 as saying that a weakly enforced EU model means that tech companies continue to rule the world, and the Session 1 slides list regulation, including regulation of technology, among the aspects of the EU’s external power.

cards.question: EU weakness in defence has led to a less robust response to the Trump administration’s push against regulating big tech in Europe, an example of _____ among the limits of the Brussels effect.
cards.abstract:
Cross-issue bargaining means exchanging concessions across different policy areas, which economists also call issue linkage. Conconi and Perroni explain that even when issues are not directly interdependent, countries may reach cooperation by trading concessions across policy dimensions where there would otherwise be no scope for mutual gains. Conconi’s later survey notes that international negotiations usually deal with one policy issue at a time, yet there are several examples of linked issues, mostly trade tied to other policies. Scholars disagree on its worth, since some see the joint settlement of several issues as a key instrument for securing agreement, while others say linkage produces symbolic statements and weakens agreements. Bartram and Witney write that the Brussels effect works because it is efficient for businesses to apply European standards internationally.

The slides give cross-issue bargaining as one of the limits of the Brussels effect, with a single example: EU weakness in defence has led to a less robust response to the Trump administration’s push against regulating big tech in Europe. They give no wider definition, and the same slide quotes the statement that the era of the EU being able to offer countries in Africa conditional deals is over. The Session 3 slides describe issue linkage separately, as a strategically used vote under unanimity in foreign policy or related areas, and they do not connect it to cross-issue bargaining. In March 2025 Bartram and Witney wrote that the Trump administration was waging a war on the EU’s extra-territorial regulation of international technology businesses, with tariffs as an important weapon. Lehne wrote in 2026 that the EU’s digital rules had become a prime target and that securing Ukraine had led some Europeans to accept almost any price for continued US engagement, while Bergmann argued in 2025 that dependence on the US through NATO sapped the willingness of European states to back a strong retaliatory move on trade.
questions: Alongside a quotation that the era of conditional deals for countries in Africa is over, the limits of the Brussels effect include _____, illustrated by defence weakness and big tech.
Weakness in one policy area, defence, has weakened the EU’s answer on another, the regulation of big tech in Europe, an example labelled _____ among the limits of the Brussels effect.

cards.question: Whether the EU is perceived as a unitary actor raises the question of its _____, an important question in the scholarly debate on foreign policy.
cards.abstract:
Actorness is the condition of being an actor in international affairs, traced by Pavese and Torney to Sjöstedt’s 1977 view of the European Community as a genuine actor whose degree of actorness varies by issue area. Bretherton and Vogler later argued that it emerges from an ongoing process shaped by opportunity, presence and capability. Jupille and Caporaso measure it by recognition from third parties, authority delegated by member states, autonomy from them and cohesion in policy preferences. Huigens and Niemann applied them to the Group of Eight summits and found the EU’s actorness questionable, with cohesion differing most between contexts. Michaels and Sus report that the first phase of the strategic autonomy debate, from late 1998 to mid-2013, was dominated by an evaluation of the EU’s actorness.

The slides raise the question of the actorness of the EU under the heading asking whether the EU is perceived as a unitary actor, and they call it an important question of the scholarly debate on foreign policy. They set out contradictory views: that the EU is a unitary actor, attributed to Elgström, and that this does not hold in every part of the world, attributed to the Perceptions report of 2015. Elgström’s report found outsiders seeing the EU as one actor at the World Trade Organization and as a ‘monolithic bloc’ in talks on endangered species, and his 2007 article found it a key actor there but not necessarily a leader. In the Eastern partnership study member states dominate news about the EU and in the China study they are prominent, and the TV study behind the first finds news featuring EU member states together outweighing news featuring Russia as a main actor. The slides list EU cohesiveness or lack thereof among the factors affecting perceptions, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops note a finding that the 2022 invasion of Ukraine had limited effects on the EU’s international actorness but a major impact on community building.

cards.question: Studying perceptions of the EU in other parts of the world amounts to _____, since it challenges the EU’s self image as better and different.
cards.abstract:
De-centring the EU is the slides’ name for the effect of studying how others see the Union, which shifts the point of view from the EU to those who watch it. Elgström argued in 2006 that analysing the perceptions of other actors complements studies of EU documents and behaviour, because it shows how the EU is judged as an international actor. He added that others’ views help shape EU identity and roles, and that their expectations influence how far its policies reach. Elgström’s 2007 article tested the picture of the EU as a leading actor in trade talks, drawn by academics and EU representatives, against the views of non-members and found it seen as a key actor but not necessarily a leader. Larsen noted in 2014 that research on the EU as a normative power and on external perceptions had run largely apart for more than a decade, and a 2015 volume examines how the EU is viewed in Eastern Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa.

The slides list de-centring the EU first among the reasons for studying perceptions of the EU in other parts of the world, writing that such study de-centres the EU. They say that it challenges the EU’s self image as better and different and that European political identity is also constructed by interactions with the outside. Two further reasons are a better understanding of how the EU can be more effective and a link between perceptions of legitimacy and distinctiveness and the possibilities to act. The slides quote Elgström 2007b that an actor perceived to be legitimate has to use less tangible power and base its support on normative consent, and cite Larsen 2014 for the point that for the EU to be a normative power the rest of the world should see it as such. Larsen finds only a limited perception of the EU as a normative power, which the slides place in neighbouring countries and in Mexico, the Philippines and Singapore.

cards.question: A 2014 argument by _____ holds that, for the Union to be a normative power, the rest of the world should see it as such.
cards.answerDate: Cited work2014
cards.abstract:
Henrik Larsen is the author of the article The EU as a Normative Power and the Research on External Perceptions: The Missing Link, published in 2014. Manners had proposed in 2002 that the EU is best understood as a ‘normative power Europe’, taking its international pursuit of the abolition of the death penalty as the case study. Larsen starts from the observation that the study of the EU as a normative power and the study of external perceptions had run relatively independently for more than a decade. His argument is that the literature on external perceptions points to a limited but identifiable perception of the EU as a normative power, depending on the geographical area. By comparison, he writes, the image of a powerful economic actor is prevalent, and he asks whether such thin and geographically varied perceptions justify the general label, outlining an agenda of geographical differences and interaction with other sources of power.

The slides cite him as ‘Larsen 2014’ under the heading ‘Is the EU perceived as a normative power?’, and they give the surname and the year only. They credit him with the claim that we need to look at the power of an actor in the context of the meaning in which it is embedded. They credit him with a second claim, that for the EU to be a normative power the rest of the world should see it as such. They credit him with a third, that perceptions of the EU as a normative power are most prominent in the countries neighbouring the EU and a few others: Mexico, the Philippines and Singapore. Elgström’s 2006 report makes a related point, that outsiders’ expectations and perceptions influence the impact of EU foreign policy, and a 2015 volume applies the approach to Eastern Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa.

cards.question: Self-perception, a dynamic shaping of representation through _____, is an individual-level source of citizens’ perceptions, and Chinese views of the EU are often formed through the lens of how people view themselves.
cards.answerDate: Cited study2023
cards.abstract:
Othering is, in Jensen’s definition, a set of discursive processes by which powerful groups define subordinate groups into existence in a reductionist way, ascribing problematic or inferior characteristics to them. Jensen traces the idea to a reading of Hegel in which the self forms by contrast with the other, to de Beauvoir on women and to Said on the Orient. Spivak first used the notion systematically in 1985, in an essay on British colonial archives in India, and Lister, whom Jensen quotes, describes it as drawing a line between ‘us’ and ‘them’. In European Union studies, Elgström argued in 2006 that others’ views help shape EU identity and roles, which form through interaction between its own role conceptions and the expectations of others. Others also build representations of the EU, as Toshkov, Mazepus and Dimitrova note of Kremlin narratives that depict it as an aggressive enemy, a weak union and one lacking moral values.

The slides describe self-perception as a dynamic shaping of representation through ‘othering’ and credit this to Woo, Dong and Kübler 2023, under the individual level of where citizens’ perceptions come from. That level also lists characteristics such as age, education and language and interactions such as travel, meetings and business, while the societal level lists bilateral relations, economic interdependence, the political system and cues by elites. On the slide about Chinese perceptions in 2011, they report Wang’s argument of 2009, quoted in Woo, Dong and Kübler 2023, that because Chinese understanding of the EU is limited compared with that of the US, perceptions are often formed through the lens of how the Chinese view themselves. The slides do not define othering beyond this, and unlike Jensen’s definition they do not describe it as ascribing inferior traits. Outsiders’ pictures can differ from the EU’s own, as Elgström found non-members seeing it as a key trade actor but not necessarily a leader and Fox and Godement argued in 2009 that China was exploiting EU divisions.

cards.question: In _____, a country’s self-image and how assertive it is make a difference to how it sees the EU, as in the cases of China, Russia and Brazil.
cards.answerDate: Chinese findings2011Perceptions report2015
cards.abstract:
Relational perception is the slides’ idea that how a country sees the EU depends on the viewer’s own self-image and assertiveness as well as on the EU itself. Power is relational in Nye’s definition, the ability to affect others to get the outcomes one prefers, and soft power does so by attraction rather than coercion or payment. Nye adds that Chinese leaders saw soft power as a way to make growing hard power more acceptable to neighbours, who might otherwise form balancing coalitions. Elgström’s role theory makes a similar point for the EU, since foreign policy roles arise from continuous interaction between its own role conceptions and the expectations of others. Toshkov, Mazepus and Dimitrova find in Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine that national channels portray the EU no worse than Russia, while adding Russian channels makes news largely positive about Russia and more likely negative about the EU.

The slides call this relational effects: a country’s self-image and how assertive it is make a difference to how it perceives the EU, as in China, Russia and Brazil. They add a contrast between global and moderately important powers, with a stable image of the EU in the moderate ones, citing a 2015 Perceptions report. On the slide about Chinese perceptions in 2011 they mark the findings ‘But: relational’ and quote Wang 2009, cited in Woo, Dong and Kübler 2023, that limited Chinese understanding of the EU compared with the US means perceptions are often formed through the lens of how the Chinese view themselves. For 2020 they quote Woo, Dong and Kübler on a reconstructed image of the EU suffering a declining global status, especially against the augmented self-image of the Chinese, and Fox and Godement argued in 2009 that China was exploiting EU divisions. The opening of Session 5 lists a relational theory of perceptions as last time’s theory, and a Session 2 slide citing Nye 2021 calls soft power relational and dependent on the minds of audiences.

Chinese views of the EU in 2011 were often formed through the lens of self-image because understanding of the EU was limited, an instance of _____ in studies of perceptions.

cards.question: Under the heading of history, the way outsiders perceive the EU is said to be shaped by an influential factor, _____, alongside culture, education and information.
cards.answerDate: Report cited2015
cards.abstract:
The colonial legacy of European states is the remembered history of empire that colours how people in former colonies see Europe and, by extension, the European Union. The European Commission’s perception study of 2015 found that research across countries treats historical ties as important factors shaping how citizens abroad view EU policies. It reports that the colonial past of European states causes resentment among the general public in Asian and African countries, where the EU is often accused of a civilising agenda that lacks respect for other countries’ goals. The same study names culture and education as further influences, since a lack of knowledge of the EU breeds a sense that its decisions are opaque, while studying in the EU helps build a positive image. The effect is not uniform, because the 2021 update finds that European colonialism weighs on views of the EU in Nigeria, South Africa and Brazil but not in Indonesia.

The lecture slides name colonial legacy as an influential factor listed under ‘History’ on the slide headed ‘Political system and history’, with culture, education and information as the other factors. They cite pages 54 and 55 of a 2015 Perceptions report for this list, and the Commission’s perception study of that year names the same three influences of historical ties, culture and education. On the same slide the political system is said to influence how the EU is portrayed, and media in systems that circulate realist and power concepts are said not to portray it as a normative power, with China and the US as examples. A Chinese survey of 2010 illustrates the other factors, since few respondents had visited EU countries, television was the main source of information about the EU, and only 9 per cent knew that it had 27 member states. The slide gives colonial legacy no example of its own, whereas Toshkov, Mazepus and Dimitrova found that Moldovan TV news gave Russia substantial coverage in items on history and commemorations.
questions: Beyond the political system and informational monopolies, a country’s history can colour how it sees the EU, with _____ singled out as influential.
Culture, education and information are ‘other factors’, but _____ is the historical factor singled out as influential in how people outside the EU perceive it.

cards.question: Alongside colonial legacy, culture and education, the existence of an _____ in certain political systems is said to make a difference to how the EU is portrayed.
cards.answerDate: Report cited2015
cards.abstract:
Informational monopolies arise where those in power control the main channels of news, a feature that Guriev and Treisman place at the centre of modern authoritarian rule. They argue that such regimes rely less on mass repression and more on propaganda, and on silencing informed elites through co-optation or censorship. Television is the channel at issue in the EU’s eastern neighbourhood, where a monitoring of 2015 called it the most efficient method of influencing public opinion in the Eastern Partnership countries. The same monitoring found that the main Russian channels, which are freely available in Armenia, Belarus and Moldova, offered an exceptionally limited range of political actors. It also found that the state of media freedom in Belarus and Armenia stopped national broadcasters from serving as an alternative to Russian propaganda.

The lecture slides list informational monopolies in certain political systems among the factors that make a difference to how the EU is perceived, on the slide headed ‘Political system and history’. On that slide media in political systems that circulate realist and power concepts are said not to portray the EU as a normative power, with China and the US as the examples. At the societal level the slides list cues by elites, via education or media, among the sources of citizens’ perceptions, and a Chinese survey of 2010 found television the most important source of information about the EU. The Commission’s perception study of 2015 reports that countries which did not regard themselves as democracies were not aware of the EU as a normative power or leader, citing Vietnam and the Pacific states. The slides give no definition or example of an informational monopoly, but Toshkov, Mazepus and Dimitrova link the more positive Belarusian coverage of Russia to media freedom limits that bring channels closer to transmission belts for official views.

cards.question: In China, the geopolitical context shapes perceptions of the EU through its role as a _____, while nine out of ten countries covered find it a desirable partner.
cards.answerDate: Chinese findings2011Later findings2020
cards.abstract:
A counterweight to the United States is a power that others hope will balance American dominance, a role that the Commission’s perception study of 2015 found Mexico, Japan and Brazil attributing to the EU. For China the same study records the EU as an important strategic partner in pursuing peaceful development and multipolarity, though only one great power among many. It adds that the Chinese viewed the EU more favourably than the US, Japan and Russia and as a unitary actor, but not as a major security actor. A Nottingham survey of 3,019 urban residents in six Chinese cities in 2010 found favourable impressions of the EU and Russia at 74 per cent, the US at 60 and Japan at 38. Yet the project’s own report says that the public still saw the US as the most influential actor politically and economically and placed China ahead of the EU.

The lecture slides give the role of the EU as a counterweight to the US as the Chinese example of how the geopolitical context shapes public perceptions of the EU. On the same slide societies place the EU’s role as a partner in their own context, and nine out of ten countries covered find it a desirable partner and leader in world affairs, with Russia the exception. The 2021 update is more guarded, finding the EU seen as benevolent but less potent than other global actors, with Chinese, Russian and American publics seeing their own country as the most likely and desirable leader. The slides quote Woo, Dong and Kübler, who compared surveys of 3,000 Chinese citizens in 2010 and 2020, on a dip from 71.7 to 44.2 per cent for the USA as most influential and a rise from 4 to 14.1 for the EU. The slides do not tie these figures to the counterweight role, and the 2021 update finds Chinese experts and focus groups describing the EU as following the lead of the US.

Societies place the EU’s role as a partner in their own context, depending on whether it resonates with local reality, as with its role as a _____ in China.

cards.question: A 2023 study in Comparative European Politics of survey data from Chinese urban residents, by _____, reports a consistent decrease across the board in viewing the EU’s role positively.
cards.answerDate: Published2023Earlier findings2011Comparison2010 to 2020
cards.abstract:
Woo, Dong and Kübler are Su Yun Woo, Lisheng Dong and Daniel Kübler, who published their study in Comparative European Politics 21, issue 5, in 2023. Their article starts from the observation that China–EU relations have become more challenging, with China being labelled a ‘systemic rival’, and asks whether Chinese perceptions of the EU have changed. It compares original surveys of 3000 Chinese citizens in six major cities, conducted in 2010 and in 2020. The authors find that respondents are reconstructing the image of the EU and reconsidering its global role, while the overall assessment of China–EU relations remains one of general goodwill. The 2010 wave resembles the Nottingham-led survey of 3,019 urban residents in six cities, which found 74 per cent favourable to the EU and only 9 per cent aware that it had 27 member states.

The lecture slides quote the article on a consistent decrease across the board in viewing the EU’s role positively, with the most significant drops for the international economy, from 75.4 per cent in 2010 to 58.1 in 2020, and for fighting poverty, from 62.2 to 37.8. They quote a considerable increase, from 4 to 14.1 per cent, in Chinese citizens who now see the EU as the most influential in world politics, and a big dip, from 71.7 to 44.2, for the USA. A further quotation reads this as a reconstructed image of the EU suffering from declining global status, with knowledge of its membership up from 9.3 to 38.7 per cent. For 2011 the slides list findings that knowledge of the EU was limited except among elites, and the project’s report adds that the more people knew about the EU the more positively they viewed it. The Commission’s 2021 update likewise finds the EU’s image in China deteriorated considerably since 2015, while the slides also quote the article, citing Campbell 2020, on bots creating 37 per cent of the Italian gratitude hashtags.

cards.question: Credited with boosting the Chinese government’s credibility while generating goodwill toward Italy among Chinese people, _____ accounted for 37 per cent of the hashtags expressing Italian gratitude toward China.
cards.answerDate: Research cited2020Quoted in2023
cards.abstract:
Bot-generated hashtags are hashtags pushed by automated accounts rather than by people, and an Italian analysis of March 2020 found bots behind 46.3 per cent of the tweets with #forzaCinaeItalia. The same analysis by Alkemy’s R&D Lab, which examined 47,821 tweets between 11 and 23 March 2020, put the bot share of tweets with #grazieCina at 37.1 per cent. The Chinese embassy in Rome had greeted an aid mission with #forzaCinaeItalia on 11 March, and the DFRLab counted over 60 million Twitter impressions for the hashtag by 3 April. The DFRLab also found that three versions of a video of Italians supposedly thanking China were filmed in one Rome location with the same audio, and that Chinese state media and officials amplified them. The European External Action Service’s report of April 2020 noted a bot network in Italy that amplified Chinese embassy messages and attacked the EU, while an SWG poll showed more Italians seeing China as friendly and less trust in EU institutions.

Under the heading ‘But there is also manipulation’, the slides quote Woo, Dong and Kübler 2023, who cite Campbell 2020, on research finding that bots created 37 per cent of the hashtags expressing Italian gratitude toward China. The quotation says this boosted the Chinese government’s credibility and generated goodwill toward Italy among the Chinese people, who appreciated the gratitude supposedly expressed by Italy. It adds that although this pertained to Italy, it may very well extend to the EU as well, in an article whose surveys of 3000 Chinese citizens in 2010 and 2020 ask whether the EU’s image has changed. The closest figure in the Italian analysis is 37.1 per cent of tweets with #grazieCina, which suggests that the slides’ figure counts tweets rather than hashtags, though Campbell 2020 could not be checked. The slide follows the findings on Chinese perceptions of the EU, and the opening slide of Session 5 recaps that propaganda and disinformation play an increasing role in forming perceptions.

cards.question: In the scholarly debate on the actorness of the EU in foreign policy, one view holds it to be a _____, though a 2015 report says it is not seen so everywhere.
cards.answerDate: Chinese findings2011Report cited2015
cards.abstract:
A unitary actor is an organisation that acts as one body in world affairs, and the Commission’s perception study of 2015 ties this to ‘actorness’, whether the EU is perceived as active and its actions as cohesive. In law the Union has one voice to point to, since Article 47 of the Treaty on European Union gives it legal personality and Article 27 has the High Representative represent it on foreign and security policy. The perception study found a strong propensity in China to view the EU as a unitary actor and an active player in world affairs. Across countries, however, it found the EU often overshadowed by its member states, with publics in the United States, Brazil and Australia seeing their actorness as equally important. The 2021 update adds that Russian experts see Poland and the Baltic states as spoilers of EU–Russia relations.

The lecture slides ask whether the EU is perceived as a unitary actor and say that its actorness has been an important question in the scholarly debate on foreign policy. They set out contradictory views, that the EU is a unitary actor, credited to Elgström, and that a 2015 Perceptions report says it is not seen so in every part of the world. They give two studies from outside the EU, an Eastern Partnership study cited as EU-STRAT, which finds that member states dominate news about the EU, and a China study, which finds that member states are prominent. Toshkov, Mazepus and Dimitrova coded TV news in Belarus, Moldova and Ukraine and found Russia a main actor in 30 to 37 per cent of items, more than the EU but less than the EU’s member states combined. For China in 2011 the slides list an image of the EU dominated by perceptions of France, the UK and Germany, and elsewhere they list EU cohesiveness, or the lack of it, among the factors affecting perceptions.

cards.question: Covering February 2023 to May 2025, the _____ found 72 per cent of Ukrainians with a positive image of the EU, against 49 per cent in 2016.
cards.answerDate: SurveysFebruary 2023 to May 2025Comparison2016
cards.abstract:
The EU Neighbours East opinion surveys are annual face-to-face polls of about 1,000 people in each Eastern Partnership country, run by the EU NEIGHBOURS east programme and tracking attitudes since 2016. In 2017 the programme worked with the polling firm ACT LLC and found a positive image of the EU among 44 per cent across the six countries, with Georgia highest at 59 per cent. The countries polled belong to the Eastern Partnership, launched in 2009 as the eastern dimension of the European Neighbourhood Policy, from which Belarus suspended its participation in 2021. The wave of January and February 2026, released on 18 June 2026, found 82 per cent of Ukrainians calling relations with the EU good, 21 points up since 2016, and trust in the EU at 82 per cent. In the same wave 62 per cent of Azerbaijanis called relations good but only 22 per cent had a positive image of the EU, while Georgians’ trust in it stood at 67 per cent.

The lecture slides report survey figures under the heading ‘Eastern neighbours’ perceptions of the EU’, with the period February 2023 to May 2025, and give a page on euneighbourseast.eu as their source. The slide sets two columns of figures side by side for Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, and its text does not say which column belongs to which date. One column gives Azerbaijan 61 per cent with a positive image against 27 per cent in 2016, Georgia 54 per cent with the EU the most trusted organisation at 78, and Ukraine 72 per cent against 49 in 2016. The other gives Armenia 69 per cent trusting the EU, Georgia 67 and 74 per cent who would vote for membership, Moldova 71 and 63, and Ukraine trust at 76 and 70 per cent who would vote to join. The opening of Session 5 recaps that the EU’s soft power is mostly evident in its neighbourhood, based on recent polls.

cards.question: In 2016, a _____ of Belarus, Ukraine and Moldova covered 607 news broadcasts, 377 hours and 1,805 news items to see how the EU and Russia were portrayed.
cards.answerDate: Analysis2016
cards.abstract:
TV news monitoring records bulletins and codes each item by topic, tone and source, as the Leiden study did for items in Belarus, Ukraine and Moldova mentioning Russia, the EU or its member states. Its authors noted that Russian outlets such as Russia Today and Sputnik had drawn attention while national TV news was less understood, and the work was supported by the project EU-STRAT. They watched the main evening bulletins of seven channels for four months and coded 607 broadcasts, 377 hours and 1,805 news items, of which 55 per cent carried no tone. A monitoring of eight Russian channels in March 2015 found them used as instruments of propaganda over Ukraine, while national broadcasters in Georgia, Ukraine and Moldova strove for an alternative. The EU had already acted, as the European Council of March 2015 stressed the need to challenge Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns, and its EUvsDisinfo site summarised pro-Kremlin portrayals of the EU as aggressive, collapsing and decadent.

The slides describe a TV news monitoring in Belarus, Ukraine and Moldova dated 2016, whereas the paper’s coding ran from 16 January to 15 May 2017. The slides say it asked what TV news say about the EU and Russia, in what tone and on which topics, with the same totals of 607 broadcasts, 377 hours and 1,805 items. They label Belarus 1, ONT and First National TV as state channels, 1+1 TV, Prime TV and Pro TV Chisinau as private and Moldova 1 as state, which the paper’s table confirms. The slides give four key findings, the first that a large portion of domestic, non-Russian TV news items has no tone, the second that Belarusian channels cover Russia more positively and Ukrainian channels almost entirely negatively. The third finding is that, not counting Russian channels, TV news in Moldova and Belarus are balanced, and the fourth that EU member states receive substantial coverage next to the EU, together more than Russia and the EaEU.

cards.question: Interactions through which the Union works with actors next to governments to support reform and adjustment, relying mainly on conditionality, are known as _____ in the context of accession.
cards.abstract:
Enlargement governance is the name the lecture slides give to the way the Union interacts with actors next to governments to support reform and adjustment in states that wish to join. Scholars place it within external governance, described by Lavenex and Schimmelfennig as the extension of the Union’s rules and policies beyond its formal members. They call enlargement the most prominent case of external action projecting the acquis, the Union’s body of law, and note that the Commission rated it the Union’s most successful foreign policy. Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier write that the candidates’ wish to join and the intrusiveness of the rules attached to membership gave the Union unprecedented influence over their domestic institutions and policies. They find that the Union used conditionality, setting rules as conditions for rewards up to full membership, and that for the acquis the credibility of the membership promise mattered most.

The slides of Session 6 define enlargement governance as the interactions between candidate states and a variety of EU actors and institutions at different levels, and list enlargement and the European neighbourhood policy as examples of the hierarchical mode of external governance. The slides name EU conditionality as the main tool, relying on the credibility of threats and promises of accession, with capacity building as another, and the Commission’s 2020 communication calls conditionality the core element of the process. They say these interactions ensure success in reform and that the strength of domestic civil society and its key norms can help, and the Commission’s guidelines treat civil society as an essential player in the enlargement agenda. They add that economic support is enhanced by investment in anticipation of accession and that enlargement leads to some economic convergence, which Kok’s 2003 report called a long-term process of decades. A critical assessment on the slides says enlargement extends the EU’s regulatory framework beyond its borders, which is by definition external governance, and one slide calls it challenged by a Chinese ‘systemic rival’ in the Balkans.
questions: Conditionality, capacity building and investment in anticipation of accession are the features of _____, where the strength of domestic civil society and its norms can help reforms in candidate states succeed.

Defined as the interactions between candidate states and a variety of EU actors and institutions at different levels, _____ supports reform and adjustment alongside the governments of the candidates themselves.

cards.question: Stable institutions guaranteeing democracy and the rule of law, a functioning market economy and the ability to take on the obligations of membership make up the _____ for accession set in June 1993.
cards.answerDate: Set outJune 1993
cards.abstract:
The Copenhagen criteria are the conditions for membership that the Copenhagen European Council set out on 21 and 22 June 1993 for the associated countries of Central and Eastern Europe. The European Council agreed that these countries could join as soon as each could assume the obligations of membership by satisfying the economic and political conditions. The text asks for stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities, a functioning market economy able to cope with competitive pressure within the Union, and the ability to take on the obligations of membership. It adds that the Union’s capacity to absorb new members while maintaining the momentum of integration is also an important consideration. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union lets any European state that respects the Union’s values and is committed to promoting them apply, and says the conditions of eligibility agreed by the European Council shall be taken into account.

The Commission now groups the criteria as political, economic, and the administrative and institutional capacity to implement the acquis, the Union’s body of law, and says the Union reserves the right to decide when a candidate has met them. On the slides the first criterion reads as democracy, the rule of law, and respect for and protection of minorities, while the Copenhagen text also names human rights. The slides list explicit criteria among the features of the enlargement to the East of 2004 to 2007 and say negotiations between governments mainly concern how candidates will comply with the criteria and adopt the acquis. They also list reforms to fulfil the accession criteria as part of the second important component of enlargement. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the criteria were introduced to clarify and supplement existing treaty provisions on membership, while Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier distinguish democratic conditionality from acquis conditionality, which concerns the specific rules.
