cards.question: The EU’s main tool for encouraging candidates to adopt its rules and norms, which relies on the credibility of its threats and promises of accession, is _____, backed by regular reports and safeguard clauses.
cards.abstract:
Conditionality is the practice of setting the Union’s rules as conditions for rewards, which for candidates range from trade and association agreements to full membership. Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier describe its logic as reinforcement by reward, in which the Union pays the reward if the government complies and withholds it if not. The European Council used the idea at Copenhagen in 1993, saying that accession would follow once an associated country met the conditions and that it would follow progress closely and draw the appropriate conclusions. Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier add that threats are credible only if the Union has superior bargaining power, and that interdependence was highly asymmetrical in its favour. In April 2008 Olli Rehn described the renewed consensus on enlargement of December 2006 as resting on consolidation, conditionality and communication, and said progress depends on how and when countries meet the conditions.

The slides name conditionality as the main tool of enlargement governance, relying on the credibility of threats and promises of accession, and say the approach was technocratic until 2020 and then became more political. The slides of Session 2 list it first among three ways of exercising transformative power, with capacity building and socialisation, a power that depends on candidates having a membership perspective. A slide titled conditionality, monitoring, money lists regular reports, which it gives as the Commission’s yearly assessment, with rule of law reporting, ad hoc monitoring reports and safeguard clauses that can remain up to three years after accession. The Commission’s 2020 communication calls conditionality the core element of the merit-based accession process, promising increased funding for reform, while the slide lists the Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans and the Ukraine facility as money. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that in the 1990s and early 2000s the Union developed conditionality with regular reports, monitoring missions and suspension clauses, which reinforced the asymmetry of the negotiations, and the slides list reform driven by conditionality versus rent seeking among the dilemmas.
questions: Along with capacity building and socialisation, _____ is one of the ways in which the Union’s transformative power is exercised on candidates that have a membership perspective.

Developed in the 1990s and early 2000s, with regular reports, monitoring missions and suspension clauses, _____ reinforced the asymmetric character of the negotiations between the Union and the candidate states.

cards.question: Candidate states must adopt the EU’s rules, policies and case law, known as the _____, which the negotiations divide into chapters that are nowadays united in six clusters.
cards.abstract:
The acquis communautaire, which the slides call simply the acquis, is the body of EU rules, policies and case law that candidate states adopt. The Commission defines it as the body of common rights and obligations binding on all member states, including the Treaties, legislation under them and Court of Justice case law, which candidates must accept before they join. Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier call the demand for its adoption acquis conditionality, which began with alignment programmes such as the 1995 White Paper and was most pronounced once accession negotiations began in 1998 and 2000. They call the new members’ adoption of the acquis an astonishing achievement, but warn that often it meant formal transposition while implementation lagged. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the revised approach of 2020 used clusters instead of chapters to speed up the negotiations and stressed the rule of law, good governance and anti-corruption as the fundamentals.

The slides say negotiations take place between governments, mainly about how candidates will comply with the Copenhagen criteria and adopt the acquis, and that a draft Treaty of Accession is agreed when all chapters have been opened and closed. They divide the rules into chapters, nowadays united in six clusters, and date both from 2020, while the Commission proposed on 5 February 2020 to organise the negotiating chapters into thematic clusters. The slides list 33 chapters, beginning with free movement of goods, while the Commission counts 35, of which chapters 34, institutions, and 35, other issues, are handled apart from the clusters. The six clusters are fundamentals, internal market, competitiveness and inclusive growth, green agenda and sustainable connectivity, resources, agriculture and cohesion, and external relations, and the fundamentals open first and close last, setting the overall pace. The slides of Session 6 add that Switzerland takes over the acquis in the areas covered by its EU agreements and contributes to the EU cohesion fund, a case of what Lavenex and Schimmelfennig call negotiated bilateralism.

cards.question: In 2004 ten states, among them Poland, Hungary, Cyprus and Malta, joined the Union, and Bulgaria and Romania followed in 2007, together forming the so-called _____, which demanded extensive adjustments from the Union.
cards.answerDate: Ten states2004Two more states2007
cards.abstract:
The big bang enlargement is the phrase the slides use, in inverted commas, for the enlargement of the EU to the East, which they date to 2004 to 2007. Its starting point was the Copenhagen European Council of June 1993, which agreed that the associated countries of Central and Eastern Europe that so desired shall become members once they met the conditions. Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier date the start of accession negotiations to 1998 and 2000, and found that the credibility of the membership promise rose once the talks started. Ten countries joined on 1 May 2004, taking the Union from 15 to 25 members, and Bulgaria and Romania followed on 1 January 2007, bringing it to 27. Kok’s report of March 2003 called the accession of the ten only a stage in a process that began more than a decade earlier and would continue for many years.

The slides say the biggest changes to the method of enlargement took place in the 1990s to prepare for it, bringing changed principles, more institutional and policy reform in advance, explicit criteria and a more profound adaptation of candidates. On their list, ten states joined in 2004, the Czech Republic, Cyprus, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia, then Bulgaria and Romania in 2007 and Croatia in 2013. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that it demanded the most extensive adjustments from the Union, and that despite the complexity of preparing 12 new member states, most of them not market economies at the start, it was viewed as a success. Kok judged large-scale migration unlikely, although present members could restrict labour inflow from Central and Eastern Europe for up to seven years, and in April 2008 Rehn said that trade between old and new members had quadrupled and migration had been rather limited. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops add that enlargement fatigue appeared before it was complete, as increased labour mobility affected public opinion in the older member states.

cards.question: A quotation from a March 2003 report to the European Commission by _____ calls enlargement the most ambitious project the Union is undertaking and the reunification of the European continent.
cards.answerDate: ReportMarch 2003
cards.abstract:
Wim Kok was Prime Minister of the Netherlands from 1994 to 2002, after leading the Dutch trade union federation and serving as finance minister. Commission President Romano Prodi invited him to report on enlargement by the end of March 2003, and Kok consulted experts, civil society groups and the future member countries. The report, titled Enlarging the European Union: Achievements and Challenges, is dated 26 March 2003 and was published by the Robert Schuman Centre at the European University Institute. Kok wrote that it aimed to answer citizens’ questions as ten new members prepared to join on 1 May 2004, and to set out the obstacles, costs and risks as well as the benefits. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on the day of its release that Kok said the benefits of enlargement far outweighed the costs, with Prodi as co-sponsor.

The slides name Wim Kok as the source of a quotation from a report to the European Commission of March 2003, placed on the slide on the enlargement to the East of 2004 to 2007 beside a list of what changed. The slides quote it as calling enlargement the most ambitious project the EU is undertaking and, in fact, the reunification of the European continent, divided in the aftermath of the last world war, where the report itself says ‘in effect’. The report names peace and stability on a European scale as the main benefit of enlargement, and the Copenhagen conclusions of 1993 had already tied peace and security in Europe to the success of Central and Eastern European reforms. It adds that earlier enlargements took place in a divided Europe, but this one helps to achieve the founding fathers’ dream of a Europe whole and free. The Union’s history page says the split between Eastern and Western Europe was healed in 2004, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops note that the EU spoke of uniting the continent earlier and that post-2022 arguments build on such statements.

cards.question: Quoted on a slide about the EU’s power of attraction as an anchor of stability, _____ is credited with a 2008 line that enlargement policy is the Union’s most important foreign policy tool.
cards.answerDate: Quoted2008
cards.abstract:
Olli Rehn is a Finnish politician who was the European Commissioner for enlargement from 2004 to 2010 and for economic and monetary affairs from 2010 to 2014. He holds a doctorate in international political economy from the University of Oxford, awarded in 1996, and has been Governor of the Bank of Finland since 12 July 2018. On 22 January 2008, in a speech titled ‘What’s the future for EU enlargement?’ to an AmCham EU luncheon, he called enlargement ‘our most powerful foreign policy tool’ and a vital part of the EU’s external policies. On 8 April 2008 he said that enlargement policy ‘has been called the EU’s most successful foreign policy tool’, and he described the renewed consensus of December 2006 as resting on consolidation, conditionality and communication. Lavenex and Schimmelfennig also write of enlargement as the EU’s most successful foreign policy ‘according to the European Commission’, citing a Commission text of 2003.

The slides of Session 2 quote the line as Rehn 2008, saying that enlargement policy is the EU’s most important foreign policy tool. The quotation closes a slide headed transformative power, which describes the power of attraction as an anchor for stability, an EU model that guided political transformations in CEE in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and the adoption of the acquis by candidates. Neither of the two Commission texts quoted above contains the slides’ phrase ‘most important foreign policy tool’. The title of the Session 5 slides asks whether enlargement is still the EU’s ‘most effective foreign policy tool’, a wording that differs from Session 2’s ‘most important’ and that the slides credit to no one. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops cite Rehn for the view that the Eastern enlargement was a success, and their reference list names his speech ‘What’s the Future for EU Enlargement?’ as given at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, though the Commission’s text of that title is of the AmCham EU speech.

cards.question: In 1973 the United Kingdom, Ireland and Denmark joined the Union in the _____, which raised issues of agriculture, fisheries, poorer regions and neutrality, with referenda for approval.
cards.answerDate: Joined1973Regional fund1975
cards.abstract:
The first enlargement of the European Communities took effect on 1 January 1973, when Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom joined and membership rose from six to nine. A Council decision of 22 January 1972 on accession to the Coal and Steel Community named Denmark, Ireland, Norway and the United Kingdom and fixed 1 January 1973 as the date accession would take effect. Norway did not join, because its voters rejected membership in September 1972, while Ireland voted yes on 10 May with about 83 per cent and Denmark on 2 October. The Community had adopted equal access to each member state’s fishing grounds in 1970, and the 1972 Act of Accession laid down a derogation that let coastal states restrict access to their nearest waters. A pro-European journal’s editorial of November 1972 put Norway’s no down largely to fear that French fishermen would fish in Norwegian waters.

The slides name Denmark, the UK and Ireland as the candidates and add Norway, which their list does not show joining. They give the key issues linked to the candidates as agriculture, fisheries, poorer regions and neutrality, with referenda for approval, and present the EU’s response as incremental adjustment. Among the adjustments the slides list the European Regional Development Fund, established in 1975, and the Union’s history page says leaders agreed on 10 December 1974 to set up a fund moving money to poorer regions. The slides also list the Common Fisheries Policy, developed in the 1970s with the principle of exclusive economic zones, and in November 1976 the Council agreed that members would extend their fishing limits to 200 miles off their North Sea and Atlantic coasts from 1 January 1977. The slides add that the UK budgetary rebate was part of the 1984 Single European Act negotiations, although the Act was signed only in February 1986, and Schimmelfennig and Sedelmeier cite British and Spanish experience to show that deals felt to be unfair leave newcomers trying to renegotiate.
questions: After the _____, the Union answered the candidates’ issues with incremental adjustment, setting up a regional development fund in 1975 and developing a fisheries policy with exclusive economic zones in the 1970s.
Greece joined in 1981 and Portugal and Spain in 1986, but before them came the _____ of 1973, with Denmark, the United Kingdom and Ireland, and Norway also among the candidates.

cards.question: Established in 1975, the _____ was one of the incremental adjustments the Union made after its first enlargement, when poorer regions were among the issues linked to the candidates.
cards.answerDate: Established1975
cards.abstract:
The European Regional Development Fund is the fund for investment in poorer regions that the European Economic Community set up by a Council regulation of 18 March 1975. The regulation gave it the task of correcting the principal regional imbalances in the Community, resulting in particular from agricultural preponderance, industrial change and structural under-employment. The idea came from the Paris summit of October 1972, which invited the Community institutions to create such a fund, and the Commission’s report of May 1973 on regional problems in the enlarged Community said it should spend by need and not by juste retour, meaning a return matching each state’s payments. The fund was meant to start alongside the first enlargement of 1973, but the oil crisis delayed it, and it began work in March 1975. For 1975 to 1977 it received 1,300 million units of account, shared in national quotas that gave 40 per cent to Italy, 28 per cent to the United Kingdom and 6 per cent to Ireland.

The lecture slides name the fund, established in 1975, among the incremental adjustments the Union made after its first enlargement to address the issues linked to the candidates. The slides give agriculture, fisheries, poorer regions and neutrality as those issues for Denmark, the UK and Ireland, with Norway, whose voters rejected accession in a referendum. The Common Fisheries Policy, which the slides date to the 1970s, was one such adjustment, since fisheries mattered in the accession talks, which produced a ten-year derogation reserving each state’s 12-mile coastal waters for its own fleet. The slides also say the UK budgetary rebate was part of the 1984 Single European Act negotiations, but the Fontainebleau European Council of June 1984 fixed it, correcting 66 per cent of the gap between the UK’s VAT payments and its share of expenditure from 1985. The Single European Act, signed in February 1986, gave the fund a renewed mandate through its new powers on economic and social cohesion.

cards.question: Listed among institutional reforms made in anticipation of enlargement, the reform of the Common Agricultural Policy is known as _____, alongside the treaties of Amsterdam and Nice and the rise of trilogues.
cards.abstract:
The Agenda 2000 package was the Commission’s programme of July 1997, For a Stronger and Wider Union, on how the Union’s policies and finances should change to take in the applicant countries. The Commission wrote that enlargement played a far greater role in it than in any earlier financial package, as the applicants would all be net recipients. For farming it proposed to move further towards world market prices coupled to direct income aid, and listed enlargement among its reasons. It proposed to cut the cereals intervention price, at which the Union buys surplus grain, from 119.19 to 95.35 ECU a tonne, but the Berlin European Council of March 1999 agreed a cut of 15 per cent. Schrader of the Kiel Institute sees three elements in it, farm reform, structural fund reform and a decision on own resources, and notes concessions in the final agreement.

The lecture slides name Agenda 2000 as the reform of the Common Agricultural Policy on their list of reforms in anticipation of enlargement, using the name for the farm reform alone, whereas the Commission and the Berlin summit applied it to the whole package. The same list holds the Treaty of Amsterdam, voting weight adjustments in the Treaty of Nice, further changes in weights after 2014 under the constitutional treaty and the Lisbon Treaty, and the rise of trilogues. Nice dealt with the ‘Amsterdam leftovers’ of Commission size, vote weighting and qualified majority voting, and cut the big states’ share of Council votes from 55 to 45 per cent in 2004. Trilogues are informal meetings between Parliament and Council that began in conciliation, and Héritier shows that Amsterdam, by allowing agreement at first reading, made them common at earlier stages. The slides present such reforms as new in the enlargement to the East of 2004 to 2007, which brought more reform in advance, and they make agriculture a key issue of the first enlargement and chapter 11 of the negotiations.

cards.question: Enlargement negotiations involve bargaining about accession under conditions of _____, in which the EU’s bargaining power is greater than that of the candidate state.
cards.abstract:
Asymmetric interdependence is the condition in which parties need one another unequally, so that the party which gains less from a deal holds more bargaining power. Moravcsik and Vachudova, drawing on Keohane and Nye’s Power and Interdependence of 1977, put it as relative bargaining power tracking relative intensity of preference, so that those who gain most from cooperation compromise most. They apply it to enlargement and note that the next ten applicants’ combined economy was no more than 3 to 5 per cent of the EU-15’s, smaller than in any earlier round apart from Greece’s entry. The Union also set the terms, since the Copenhagen European Council of June 1993 said that membership requires stable institutions, a functioning market economy and the ability to take on the obligations of membership. Parliament’s fact sheet describes a procedure in which the Council, the Commission and the European Council act at successive stages, mostly by unanimity, and which ends in an accession treaty.

The lecture slides name asymmetric interdependence as the condition under which bargaining about accession takes place in the negotiations on joining, the most important of the several processes that make up enlargement. They call enlargement negotiations an asymmetric process in which the EU’s bargaining power is greater than that of the candidate state. On the EU side, the slides say, decision-making is intergovernmental and by unanimity, and the Commission leads the process as a gatekeeper, in their phrase a friend who tells the truth. Because negotiations take place between governments, the slides say, they strengthen the executive power of governments and the Council of Ministers at the expense of parliaments, and a Parliament study of 2025 reports that early Commission assistance for administrative reform went mainly to executive branches and ministries. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that conditionality, developed in the 1990s and early 2000s with regular reports, monitoring missions and suspension clauses, reinforced the asymmetric character of enlargement negotiations.

cards.question: On the EU side of enlargement negotiations the Council acts together with _____, while the Commission leads the process and serves as a gatekeeper, in one phrase a friend who tells the truth.
cards.answerDate: Informal dinner4 March 2026
cards.abstract:
COREPER is the Committee of Permanent Representatives of the member states’ governments, the body that prepares the work of the Council of the European Union and carries out the tasks the Council gives it. Its acronym comes from the French Comité des représentants permanents, and it meets in two forms, Coreper I of the deputy permanent representatives and Coreper II of the permanent representatives, who are the member states’ ambassadors. Coreper I prepares technical areas such as agriculture, employment, education and the environment, while Coreper II handles matters of ‘high politics’, among them foreign, economic and monetary affairs and justice and home affairs. The two committees meet at least weekly and work in parallel, neither being subordinate to the other, and some 150 specialised working parties serve them. In enlargement the Commission says negotiations cannot start until all governments agree unanimously on a framework, and that the talks take place between ministers and ambassadors of the EU governments and the candidate in an intergovernmental conference.

The lecture slides list COREPER among the EU institutions that act in enlargement negotiations, under the Council together with COELA. They give the EU side as the Council and COREPER, and the Commission, which leads the process and is also a gatekeeper, in their words a friend who tells the truth. They add that decision-making is intergovernmental and by unanimity, and that the Council decides unanimously whether to open negotiations, whereas Parliament’s fact sheet gives that decision to the European Council and leaves the Council to decide on clusters. The slides report that on 4 March 2026 member states rejected reverse enlargement during an informal dinner with the Commission and COREPER ambassadors. Euronews reported that ambassadors largely rejected the Commission’s idea of reversed membership for Ukraine, under which it would be a formal member without voting rights, farm payments or cohesion funds until it earned them, and that the Commission never put the idea on paper.

cards.question: After a country submits its application, the Council asks for a _____ on it, and that assessment comes before the unanimous decision to grant candidate status.
cards.answerDate: Ukraine opinionJune 2022Ukraine status23 June 2022Ukraine talks14 December 2023
cards.abstract:
A Commission opinion is the Commission’s assessment of a country’s application for membership, a step that Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union builds in by requiring the Council to act unanimously after consulting the Commission. The applicant addresses its application to the Council, which asks the Commission for an opinion, and the European Parliament and national parliaments are notified of the application. The Commission’s opinions of 17 June 2022 on Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia rested on political criteria, economic criteria and the ability to take on the obligations of membership, the acquis. Ukraine applied on 28 February 2022, the Council invited the opinion on 7 March, questionnaires followed in April and the opinion came on 17 June. The practice is older, since the Commission prepared an opinion on each application in 1997, starting from replies to questionnaires sent in April 1996, and presented them with Agenda 2000.

The lecture slides place the opinion at the start of the procedure: a candidate applies, the Council asks the Commission for an opinion and the Commission delivers it to the Council. The slides add that the European Council grants candidate status unanimously, and that the candidate then meets any pre-conditions, judged on the Commission’s assessment, before the Council can decide unanimously to open negotiations. They call the Commission the leader of the process and its gatekeeper, ‘a friend who tells the truth’, and list its ‘technocratic’, ‘objective’ assessments among the elements of the EU’s transformative power. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report that the opinion of June 2022 outlined seven steps for Ukraine, that the European Council granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova on 23 June 2022 and that it decided on 14 December 2023 to open accession negotiations with Ukraine. At the far end of the procedure the slides have the Commission deliver another, brief opinion, this time on the Treaty of Accession, before the European Parliament gives its assent and the Council approves the treaty unanimously.
questions: In June 2022 the _____ on Ukraine’s application outlined seven steps the country had to take to progress on its path to the EU, in the same month it became a candidate.
Once a draft Treaty of Accession has been agreed, another, brief _____ on it is delivered, before the European Parliament gives its assent and the Council approves the treaty unanimously.

cards.question: Through a questionnaire covering all EU policies, the Commission carries out _____, an analysis of a candidate’s readiness whose results set reform priorities by cluster.
cards.answerDate: Screening openedJuly 2022
cards.abstract:
Screening is the Commission’s analytical examination of how far a candidate country’s legislation matches the body of EU law, which the Commission carries out jointly with the candidate before negotiations on the chapters begin. Its findings, chapter by chapter, reach the member states in a screening report, whose conclusion is a Commission recommendation either to open negotiations directly or to require that opening benchmarks are met first. The revised methodology of February 2020 groups the chapters in thematic clusters, so screening is carried out per cluster and priorities for accelerated integration and key reforms are agreed between the EU and the candidate. Parliament’s fact sheet records that North Macedonia completed the screening process in December 2023, after accession negotiations with it and Albania were formally opened in July 2022. On Parliament’s account it follows the European Council’s decision to open negotiations and precedes the Council’s decision to open any chapters or clusters.

The lecture slides say the Commission provides candidates with a questionnaire regarding all EU policies to establish how ready they are, and they call this screening. They add that screening results in the setting of reform priorities by cluster, the EU’s rules, policies and case law being divided into chapters that are nowadays united in six clusters. In the slides’ list of steps, the questionnaire comes after the Council asks the Commission for an opinion on the application and before the Commission delivers that opinion to the Council. The record matches that sequence but not the label, since the Commission sent Ukraine questionnaires on 8 and 13 April 2022 for its opinion of 17 June, whereas its page on the steps towards joining lists screening among the elements of the membership negotiations. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report that in July 2022, the month after the European Council granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova, the screening processes with Albania and North Macedonia were officially opened, ending the dormant phase in their accession.

cards.question: After the Council unanimously decides to open negotiations, the Commission proposes a draft _____, which the Council agrees by unanimity while setting opening benchmarks for each cluster.
cards.abstract:
The negotiating framework is the document that sets out the guidelines and principles for the accession negotiations with each candidate country. The Commission’s glossary says that the Commission draws up a draft, the member states adopt it and the Council Presidency presents it at the start of the negotiations. The Commission adds that negotiations cannot start until all EU governments agree, in a unanimous decision of the Council, on a framework or mandate for them. The step can take long, since the Commission presented the draft framework for Albania and North Macedonia to the member states in July 2020, and negotiations were formally opened only in July 2022 after long delays. The Commission’s communication of February 2020 on the revised methodology said its changes could be accommodated within existing frameworks, so those for Serbia and Montenegro were not amended.

The lecture slides have the Commission propose a draft negotiation framework once the Council has decided unanimously to open negotiations, and the Council agrees it by unanimity while setting opening benchmarks for each cluster. The Commission then proposes, and the Council adopts by unanimity, a common negotiating position, and the Council decides by unanimity whether to open a cluster. The candidate and the EU then provisionally open and close clusters and negotiate over the candidate’s readiness, and the slides say negotiations on the fundamentals cluster open first and close last, as the Commission’s communication of 2020 also states. Where the slides give the decision to open negotiations to the Council, Parliament’s fact sheet gives it to the European Council, acting unanimously on a Commission recommendation, and leaves the Council to decide on chapters and clusters. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops record that the European Council decided on 14 December 2023 to open accession negotiations with Ukraine, the kind of decision that the slides place before the draft framework.
questions: Before the Council adopts a common position and decides unanimously whether to open each cluster, it agrees on the _____ that the Commission proposed in draft form.
Provisional opening and closing of clusters by the candidate and the EU follows the adoption of a common position and, before that, of the _____ with its opening benchmarks.

cards.question: Since 2020 the 33 negotiating chapters have been united in six thematic groups, and the Council decides unanimously whether to open each _____ after setting opening benchmarks for it.
cards.answerDate: Clusters from2020
cards.abstract:
A cluster is a thematic group of negotiating chapters, introduced by the Commission’s communication of 5 February 2020 so that talks could proceed on a whole sector at a time instead of chapter by chapter. The communication named six clusters, which are Fundamentals; Internal market; Competitiveness and inclusive growth; Green agenda and sustainable connectivity; Resources, agriculture and cohesion; and External relations. Its annex sorts 33 numbered chapters into the clusters and handles chapter 34, ‘Institutions’, and chapter 35, ‘Other issues’, separately. Negotiations on a cluster open as a whole once the opening benchmarks are met, the communication says, and closing benchmarks are then set for each chapter. Parliament’s fact sheet reports that Albania opened Cluster 1, the fundamentals, with five chapters on 15 October 2024 and had opened all six clusters by November 2025.

The lecture slides say that the EU’s rules, policies and case law are divided in chapters, nowadays united in six clusters, and they list the same six. They add that screening results in reform priorities by cluster, that the Council sets opening benchmarks for each cluster and decides unanimously whether to open one, and that the candidate and the EU provisionally open and close clusters. The slides date the arrangement of 33 chapters and six clusters to 2020, which matches the Commission’s annex, though the Commission’s glossary counts 35 chapters of the acquis in all. The slides list a flexible enlargement methodology, with political steering from the member states since 2020, among the elements of the EU’s transformative power. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the 2020 approach was meant to speed up negotiations by working with clusters instead of chapters and to give the Council a central role, but conclude that it did not really change the policy substantially, because the proposed increase in funding was rejected, partly due to Covid-19, and that it did not break the deadlock.
questions: Fundamentals, Internal market and External relations are each the name of one _____, a bundle of chapters for which screening sets reform priorities and the Council sets opening benchmarks.
The 2020 revised approach tried to speed up talks by working with each _____ rather than each chapter, and aimed at a more political process with a central role for the Council.

cards.question: Of the six negotiating clusters, talks on the _____ are the first to open and the last to close, bracketing everything the candidate negotiates in between.
cards.answerDate: Revised approach2020
cards.abstract:
The Fundamentals cluster is the first of the six thematic groups into which the European Commission proposed in February 2020 to sort the chapters of accession negotiations. The Commission’s Communication Enhancing the accession process answered requests from member states, above all French calls for reform, after the Union failed in 2019 to open talks with North Macedonia and Albania. Its annex puts chapter 23 on the judiciary and fundamental rights and chapter 24 on justice, freedom and security into this cluster, with economic criteria, democratic institutions, public administration reform, procurement, statistics and financial control. The other five clusters are internal market, competitiveness and inclusive growth, green agenda and sustainable connectivity, resources, agriculture and cohesion, and external relations, as the lecture slides also list them. Chapters 34 and 35, on institutions and on other issues, are handled separately, so the six clusters hold chapters 1 to 33, the number of chapters the slides give.

The Commission wrote that negotiations on the fundamentals would be opened first and closed last, that progress on them would determine the overall pace of negotiations, and that no other chapter would be provisionally closed before the rule of law benchmarks were met. The Council adopted conclusions on 25 March 2020 that endorsed the Communication and called the fundamental democratic, rule of law and economic reforms the core objective of the accession process. In May 2021 the Council applied the method to Montenegro and Serbia, noting that Serbia had opened every chapter of the fundamentals cluster but only some chapters, or none, in the others. The lecture slides say that negotiations on the fundamentals cluster open first and close last, and that agreement on a draft Treaty of Accession is reached once all chapters have been opened and closed. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the 2020 revised approach emphasised the rule of law, good governance and anti-corruption measures as ‘the fundamentals’, a step meant to refocus reforms and restore the credibility of enlargement.
questions: Listed ahead of Internal market, Competitiveness and inclusive growth, Green agenda and sustainable connectivity, Resources, agriculture and cohesion, and External relations, the _____ is the first of the six clusters.
The 2020 revised approach stressed the rule of law, good governance and anti-corruption as core reforms to restore credibility, and the _____ is the cluster that opens first and closes last.

cards.question: The Union’s rules, policies and case law that candidates must adopt are divided into 33 _____, which since 2020 have been united in six clusters.
cards.answerDate: Clusters from2020
cards.abstract:
The chapters of the acquis are the policy fields, 35 in all, into which accession negotiations divide the body of EU law that a candidate must adopt. ‘Acquis’ is French for something agreed, and the European External Action Service puts the whole body at about 130,000 pages of legal text. It counts as part of the acquis the aims of the Treaties, the legislation adopted under them, the case law of the Court of Justice and acts agreed in foreign, security, justice and home affairs. A candidate does not negotiate the acquis itself, which it must adopt in full, but only the conditions and timing for applying it. Hillion notes that the list of chapters has grown from 30 at the fifth enlargement to 35, and with it the number of benchmarks and of points at which member states can halt the process.

The lecture slides number the chapters at 33 and list the first fifteen, from free movement of goods as number 1 through competition policy as number 8 to energy as number 15, which matches the Commission’s numbering. The slides count 33 because chapters 34 on institutions and 35 on other issues are handled separately, so the Commission’s six clusters of 2020 hold chapters 1 to 33. The slides say the main subject of the negotiations is how a candidate will comply with the Copenhagen criteria and adopt the acquis, and the lecture on transformative power equates the acquis with the EU’s rules, policies and case law. The slides add that agreement on a draft Treaty of Accession is reached when all chapters have been opened and closed, and the Union’s diplomatic service says that treaty is drawn up once every chapter is agreed. The slides say that the chapters are nowadays united in six clusters, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the 2020 revised approach aimed to speed up negotiations by working with clusters instead of chapters.

Agreement on a draft Treaty of Accession is reached only when all 33 _____ have been opened and closed, although they are now bundled into six thematic clusters.

cards.question: Once all chapters have been opened and closed, a draft _____ is agreed, on which the Commission gives a further, brief opinion before Parliament’s assent and the Council’s unanimous approval.
cards.abstract:
The Treaty of Accession is the agreement between the member states and an applicant that Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union requires for admission. Article 49 says that the conditions of admission and the adjustments to the Treaties that admission entails are the subject of this agreement, which every contracting state must ratify under its own constitutional rules. In the 2005 treaty for Bulgaria and Romania those conditions and adjustments were set out in an Act annexed to the treaty, which formed an integral part of it. The Commission describes an accession treaty as holding the detailed terms of membership, all transitional arrangements and deadlines, the financial arrangements and any safeguard clauses. It is not final until the Council, the Commission and Parliament support it, the candidate and all member states sign it, and each of them ratifies it by a parliamentary vote or a referendum.

The lecture slides make it the document that closes the accession procedure, and say that agreement on a draft is reached when all chapters have been opened and closed. The Commission’s guide adds that the Commission then gives its opinion on the candidate’s readiness, the member states decide unanimously to close the negotiations, and Parliament must give its consent, and the slides call this opinion another, brief, one. The Bulgarian and Romanian case shows the order, with the Commission’s opinion on 22 February 2005, Parliament’s assent on 13 April and the Council’s decision to accept the applications on 25 April, the day the treaty was signed. Article 49 now speaks of Parliament’s consent, where the 2005 documents and the slides say assent, and it has Parliament act by a majority of its component members and the Council act unanimously. The slides add that the negotiations strengthen the executive power of governments and the Council at the expense of parliaments, and a study for the European Parliament quotes a Commission project note saying the balance of power shifts to the executive during integration.
questions: For the _____ to come into force, the Council must approve it unanimously, the European Parliament must give its assent, and all member states and the candidate must ratify it.

Negotiated between governments, in a process that strengthens executive power at the expense of parliaments, the _____ still needs the European Parliament’s assent and ratification by every member state to take effect.

cards.question: Enlargement leads to some economic convergence, and a 2012 World Bank report, in the words of its chief economist for Europe and Central Asia, described the Union as a _____ taking in poor countries.
cards.answerDate: Report2012
cards.abstract:
The convergence machine is the World Bank’s image of the European Union as a system that takes in poor countries and helps them become high income economies. It comes from Golden Growth, a 2012 World Bank study that assesses six parts of the European growth model, namely trade, finance, enterprise, innovation, labour and government. The Bank’s page quotes Indermit Gill, its chief economist for Europe and Central Asia, saying one can claim without exaggeration that Europe invented such a machine. The report traces three waves, from Western Europe catching up with the United States in 1950 to 1973, to over 100 million people in the southern periphery drawing closer until the early 1990s, and another 100 million in Central and Eastern Europe after 1994. It adds that over four decades consumption per head grew by 4 per cent a year in poorer Europe against 2 per cent in richer Europe, while the world beyond East Asia saw little convergence.

The lecture slides quote this line under the heading ‘The European Union as a convergence machine’ and credit it to Gill, with a World Bank chart headed GDP growth, 1990 to 1995. The slides list among the features of enlargement governance that enlargement leads to some economic convergence and that economic support is enhanced by increased investment in anticipation of accession. They describe capacity building as a transfer of funds and expertise that helps candidates converge towards EU standards of governance and regulation, and they treat domestic reforms as one of the major benefits of enlargement. Próchniak and Rapacki find that eleven members from Central and Eastern Europe stood at 44.5% of the EU15 average income per head in 2004 and narrowed the gap by nearly 31 percentage points over twenty years. The report itself warns that the machine ground to a halt in the south while it turned smoothly in the east, and Próchniak and Rapacki caution that weak institutions may offset the benefit for today’s candidates.

cards.question: Alongside conditionality and socialisation, _____ is one of the three ways in which the EU exercises transformative power on candidates that have a membership perspective.
cards.abstract:
Capacity building is the help the EU gives a candidate’s administration so that it can adopt, apply and enforce EU law. One instrument is Twinning, which since 1998 has paired civil servants from member states with those of a partner country to support the transposition, implementation and enforcement of the acquis. Twinning projects last up to 3 years and rest on peer to peer exchanges between public administrations. Money comes through the Instrument for Pre-accession Assistance, which has supported reforms in the enlargement region since 2007 and was allotted €11.5 billion for 2007 to 2013, €12.8 billion for 2014 to 2020 and €14.162 billion for 2021 to 2027. A study for the European Parliament reports interviewees saying that early assistance for public administration reform focused mainly on executive branches and ministries and less on parliaments.

Börzel and Risse describe the accession of the Central, Eastern and South Eastern European countries as resting mostly on rewards, on the one hand, and capacity building, on the other. They add that conditionality works far less well where states lack the capacity to make the required changes, and they set socialisation beside it, a process in which actors take on new norms to belong. The lecture slides list capacity building as one of three ways in which the EU exercises transformative power, alongside conditionality and socialisation, on candidates that have a membership perspective. The slides on enlargement governance call conditionality the main tool, relying on the credibility of the EU’s threats and promises of accession, and capacity building another tool, described as support for administrative capacity. They list it next to enlargement driven financial and technical assistance and say it involves a transfer of funds and expertise that helps candidates converge towards EU standards of governance and regulation.
questions: Support for the administrative capacity of candidates, through a transfer of funds and expertise that helps them converge towards EU standards of governance and regulation, is known as _____ in enlargement.

cards.question: Listed among the elements of the EU’s transformative power, a _____ can remain in place for up to three years after a country has joined the Union.
cards.abstract:
A safeguard clause is a provision in an accession treaty that lets the EU withhold the benefits of membership or take protective measures if a new member fails to complete promised reforms. The Commission’s guide says an accession treaty contains the terms of membership, all transitional arrangements and deadlines, the financial arrangements and any safeguard clauses. The 2005 treaty with Bulgaria and Romania has three such clauses, on economic difficulties in Article 36, on the internal market in Article 37 and on justice and home affairs in Article 38. Each applies until the end of a period of up to three years after accession. The internal market and justice clauses could be invoked even before accession on the basis of monitoring findings, and their measures may continue beyond the three years while the commitments remain unfulfilled.

The European Council of 16 and 17 December 2004 said that safeguard clauses would address serious problems arising before accession or in the three years after it, and asked the Commission to keep reporting each year. Trauner notes that such clauses were nothing new, since earlier Central and Eastern European treaties had them, but that their use was never seriously discussed in 2004, and that activating them may mean suspended EU funds or export food bans. He adds that the Commission had so far advised against activating them and instead set up a cooperation and verification mechanism, with benchmarks on corruption, organised crime and judicial reform. The lecture slides list safeguard clauses among the elements of transformative power, under conditionality, monitoring and money, beside regular reports, rule of law reporting and ad hoc monitoring reports, and say they can remain up to three years after accession. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that in the 1990s and early 2000s the EU developed conditionality, introducing regular reports, monitoring missions and suspension clauses, but they do not use the term safeguard clause.

cards.question: Listed first among the instruments of conditionality and monitoring, a _____ on candidates’ progress is the Commission’s yearly assessment, followed by rule of law reporting and ad hoc monitoring reports.
cards.abstract:
A regular report is the Commission’s periodic assessment of how far each candidate has progressed towards accession. The European Council at Luxembourg in December 1997 decided that from the end of 1998 the Commission would make regular reports to the Council on each Central and Eastern European applicant, in the light of the Copenhagen criteria and above all the rate at which it adopted the acquis. Hillion notes that this contrasted with earlier procedures, in which the Commission gave only two opinions on a membership application, and that the reports were to be the basis for Council decisions on the conduct of the negotiations. Pre-accession financial assistance could also be reviewed if progress on the Copenhagen criteria was judged insufficient. Today the Commission publishes its assessments each year in an Enlargement Package, whose country reports give a detailed annual assessment of reform progress with recommendations and guidance on reform priorities.

The lecture slides list regular reports first among the instruments under conditionality, monitoring and money, and describe them as the Commission’s yearly assessment of candidates’ progress. They sit beside rule of law reporting, ad hoc monitoring reports and safeguard clauses, while the money side of the slide names the Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans and the Ukraine Facility. The slides list technocratic and objective, merit based assessments by the Commission among the elements of transformative power, and say that enlargement was developed as a technocratic approach until 2020 and then became more political. The 2020 Communication invited member states to contribute directly to the annual reports and to review progress more regularly, while Parliament gives its opinion on the annual Commission reports. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that in the 1990s and early 2000s the EU developed conditionality as an underlying principle and tool, introducing regular reports, monitoring missions and suspension clauses and reinforcing the asymmetric character of enlargement negotiations.
questions: Introduced with monitoring missions and suspension clauses in the 1990s and early 2000s, the _____ belonged to a conditionality that reinforced the asymmetric character of enlargement negotiations.

The Commission’s yearly assessment of candidates’ progress, introduced with conditionality in the 1990s and early 2000s, is called the _____, one of three kinds of report listed beside safeguard clauses.

cards.question: Under the heading of conditionality, monitoring and money, the Union lists the Commission’s yearly assessment, _____, ad hoc monitoring reports and safeguard clauses that can remain up to three years after accession.
cards.abstract:
Rule of law reporting is the Commission’s annual monitoring of developments in the justice system, the anti-corruption framework, media pluralism and other institutional checks and balances. The Commission’s Rule of Law Report has been issued since 2020 and is the foundation of an annual rule of law cycle, a preventive tool that opens a yearly dialogue with the Council, Parliament, national parliaments and civil society. The 2024 report was the first to include country chapters on four enlargement countries, Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia, to support irreversible progress on democracy and the rule of law ahead of accession. As of 2024 those four countries also take part as observers in the network of national contact points that helps prepare the report. The rule of law is part of the first Copenhagen criterion, which Parliament’s enquiries unit lists as stable institutions that guarantee democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities.

The lecture slides list rule of law reporting among the instruments of the EU’s transformative power, under conditionality, monitoring and money. They place it beside regular reports on candidates’ progress, which they describe as the Commission’s yearly assessment, ad hoc monitoring reports, and safeguard clauses that can remain up to three years after accession. The slides’ own wording of the first Copenhagen criterion names the stability of institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, and respect for and protection of minorities. A study for the European Parliament calls screening and rule of law reports important for the Commission’s assessment of democratic institutions, and quotes officials saying that the 2020 methodology set no fixed benchmarks for them. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the 2020 revised approach emphasised the rule of law, good governance and anti-corruption measures as ‘the fundamentals’ to refocus reforms and restore credibility, and the Council of March 2020 called these reforms the core objective of accession.

cards.question: Listed under money among the elements of the Union’s transformative power, the _____ for the Western Balkans is dated 2024 and comes with a scoreboard.
cards.answerDate: Dated2024
cards.abstract:
The Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans is a financing instrument of €6 billion for 2024 to 2027, set up by Regulation (EU) 2024/1449. The Commission proposed it on 8 November 2023 as the financial pillar of a Growth Plan for a region whose economic convergence stands at around 35% of the EU average. Of the €6 billion, €2 billion are grants and €4 billion are concessional loans and at least 50% of the total goes to investments through the Western Balkans Investment Framework. Parliament endorsed the compromise text on 24 April 2024 and the Council on 7 May, and the regulation entered into force on 25 May 2024. It complements the existing pre-accession instrument IPA III, and what sets it apart is a payment mechanism tied to the achievement of reforms.

The lecture slides list it, dated 2024 and paired with a scoreboard, as one of two items under money on their slide about conditionality, monitoring and money, the other being the Ukraine facility for recovery, reconstruction and modernisation. The same slide lists regular reports on candidates’ progress, rule of law reporting, ad hoc monitoring reports and safeguard clauses that can remain up to 3 years after accession, and the slides count enlargement-driven financial and technical assistance among the elements of the EU’s transformative power. The scoreboard is the Commission’s public tracker of the Facility, showing the steps fulfilled and the amounts disbursed, and the European Economic and Social Committee had recommended such a scoreboard on the model of the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Behind it, each Reform Agenda splits reforms into quantitative and qualitative steps that serve as payment conditions, payments are made twice a year after the Commission verifies them, and the Commission suspends or deducts a payment if conditions fail. The Court of Auditors warned in January 2024 that the disbursement conditions might not be ambitious enough or sufficiently measurable, while Velinovska argues that the EU is now “conditioning financing on reform itself”.

cards.question: Launched in June 2023 for long-term support during the war and in view of accession, the _____ involves commitments of 50 billion euros for 2024 to 2027 across three pillars.
cards.answerDate: LaunchedJune 2023Created29 February 2024Period2024 to 2027
cards.abstract:
The Ukraine Facility is the EU’s single mechanism for up to €50 billion of support to Ukraine over 2024 to 2027, made up of €33 billion in loans and €17 billion in grants. The Commission presented the proposal on 20 June 2023, and Regulation (EU) 2024/792 of 29 February 2024 entered into force on 1 March. Pillar I, the Ukraine Plan, gives the Ukrainian state €5.27 billion in grants and the full €33 billion of loans, released against conditions set in a plan for recovery, reconstruction and modernisation. Pillar II, the Ukraine investment framework, offers guarantees of up to €6.97 billion to attract investment, while Pillar III pays for technical assistance, support for civil society and borrowing-cost subsidies. Ukraine submitted its plan on 20 March 2024 and the Council approved it on 14 May, with conditions for each quarter until 2027 that the Commission checks before each regular payment.

The lecture slides list the Ukraine facility, given as recovery, reconstruction and modernisation, as one of two items under money on their slide about conditionality, monitoring and money. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that it was launched in June 2023 for long-term support to Ukraine during the war and in view of its accession, and officially created on 29 February 2024 after negotiations between Parliament and Council. They say €50 billion across three pillars closely related to accession preparedness exceeds the EU’s earlier commitments to Ukraine and any support to another candidate, and contrast it with the European Peace Facility, which funded military deliveries. In their conclusion they describe the accession funding as separate from defence funding, and note that enlargement has reached only funding and organisational change, while institutional change is still obstructed by veto players. Volintiru and Bodnya argued before adoption that the plan could anchor a unified assistance strategy but covers only some reforms, and Larsen argues that payments should rest on results such as corruption convictions, not on new laws.

cards.question: Introduced in 2020, the _____ works with six clusters instead of 33 chapters and gives the member states political steering over negotiations with candidates.
cards.answerDate: Since2020
cards.abstract:
The revised enlargement methodology is the reform of the accession process that the Commission set out on 5 February 2020 in a Communication titled Enhancing the accession process: a credible EU perspective for the Western Balkans. It followed the European Council of 17 and 18 October 2019, which discussed enlargement and decided to return to the issue before the Zagreb summit of May 2020. Hoxhaj traces the idea of reversibility in it to a French non-paper of November 2019, which proposed that member states could cancel talks if a candidate backslides. The Communication aimed to make the process more predictable, more credible, more dynamic and subject to stronger political steering, with positive and negative conditionality and reversibility. The Council endorsed it on 25 March 2020 and said the changes could fit the negotiating frameworks of Montenegro and Serbia if both agreed.

The lecture slides list a flexible methodology with political steering from the member states among the elements of transformative power since 2020, and say enlargement was developed as a technocratic approach until 2020 and then became more political. They show 33 chapters of EU rules now united in six clusters, from fundamentals to external relations, and the Communication confirms that each cluster opens as a whole after its opening benchmarks while chapters 34 and 35 are handled separately. The slides add that the fundamentals cluster opens first and closes last, as the Communication also states. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that clusters were meant to speed up negotiations and to switch from a technical process, led by Commission assessments, to a political one with a central role for the Council, the member states and candidate leaders. They judge that, because the EU rejected a substantially increased funding mechanism, partly as Covid-19 redirected funds, the methodology did not really change the policy or break the deadlock, and Madhi had warned that more member state steering could weaken the Commission’s technical assessments.

A substantially bigger funding mechanism proposed with it was rejected, partly because Covid-19 redirected funds, so the 2020 _____ neither changed policy substantially nor broke the deadlock on further enlargement.

cards.question: Challenging the Union’s enlargement governance with a Chinese ‘systemic rival’ in the Balkans, the _____ is described through bank loans, a focus on Serbia and special laws regulating public tenders.
cards.answer: Belt and Road in the Western Balkans
cards.abstract:
Belt and Road in the Western Balkans is the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative as it reaches the six non-EU states of the region, where Clingendael finds China acts mainly as an infrastructure financier and investor. The Clingendael report adds that China has no unified regional strategy but builds bilateral ties inside the 17+1 platform, with Serbia its preferred partner and Kosovo the weakest tie. On 12 March 2019 the Commission and the High Representative called China “a systemic rival promoting alternative models of governance”. For the Western Balkans the same text asked the EU to pursue enlargement to secure adherence to its standards in areas such as public procurement. The Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies finds that Chinese loans equal about 1.2% of regional GDP a year against 1.5% for EU loans, and in Serbia exceed them.

The lecture slides describe the Belt and Road Initiative as China’s strategy in the Balkans, through investments and projects, on a slide titled “Enlargement governance is challenged by Chinese ‘systemic rival’ in the Balkans”. Its first point reads “12 billion euro Chinese banks loans, 60% of all China’s bank loans are for the Western Balkans”, and its second “Focus on Serbia: 1/3 of all Chinese loans in the region are in Serbia, FDI grows dramatically”, citing Zweers 2020. Those figures are the slide’s own, and the trackers wiiw uses differ: AidData counts 60 projects worth USD 14.2 billion by 2021, USD 7 billion in Serbia, and the American Enterprise Institute USD 19 billion from 2010 to 2024, USD 14.7 billion in Serbia. The slide’s third point reads “Different - intergovernmental modes of governance: special laws regulate public tenders when Chinese projects are involved”, and Vladisavljev cites a special Expo-related law that exempts key Surčin projects in Serbia from the Law on Public Procurement. Shopov argues that the EU still has no clear China conditionality for aspirant countries, although Clingendael had urged using accession conditionality to shape Chinese involvement.

cards.question: Five days after Russia’s full-scale invasion began, the _____ was submitted by President Zelenskyy, and it restarted an enlargement process that had been deadlocked for the last 13 years.
cards.answerDate: Invasion24 February 2022Candidate status23 June 2022Talks decided14 December 2023
cards.abstract:
Ukraine’s membership application was presented on 28 February 2022, which the Commission’s Opinion dates five days after Russia launched its full-scale aggression. Under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, a European state that respects the Union’s values may apply, and the Council then acts unanimously after consulting the Commission and receiving Parliament’s consent. On 7 March 2022 the Council asked the Commission for its Opinion, which the leaders endorsed at the informal meeting in Versailles. The Commission delivered the Opinion on 17 June 2022 and recommended candidate status on the understanding that seven steps were taken, from judicial appointments and anti-corruption work to an anti-oligarch law, a media law and minority rights. The European Council decided at its meeting of 23 and 24 June 2022 to grant candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova, and on 14 and 15 December 2023 decided to open accession negotiations.

The lecture slides show Ukraine’s membership application, submitted by its President Zelenskyy, as the event that restarts the enlargement process after a deadlock of the last 13 years. They quote the European Council acknowledging “the European aspirations and European choice of Ukraine” and saying that “Ukraine belongs to our European family”, citing European Council 2022a, and the Commission notes that the Association Agreement’s preamble had already acknowledged Ukraine’s European aspirations. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops place that statement at the informal Versailles summit, and write that Ukraine applied five days after the full-scale invasion began on 24 February 2022 and Moldova followed in March. They say that with Ukraine it was the first time the EU decided to start negotiations with a country facing a large-scale, active war, and that until 2022 the prospect of membership was non-existent for Ukraine, Georgia and Moldova, covered by the Neighbourhood Policy and the Eastern Partnership. Darvas and colleagues add that the EU approved the application quickly yet tied the opening of negotiations to further reforms on the rule of law and good governance.

cards.question: A Ukrainian case that could mean a simpler, shorter procedure, with the process sped up or certain stages postponed, is discussed as _____, though the debate is still open.
cards.answerDate: OpinionJune 2022Talks decided14 December 2023
cards.abstract:
Accession through war is the question of how the accession procedure should treat a candidate that is fighting a war, a case the EU faced for the first time when it decided to start negotiations with Ukraine. The Commission assessed Ukraine’s application in the usual way, against the Copenhagen criteria, with questionnaires sent in April 2022 and answered by 9 May. Its Opinion of 17 June 2022 recommended candidate status on seven steps and stressed that steps towards the EU can be reversed if conditions are no longer met. On 14 and 15 December 2023 the European Council decided to open accession negotiations and asked the Council to adopt negotiating frameworks once the steps in the Commission’s recommendations of 8 November 2023 were taken. Darvas and colleagues propose progressive integration into EU policies alongside the formal talks, so that Ukrainians see benefits early, but warn against gatekeeping that adds hurdles before accession.

The lecture slides ask whether accession through war for Ukraine could mean a simpler, shorter procedure, with the process sped up or certain stages postponed to a later moment. They add that the debate is still open, that it is therefore difficult to develop a template for such a peculiar accession, and that the issue must be discussed, citing a 2022 article by Petrov and Hillion on Ukraine’s road to the EU in the Common Market Law Review. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report that the European Council decided on 14 December 2023 to open accession negotiations, after the Commission’s opinion of June 2022 outlined seven steps that Ukraine needed to take. Zuleeg argued in April 2025 for near-term membership with transition periods and derogations and voting rights granted gradually, while Paul and Taran, calling accession with a candidate at war unprecedented, urged keeping the merit-based process and avoiding unnecessary delays. Litra reports that the ‘fast-track’ and ‘reverse accession’ models were debated informally in early March 2026 and rejected by member state ambassadors.

cards.question: Proposed for Ukraine in early 2026, _____ meant fast accession without compliance with the Copenhagen criteria, and a geopolitical discourse presented it as a radical policy change.
cards.answerDate: ProposedEarly 2026Requested2027Rejected4 March 2026
cards.abstract:
Reverse enlargement is an option for Ukraine that would depart from the usual order of accession, in which, under the European Council’s Copenhagen conclusions of June 1993, membership follows once a country satisfies the required economic and political conditions. Those conditions are stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law and human rights, a functioning market economy, and the ability to take on the obligations of membership. In June 2022 the European Council said that Ukraine’s progress would depend on its own merit in meeting the Copenhagen criteria, taking into consideration the EU’s capacity to absorb new members. In December 2023 it called enlargement a geo-strategic investment and said that aspiring members must step up reforms in line with the merit-based nature of the process, while the Union prepares itself in parallel. Darvas and colleagues note that the strongest motivation for difficult reforms has been a credible and predictable accession process based on rewarding reforms.

The lecture slides report that in early 2026 the Commission proposed reverse enlargement for Ukraine, meaning fast accession without compliance with the Copenhagen criteria, and that Zelenskyy requested an accession date of 2027 as part of a peace deal. On their slide titled “Discursive divide mirrors policy disagreement”, these points sit in the geopolitics column, where the geopolitical discourse is said to present a radical policy change with the reverse enlargement option. The merit column records that on 4 March 2026 member states rejected the idea during an informal dinner with the Commission and COREPER ambassadors, citing concerns about the credibility of the enlargement process. It quotes a diplomat who censured the Commission for building up hype and creating the “illusion” that enlargement can be exclusively political, rather than merit-based. Litra reports that ‘fast-track’ and ‘reverse accession’ models were debated informally in early March 2026 and rejected by member state ambassadors, while Zuleeg had argued in 2025 for fast accession with derogations and gradually granted voting rights.

cards.question: Whether enlargement means exporting stability or _____ is debated, and one side holds that with the war against Ukraine Ukraine’s vulnerability becomes the Union’s and the costs of aggression spill over.
cards.answerDate: Stability gains2000 to 2010
cards.abstract:
Importing instability is the worry that enlarging towards a country at war brings its insecurity into the Union, the opposite of exporting stability. The Commission wrote in 2020 that a credible accession perspective is the key driver of transformation in the Western Balkans and a geostrategic investment in a stable, strong and united Europe. The European Council repeated in December 2023 that enlargement is a geo-strategic investment in peace, security, stability and prosperity. Darvas and colleagues observe that the EU has no experience of accepting a candidate at war, and recall that Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union obliges members to give a victim of armed aggression aid and assistance by all the means in their power. They add that Ukraine’s membership would significantly increase the EU’s military and security capabilities, while lengthening the EU–Russia border.

The lecture slides ask whether enlargement means exporting stability or importing instability, and set two readings side by side, one citing Leigh 2025 for instability and one citing Anghel 2025 for stability. On the instability side they say that, given the state of the war, Ukraine’s vulnerability becomes the EU’s vulnerability, and that the cost of external aggression to candidates spills over to the EU, citing Jones 2025. On the stability side they quote the view that enlargement is the EU’s strategic gamble for managing risk, and the claim that Russia’s assault on Ukraine, military threats to Moldova and Georgia and destabilising actions in the Western Balkans now pose a direct threat to the integrity of the European project. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops quote High Representative Borrell in 2022 calling a credible enlargement policy a geostrategic investment in peace, stability, security and economic growth in the whole of Europe. The slides credit enlargement with extending stability and values in 2000 to 2010, with rising authoritarianism challenging these gains since, and Litra reports officials warning that the cost of non-enlargement could be higher than the cost of enlargement.

cards.question: In a diagram of the discursive divide among policy makers, acceleration is set against _____, while security is set against rule of law and geopolitics against merit.
cards.abstract:
The absorption capacity of the Union is its ability to take in new members while its institutions still function effectively and its policies stay sustainably financed. Lehne traces the idea to the Copenhagen European Council of June 1993, whose membership criteria cited the Union’s capacity to absorb new members. The December 2006 European Council made it part of a renewed consensus on enlargement and stated that the pace of enlargement must take into account that capacity. It also asked the Commission for impact assessments on key policy areas in its opinion on a country’s application and again during the accession negotiations. Lehne calls the concept deeply political and links it to more majority voting in the Council, a smaller Commission and extra money in the next multiannual budget.

A slide titled “Recent research: Discursive divide on enlargement among policy makers” sets acceleration against absorption capacity as one of four contrasts. The other three contrasts are security against rule of law, geopolitics against merit, and constitutionalisation against bilateralisation, and the slides’ separate list of dilemmas adds reform driven by conditionality against rent seeking. Both sides appear in official texts, since in June 2022 the European Council called for the acceleration of the Western Balkans’ accession process and still tied progress to the Union’s capacity to absorb new members. The Commission’s communication of November 2025 likewise notes an accelerating pace for some candidates and adds that the Union must adapt to welcome a larger family. Dimitrova describes the first dilemma as the ostensibly geopolitical logic against merit-based assessment, and Staelens adds that leaders doubted the Union’s absorption capacity before 2022 but now see the geopolitical imperative and merit clash again.

cards.question: In a diagram of the discursive divide among policy makers on enlargement, the pair _____ is noted with the word vetoes and sits beside acceleration versus absorption capacity.
cards.abstract:
The pair constitutionalisation versus bilateralisation is one of four contrasts on the course’s diagram of the discursive divide among policy makers, and the slide marks it with the word vetoes. The treaty rule behind such vetoes is Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, under which the Council acts unanimously on an application after consulting the Commission and receiving the Parliament’s consent. The Commission’s guide adds that membership negotiations cannot start until all governments agree and that no chapter closes until every government is satisfied. Hillion argues that unanimous decisions have proliferated since the accession wave of 2004 and 2007, which inflated veto opportunities and amounted to a nationalisation of enlargement policy. He adds that Article 49 itself gives the member states a decisive say at only two procedural points, the decision to start and the acceptance of the conditions of admission.

The slides say that decision-making in enlargement is intergovernmental and by unanimity, and that the Council decides unanimously whether to open each cluster of negotiating chapters. Session 3 lists a delay in the start of negotiations with North Macedonia among the consequences of foreign policy voting under unanimity. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that enlargement has reached the stage of funding and organisational change while institutional change is still obstructed by veto players. They add that further progress stumbles against unanimous decision-making and a lack of appetite for treaty reform. Grabbe counts about 150 veto points in the current accession process, notes that North Macedonia has suffered from vetoes in disputes with Greece and Bulgaria, and reports a Commission proposal of 6 October 2026 to use qualified majority voting to speed up negotiations.

cards.question: Counted among the elements of the Union’s transformative power through technocratic and objective Commission assessments, _____ is set against geopolitical enlargement in a list of enlargement dilemmas.
cards.answerDate: Political turn2020Dinner4 March 2026
cards.abstract:
Merit-based enlargement means that a candidate advances according to its own progress in meeting the conditions of membership, as the Commission assesses it. The Commission’s methodology of February 2020 calls conditionality the core element of the merit-based accession process and asks for conditions that are objective, precise, detailed, strict and verifiable. The same communication adds that the member states’ commitment to the Western Balkans is a significant political and not simply technical undertaking. In December 2023 the European Council called enlargement a geo-strategic investment and asked aspiring members to step up reforms in line with the merit-based nature of the accession process. The Commission’s communication of November 2025 still calls the process strict, fair and merit-based, and Staelens notes that it is formally merit-based under the Copenhagen criteria but also works as a political tool.

The slides list merit-based enlargement among the elements of the EU’s transformative power as technocratic and objective assessments by the Commission. They say that enlargement was developed as a technocratic approach until 2020 and then became more political, and their dilemmas of enlargement begin with geopolitical versus merit-based enlargement. On the slide about policy disagreement, the merit column records that member states rejected reverse enlargement on 4 March 2026 over the credibility of the process, and a quoted diplomat censured the Commission for the “illusion” that enlargement can be exclusively political. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the 2020 methodology aimed to switch from a technical process, in which the Commission’s assessments matter most, to a more political one with a central role for the Council and the member states. Dimitrova adds elsewhere that the geopolitical logic undermines the threat of non-membership for reform laggards.
