cards.question: Once the Commission has delivered its opinion to the Council, the Council grants _____ unanimously, and pre-conditions, if any, must then be met before negotiations can open.
cards.answerDate: Ukraine, Moldova23 June 2022Georgia, BosniaDecember 2023
cards.abstract:
The candidate status that the slides describe is a political step, because Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union does not use the term. It has the applicant address the Council, which acts unanimously after consulting the Commission and receiving the Parliament’s consent. In practice the Commission delivers an opinion first, and on 17 June 2022 it recommended candidate status for Ukraine on the understanding that listed reform steps were taken. On 23 and 24 June 2022 the European Council granted the status to Ukraine and Moldova and said it was ready to grant it to Georgia once the priorities in the Commission’s opinion had been addressed. It granted the status to Bosnia and Herzegovina on 15 December 2022, on condition that the country carry out the steps in the Commission’s communication of October 2022.

The slides say that the Council, or the European Council, grants candidate status unanimously after the Commission has delivered its opinion to the Council, and that any pre-conditions must then be met before the Council can decide unanimously to open negotiations. Their table of candidate countries lists Turkey, Montenegro, Serbia, Albania and North Macedonia beside Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that on 23 June 2022 the European Council granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova, while Georgia, which applied in March 2022 with Moldova, was held back by domestic political developments. They place the grants to Georgia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in December 2023, but the record dates Bosnia and Herzegovina’s to December 2022, and the European Council of 14 and 15 December 2023 granted Georgia’s on the understanding that steps from the Commission’s recommendation of 8 November 2023 were taken. They add that Georgia was the first candidate sharing neither land nor sea borders with the Union, yet the Commission reported in November 2025 that the European Council had found in 2024 that the Georgian authorities’ course of action de facto halted the accession process.

cards.question: Provided for the Western Balkan candidates in 2003, the _____ did not prevent a decade without significant progress on enlargement, even after Croatia’s accession in 2013.
cards.answerDate: Perspective2003Croatia joins2013
cards.abstract:
The European perspective is the Union’s promise that the Western Balkan countries will in the end become members, and the summit of 21 June 2003 in Thessaloniki declared that the future of the Balkans is within the European Union. The declaration listed Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, and Serbia and Montenegro as potential candidates, and made each country’s progress depend on its own merits in meeting the Copenhagen criteria. The Commission’s methodology of 2020 recalls that the Union has expressed unequivocal support for this perspective since the summits of 2000 and 2003. O’Brennan notes that Croatia joined on 1 July 2013 as a template for its neighbours, yet he describes the process in the region as on life support despite the promise made at Thessaloniki. Juncker announced on 15 July 2014 that the Western Balkans would keep a European perspective and negotiations would continue, but that no further enlargement would take place over the next five years.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that a European perspective was provided for the Western Balkan candidates in 2003. They write that, despite this perspective and Croatia’s successful accession in 2013, there was no significant progress on EU enlargement during the last decade, in their account of the period before 2022. They add that Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia were left outside the enlargement process, in contrast to the Western Balkan candidates, and that until 2022 their prospect of membership was non-existent. Dimitrova warns elsewhere that citizens of candidate states engaged since 2003, when Thessaloniki agreed an accession perspective, risk disillusionment with ever-receding prospects of enlargement. The slides on the Union’s transformative power say that it depends on candidates having a membership perspective, exercised through conditionality, capacity building and socialisation.

cards.abstract:
The North Macedonia veto was Bulgaria’s refusal on 17 November 2020 to approve the negotiating framework for North Macedonia, which blocked the official start of accession talks. Bulgaria had approved the framework for Albania, its foreign minister cited open disputes over history and language, and it wanted guarantees that Skopje would meet the 2017 Friendship Treaty. The block came after the Council decided on 25 March 2020 to open negotiations with North Macedonia, subject to endorsement by the European Council, because the country had met the conditions set in June 2018. Those conclusions also stressed the good-faith implementation of bilateral agreements, including the Treaty on Good Neighbourly Relations with Bulgaria. In December 2023 the European Council said it was ready to complete the opening phase once North Macedonia completed the constitutional changes referred to in the Council conclusions of 18 July 2022.

The slides list the North Macedonia veto, a delay in the start of negotiations with North Macedonia, among the consequences of foreign policy voting under unanimity. On the same list they name issue linkage, the strategic use of a vote under unanimity in foreign policy or related areas, and a delay in adopting sanctions against Belarus after the protests that followed the 2020 presidential election, due to the position of Cyprus. Cyprus held up those sanctions on 21 September 2020 by tying them to measures against Turkey over drilling in its exclusive economic zone, and the Council listed 40 Belarusian individuals only on 2 October 2020. Session 3 defines veto players, citing Tsebelis 2002, as individual or collective actors whose agreement is necessary for a change in the status quo, and Session 5’s table of candidate countries carries the words preparing to start followed by veto. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that in the month after the European Council’s decisions of 23 June 2022 the screening processes with Albania and North Macedonia were officially opened, and that institutional change in enlargement is still obstructed by veto players.

cards.question: Numbering more than a hundred since 1999 and managed by over 20 joint committees, the _____ have a non-member take over the acquis in the areas covered.
cards.answerDate: Free trade1972Bilateralsfrom 1999Package2024
cards.abstract:
The Swiss bilateral agreements are the sector treaties through which Switzerland, a member of neither the EU nor the European Economic Area, joins much of the single market. The Commission calls the free trade agreement of 1972 the cornerstone, and says that after Swiss voters rejected the European Economic Area in 1992 the sides agreed seven agreements, signed in 1999. Those seven are tied by a ‘guillotine clause’, so that ending one ends all the others six months later, and a second set in 2004 added Schengen and Dublin. Almost every agreement has its own joint committee, which meets once a year and can add new EU legislation, subject to the consent of the Swiss Federal Council. Lavenex calls this a deep form of external governance close to quasi-membership, yet the agreements are as a rule static, with dynamic alignment only in air transport and Schengen and Dublin.

The lecture slides list the series, beside the European Economic Area, as a comprehensive form of association, with the free trade agreement of 1972 and over a hundred agreements from 1999, managed by over 20 joint committees. The slides say Switzerland takes over the acquis, the body of EU law, in the areas covered and contributes to the EU cohesion fund, while Lavenex notes that later adaptation is voluntary, checked for ‘euro-compatibility’ since 1992. The slides add that Switzerland has aligned extensively, though not automatically, with EU sanctions, and Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley note that its refusal to allow Swiss-made ammunition to reach Ukraine led European governments to avoid Swiss equipment. In 2022, the slides say, 50% of Swiss exports went to the EU and 69% of imports came from it, and the Commission ranks Switzerland fourth among EU trade partners, with goods trade above €362 billion in 2025. The slides trace a revision in 2019 to 2021 and the Bilaterals III package, finalised between March and December 2024 and awaiting ratification in Switzerland after signature on 2 March 2026.

cards.question: Finalised between March and December 2024 and not yet in force, the _____ package includes dynamic harmonisation with EU law and new agreements in health, electricity and food safety.
cards.answerDate: FinalisedMarch–December 2024Programmesfrom 2025Upper house vote30 September 2026
cards.abstract:
Bilaterals III is the Swiss name for the package of agreements between Switzerland and the EU that was negotiated from 18 March to 20 December 2024. It followed a Common Understanding of November 2023, reached after 18 months of exploratory talks, and the negotiators held more than 200 meetings. One part updates five agreements of 1999, on free movement of persons, air transport, rail and road transport, mutual recognition and farm trade, while a second part adds new agreements on electricity, health and food safety. The updates are meant to ensure Switzerland’s dynamic alignment with EU law, to set up dispute resolution and to extend EU state aid rules to air and land transport. Lavenex and Veuthey argued in 2023 that, without regular updates, the substance of the bilateral agreements, and so market access, would gradually erode.

The lecture slides say the package was finalised between March and December 2024 and is for ratification in the Swiss Parliament, not yet in force, and the Swiss government records its signature on 2 March 2026. The slides place it after a revision in 2019 to 2021, when talks on the draft Institutional Framework Agreement were suspended and new negotiations failed, whereas the Swiss Federal Council records a decision on 26 May 2021 not to sign. The slides list dynamic harmonisation, which the Commission calls dynamic alignment, and new agreements in health, electricity and food safety, and they say Swiss participation in EU programmes has moved ahead separately since 2025. The slides call ratification a high hurdle, because on 30 September 2026 the upper house voted that a referendum would need a majority of voters and a majority of the 26 cantons, by 23 votes to 17 with 3 abstentions according to blue News. The Federal Council had preferred an optional referendum, which needs only a popular majority, and the National Council, which has yet to vote on the proposal, is expected to take up the package in its winter session.

cards.question: In May 2021 negotiations on the draft EU–Switzerland _____ were suspended, and new negotiations were unsuccessful, before the Bilaterals III package was finalised between March and December 2024.
cards.answerDate: Revision2019–2021SuspendedMay 2021Package2024
cards.abstract:
The Institutional Framework Agreement was a draft treaty meant to give Switzerland’s access to the EU internal market common rules, covering five existing market access agreements and all future ones. It grew out of EU dissatisfaction, since in 2010 the Council said that the system of bilateral agreements had ‘clearly reached its limits’ and asked for dynamic adaptation, homogeneous interpretation, surveillance and dispute settlement. Negotiations began in 2014, and a full draft text was agreed at political level in November 2018. The draft provided for dynamic updating of the agreements, state aid rules for air transport and an arbitration tribunal that would send questions of EU law to the Court of Justice for a binding ruling. The European Parliament recommended on 26 March 2019, by 393 votes to 132 with 81 abstentions, that the Swiss Federal Council conclude it once its consultation of Swiss stakeholders gave a positive result.

The lecture slides place the suspension of negotiations in May 2021 inside a revision of the relationship running from 2019 to 2021, after which new negotiations were launched but were unsuccessful. The record is blunter, since on 7 June 2019 the Federal Council told the Commission it wanted clarifications on state aid, wage protection and free movement of persons, and on 26 May 2021 it decided not to sign, which ended the talks. Lavenex and Veuthey call that a unilateral decision and warn that the existing agreements would lose substance and market access without regular updates. The slides describe the relationship as more than a hundred bilateral agreements from 1999 onwards, managed by more than 20 joint committees. Talks resumed after exploratory contacts in 2022 and 2023 and a Common Understanding in November 2023, and the Bilaterals III package, finalised between March and December 2024, adds the dynamic adoption of legislation that the slides call dynamic harmonisation, and awaits ratification.

cards.question: The Bilaterals III package between the EU and Switzerland includes _____ with EU law, alongside new agreements in health, electricity and food safety.
cards.answerDate: FinalisedMarch–December 2024
cards.abstract:
Dynamic harmonisation is the slides’ name for an arrangement in which a partner’s rules in a sector keep pace with EU law as that law changes, which EU texts call dynamic alignment and Swiss texts dynamic adoption. Lavenex contrasts the European Economic Area, whose rules adapt steadily to the evolving acquis, with the Swiss bilateral agreements, which are as a general rule static because they fix the scope of adaptation at signature. Only the agreements on air transport and on Schengen and Dublin provide for dynamic alignment with future EU law, and the air transport agreement also recognises the case law of the Court of Justice. Switzerland has also adapted voluntarily since 1992, checking each new law for ‘euro-compatibility’, and joint committees can add EU legislation to the agreements with the Federal Council’s consent. The EU pressed for more, and the draft institutional agreement of 2018 provided for the dynamic updating of the agreements within its scope.

The slides list dynamic harmonisation with EU law as the first item of the Bilaterals III package, ahead of new agreements in health, electricity and food safety, and say it was finalised between March and December 2024 and is not yet in force. They present Switzerland as their example of external governance, the extension of the EU’s legal rules, policies, standards and regulatory arrangements to third countries without membership, which needs no institutional expansion. The Commission says the updates to five agreements of 1999 ‘ensure Switzerland’s dynamic alignment with EU law’, as does the new food safety agreement, and the Federal Council adds dynamic adoption to all market access agreements. In return the Commission says Switzerland will be able to influence the design of relevant EU legislation, as the draft of 2018 already provided for Swiss experts in preparatory work. Lavenex and Veuthey note that omitting dynamic adoption formally preserved Swiss sovereignty, though voluntary adaptation compromised it in practice, and that the EU now expects such partners to accept it.

cards.question: On 30 September 2026 the Swiss upper house voted that a referendum on the EU package would need a _____: approval by a majority of voters and a majority in the 26 cantons.
cards.answerDate: Upper house vote30 September 2026Package2024
cards.abstract:
A double majority is a voting rule under which a proposal passes only if it wins both a majority of those voting and a majority of the cantons. Under Article 142 of the Swiss Federal Constitution, each canton’s vote follows the result of its own popular vote, and six cantons, among them Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, count for only half a cantonal vote. Article 140 requires it for revisions of the Constitution and for joining organisations for collective security or supranational communities, whereas Article 141 sends certain other treaties to an optional referendum, which a popular majority decides. The rule protects small cantons, and swissinfo reported in 2020 that only two of 481 popular initiatives voted on since 1891 had failed because the cantons overturned a popular majority. Australia also requires a double majority for constitutional changes.

The lecture slides say that on 30 September 2026 the Swiss upper house voted that a referendum on the EU package would need approval by the majority of voters and a majority in the 26 cantons, and that the lower house is to vote on the proposal. Blue News reported on 30 September 2026 that the vote was 23 in favour, 17 against and 3 abstentions, for a mandatory referendum ‘sui generis’, meaning of its own kind, which needs no amendment of the Constitution. Earlier, on 11 June 2026, the Council of States had only postponed the question, by 24 votes to 20, until a draft existed. The Federal Council had called for an optional referendum, which needs only a nationwide majority, and the slides call the double majority a high hurdle for Bilaterals III, which was finalised between March and December 2024 and is not yet in force. The National Council is expected to debate the package in its winter session, and Le News says a nationwide vote before the federal elections of autumn 2027 remains possible but would need a fast timetable.

cards.question: Listed with the dates 1963 and 1996 among examples of external governance, the _____ is accompanied by figures showing 42.7% of one partner’s goods exports going to the EU in 2025.
cards.answerDate: First date1963Second date1996Trade figures2025
cards.abstract:
The EU–Turkey Customs Union lets industrial goods move freely between the EU and Turkey, which applies the common customs tariff of the EU to other countries. Its legal basis is mainly Article 28 of the association agreement of 1963, an interim step towards the membership that Turkey had applied for in 1959. Decision No 1/95 of the EC–Turkey Association Council, adopted on 22 December 1995, set the rules for the final phase and entered into force on 31 December 1995, and the Commission dates the end of that phase to 1 January 1996. The union covers industrial goods but excludes agriculture except processed products, services, establishment and public procurement. Turkey must also align with the preferential trade regime of the EU within five years, whereas EU free trade agreements with third countries do not automatically cover Turkey.

The lecture slides list it with the dates 1963 and 1996 among their examples of external governance, beside the EU–Switzerland free trade agreement of 1972, EU–Norway of 1973 and EU–Japan, dated 2017 and in force from 2019. The slides also name accession association, with Turkey in the past, among the kinds of agreement around which external governance develops, although accession talks opened in October 2005 and in June 2018 the Council ruled out work on modernising the union. The slides rank Turkey as the 5th-largest EU trade partner, after Switzerland in 4th place and before Norway in 6th, and the Commission agrees, with 4.2% of EU goods trade in 2025. In 2025, the slides say, 42.7% of Turkey’s goods exports went to the EU and 35.3% of its imports came from it, and bilateral goods trade reached 217.6 bn, a record of over €217.6 billion by the Commission’s figure. El-Sahli notes that the EU can sign free trade agreements with third countries without Turkey while Turkey must apply the same external tariffs, and an SWP Comment of 2020 urged the EU to separate its accession framework from modernising the union.

cards.question: In force since February 2019, the _____ involves no policy or institutional integration and is described as a more conventional free trade relationship, though it can be seen as geopoliticization on both sides.
cards.answerDate: Listed2017In forceFebruary 2019Trade growth2018 to 2025
cards.abstract:
The EU–Japan Economic Partnership Agreement is, according to the European Parliament’s research service, the largest bilateral trade agreement the EU has concluded, covering around 640 million consumers and roughly a third of world GDP. Negotiations opened in March 2013, leaders agreed in principle on 6 July 2017, and the text was finalised on 8 December 2017, which Juncker and Abe welcomed. It was signed on 17 July 2018 and entered into force on 1 February 2019. At the end of the staging period Japan removes 97% of tariff lines on EU exports and the EU 99% on imports from Japan, and rice and seaweeds are the only items both sides excluded. It was negotiated amid the Brexit referendum and paused TTIP talks, and Bruegel notes that it gained heightened geopolitical importance after the US tariffs on steel and aluminium in 2018.

The lecture slides list EU–Japan among the agreements around which external governance develops, with 2017 as one date and 2019 as the year it came into force, while the record puts the final text in December 2017. The slides say it involves no policy or institutional integration and is a more conventional free trade relationship, and the research service adds that its regulatory cooperation is voluntary, each party keeping the right to regulate. The slides add that it can be seen as geopoliticization on both sides, citing Meunier and Nicolaidis for the idea that the geopoliticization of trade is the external face of economic statecraft, with trade policies embedded in power rivalries. Christou and Damro find that the Commission’s trade department still follows a market-liberal frame, while geopolitical pressure produces a counter-frame that links trade to security. The slides say numerous committees and working groups set up by the agreement let the two sides meet regularly, and that total trade rose 23.1% between 2018 and 2025, with services up 59%, goods up around 11% and Japan the 7th-largest partner.

cards.question: Listed as an example of other association among the agreements around which EU external governance develops, the _____ followed an association dated 2002.
cards.answerDate: Association2002Framework2022
cards.abstract:
The EU–Chile Advanced Framework Agreement is the treaty meant to modernise and replace the association agreement of 2002 between the EU and Chile. The agreement of 2002 had three pillars, political dialogue, cooperation and trade, and its trade part has applied since February 2003. Negotiations began in November 2017 under Council directives that were the first ever published before talks started, and the two sides reached a political conclusion on 9 December 2022. The new agreement has two parts, political dialogue and cooperation, and trade and investment, and because it falls under shared competence every member state must also ratify it. It was signed on 13 December 2023 beside an interim trade agreement, which repeats the trade pillar except investment protection and expires once the framework agreement enters into force.

The lecture slides give the EU–Chile Advanced Framework Agreement of 2022 as their example of other association, beside an association dated 2002, while the record dates the political conclusion to December 2022 and the signature to December 2023. The slides list it among the agreements around which external governance develops, with the European Economic Area, the Swiss treaties, EU–Japan, development cooperation with African, Caribbean and Pacific states, the new generation association agreements with Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, and the Armenia CEPA. The EU delegation says the new texts add articles on democratic principles, human rights and the rule of law, extend political dialogue to peace, justice and security, and make nearly all EU exports tariff-free. Dammert and Torreblanca note that the EU imports 80 per cent of its lithium from Chile, and they read the deal, with a memorandum on critical materials signed in July 2023, as progress in an à la carte multipolar world. The slides on the European Parliament list approving association and trade agreements, by assent, among its powers, and its foreign affairs and trade committees recommended consent to the agreement on 24 January 2024 by 66 votes to 12.

cards.question: Provisionally applied from May 2026, the _____ is the EU-level-only trade part of a deal that was separated in two for easier ratification, with a mixed agreement making up the other part.
cards.answerDate: Talks finished2019ConcludedDecember 2024Court requestJanuary 2026Provisionalfrom May 2026
cards.abstract:
The EU–Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement, which the slides call the iTA, is the trade part of a deal that, they say, was separated in two for easier ratification, the other part being the EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement, the EMPA. The Commission presented the deal as two parallel legal texts on 3 September 2025, and the iTA covers only provisions that fall under the exclusive competence of the Union. Its text has a preamble and 23 chapters, and the Commission says it will be repealed and replaced by the EMPA once that agreement is fully ratified. The negotiation behind it began formally in April 2000, was suspended in 2004 and produced a political agreement on 28 June 2019 that was never ratified. Talks were relaunched in March 2023, and the Commission President and four Mercosur presidents finalised the negotiations on 6 December 2024.

The slides say the iTA is at EU level only, whereas the EMPA is a mixed agreement that needs member state ratification, and that separating the two was politically and legally controversial. Parliament’s resolution of 21 January 2026 states that the EMPA needs unanimity in the Council and ratification by all 27 member states, whereas the iTA needs only a qualified majority in the Council and Parliament’s consent. In that resolution Parliament voiced concern that the split may be incompatible with Article 218 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and it decided to seek an opinion from the Court of Justice. The slides say this has effectively paused Parliament’s consent procedure with the Court’s decision awaited, and they describe the deal as partly in force but not fully ratified. The Commission announced on 27 February 2026 that it would apply the iTA provisionally, which began on 1 May 2026 as the slides say, while one legal commentator doubts that the agreement should be provisionally applied as it stands while the Court’s opinion is pending.

cards.question: Described in a Commission press release as the deal with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia, the _____ will create the world’s biggest free trade zone covering over 700 million consumers.
cards.answerDate: Talks finished2019ConcludedDecember 2024Court requestJanuary 2026
cards.abstract:
The EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement, which the slides call the EMPA, is the framework deal between the European Union and its member states, on one side, and the Common Market of the South with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, on the other. The Commission’s trade site says it has a political and cooperation pillar and a trade pillar. Its roots lie in the 1995 Interregional Framework Cooperation Agreement, a stepping stone towards an association agreement, and in Council directives of 17 September 1999 that sketched three pillars. Parliament’s resolution of 21 January 2026 notes that those directives authorised an association agreement, which requires Council unanimity and ratification by national parliaments. A political agreement of 28 June 2019 was never ratified, and the negotiations were finalised anew on 6 December 2024.

The slides quote a Commission press release that names the deal with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia as the EMPA and says it will create the world’s biggest free trade zone, covering a market of over 700 million consumers. The press release of 6 December 2024 quotes Kaja Kallas on a market for over 700 million people and names four Mercosur countries, and the Commission’s trade site likewise lists only Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. According to the slides, the EMPA is a mixed agreement with member state ratification needed, whereas the interim trade agreement is at EU level only, and the deal was separated in two for easier ratification, which was controversial. Parliament’s resolution says the EMPA needs unanimous approval in the Council, Parliament’s consent and ratification by all 27 member states, and the slides say its consent procedure has effectively been paused since the January 2026 request for a Court opinion. The slides use the same word for the EU–Ukraine association agreement, whose ratification they call slow and problematic, and a consultative Dutch referendum on 6 April 2016 rejected that agreement with 61 per cent of voters against.

cards.question: Negotiated in 2017, in force from 2021 and running to 386 articles, the _____ sets up a Partnership Council, a Partnership committee, a Parliamentary partnership committee and a civil society platform.
cards.answerDate: Negotiated2017In force2021Articles386
cards.abstract:
The Armenia CEPA is the Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement between the EU, Euratom and their member states and Armenia, which the slides list as a new generation trade and cooperation agreement. It is to replace the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement that entered into force on 1 July 1999 for ten years and was renewed automatically. It was signed in Brussels on 24 November 2017, substantial parts applied provisionally from 1 June 2018, and it entered into force on 1 March 2021 after ratification by Armenia, all member states and the European Parliament. Its text runs to 386 articles in eight titles, from objectives and general principles to institutional and final provisions. Article 2 makes respect for democratic principles, the rule of law and human rights an essential element of the agreement, and the Commission adds that it promotes legislative approximation to EU norms in many sectors.

The slides list a Partnership Council, a Partnership committee, a Parliamentary partnership committee and a civil society platform, and the text sets up all four in its institutional chapter. The Partnership Council meets at ministerial level at least once a year and takes decisions that bind the parties. The slides quote the preamble’s wish to develop regular political dialogue on bilateral and international issues of mutual interest, including regional aspects, taking into account the common foreign and security policy of the EU and the relevant policies of Armenia. The same recital recognises the importance Armenia attaches to its participation in international organisations and cooperation formats and its existing obligations arising from them. Górecki says Armenia dropped an association agreement in 2013 under Russian pressure to stay free to join the Eurasian Economic Union, and Parliament noted that the CEPA cannot remove tariff barriers for that reason, while the slides set it beside the Azerbaijan agreement of 1999 under the heading that different agreements reflect different political relations.

cards.question: In force from 1999, initially for ten years and then automatically renewed, the _____ has more than 100 articles, and a new agreement is in negotiation.
cards.answerDate: In force1999
cards.abstract:
The Azerbaijan PCA is the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement between the European Communities and their member states and Azerbaijan, which the slides set beside the Armenia CEPA under the heading that different agreements reflect different political relations. It was signed in Luxembourg on 22 April 1996, and the slides give it as in force from 1999, more exactly 1 July 1999 on the Official Journal record. It has 105 articles and aims at political dialogue, support for Azerbaijan’s democracy and market economy, trade and investment, and wider cooperation. Article 97 concluded it for an initial period of 10 years and renews it automatically year by year unless a party gives six months’ notice of denunciation. The Commission adds that it has no tariff preferences but eliminates trade quotas between the EU and Azerbaijan.

The slides give Article 2 as saying that respect for democracy and human rights underpin the partnership, and the text names democracy, international law, human rights and market economy principles as essential elements of the partnership. The slides quote the preamble’s commitment to strengthening the political and economic freedoms ‘which constitute the very basis of the partnership’, and the preamble also believes that full implementation will depend on and contribute to reforms in Azerbaijan, notably in the light of the conclusions of the CSCE Bonn Conference. The preamble is desirous of regular political dialogue on bilateral, regional and international issues, and Article 81 sets up a Cooperation Council that meets at ministerial level once a year, which Parliament’s summary lists with a Cooperation Committee and a parliamentary body. For comparison the Armenia CEPA has 386 articles and four joint bodies, as the slides list, against one ministerial council and two supporting bodies in the Azerbaijan text. The slides say a new agreement is in negotiation, while the Commission says talks opened in February 2017 and have been on hold since February 2022, and the External Action Service said in 2021 that discussions were ongoing.

cards.question: Trade is a key instrument of EU civilian power, leading some to apply the idea of _____ to the Union, whose link between market access and human rights was stronger in the late 1990s.
cards.answerDate: First cited2012Cited again2017Lisbon point2019
cards.abstract:
Market power Europe is the idea, set out on the slides about trade and EU power, that trade is a key instrument of EU civilian power, leading some to characterise the EU as a ‘market power’. The slides cite Damro 2012 and Meunier and Nicolaidis 2017 for that characterisation. Damro’s article of 2012 argues that the EU is fundamentally a large single market with significant institutional features and competing interest groups, and that it is best understood as a market power Europe. In his account the EU exercises power by externalising its economic and social market-related policies and regulatory measures, whether intentionally or not, with persuasive and coercive means. Damro’s article of 2015 offers the idea as a dynamic conceptual framework for the wider debate on the EU as a power.

The slides link access to EU markets to human rights, labour and environmental rights, and they say that this link was stronger in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Article 207 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires the common commercial policy to be conducted in the context of the principles and objectives of the Union’s external action. Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union lists among those principles democracy, the rule of law and human rights, and the slides add that the Lisbon treaty assigned non-commercial objectives to commercial policy but that this has been challenged, citing Meunier and Nicolaidis 2019. That article of 2019 argues that the most important recent development is the geopoliticization of trade and investment policy, which may challenge the interdependence and multilateralism that the EU has long safeguarded. The slides of the first session say that the EU’s trade power has been part of its geopolitical power for most of its existence, and they quote Mario Draghi saying that for years the Union believed its 450 million consumers would bring geopolitical power, an illusion that he expected the year of his speech to end.

cards.question: Trade is a key instrument of EU civilian power, a statement credited to a 2012 work by _____ and to a second work from 2017 by two other authors.

cards.abstract:
The slides cite Chad Damro as ‘Damro 2012’, giving the surname and the year only. An article that fits the slides’ idea of a ‘market power’ is his ‘Market Power Europe’, published in 2012 in the Journal of European Public Policy, volume 19, issue 5, pages 682 to 699. In it Damro argues that the EU is fundamentally a large single market with significant institutional features and competing interest groups. He proposes that the EU may be best understood as a market power Europe that exercises power through the externalisation of its economic and social market-related policies and regulatory measures. Such power, he adds, may be intentional or unintentional behaviour, and the EU is fully capable of using both persuasive and coercive means to influence international affairs.

The slides cite Damro 2012, together with Meunier and Nicolaidis 2017, for the statement that trade is a key instrument of EU civilian power, leading some to characterise the EU as a ‘market power’. The citation sits on the slide headed Trade and EU power, which also notes that access to EU markets was linked to human rights, labour and environmental rights, more strongly in the late 1990s and early 2000s. In 2015 Damro returned to the concept in a second article, which presents it as a dynamic conceptual framework for researching the EU as a power. The treaty basis for such trade power is Article 207 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which has the common commercial policy conducted in the context of the principles and objectives of the Union’s external action. The slide adds that the Lisbon treaty assigned non-commercial objectives to commercial policy but that this has been challenged, a point it cites to a 2019 work of Meunier and Nicolaidis, who describe a geopoliticization of trade and investment policy.

cards.question: Trade policies come to be embedded in power rivalries in the _____, defined as the external face of economic statecraft and set beside the politicisation of trade agreements seen in protests.

cards.abstract:
Geopoliticisation of trade is defined on the slides, after Meunier and Nicolaidis, as the external face of economic statecraft, whereby trade policies come to be embedded in power rivalries. Meunier and Nicolaidis argue in 2019 that the most important recent development is the geopoliticization of trade and investment policy, shown by tariffs, retaliatory measures and counter-retaliation. They see it as a challenge to the interdependence and multilateralism that the EU has long safeguarded. The European Parliament’s research service noted in 2016 that TTIP was promoted for commercial and geopolitical reasons and as a model for new trade rules. The slides add, with the date 2019, that geopolitics is both a product and a tool of security policies, and they set the idea beside the politicisation of trade agreements, shown by protests against TTIP and CETA.

The slides use the EU–Ukraine agreement as a case, citing Dimitrova and Dragneva 2022 for Russia geopoliticising it in 2011 to 2013, which their abstract describes as contestation fuelled by Russia’s grievances. According to the slides, Russia first argued that the agreement would negatively affect Russia–Ukraine trade, the European Commission convened a joint tripartite commission to examine such effects, and Russian grievances also targeted the agreement’s foreign and security cooperation. Dragneva and Wolczuk wrote in 2012 that Russia’s opposition did not seem premised on economic grounds and that Putin had threatened protective measures in April 2011. The slides quote Deyermond 2016, as cited by Dimitrova and Dragneva, saying that Russia sought to assert the precedence of its regional project, the Eurasian Economic Union or EEU, launched on 1 January 2015, and framed the EU as a ‘spoiler’ of its legitimate interests, in line with perceptions of limited sovereignty of its post-Soviet neighbours. The slides also see the EU–Japan agreement as geopoliticisation on both sides and ask whether the EU is winning or losing, while the Commission calls that agreement, signed on 17 July 2018, a key political priority.
questions: The EU–Ukraine agreement became a case of _____ when Russia, in 2011 to 2013, argued that it would hurt Russia–Ukraine trade and targeted its foreign and security cooperation.
Russia’s assertion of the precedence of its regional project, and its framing of the EU as a ‘spoiler’ of its legitimate interests, are examples of _____ affecting an association agreement.

cards.sub: Lecture 6 · Trade, agreements and external governance

cards.question: The 2019 work of _____ is cited for the point that the Lisbon treaty assigned non-commercial objectives to commercial policy, though this has been challenged.
cards.answerDate: Cited work2017Cited again2019
cards.abstract:
The slides cite Meunier and Nicolaidis by surnames and years only, for works of 2017 and 2019 and for a definition of the geopoliticisation of trade. The authors are Sophie Meunier and Kalypso Nicolaïdis, and their review of 2019 is called ‘The Geopoliticization of European Trade and Investment Policy’, published in volume 57 of the Journal of Common Market Studies. Their abstract says that the academic debate on EU trade policy had been dominated by claims about its new politicisation, with the mobilisation against TTIP and Wallonia’s blocking of CETA as the leading cases. They push back on two counts, arguing first that internal politicisation is nothing new, since member states had long fought hard political fights over competences and interests behind the scenes. Second, they argue that the most important recent development is geopoliticization, as the rhetoric of trade negotiations gave way in 2018 to ‘the language of economic battlefields and trade warfare’.

The 2017 citation on the slides sits beside Damro 2012 and supports the statement that trade is a key instrument of EU civilian power, leading some to characterise the EU as a ‘market power’. Damro’s article argues that the EU is best understood as a market power Europe that exercises power by externalising its market-related policies and regulatory measures. The 2019 citation supports the point that the Lisbon treaty assigned non-commercial objectives to commercial policy, but that this has been challenged. Article 207 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union puts the common commercial policy in the context of the Union’s external action, whose principles in Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union include democracy, the rule of law and human rights. The slides also credit the two authors with the definition of geopoliticisation as the external face of economic statecraft, whereby trade policies come to be embedded in power rivalries, and add, with the date 2019, that geopolitics is both a product and a tool of security policies.

cards.sub: Lecture 6 · Trade, agreements and external governance

cards.question: Protests against the _____ and against CETA are given as an example of the politicisation of trade agreements, with polarisation of opinions and debates.
cards.abstract:
TTIP, the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership, was a proposed comprehensive trade and investment agreement between the European Union and the United States, for which the Council issued negotiating directives in June 2013 and declassified them in October 2014 after an inquiry by the European Ombudsman. The Parliament’s research service reports that it was championed for commercial reasons, as a means of building a new model for trade rules, and also for geopolitical ones. The same briefing records that the 13th round of talks, held in New York in April 2016, covered every chapter of the agreement. Still disputed that summer were the EU’s proposed investment court, meant to replace the arbitration the United States favoured, and food safety rules. CETA, the agreement with Canada, was signed on 30 October 2016 and has applied provisionally since 21 September 2017, but as a mixed agreement it needs ratification by every member state.

The lecture slides name TTIP, together with CETA, as the trade agreements that were protested against, in their point on the politicisation of trade agreements. They describe that politicisation as protests, a polarisation of opinions and debates, and set it beside the definition by Meunier and Nicolaidis of the geopoliticisation of trade as the external face of economic statecraft, whereby trade policies come to be embedded in power rivalries. De Bièvre and Poletti define politicisation as polarised opinion, public salience and a growing number of societal actors, and observe that TTIP and CETA were strongly contested while other EU trade negotiations proceeded with far less of it. Garcia-Duran Huet and Eliasson argue that a large and professionally organised campaign by European civil society groups shifted public opinion and affected policy, and that the TTIP talks were frozen in late 2016. In May 2017 the General Court annulled the Commission’s refusal to register the ‘Stop TTIP’ citizens’ initiative, which sought to prevent negotiations on TTIP and CETA.

The politicisation of trade agreements is illustrated by protests against CETA and against the _____, a point set beside the external face of economic statecraft.

cards.question: Asserting the precedence of its regional project, the _____, Russia framed the EU as a ‘spoiler’ of its legitimate interests, in line with perceptions of limited sovereignty of its post-Soviet neighbours.
cards.abstract:
The Eurasian Economic Union was launched on 1 January 2015 as the third stage of economic integration among post-Soviet states, following the customs union and the Single Economic Space. Russia, Belarus and Kazakhstan signed the treaty establishing it on 29 May 2014, extending the provisions of the existing Eurasian Customs Union. By February 2015 its members were Russia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, with Kyrgyzstan expected to join in May 2015. Dragneva and Wolczuk wrote in 2012 that Russia saw the customs union as a vehicle for reintegrating the post-Soviet space, with an institutional framework explicitly modelled on the EU and intended as a modernising alternative to it. They called this a normative rivalry, because Russia now competed in exporting governance to the shared neighbourhood, a field the EU had held alone until then.

The slides quote Deyermond 2016, as cited by Dimitrova and Dragneva, on the EU–Ukraine agreement: in putting forward its concerns Russia sought to assert the precedence of its regional project, the EEU, and framed the EU as a ‘spoiler’ of its legitimate interests, in line with perceptions of limited sovereignty of its post-Soviet neighbours. The slides place this in Dimitrova and Dragneva 2022, who say that Russia geopoliticised the agreement in 2011 to 2013, arguing first that it would harm Russia–Ukraine trade and also targeting its foreign and security cooperation. That article argues that the agreement influenced the EU only indirectly, through the power imbalance between the parties, its politicisation at home and the geopolitical contestation driven by Russia’s objections. Oleksandr Sushko reported in September 2013 that the Russian presidential aide Sergey Glazyev had said Ukraine could not take part in the Customs Union, or be an observer in the future Union, if it signed an Association Agreement. Susan Stewart adds that from August 2013 Russia created problems at the border for Ukrainian exports, and that President Yanukovych then refused to sign the agreement and made a deal with Putin instead.

A quotation from 2016 cited in a 2022 work describes Russia’s regional project, the _____, as the project whose precedence Russia sought to assert.

cards.question: Also called the ‘Revolution of dignity’, the _____ was the name of the mass protests in Ukraine in favour of the Association Agreement between the EU and Ukraine.
cards.answerDate: Signing rejectedNovember 2013Crimea annexedMarch 2014SignedJune 2014In forceDecember 2016
cards.abstract:
The Euromaidan, also called the Revolution of Dignity, was the wave of mass protests that began in the Maidan Square in Kyiv in November 2013. It began on 21 November 2013, when Ukraine’s government suspended plans to sign the EU Association Agreement, and more than 1,500 people marched to the square that evening. Susan Stewart writes that the protests quickly went beyond Ukraine’s relationship with the EU and became a struggle against corruption and against President Yanukovych, and spread to other cities. On the night of 30 November the government ordered the Berkut police to clear the square, and on 19 January 2014 over 200,000 people protested in central Kyiv. More than 100 people died in the protests of 18 to 20 February, and on 22 February Yanukovych fled, first to Donetsk and then to Crimea, while parliament voted to remove him.

The slides describe the Euromaidan as politicisation in Ukraine in favour of the agreement, and say that signing it in November 2013 was rejected by Yanukovych under Russian pressure. Oleksandr Sushko called the agreement in September 2013 the most extensive international agreement the EU had ever concluded with a third country, and said the Kremlin was trying to derail it. The slides say that negotiating the agreement took more than seven years and was led by different presidents, and that Poroshenko signed it in June 2014, after the Russian annexation of Crimea in March 2014. The Commission and the European External Action Service date the negotiations to 2007 to 2011 and the signing to 21 March and 27 June 2014, with the free trade part applied since 1 January 2016 and entry into force on 1 September 2017, where the slides say December 2016. The slides call the agreement mixed and a template for reforms, and Dimitrova and Dragneva argue that the EU innovated at institutional, constitutional and policy levels to support its implementation, secure ratification and answer Russia’s geopolitical moves.
questions: Mass protests, the _____, marked the politicisation in Ukraine in favour of the agreement that Poroshenko eventually signed in 2014 and that entered into force in December 2016.
Under Russian pressure, signing the Association Agreement was rejected in November 2013, and the _____ was the politicisation in Ukraine, as mass protests, in favour of it.

cards.question: The negative result of the _____, held in April 2016, showed that the issue was easily politicised among citizens and where the red lines were for bringing Ukraine closer to the Union.
cards.answer: Dutch referendum on the Association Agreement
cards.answerDate: ReferendumApril 2016In forceDecember 2016
cards.abstract:
The Dutch referendum on the Association Agreement was a consultative vote held in the Netherlands on 6 April 2016 on the EU–Ukraine Association Agreement. A law in force from 1 July 2015 let citizens demand a consultative referendum with at least 300,000 signatures, and three Eurosceptic groups collected 470,000, which obliged the authorities to hold it. Of those voting 61 per cent were against, on a turnout of about 32 per cent that only just cleared the 30 per cent needed for the result to be valid. Prime Minister Mark Rutte said the agreement could not be ratified in its present form, although the other 27 member states had already ratified it. Boersma argued at the time that the vote was not really about Ukraine, noting that opponents called the deal a first step towards Ukrainian membership and that the organisers reportedly cared little about Ukraine itself.

The slides give the referendum as their example of the slow and problematic ratification of the EU–Ukraine agreement, which they call a mixed agreement, one of the EU and its member states. They date the agreement’s entry into force to December 2016, but the Commission and the European External Action Service give 1 September 2017, after ratification by all member states, with the free trade part applied provisionally since 1 January 2016. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops say the negative result showed that the issue was easily politicised among citizens and where the red lines were for bringing Ukraine closer to the Union. In December 2016 the leaders of the 28 member states adopted a Decision, binding on themselves, that took effect once the Netherlands ratified, and Wessel calls it a self-binding common understanding that cannot bind the EU or Ukraine. Dimitrova and Dragneva count among the EU’s innovations a constitutional one, securing ratification despite politicisation in the Netherlands, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops add that until 2022 member states were constrained by public opinion about closer relations with Ukraine.

cards.question: The EU has been forced into survival mode by a crisis of _____, which it answers by defending institutions such as the WTO, reforming them with a mixed record and extending them.
cards.answerDate: Cited work2023
cards.abstract:
Multilateralism, cooperation among many states through shared institutions and rules, is written into the Treaty on European Union, whose Article 21 says the Union shall promote multilateral solutions to common problems, in particular in the framework of the United Nations. The same article lists among its aims an international system based on stronger multilateral cooperation and good global governance. The EU Global Strategy of June 2016 repeats the commitment, saying the Union will promote a rules-based global order with multilateralism as its key principle and the United Nations at its core, and that its trade agreements should support returning the World Trade Organization to the centre of global negotiations. It adds that the commitment means reforming the UN, since resisting change risks the erosion of such institutions. Dworkin and Gowan of the European Council on Foreign Relations argued in 2019 that the multilateral system faced three linked crises, of power, relevance and legitimacy, and called the EU its most consistent supporter.

The lecture slides, in a section headed Beyond external governance, say that a crisis of multilateralism has forced the EU and multilateral institutions into survival mode. They list three efforts to sustain multilateralism: to defend its institutions, with the WTO as the example, to reform them, with what the slides call a mixed record, and to extend them, a point cited to Schuette and Dijkstra 2023. Schuette and Dijkstra sort the EU’s efforts since 2016 into the same three kinds, defending, reforming and extending, and find the EU fairly effective at temporarily defending institutions but largely unsuccessful at reforming or extending them. The WTO shows the strain, because since 11 December 2019 its Appellate Body has been unable to deliver binding rulings on trade disputes, as new appointments to it are blocked. The EU answered with the multi-party interim appeal arbitration arrangement, effective from 30 April 2020, and pursues WTO reform that would ease plurilateral agreements and find a lasting solution to the Appellate Body problem.

A 2023 work is cited for the effort to extend institutions, one of three ways of sustaining _____, alongside defending the WTO and reforming with a mixed record.

cards.question: The extension of the EU’s legal rules, policies, standards and regulatory arrangements to third countries, without those countries moving towards membership, is known as _____ in the literature on the Union’s reach.
cards.abstract:
External governance is the concept political scientists use for the expanding scope of EU rules beyond the Union’s borders. Sandra Lavenex wrote in 2004 that its crucial criterion is the extension of the legal boundary of the Union’s authority beyond institutional integration, which happens when parts of the acquis, the body of EU law, are extended to non-member states. She presented the ‘wider Europe’ initiative, ‘everything but institutions’ as an alternative to membership, as a way to manage the Union’s new interdependence with its near abroad. Lavenex and Schimmelfennig added in 2009 that enlargement is the most prominent case of projecting the acquis, but that the ‘enlargement model’ might soon reach exhaustion, so forms of integration into EU rules below membership deserve study. Dragneva and Wolczuk called the Association Agreement the most ambitious mechanism for exporting EU governance to the post-Soviet countries, and urged the EU in 2012 to revisit its external governance approach to its eastern neighbourhood.

The slides define external governance as the extension of the EU’s legal rules, policies, standards and regulatory arrangements to third countries without these countries moving towards membership, and cite Lavenex 2004 and Lavenex and Schimmelfennig 2009. They add that the legal boundaries of the EU can be extended without an institutional expansion, and that legal, institutional and transactional boundaries move in different degrees. They say the expansion of such activities was driven by perceptions of interdependence and by the EU’s own responsibilities to contribute to problem solving in given geographical areas. Their example is Switzerland, with more than a hundred bilateral agreements from 1999 onwards, managed by more than 20 joint committees, under which it takes over the acquis in the areas covered and contributes to the EU cohesion fund, though the European Parliament counts over 120 agreements, beginning with a free trade agreement of 1972. The Session 5 slides say that the enlargement approach extends the EU’s regulatory framework beyond its borders, which they call by definition external governance.

Because legal boundaries can be extended without an institutional expansion, and legal, institutional and transactional boundaries move in different degrees, the Union’s rules can reach third countries through _____ rather than through membership.

cards.question: Cited for defining external governance as the movement of the EU’s institutional and regulatory boundaries beyond its borders, _____ also wrote a 2004 article on EU external governance in ‘wider Europe’.
cards.answerDate: Article2004Joint work2009Later article2024
cards.abstract:
Sandra Lavenex is a political scientist, Professor of European and International Politics at the University of Geneva and a visiting professor at the College of Europe. In August 2004 she published the article ‘EU external governance in “wider Europe”’ in the Journal of European Public Policy, in volume 11, number 4, on pages 680 to 700. Its abstract presents the ‘wider Europe’ initiative, which offered the eastern and southern neighbours ‘everything but institutions’ as an alternative to membership, as part of an ambitious agenda to manage the enlarged Union’s new interdependence. Her argument was that external governance seeks to expand the Union’s ‘legal boundary’ with only limited openings of its ‘institutional boundary’, so that the EU oscillates between an inclusionary and an exclusionary approach towards its near abroad. With Frank Schimmelfennig she developed the concept in 2009 as the expanding scope of EU rules beyond EU borders, and distinguished three institutional modes of external governance, hierarchy, networks and markets.

The lecture slides credit Lavenex 2004 with defining external governance as the movement of the EU’s institutional and regulatory boundaries beyond its borders, and list the article as additional literature. They also cite Lavenex and Schimmelfennig 2009 for expanding the scope of EU rules beyond its borders, and the slide on the modes of external governance ends with the same citation. In the 2004 article itself Lavenex writes that the institutional and the legal form different boundaries which need not always move together, so that the legal boundary can be extended without a parallel institutional expansion. Policy analysts took up the term, as when Dragneva and Wolczuk urged the EU in 2012 to revisit its ‘external governance’ approach to its eastern neighbourhood. Lavenex is one of six authors of a 2024 article on EU and NATO enlargements after 2022, which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops cite for the EU’s decisions in the three years after the invasion, and her contribution to it examines geopolitical enlargement and organised hypocrisy.

cards.sub: Lecture 6 · Trade, agreements and external governance

cards.question: Hierarchical, networks and markets are the three _____, with enlargement and the neighbourhood policy given as examples of the hierarchical kind and the European Economic Area as an example of markets.
cards.abstract:
The modes of external governance are the institutional forms through which EU rules reach third countries, and Lavenex and Schimmelfennig named three in 2009: hierarchy, networks and markets. Lavenex had earlier sorted the EU’s outer ties by type of association, from quasi-membership, such as the European Economic Area and the Swiss bilateral treaties, through accession and neighbourhood association to development and transatlantic co-operation. Hierarchy means a formal relationship of domination and subordination with binding rules, and the authors call the European Economic Area the clearest quasi-hierarchical case, although non-members formally keep their sovereignty. The European Parliament adds that new internal market law enters the EEA by a Joint Committee decision, and that Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein cannot change its substance when they transpose it. Networks are horizontal, with formal equality of partners and coordination of rules, while markets are loosely institutionalised, with competition and mutual recognition as the mechanisms, and in governance by externalisation firms that want access to the EU market follow its rules.

The lecture slides give the same three modes, hierarchical, networks and markets, and list enlargement and the European neighbourhood policy as examples of the hierarchical mode. For networks they say that relations are formally equal, with ongoing coordination. The markets mode lists the European Economic Area, free movement of persons and governance by externalisation, and the slide ends with a citation of Lavenex and Schimmelfennig 2009. That placement is looser than the article, which calls the EEA the clearest quasi-hierarchical case, finds network features in its Joint Committee, and says the neighbourhood policy lacks the legal formalisation of association with western neighbours, although the European Parliament describes that policy as primarily bilateral and built on association agreements. The Session 5 slides say that enlargement relies on conditionality for rule and norm adoption by candidates, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia had been governed by the Neighbourhood Policy and also had a close Eastern Partnership relationship.

Enlargement, which relies on conditionality and extends the EU’s regulatory framework beyond its borders, is the example of the hierarchical type among the three _____ by which the Union projects its rules.

cards.question: The contrast of _____ turns on whether objectives are defined by one state or organisation and directed one-sidedly, or defined jointly among actors in a decentralised way with repeated interactions.
cards.abstract:
Governance versus policy contrasts a foreign policy view and an external governance view of how the Union affects states outside it. Lavenex and Schimmelfennig say the foreign policy view treats countries or regions as its units, whereas the governance view starts from systems of rules and looks at norm diffusion and policy transfer. They understand governance as institutionalised forms of coordinated action that aim at collectively binding agreements, and in its network form no party can bind another without its consent. Lavenex wrote in 2004 that governance is less than government but more than co-operation, since it implies a system of rules beyond voluntary co-operation. Lavenex and Schimmelfennig find network elements in the joint evaluation of progress in Association Councils, and the Parliament’s fact sheet says action plans are drawn up between the EU and most partner countries.

The lecture slides contrast governance versus policy in two columns, and under policy they say that objectives are defined by a state or organisation, that policy evolves with internal political change and change in the international context, and that it is mostly one-sided and directed towards specific countries or regions or, domestically, sectors. Under governance they say that objectives are jointly defined among actors and that governance is decentralised, with repeated interactions that also involve lower-level actors: experts, civil society and business. The Session 5 slides use the term for enlargement: the EU interacts with actors next to governments to support reform and adjustment, which the slides call enlargement governance. They add that these interactions ensure success in reform and common standards setting, and that domestic civil society and its key norms can contribute to a positive outcome. The Session 6 slides list expert joint bodies, technical committees, working groups and civil society fora among the joint bodies of agreements, as in the Ukraine agreement, which sets up an association council, an association committee, a parliamentary association committee and a civil society platform.
questions: Experts, civil society and business join repeated interactions on one side of the contrast of _____, while the other side evolves with internal political change and changes in the international context.

cards.question: Dated 1994, the _____ brings together the EU member states and EFTA members such as Iceland and Norway, with no access to decision making but input in working groups.
cards.answerDate: Slide date1994
cards.abstract:
The European Economic Area, the EEA, extends the EU’s internal market to the European Free Trade Association countries that join, and its agreement was signed on 2 May 1992 and took effect on 1 January 1994. It covers the 27 EU member states and three of the four EFTA members, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, while Switzerland arranges access to the single market through bilateral agreements. Members take on the four freedoms of goods, persons, services and capital, with competition rules and horizontal policies such as consumer protection. It leaves out the common agricultural and fisheries policies, the customs union, the common trade policy and the common foreign and security policy. In December 2002 Commission President Romano Prodi called the EEA a working economic area as close to the EU as possible without membership and proposed using its experience as a model for the neighbours.

The lecture slides date the EEA to 1994 and list the EU member states plus the EFTA members Iceland, Norway and Lichtenstein, as the slide spells the third. The slides describe the arrangement as no access to decision making but input in working groups, and EFTA agrees that the three states have no formal access to EU decision making but may sit in Commission expert groups. They name it first among the comprehensive forms of association, with the multiple bilateral treaties with Switzerland, and first under the markets mode of external governance, with free movement of persons and governance by externalisation. Lavenex and Schimmelfennig call the EEA the clearest quasi-hierarchical system of external governance, though mutual recognition also reaches it through the full transfer of Single Market legislation. The slide expands EFTA as the European Free Trade Area, but the body is an Association, as in Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley, who report that the White Paper for European Defence lets €150 billion of new EU financed spending go to Ukraine and to members of EFTA and the EEA, in practice Switzerland and Norway.

cards.question: Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are tied to the EU by the new generation kind of _____, built around a Deep and Comprehensive Trade agreement and summed up as everything but the institutions.
cards.answerDate: EU–Chile2002Ukraine signedJune 2014Dutch voteApril 2016Ukraine in forceDecember 2016
cards.abstract:
An association agreement is concluded under Article 217 TFEU and establishes an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure. The Ukrainian agreement was signed on 21 March and 27 June 2014 and applied provisionally from November 2014, its free trade area from 1 January 2016. The European External Action Service announced on 1 September 2017 that the agreement entered fully into force, later than the December 2016 that the slides give. Its institutional chapters set up an association council, an association committee, a parliamentary association committee and a civil society platform, the council meeting at ministerial level at least once a year. The Dutch consultative referendum of 2016 had 32.3% turnout and 61% against, and the Dutch Parliament proceeded with ratification only in 2017, after a decision of the Heads of State or Government in December 2016 gave clarifications.

The slides sort the kinds into comprehensive association such as the EEA and the Swiss treaties, other association such as EU–Chile, accession association, once covering Central and Eastern Europe and Turkey, and new generation association agreements for Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, summed up as everything but the institutions. The Session 3 slides on the European Parliament list approving association and trade agreements by assent among its roles. For the Ukrainian case the slides say negotiating took more than 7 years, led by different presidents, and that Yanukovich rejected signing in November 2013 under Russian pressure, and a Warsaw analysis dates the suspension of preparations to 21 November, on the eve of the Vilnius summit. Politicisation in Ukraine in favour of the agreement brought mass protests, the Euromaidan or ‘Revolution of dignity’, and the slides date the Russian annexation of the Crimea to March 2014 and Poroshenko’s signing to June 2014. The slides call ratification slow and problematic, with the Dutch referendum as an example, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that its negative result showed the issue was easily politicised and where the red lines lay.

cards.question: Ukraine’s Association agreement with the EU, which contains the _____ and offers a template for reforms, faced Russian arguments that it would negatively affect Russia–Ukraine trade.
cards.answerDate: Geopoliticised2011–2013Ukraine signedJune 2014Ukraine in forceDecember 2016
cards.abstract:
The DCFTA, the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area, is an integral part of the EU–Ukraine Association Agreement and, the Commission says, opens markets for goods and services on both sides under predictable and enforceable trade rules. It eliminated the majority of tariffs, 98.1% on the EU side and 99.1% on the Ukrainian side, and makes customs procedures more efficient. It also gradually approximates Ukrainian legislation, rules and procedures, including standards, to those of the EU. It has applied provisionally since 1 January 2016, and a Parliament study of 2020 notes that the EU was then Ukraine’s largest trading partner, with 40% of trade flows. In 2025 the EU and Ukraine reviewed it under Article 29 of the association agreement, and the upgraded text entered into force on 29 October 2025.

The slides say that the EU–Ukraine Association agreement contains a Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade agreement, offers a template for reforms and is a mixed agreement of the EU and the member states. Citing Dimitrova and Dragneva 2022, the slides say the agreement became geopoliticised by Russia in 2011–2013, when Russia argued that it would negatively affect Russia–Ukraine trade and the Commission convened a joint tripartite commission to examine such effects. The slides quote Deyermond as saying that Russia sought to assert the precedence of its regional project, the EEU, framing the EU as a ‘spoiler’ of Russia’s legitimate interests, and a Warsaw analysis of 2013 notes that Russia’s market took about a third of Ukraine’s exports. The Commission dates its trilateral talks with Ukraine and Russia from July 2014 to 21 December 2015, when the final ministerial meeting ended without agreement and Commissioner Malmström said the DCFTA could not be amended, directly or indirectly. Dimitrova and Dragneva argue that the agreement influenced the EU indirectly through power asymmetry, politicisation and Russia’s geopoliticisation, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia stayed outside enlargement, with no prospect of membership until 2022.

cards.sub: Lecture 6 · Trade, agreements and external governance

cards.question: Association with Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine of the Deep and Comprehensive Trade kind is summed up in the phrase _____, in a list that also names the EEA, EU–Chile and accession association.
cards.answerDate: Ukraine in forceDecember 2016Candidate status23 June 2022Georgia statusDecember 2023
cards.abstract:
Everything but the institutions is a phrase of Romano Prodi, then President of the European Commission, who in December 2002 described his offer to the neighbours as ‘sharing everything with the Union but institutions’. He spoke in Brussels a week before the Copenhagen summit that was to invite up to ten new members, offering more than partnership and less than membership, without precluding membership. The offer centred on a common market with free trade, an open investment regime and approximation of legislation, and he named the European Economic Area as a working example. Lavenex wrote in 2004 that the ‘wider Europe’ initiative, by offering ‘everything but institutions’, proposed an alternative to membership, while the EU expected these countries to align legislation with the acquis. The Eastern Partnership, inaugurated in 2009 on the basis of the Neighbourhood Policy, upgraded relations with Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine.

The slides use the phrase to sum up the new generation association agreements that they list for Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, described as Deep and Comprehensive Trade agreement association. It appears on the slide on how EU external governance develops around agreements, whose other entries include the EEA and the Swiss treaties, EU–Chile, EU–Japan, development cooperation with ACP states, the Armenian CEPA and accession association. The slides add that the Association agreement with Ukraine contains a Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade agreement and is a mixed agreement of the EU and the member states. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the relations of Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia had been governed by the Neighbourhood Policy and that, despite the Eastern Partnership and their comprehensive association and trade agreements, they were left outside enlargement, with no prospect of membership until 2022. The European Council granted Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022, Moldova the same day and Georgia in December 2023, and the authors say the EU’s discourse shifted from ‘creating a ring of friends’ to ‘creating one of us’.

cards.question: An agreement with Ukraine that involves both the EU and its member states is a _____, and its ratification was slow and problematic, as the Dutch referendum of April 2016 showed.
cards.answerDate: Mercosur textDecember 2024Dutch voteApril 2016Ukraine in forceDecember 2016
cards.abstract:
A mixed agreement is an international agreement that the Union and its member states conclude together, because some of its provisions fall within competences shared between them. Under Article 218 TFEU the Council concludes an association agreement unanimously, after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament. The Court of Justice ruled on 16 May 2017, in Opinion 2/15, that the free trade agreement with Singapore could not, in its current form, be concluded by the EU alone. It found exclusive EU competence over most of the agreement, but not over non-direct ‘portfolio’ investment or the settlement of disputes between investors and states. The Dutch consultative referendum of 2016 on the Ukraine agreement had 32.3% turnout and 61% against, and led the Prime Minister to put ratification on hold.

The slides call the EU–Ukraine Association agreement a mixed agreement, involving the EU and the member states, and list slow and problematic ratification for it, with the Dutch referendum as an example. For EU–Mercosur they say that the new version, concluded in December 2024 and proposed for adoption in 2025, was separated in two parts for easier ratification, the iTA and the EMPA. The iTA is at EU level only, while the EMPA is a mixed agreement for which member state ratification is needed, and the Commission presented the two texts on 3 September 2025. The slides give the decision route for the new version as European Parliament consent and Council qualified majority voting and call the separation politically and legally controversial, and on 21 January 2026 Parliament voted by 334 to 324 to seek a Court of Justice opinion, citing possible incompatibility of the split with Article 218(2) and (4) TFEU. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the negative result of the consultative referendum held in the Netherlands in April 2016 showed that the issue was easily politicised among citizens, and where the red lines were for bringing Ukraine closer to the Union.
