cards.question: Listed beside the Partnership Council among the joint bodies that structure relations between the EU and its partners, the _____ comes before parliamentary, expert and civil society bodies in the same list.
cards.abstract:
The Association Council is the ministerial body that an association agreement sets up to supervise and monitor how the agreement is applied and to review its functioning in the light of its objectives. In the agreements with Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine it is one of four bodies, with an association committee, a parliamentary association committee and a civil society platform, and it meets at ministerial level at least once a year. The Azerbaijan partnership agreement of 1996 has a counterpart under another name, a Cooperation Council that supervises the agreement and meets at ministerial level once a year. That council consists of members of the Council of the European Union and the Commission and of the Azerbaijani government, and a Cooperation Committee of senior civil servants assists it, while a separate Parliamentary Cooperation Committee joins members of the two parliaments. Under Article 218(9) TFEU the Council fixes the Union’s position in a body set up by an agreement when that body adopts acts with legal effects.

The slides name the Association Council as one of the joint bodies through which agreements structure relations between the EU and its partners, beside the Partnership Council. The slide lists six things agreements contain: the legal framework of the treaties, trade, regulation, dispute resolution, special clauses on democracy, human rights and rule of law, and joint bodies. After the two councils the joint bodies listed are parliamentary joint bodies, expert joint bodies, technical committees and working groups, and civil society fora. The slides give two examples, the Cooperation Council of the Azerbaijan agreement and the Partnership Council, Partnership committee, Parliamentary partnership committee and civil society platform of the Armenian one, and add that more than 20 joint committees manage the Swiss agreements. The Commission’s report of 2022 on Armenia calls the Partnership Council the highest-level body set up under the agreement, and the European Economic and Social Committee says the civil society platform helps prepare recommendations for it.

cards.question: Special clauses linking the functioning of an agreement with democracy, human rights and rule of law make up the _____, which is among the things agreements contain but is not in all of them.
cards.answerDate: PCA in force1999CEPA negotiated2017CEPA in force2021
cards.abstract:
A democracy and human rights clause writes into an agreement values that Article 21 TEU says guide the Union’s external action, among them democracy, the rule of law and human rights. The EU builds it as an ‘essential elements’ clause, which lets one party take appropriate measures after serious breaches by the other. The first agreements with an explicit clause were signed in 1992 with Brazil, the Andean countries, the Baltic states and Albania, and in 1995 the Community decided to include such clauses in all new agreements. The clause rests on Article 60 of the Vienna Convention on the law of treaties, which allows suspension after a material breach, though not every clause mentions the rule of law. The Parliament’s research service reports that the EU prefers constructive engagement and has never used the clause to suspend trade preferences.

The slides define it as a special clause linking functioning with democracy, human rights and rule of law, and stress that such clauses are not in all agreements. They list these clauses among the ways agreements structure relations, and say that the link of access to EU markets to human rights, labour and environmental rights was stronger in the late 1990s and early 2000s. For the Azerbaijan Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, in force from 1999 and renewed automatically after ten years, the slides cite Article 2, and the treaty text makes respect for democracy, international law and human rights ‘essential elements of partnership and of this Agreement’. A joint declaration counts violation of those essential elements as a case of special urgency, so a party may act without first referring to the Cooperation Council, and the Parliament’s summary calls the arrangement a conditional clause allowing suspension, even unilaterally. The slides add that the Armenian Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement, negotiated in 2017, has 386 articles and records a commitment to democratic principles and rule of law, and the Commission dates its full entry into force to 1 March 2021.

cards.question: Begun on 18 August 2026 by ING's chief economist, the weekly series _____ borrows its name from a bank's sales presentation and sets out to rebalance how Europe's economy is seen.
cards.answerDate: Idea set out12 February 2026Series began18 August 2026
cards.abstract:
Europe's Pitch Book is a series of weekly opinion articles offering a glass-half-full perspective on the European economy, by Marieke Blom, Chief Economist and Global Head of Research at ING, whose first instalment appeared on 18 August 2026. It starts with demographics and productivity, turns to defence, energy, digital technology, trade and the financial landscape, then to Poland, Spain, Italy and Romania, and ends with health and happiness. The name borrows from investment banking, where a pitch book is a presentation that tries to win a client's business by explaining why the bank is best placed to lead a deal. Blom set out the idea in an ING article of 12 February 2026, which asked what would belong on the first slide if Europe were sold to Europeans. Both pieces respond to the report on European competitiveness that Mario Draghi delivered in September 2024, which called the need to raise Europe's productivity an 'existential challenge'.

Blom argues that the European storyline has become systematically more negative than the underlying reality, while stressing that this is not an 'everything is fine' argument. The idea that popular stories spread and move economic behaviour is the subject of narrative economics, which Robert Shiller set out in his 2017 address to the American Economic Association. A European Central Bank survey in November 2025 found euro area households that struggled to predict their finances likelier to plan cuts in spending, 53% against 42%, and delays to big purchases, 37% against 26%. In February Blom suggested that gloom may be contributing to hesitant corporate investment and high savings, noting that 46% of Europeans said in October 2025 that the economic situation was bad. The first article ends with evidence she found more positive than expected, including Europeans increasingly feeling European and foreign buying of euro area assets at a peak, and says momentum may be turning.

cards.question: Having started as a trainee at ABN AMRO in 1999, _____ became ING's chief economist for the Netherlands in 2014 and its global head of research on 1 August 2022.
cards.answerDate: Career began1999Joined ING2014Global role1 August 2022
cards.abstract:
Marieke Blom is Chief Economist and Global Head of Research at ING Group and part of the ING Think team for Europe and the Netherlands. She has worked at ING since 2014 and has been the Netherlands' chief economist since that year, and she was appointed global chief economist with effect from 1 August 2022. In that role she leads ING Research, which ING described in 2022 as a team of more than 60 economists and analysts who interpret economic trends and events every day. Before ING she was a senior manager at the Amsterdam consultancy De Argumentenfabriek, having started as a trainee and economist at ABN AMRO in 1999. She holds a master's degree in monetary economics and wrote her thesis at the research department of the Dutch Central Bank, and ING's profile lists her as a board member of the Dutch Royal Economic Society.

The same profile lists her on the advisory committee of the National Growth Fund, set up by decree on 4 September 2020 to advise ministers on investment proposals of at least €30 million in infrastructure, innovation and knowledge development. Under the decree its members serve in a personal capacity and must step aside from an advisory round if they have a relationship with a party involved in a proposal. In 2026 Blom argues that the European storyline has become systematically more negative than the underlying reality. In February she proposed that Europe 'sell' itself to its own citizens, starting with strengths they recognise, and in August she began a weekly series to compare perception with reality. She says she is not arguing that everything is fine, and that the series will explain where criticism is justified while adding nuances she thinks the debate lacks.

cards.question: When households expecting a downturn cut spending and firms hold back investment, the gloom helps cause the slump it fears, a loop called _____ that can begin with beliefs unrelated to fundamentals.
cards.abstract:
Self-fulfilling pessimism is the process by which a widespread expectation of weak economic conditions helps to produce them, because people who expect bad times act in ways that make bad times more likely. John Maynard Keynes argued in 1936 that most decisions to do something positive rest on animal spirits, a spontaneous urge to action, so that if they dim, enterprise will fade and die. Robert Shiller later argued that popular stories about the economy can make a recession more severe by changing how many people decide to spend, to hire and to start businesses. Uncertainty, which is related to pessimism but not the same, can also freeze firms: a model estimated on firm-level data finds that a jump in uncertainty makes them pause investment and hiring for a time. Theory allows 'sentiment shocks', changes in beliefs unrelated to economic fundamentals, to move spending on their own, but they are hard to measure because sentiment often moves with fundamentals such as expected income.

Marieke Blom argues that excessively pessimistic households spend less, that pessimistic firms invest less, and that investors need to see some upside before they commit capital, so that pessimism can become self-fulfilling. The European Central Bank reports that euro area households who find their finances hard to predict are likelier to plan spending cuts, and counts elevated uncertainty as an important factor behind the persistently high saving rate. Evidence that sentiment moves spending beyond fundamentals is weaker, since a 2025 study at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City found the link between consumer sentiment and real spending growth modest historically. A study of US counties found that large partisan swings in optimism about government policy after presidential elections had a very small effect on spending, one that could not be told from zero. The strength of self-fulfilling pessimism is therefore an open empirical question, and Blom's argument is a claim about how far it applies to Europe, not a measured result.

cards.question: An ING economist calls _____ the drift in which policymakers, fearing they could capsize the economy, turn from core principles with more state aid, reviewed merger guidelines and a delayed carbon market.
cards.abstract:
Panic politics is Marieke Blom's name for policymakers turning from core principles of the European Union on state aid, protectionism, mergers, trade deals and climate policy because they fear they could capsize the economy. Under Article 107 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, state aid that favours certain firms is incompatible with the internal market where it distorts competition and affects trade, with listed exceptions. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine the Commission adopted a Temporary Crisis Framework on 23 March 2022, widened it to the net-zero transition in 2023, and on 25 June 2025 replaced it with the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework. It is also rewriting its merger guidelines of 2004 and 2008, publishing a draft on 30 April 2026 in what it calls the broadest review in two decades, while keeping the mission of merger control unchanged. The Draghi report wanted competition policy to adapt so that it is not a barrier, but warned that generous aid from the largest countries has an adverse impact on the single market.

The Emissions Trading System, launched in 2005, caps greenhouse gas emissions from power, industry and aviation, about 40% of the Union's total, and obliges polluters to surrender allowances. Parliament backed a deal on 10 February 2026 that set the 2040 target at a 90% cut and postponed ETS2, which prices emissions from buildings and road transport, from 2027 to 2028. On 17 July 2026 the Commission proposed a targeted revision of the Emissions Trading System, which it presents as strengthening industrial competitiveness and supporting the 2040 target. On 16 December 2025 it proposed lowering the 2035 CO2 target for new cars and vans from 100% to 90%, still under negotiation in the Council in June 2026. Blom reads such shifts as fear rather than strategy, while the Commission presents its car and emissions trading proposals as flexibility and competitiveness, so the label is her interpretation, not a finding.

cards.question: Newsrooms hold that _____, which is why a factory closure draws more attention than an expansion and a crisis draws more clicks than steady progress, an effect social media amplifies.
cards.abstract:
Bad news sells is the newsroom idea, often put as 'if it bleeds, it leads', that stories of crime, bloodshed and tragedy sell more papers than good news. Researchers who study news selection list 'bad news', stories with negative overtones such as conflict or tragedy, among the news values, a taxonomy dating from a 1965 study of foreign news. In 711 lead stories from 10 British newspapers in 2014, bad news was the most frequent of those values, and several titles carried about six times as much bad news as good. A 17-country experiment found stronger physical reactions to negative video news on average, and a preregistered Dutch replication found suggestive support while showing that negative news mainly produced negative feeling. A Federal Reserve study found that the tone and volume of economic reporting affect consumer sentiment and at times pulled it away from what fundamentals suggested.

On the web the pattern is measurable: in randomised tests of about 105,000 headline variants on Upworthy, each extra negative word raised the click-through rate by 2.3%. Social media can amplify hostile content, since across 2.7 million posts from news outlets and members of Congress, posts about the political out-group were shared about twice as often as posts about the in-group. Marieke Blom gives 'bad news sells' as the first of three reasons for a persistent skew in how Europe is seen: a factory closure draws more attention than an expansion, a crisis more clicks than steady progress. Her other two reasons are that economic forecasting rewards pessimism more than optimism, and a political angle in which lobbying needs urgency and opposition politicians gain by talking the economy down. The pull has limits, since 40% of respondents across markets in a 2025 survey said they sometimes or often avoid the news, up from 29% in 2017.

cards.question: Defence, energy, digital technology, trade and the financial landscape are what an ING economist labels the _____, each of which her series promises to examine against the evidence.
cards.answerDate: Introduced18 August 2026
cards.abstract:
The five ugly challenges are Marieke Blom's label, in the first article of her Europe's Pitch Book series, for defence, energy, digital technology, trade and the financial landscape. In defence the Draghi report noted twelve types of battle tank in Europe against one in the United States, and the joint White Paper of 19 March 2025 calls the industry too fragmented to supply the quantities needed. In energy the report found that EU companies paid electricity prices two to three times, and gas prices four to five times, those in the United States, a gap it put down mainly to Europe's lack of natural resources. In digital technology it said that Europe largely missed the internet-led digital revolution and had only four of the world's top 50 tech companies. In trade it observed that rapid world trade growth looked to have passed, and on 21 August 2025 the United States committed in a joint framework to apply the higher of its usual tariff or 15% to most EU goods.

The financial landscape is the fifth: the report found that EU households saved €1,390 billion in 2022 against €840 billion in the United States yet held less wealth, and named fragmented capital markets as a key reason. The Commission's savings and investments union aims to connect household savings with the funding that European businesses need to grow, innovate and create jobs. On defence the White Paper proposed SAFE, up to €150 billion in loans backed by the EU budget, and projected that defence investment could reach at least €800 billion over four years. Blom says she will offer a different perspective on each challenge, comparing perception with reality, explaining where criticism is justified and adding nuances she thinks are missing from the debate. She places them after what she calls 'the bad stuff' of demographics and productivity, and before Poland, Spain, Italy and Romania, with one article a week until just before Christmas.

cards.question: In defence policy, a _____ is unfolding, according to a March 2025 commentary: a watershed in which discussion of European defence financing takes centre stage and the Commission emerges as a key player.
cards.answerDate: Commentary11 March 2025
cards.abstract:
The European Zeitenwende is the name that Hofmann and De Vries give to a watershed in European defence policy, borrowing a German word for a historic turning point. In Germany, Chancellor Olaf Scholz told the Bundestag on 27 February 2022 that the Russian attack three days earlier “marks a watershed in the history of our continent”, in the official English translation. He announced a one-off €100 billion special fund for the armed forces and a pledge to invest more than 2% of gross domestic product in defence every year. Jana Puglierin of the European Council on Foreign Relations wrote in 2024 that the fund laid the groundwork for making up 30 years of underfinancing, but that it was expected to run out around the end of 2027. The shift then reached the EU, where the European Council said on 6 March 2025 that Europe must become more sovereign and more responsible for its own defence.

Hofmann and De Vries say the watershed is one in which discussion of European defence financing takes centre stage and the European Commission emerges as a key player in security and defence. In their account a newly aggressive Russia and an unpredictable United States forced a strategic rethink, a radical departure from the piecemeal advances in European security policy since the end of the Cold War. They add that joint procurement was once seen as a tentative step, and eight days after their commentary the Commission said its ReArm Europe plan enables spending of over €800 billion. They recall that the European Defence Community, signed by six states in May 1952, collapsed when French domestic politics led parliament to reject it, which the European Parliament dates to 30 August 1954. Later efforts faltered over concerns about undermining NATO, and as the EU moves out of NATO’s shadow, the authors argue, the stakes rise because voters who have prioritised welfare must bear the cost of rearmament.

cards.question: Voters in Europe have traditionally put social welfare ahead of defence, so rearmament forces a renegotiation of the welfare state around the _____ trade-off between military and civilian spending, a delicate balancing act.
cards.answerDate: ECFR surveymid-2024Commentary11 March 2025
cards.abstract:
Guns or butter is the old shorthand for the trade-off between military spending, the guns, and social spending, the butter. In 2025 NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told the European Parliament that a small fraction of what European states spend on pensions, health and social security would make defence much stronger. Marta Prochwicz Jazowska and Paweł Zerka of the European Council on Foreign Relations wrote in April 2025 that the belief in a choice between guns and butter makes some leaders reluctant to speak openly about raising defence spending. Jeromin Zettelmeyer of Bruegel concluded in March 2025 that higher German defence spending would be fiscally sustainable but would require cuts elsewhere and would breach EU fiscal rules. Carlo Bastasin of the Brookings Institution wrote in September 2025 that Italy’s government faces a difficult trade-off between military and welfare spending, because the former is unpopular.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley use the phrase for choices between defence and civilian spending that mobilising private capital offers governments and the EU a way to avoid. They add that the 2025 White Paper for European Defence encourages private capital investment, which brings trade-offs because private finance has its own interests and may be less reliable than EU or state financing. Hofmann and De Vries do not use the phrase, but they write that the normalisation of war is forcing a renegotiation of the European welfare state, a delicate balancing act that will decide whether defence budgets stay sustainable. They note that voters have traditionally prioritised social welfare, and report a European Council on Foreign Relations survey of mid-2024 in which majorities in France and Italy opposed more defence spending if it came at the expense of healthcare and education. That think tank’s own brief on its May 2024 poll of 19,566 adults in 15 countries said most Europeans were unprepared to spend more on defence and named Italy, Greece, Spain and Switzerland as countries with majorities against.
questions: In France and Italy a survey of mid-2024 found majorities opposed to higher defence spending if it cost healthcare and education, the kind of _____ choice that private capital might help governments avoid.

Mobilising private capital, one article on defence production argues, offers governments and the EU a way to avoid _____ choices between defence and civilian spending, though private equity brings its own risks.

cards.question: In a _____ survey from late 2023, 89% of Europeans backed humanitarian aid for those affected by the war in Ukraine, yet only 60% endorsed financing arms deliveries.
cards.answerDate: Surveylate 2023Commentary11 March 2025
cards.abstract:
The Eurobarometer is the European Union’s public opinion survey, created to track over time what Europeans think, and its first Standard Eurobarometer was published in July 1974. Academic work asks parties the same questions, and an expert survey of 269 parties in 29 countries in mid-2023 found that 97 rejected at least one of weapons, refugees, Ukraine’s path to EU membership or higher energy costs. Standard Eurobarometer 100 was in the field from 23 October to 15 November 2023, when 26,471 EU citizens were interviewed face to face in the 27 member states. The Commission published the results on 13 December 2023 and reported that almost nine in ten agreed with humanitarian support, more than eight in ten with welcoming people fleeing the war, and 72% with financial support. Around six in ten approved of granting Ukraine candidate status, at 61%, and of the EU financing military equipment for Ukraine, at 60%.

Hofmann and De Vries argue that leaders must secure long-term public support for deeper defence commitments and aid to Ukraine, but that recent polls suggest it is waning. Their first poll is this Eurobarometer, in which 89% backed humanitarian aid, 84% accepting refugees, 72% financial aid and only 60% the financing of arms deliveries. They call the 61% for Ukraine’s EU candidacy a concerning figure, given the political capital invested in Kyiv’s European integration. The next survey, Standard Eurobarometer 101, found 87% for humanitarian support and 70% for financial support, each down 2 points, while the 60% for military equipment was unchanged. The authors call such figures static and turn to the eupinions tracking, whose December 2023 survey found 60% support for Ukraine’s accession across the EU but 52% opposition in Germany, which the European Council on Foreign Relations also found unconvinced by the bid in May 2024.

cards.question: Since March 2022 survey research called _____ and conducted by the Bertelsmann Stiftung has tracked European sentiment on military aid, refugee policy, defence cooperation and Ukraine’s EU bid.
cards.answerDate: Tracking beganMarch 2022Latest figureslate 2024
cards.abstract:
The eupinions project is the Bertelsmann Stiftung’s tool for tracking European public opinion, launched in 2015 and supported by the King Baudouin Foundation since 2020. In 2022 the foundation described it as developed with Dalia Research, and by December 2023 its data came from Latana, in samples of about 13,300 people drawn each quarter from all 27 member states in 22 languages. The samples are weighted to Eurostat statistics, and country comparisons cover only seven countries with large enough samples, namely Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain. Its Ukraine tracking began in March 2022, and in October 2022 it reported that 60% of Europeans backed arms deliveries through the EU, with Italy the only one of the seven countries where a majority was against. Academic work asks parties the same questions, and an expert survey of 269 parties in mid-2023 found that 97 rejected at least one of weapons, refugees, Ukraine’s EU path or higher energy costs.

Hofmann and De Vries write that eupinions has tracked shifting European sentiment on military aid, refugee policy, defence cooperation and Ukraine’s EU bid since March 2022. They present it as showing the broader trends behind the static figures of a single poll, and say its results highlight a slow but steady erosion of support. On military aid, they report Poland’s support falling from 84% in March 2022 to 71% by late 2024, Italy the most sceptical, and the EU-wide figure for weapons deliveries down to 51% by the end of 2024. On refugees, they report approval falling from 93% to 75% in Spain and from 86% to 58% in Germany, the largest drop in the bloc, though an EU-wide 64% still backed accepting them. On defence cooperation, they report falls in Spain from 92% to 83% and in France from 87% to 71%, but note that 78% of Europeans still favoured closer military collaboration, and they see cracks appearing.

cards.question: Surveys tracking European views since March 2022 point to the _____ for Ukraine and for deeper defence commitments: backing for weapons deliveries across the EU had fallen to just 51% by late 2024.
cards.answerDate: Tracking beganMarch 2022Eurobarometerlate 2023ECFR surveymid-2024Latest figureslate 2024
cards.abstract:
Eroding public support is a gradual fall in the share of citizens who back a policy, and in October 2022 the Bertelsmann Stiftung’s eupinions survey already reported initial signs that approval of the response to Ukraine was crumbling. The Eurobarometer of autumn 2023 still found almost nine in ten agreeing with humanitarian support for Ukraine, but only 72% with financial support and 60% with the EU financing military equipment. In spring 2024 humanitarian and financial support each slipped 2 points, to 87% and 70%, while the military figure stayed at 60%. The eupinions wave of December 2023 showed a strong desire to support Ukraine alongside concerns about costs, and 52% of Germans opposed Ukraine’s accession. Research on party positions found that populist rhetoric and scepticism of the EU explain the bulk of the variation in party support for Ukraine, although many strongly populist parties take moderate pro-Ukraine positions in government.

Hofmann and De Vries identify eroding public support as a risk to Europe’s rearmament, because leaders must secure long-term backing for deeper defence commitments and aid to Ukraine, yet recent polls suggest it is waning. They warn that without it Europe’s newfound defence ambitions may prove fragile, since rearmament is expensive and citizens must not only understand but also accept the financial sacrifices it entails. They cite the late 2023 Eurobarometer and the eupinions tracking since March 2022, which they say shows a slow but steady erosion, with backing for weapons deliveries across the EU down to 51% by the end of 2024. Approval of accepting Ukrainian refugees fell from 93% to 75% in Spain and from 86% to 58% in Germany, though 64% of Europeans still backed it at the end of 2024. They add that a European Council on Foreign Relations survey of mid-2024 found majorities in France and Italy opposed to more defence spending at the expense of social priorities, and that think tank’s own brief found most Europeans unprepared to spend more.

cards.question: Failure to manage expectations about the cost of rearmament could embolden far-right populists and bring a _____ that destabilises European security, much as the Trump administration is now disrupting America’s strategic commitments.
cards.answerDate: Commentary11 March 2025ECFR surveymid-2024
cards.abstract:
A populist backlash in defence policy would be voters turning to parties that resist rearmament or its cost, and many of Europe’s populist challenger parties, the European Council on Foreign Relations found in 2025, oppose the EU’s rearmament plans and prefer a national vision of security. Research on party positions in mid-2023 found that populist rhetoric and scepticism of the EU explain the bulk of the variation in party support for Ukraine, although many strongly populist parties take moderate pro-Ukraine positions in government. In Germany, the Bertelsmann Stiftung found in December 2023 that 82% of supporters of the Alternative für Deutschland rejected arms deliveries to Ukraine and 81% opposed Ukraine’s accession to the EU. Marta Prochwicz Jazowska and Paweł Zerka argued in April 2025 that leaders should show that defence and social priorities can be reconciled, which needs sound financing. In March 2025 the Commission invited member states to activate the national escape clause of the Stability and Growth Pact, giving them room to raise defence spending by up to 1.5% of gross domestic product a year for four years within EU fiscal rules.

Hofmann and De Vries do not use the word backlash, but they warn that failure to manage expectations about the cost of rearmament could embolden far-right populists. They say this would destabilise European security in much the same way that the Trump administration is now disrupting America’s strategic commitments. Five days before their commentary the European Council had said that Europe must become more responsible for its own defence and called Russia’s war an existential challenge for the EU. They add that voters have traditionally prioritised social welfare over defence, that recent polls suggest support for Ukraine is waning, and that a mid-2024 survey found majorities in France and Italy opposed to more defence spending at the expense of healthcare and education. Without a transparent and honest dialogue about the trade-offs involved, they conclude, Europe’s security ambitions could falter at the ballot box.
questions: Because voters have traditionally prioritised welfare over defence and polls show support waning, leaders who do not explain the sacrifices of rearmament risk a _____ at the ballot box.

cards.question: A durable security strategy, one March 2025 commentary argues, needs a sustained effort to rally opinion around a compelling story of urgency and sacrifice: the _____ that leaders must forge.
cards.answerDate: Commentary11 March 2025
cards.abstract:
An honest narrative is a public account of why a policy is needed and what it will cost, and Hofmann and De Vries ask European leaders to forge one for defence. Opinion researchers had made a similar point earlier, as Isabell Hoffmann of the Bertelsmann Stiftung said in October 2022 that it was becoming increasingly important to carry the public along in terms of argumentation and communication. She warned of a risk that the desire to help and the private burdens would come into conflict, and that political conflict could arise. In Belgium, the Egmont Institute noted in March 2025, headlines such as “pensions or tanks?” had ignited public debate, and most political parties had been reluctant to support greater defence efforts. Marta Prochwicz Jazowska and Paweł Zerka of the European Council on Foreign Relations argued in April 2025 that leaders should cite concrete economic benefits and not abstract appeals, and that the right message varies by country.

Hofmann and De Vries say that maintaining a credible and durable security strategy requires a sustained effort to rally public opinion. The narrative, they say, must convey both the geopolitical urgency of the moment and the sacrifices needed to meet it. Their reason is that rearmament is expensive, citizens must not only understand but also accept its financial sacrifices, and voters have traditionally prioritised social welfare over defence. Official texts already carry the urgency half of such a story, as the European Council called Russia’s war an existential challenge on 6 March 2025 and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on 19 March that “the era of the peace dividend is long gone”. Without a transparent and honest dialogue about the trade-offs, the authors warn, security ambitions could falter at the ballot box, and they close by asking whether leaders and citizens will bear the costs of shaping Europe’s future or risk having it shaped for them.
questions: Without a transparent dialogue about the trade-offs, Europe’s security ambitions could falter at the ballot box, so leaders need the _____ about both the geopolitical urgency and the sacrifices required of citizens.

cards.question: Proposed as an analytical tool for settings where a critical juncture may be expected rather than incremental change, the _____ arranges six cumulative stages, from a change of discourse up to constitutional-level change.
cards.abstract:
The stairway of change is a tool that Antoaneta Dimitrova, Seda Gürkan and Joachim Koops built from institutionalist theory to detect whether a policy has really taken a new path after an external shock. Many historical institutionalists divide political history into long periods of continuity and critical junctures, moments of substantial institutional change that move development onto a new path. Capoccia and Kelemen define a critical juncture as a relatively short period in which the probability that agents’ choices will affect the outcome of interest is substantially heightened, and they note that the literature offers little guidance on identifying one. Hall and Taylor add that many historical institutionalists lack a well-developed account of what precipitates a juncture, although they generally stress economic crisis and military conflict. Punctuated-equilibrium theory likewise expects long stretches of stability and small adjustments to be interrupted occasionally by large-scale departures from the past.

The authors call the stairway a tool for a setting where a critical juncture can be expected, as opposed to normal circumstances, when incremental change can be expected. It has six cumulative stages, from a change of discourse through policy decisions, organisational arrangements, funds and resources and institutional arrangements below the constitutional level, up to constitutional-level change. The boxes towards the top cannot be ticked before the earlier ones have emerged, the authors hold, although the levels can overlap, and organisational and funding changes can each be an entry point. They note that funding is flexible to redirect, as the European Peace Facility, an off-budget instrument operational since 1 July 2021, was used from 28 February 2022 to support Ukraine. Applying the test, they find that enlargement reached only funding and organisational change, while security and defence reached institutional change, one step below the constitutional-level change that a critical juncture requires.
questions: Under the _____ framework, the boxes towards the top cannot be ticked before the earlier ones have emerged, and enlargement is judged to have reached only the funding and organisational stages.
In the framework called the _____, security and defence has reached institutional change, one step below the constitutional-level change that the authors say a critical juncture requires.

cards.question: In the stairway framework, the _____ asks whether decisions break with previous ones and revise the substance of policy, or are incremental and follow a clear path-dependent pattern.
cards.abstract:
Scope of change is one of two criteria, with sustainability, by which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops judge whether a policy has taken a new path, and it denotes how significant the changes are in substantive terms. Its contrast comes from historical institutionalism, in which institutions are persistent features that push development along a set of ‘paths’. In judging scope the authors ask whether decisions break with earlier ones and revise or devise policy measures, rather than being incremental and following a clear path-dependent pattern. They use four indicators: decisions that depart in substance, actors re-orienting to new incentives and constraints, changes in decision making that facilitate the policy, and constitutional-level change that locks in different rules. For enlargement the baseline is Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, under which the Council acts unanimously on an application and all the contracting states ratify the accession agreement.

On 23 June 2022 the European Council granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova and recognised the European perspective of Georgia, and on 14 December 2023 it decided to grant Georgia candidate status. The authors call this a radical shift, because it upgraded these countries from neighbours to potential members and moved the EU’s logic from “creating a ring of friends” to “creating one of us”, giving enlargement decisions unprecedented scope. In security and defence they cite the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine, which they call the first EU military training mission within member states and which the Council launched on 15 November 2022 for training on EU soil. They also cite the adaptation in March 2022 of the European Peace Facility to finance lethal equipment for the first time, while the Parliament’s research service dates the first such assistance measures from 28 February 2022. Sanctions on Russia are a mixed case, because the 17 packages now include the energy sector yet build on the 2014 response, and the authors conclude that neither policy has reached constitutional-level change.
questions: The war eased political constraints, and granting candidate status to Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia was judged a radical shift, giving enlargement decisions unprecedented _____ even though their sustainability remained in question.

Four indicators, among them relevant actors re-orienting to new incentives and constitutional-level change that locks in new decision-making rules, measure the _____, the criterion that stands beside sustainability.

cards.question: Whether decisions and organisational changes become embedded in decision-making, institutional and constitutional-level rules, rather than staying rhetorical or temporary, defines the _____, the criterion that stands beside scope in the stairway framework.
cards.abstract:
Sustainability of change is the second criterion, with scope, by which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops judge a policy, and it asks whether the policy is embedded in different decision-making, institutional and constitutional-level rules. The idea echoes historical institutionalism, in which increasing returns make the costs of exit rise with each step along a path, so that a course of action can become very hard to reverse. In the EU the highest rules are the Treaties, and Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union requires the Council to act unanimously on an application and all the contracting states to ratify accession. Article 31 requires the European Council and the Council to act unanimously on the common foreign and security policy unless the chapter provides otherwise, and its qualified majority provisions do not apply to decisions with military or defence implications. Parliament’s resolution of 29 February 2024 says that recent difficulties with sanctions decisions confirm the need to move away from unanimity, and that passerelle clauses could switch specific areas to qualified majority voting at once.

The authors ask whether decisions, initiatives, organisational changes and capacity building are becoming institutionalised through higher-level adjustments of formal and informal rules. The alternative is a mostly rhetorical response with no concrete financial or organisational consequences, or temporary, transitionary arrangements that respond only superficially to external pressures. Assistance measures under the European Peace Facility, for example, carry end dates, the first running from 28 February 2022 until 28 February 2024 and later extended to 28 February 2027. On enlargement the authors say sustainability remains in question, because progress stumbles against unanimity, a lack of appetite for treaty reform and veto players, and in security and defence they note that unanimity rules still prevail. They conclude that enlargement reached only funding and organisational change, while security and defence is a step higher at institutional change, and because both sit below the constitutional level the changes are not irreversible.
questions: Although enlargement decisions had unprecedented scope, the _____ remains in question, because progress stumbles against unanimous decision-making, a lack of appetite for treaty reform and obstruction by veto players.

A response to an external shock that stays rhetorical, brings no concrete financial or organisational consequences or consists of temporary arrangements fails the test of _____, according to the authors.

cards.question: Reached through treaty amendment, a landmark decision of the Court of Justice or recursive change such as trilogues, the _____ is the sixth and top stage of the stairway framework.
cards.abstract:
Constitutional-level change is the sixth and top stage of the stairway of change, which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops apply where higher-level constraints make policy change difficult. In the EU the constitutional level is the Treaties, which under the ordinary procedure in Article 48 of the Treaty on European Union change by common accord of the governments and take effect once all Member States ratify them. The Court of Justice can reshape the rules, as in Van Gend en Loos of 5 February 1963, when it established direct effect, the principle that individuals can rely on EU law before national courts. The Lisbon Treaty added a passerelle clause that lets the Council move from unanimity to qualified majority voting once the European Council unanimously agrees, yet the Parliament’s research service still called such clauses unused in 2020. Trilogues are informal meetings of Parliament, Council and Commission that began in the early 1990s and have no explicit reference in the Treaties.

The authors say constitutional-level change can come through treaty amendment, a landmark decision of the Court of Justice or recursive formal and informal change, such as trilogues. As an indicator of scope they describe it as change that locks in different decision-making rules, for example unanimity changing to qualified majority voting, and they accept that it may be an ambitious threshold. A critical juncture needs such change, they argue, codified in treaty change or made within the existing treaties as with trilogues or extended use of emergency powers under Article 122 TFEU, because without it changes remain reversible. They tie the threshold to veto players, since a policy can stay in deadlock, citing Tsebelis, until preference configurations or decision-making rules change, and the slides define veto players as actors whose agreement a change in the status quo needs. In their conclusion both policies still face unanimity specified in the treaties, the Lisbon provisions that could change rules without treaty change remain unused, and neither has undergone a critical juncture.
questions: Because unanimity is specified in the treaties, neither enlargement nor security and defence has yet seen _____, which the authors say a critical juncture requires.
When unanimity changes to qualified majority voting in a policy area and locks in different decision-making rules, that counts as _____; without it, the authors say, changes remain reversible.

cards.question: Policy change is seen as incremental, with small adjustments over time, but punctuated by drastic and extensive change driven by external factors or shifts in issue definition, in _____ theory.
cards.answerDate: External shock24 February 2022
cards.abstract:
Punctuated equilibrium is a theory of policy change that seeks to explain why political processes are generally stable and incremental but occasionally produce large-scale departures from the past. It was first advanced in biology, as an explanation of how differences among species develop, before political scientists applied it to public policy. Baumgartner and Jones analysed US policymaking cases in 1993 and found that policy makes leaps and rests in near stasis as issues emerge on and recede from the public agenda. The theory stresses issue definition, because as issues are defined in different ways in public discourse, existing policies are either reinforced, which obstructs all but modest change, or questioned, which opens the way to major reversals. Capoccia and Kelemen note that many historical institutionalist arguments assume a similar dual model, in which long periods of path-dependent stability are punctuated by brief phases of flux called critical junctures.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops cite the theory through Jones and Baumgartner among the institutionalist insights they build on, describing policy change as incremental, with small adjustments over time, yet punctuated by more drastic and extensive change. They say the drastic change is driven by external factors or by shifts in issue definition, which can come through political rhetoric or through new discourses, as discursive institutionalism suggests. Schmidt, whom they cite, presents that approach as a more dynamic account of institutional change than the older new institutionalisms. The authors report that before 2022 the status quo in enlargement and in security and defence had been preserved for at least a decade, which they say makes the changes triggered by the war both significant and traceable. They treat Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 as an external shock and ask whether it was a critical juncture, noting that member states broadly saw candidate status for Ukraine as a geopolitical necessity.
questions: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 is described as an external shock, the kind of external factor that _____ theory expects to interrupt long periods of small adjustments with drastic change.

A shift in issue definition, achievable through political rhetoric or new discourses, can bring drastic change after long stretches of small adjustments, according to _____ theory, which the authors cite among their institutionalist insights.

[Open access]

Daniel Kelemen, “The Study of Critical Junctures: Theory, Narrative, and Counterfactuals in Historical Institutionalism,” World Politics 59, no. 3 (2007): 341–69, https://www.critical-juncture.net/uploads/2/1/9/9/21997192/capoccia_and_keleman_the_study_of_critical_junctures.pdf. [Open access]

cards.question: Emphasising ideas as a driver of change that emerges when actors interact, _____ sees policy as embedded in institutions that specific actors can partly change by reinterpreting them.
cards.abstract:
Discursive institutionalism is an approach that Vivien Schmidt called, in her 2008 review, the newest of the new institutionalisms, one that explains the role of ideas and discourse in politics. She defines ideas as the substantive content of discourse, existing at the levels of policies, programmes and philosophies, and discourse as the interactive process of conveying them. She distinguishes coordinative discourse among policy actors from communicative discourse between political actors and the public, the second stronger in simple polities and the first in compound ones. Hall and Taylor had identified three new institutionalisms, historical, rational choice and sociological, and Schmidt later presented this approach as the fourth, aimed at explaining change. In her account institutions are not external rule-following structures but structures and constructs internal to agents, whose foreground discursive abilities explain how institutions change or persist.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops cite Schmidt for the view that ideas are a driver of change, emerging when actors interact in a discursive setting, and that policy is embedded in institutions which specific actors can partly change by reinterpreting them. They make a change of discourse the first stage of the stairway, meaning new ideas and arguments that change the issue definition or produce coordinating and communicating discourses, and expect, like Schmidt, that change cannot happen without them. They stress that it makes a difference whether actors react at the discursive level only or commit themselves to a new policy through different decisions backed by resources and organisational structures. On enlargement they find two main frames since the war began, values and identity and geopolitics, and Parliament’s resolution of 29 February 2024 calls enlargement both a moral and historic commitment and a strategic geopolitical priority. In their conclusion both policies show a substantial shift in key policy discourses, whereas in security and defence progress in missions or defence procurement since 2014 has been much weaker than at the rhetorical level.
questions: A change of discourse, meaning new ideas and arguments that change the issue definition, is the first stage of the stairway of change, a choice built on _____ and its focus on ideas.
Since the war began, EU arguments for enlargement have been framed around values and identity and around geopolitics, the kind of shift in ideas that _____ treats as a driver of policy change.

cards.question: Placing critical junctures at the centre as key moments when pivotal decisions affect later ones, _____ treats path dependence as a core aspect and identifies junctures mostly after the event.
cards.abstract:
Historical institutionalism is an approach in which institutions, meaning organisations and the rules or conventions they promulgate, are persistent features that push historical development along a set of ‘paths’. Hall and Taylor name four distinctive features, including attention to power asymmetries, to path dependence and to the role of ideas. Many historical institutionalists see continuity punctuated by critical junctures, moments of substantial institutional change that create a branching point from which development moves onto a new path. Pierson adds that this view holds that timing and sequence matter and that political development is punctuated by critical junctures that shape the basic contours of social life. Capoccia and Kelemen call critical junctures an essential building block of the approach and define one as a relatively short period in which agents’ choices have a substantially heightened probability of affecting the outcome of interest.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops present the theory as putting critical junctures at the centre, as key moments of policy change when, at pivotal periods, key decisions are taken that affect later decisions. They add that path dependence, the development of a policy along a trajectory determined by some key initial decisions, is a core aspect of the approach, whereas critical junctures are mostly identified after the event. They cite Christiansen and Verdun for junctures as moments of uncertainty when actors can shape institutions, and Collier and Collier for periods of significant change that produce distinct legacies. The slides define a critical juncture as a relatively short period when actors can take key decisions that set new trajectories, and the European Council granted Ukraine and Moldova candidate status within four months of the invasion. The authors call the war a potential juncture if it lessens the constraints on policy makers, but conclude that neither enlargement nor security and defence has yet undergone one, for want of constitutional-level change.
questions: Critical junctures, often recognised only long after the events that triggered them, are the central concept of _____, which holds that key decisions taken in pivotal periods shape what follows.

cards.question: A policy that develops along a trajectory determined by some key initial decisions shows _____, a core aspect of historical institutionalism that has been widely explored in policy analyses.
cards.abstract:
Path dependence is a term for the way earlier steps in a sequence shape later ones, and Pierson notes that writers use it in a broader and a narrower sense. In the broad sense it means that what happened at an earlier point in time affects later outcomes, which Pierson says may amount to the loose claim that ‘history matters’. In the narrower sense, which he adopts, it describes increasing returns processes, in which the probability of further steps along the same path rises with each move because the costs of exit rise. Mahoney argues that it characterises specifically those historical sequences in which contingent events set in motion institutional patterns or event chains with deterministic properties. Hall and Taylor say historical institutionalists use it to reject the idea that the same forces generate the same results everywhere, since their effects are mediated by contextual features inherited from the past, above all institutions.

Capoccia and Kelemen link it to critical junctures, because choices made in a juncture close off alternatives and establish institutions that generate self-reinforcing path-dependent processes. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops define it as the development of a policy along a trajectory determined by some key initial decisions, call it a core aspect of historical institutionalism and contrast it with critical junctures, which are mostly identified after the event. The slides define a critical juncture as a relatively short period when actors can take key decisions that set new trajectories. In judging scope the authors ask whether decisions break with previous ones or are incremental and follow a clear path-dependent pattern, and they report that before the war the status quo in both policy areas had been preserved for at least a decade. For enlargement they say the steps taken since 2022 suggest a different path, after the European Council granted Ukraine and Moldova candidate status on 23 June 2022, but without constitutional-level change policies may revert to the status quo ante and both remain stuck on the stairway.

cards.question: External shocks may provide _____, together with productive conditions, to relax constraints and facilitate policy decisions that set a policy on a new path.
cards.answerDate: External shock24 February 2022ReferendumApril 2016
cards.abstract:
The permissive conditions of a critical juncture are, in Hillel David Soifer’s account, the conditions that loosen constraints on agency, so that change becomes possible. Productive conditions then operate within that window to create differences across cases, and a juncture counts as critical if those differences are reinforced after it closes. Soifer calls it a “crisis without change or missed opportunity” when permissive conditions are present but no major, divergent change follows. Capoccia and Kelemen, as Kai M. Thaler summarises them, define critical junctures as short periods when agents’ choices have a substantially heightened probability of affecting the outcome, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops add that agents then face a broader than typical range of feasible options. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops ask whether Russia’s war against Ukraine has been a critical juncture for EU enlargement and for security and defence policy.

They say external shocks may provide permissive conditions, together with productive conditions, a pairing they cite from Soifer, and expect the war to be a potential critical juncture if it lessens the constraints on policy makers regarding their menu of policy choices. Before the war, they write, member states were constrained by public opinion, and the Dutch consultative referendum of 6 April 2016, in which about 61% voted against the Association Agreement, showed where the red lines lay. The heads of state or government then decided on 15 December 2016 that the Agreement does not confer candidate status on Ukraine, and the authors say that until 2022 the prospect of membership for Ukraine, Georgia and Moldova was non-existent. The authors say the war eased political constraints and opened the door to membership, and the European Council of 23 and 24 June 2022 granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova. The authors conclude, however, that both policies still face constitutional-level constraints, namely decision by unanimity specified in the treaties, and that neither has yet undergone a critical juncture.

cards.question: Issued by the informal European Council of 10 to 11 March 2022, the _____ described Russia’s war of aggression as a tectonic shift in European history and called Ukraine part of the European family.
cards.answerDate: Invasion24 February 2022Informal summit10–11 March 2022Candidate status23 June 2022
cards.abstract:
The Versailles Declaration is the declaration of the EU’s informal meeting of heads of state or government at Versailles on 10 and 11 March 2022, two weeks after Russia brought war back to Europe. The summit’s agenda was expanded, so that the planned topics of investment and growth were joined by Ukraine, defence, energy dependence and a more robust economic base. The leaders condemned Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified aggression, demanded that it withdraw all its forces, and said the EU remained ready to move quickly with further sanctions. They also agreed to phase out EU dependency on Russian fossil fuels, though without setting a deadline, and to take more responsibility for the Union’s own security. The declaration names three dimensions of this new reality: defence capabilities, energy dependencies and a more robust economic base.

It states that Russia’s war of aggression “constitutes a tectonic shift in European history”, which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops quote at the start of their article, while other EU actors called the war an “awakening moment for Europe”. It also states that the European Council acknowledged the European aspirations and the European choice of Ukraine, records Ukraine’s application of 28 February 2022, and adds that “Ukraine belongs to our European family”. The authors place this in the values and identity frame, where the weight of EU arguments shifted from technical preparedness to shared values and belonging, and the lecture slides carry the same passage. On 23 June 2022, the authors report, the European Council granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova, saying that their future lies within the European Union. The authors observe that, despite many declarations and significant decisions over three years, it is still not clear whether the war has truly been a critical juncture, and Richard Youngs argued in July 2022 that it had not produced a fundamental geopolitical shift in EU external action.

cards.question: Immediately after the invasion began, the Commission’s president said, “_____ and we want them in the EU”, words that frame enlargement around shared values and belonging.
cards.answerDate: Reported27 February 2022ReaffirmedFebruary 2024
cards.abstract:
Ukraine is one of us is the opening of a remark by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, which Euronews reported on 27 February 2022 as continuing “and we want them in the European Union”. She spoke after Brussels announced weapons for Ukraine and bans on Russian-backed media and aircraft, and gave no sign of the rapid accession that President Zelenskyy had demanded the day before. She pointed instead to existing ties, such as integrating the Ukrainian market into the single market and close cooperation on the energy grid. Ukraine’s president applied for membership on 28 February 2022, and the Council asked the Commission for its opinion, as the Versailles Declaration records. The older approach was Commission President Romano Prodi’s wish, in December 2002, to see a “ring of friends” around the Union, sharing everything but institutions.

The authors cite the Euronews report as an example of the values and identity frame, one of two main frames in EU arguments for making Ukraine part of enlargement, the other being geopolitics. In this frame the weight shifted from technical and economic preparedness to shared values and belonging, and virtually all high-level EU representatives reinforced it. The Versailles Declaration spoke in the same vein, saying that Ukraine belongs to the European family, and in February 2024 von der Leyen reaffirmed that Ukraine and the Western Balkans belong to it. The authors cite the reception of Ukrainian refugees, compared with earlier flows from outside Europe, as a sign of changed perception, and a 2024 study finds their initial position better than in other mass influx situations once the Council had introduced temporary protection on 4 March 2022. The authors also describe the shift from the Neighbourhood Policy and the Eastern Partnership to the accession framework as a change in the EU’s logic from “creating a ring of friends” to “creating one of us”.

cards.question: A text of 27 June 2022 by the High Representative names the _____ for the EU as being to both widen and deepen, and calls credible enlargement a geostrategic investment.
cards.answerDate: Commission text2020EP resolutionJune 2022Borrell text27 June 2022
cards.abstract:
The geopolitical imperative is the argument that the EU should enlarge because it serves the Union’s own strategic interest, not as a favour to candidates. On 5 February 2020 the Commission called a firm, merit-based membership prospect for the Western Balkans “more than ever a geostrategic investment in a stable, strong and united Europe”. In June 2022 the European Council decided that the future of Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia lies in the EU, yet said that each country’s progress depends on its own merit in meeting the Copenhagen criteria. High Representative Josep Borrell titled a blog text of 27 June 2022 “The geo-political imperative for the EU is to both widen and deepen”. He calls a credible enlargement policy “a geostrategic investment in peace, stability, security and economic growth in the whole of Europe”.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops identify the geopolitical imperative, also called the geopolitical necessity, as the second main frame in EU arguments for making Ukraine part of enlargement, alongside values and identity. They say the rhetorical link between enlargement and the EU’s security priorities has added urgency to enlargement decisions, although values remain, at least symbolically, a priority. They add that such arguments are not an abrupt change, since the Commission already called a credible accession perspective a geostrategic investment in 2020, but they judge their use for Ukraine, Georgia and Moldova, previously excluded, a shift. The same frame revived debates on institutional reform, with the Parliament’s resolution of 9 June 2022 calling on the European Council to start revising the treaties and Borrell calling the EU’s capacity to act a geopolitical imperative too. The slides list geopolitical against merit-based enlargement among the dilemmas of enlargement, and James Blanchett argues that Moldova and Ukraine fared better than four Western Balkan candidates, which compliance with the Copenhagen criteria cannot explain.

cards.question: In May 2023, nine member states launched the _____ to improve the effectiveness and speed of foreign-policy decision-making in the Common Foreign and Security Policy and to prepare the Union for the future.
cards.answer: Group of Friends on Qualified Majority Voting
cards.answerDate: Swedish termfirst half of 2023Joint statement4 May 2023Franco-GermanSeptember 2023
cards.abstract:
The Group of Friends on Qualified Majority Voting is an inclusive group of EU states launched on 4 May 2023 to foster qualified majority voting, or QMV, in the Common Foreign and Security Policy, the CFSP. Article 31(1) of the Treaty on European Union requires unanimity in the European Council and the Council for CFSP decisions, except where the treaty provides otherwise. Article 31(2) allows QMV in some cases, such as appointing a special representative, but a state may cite vital reasons of national policy to stop a vote. Article 31(3) lets the European Council decide unanimously on QMV in further cases, Article 31(4) excludes military and defence decisions, and an EPRS study found in May 2023 that the clause had never been used. Julina Mintel and Nicolai von Ondarza wrote in 2022 that publicly disputed vetoes, such as Cyprus’s on Belarus sanctions in 2020, had given the debate a new dynamic.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that nine member states formed the group in May 2023, and its joint statement names Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Spain. The statement aims to improve the effectiveness and speed of foreign-policy decision-making through practical steps within existing treaty provisions, and the authors add the aim of “preparing the EU for the future”. The authors report that talks under the Swedish Presidency in early 2023 focused on a “pragmatic” reform programme of changes in areas such as the CFSP that needed no treaty change, and that a Franco-German report of September 2023 followed. The slides list reform ideas for QMV on sanctions, human rights and civilian missions, with military aspects excluded, and state that on defence and military matters the Council always decides by unanimity. The authors read these initiatives as showing that the prospect of enlargement has prompted serious reflection on institutional reform, but they conclude that unanimity rules in foreign, security and defence policy still prevail.

cards.abstract:
The Granada Declaration is the declaration of the EU’s heads of state or government of 6 October 2023, issued at their informal meeting in Granada under the Spanish Presidency. The Spanish Presidency prepared it with ministerial discussions of the EU’s absorption capacity, including a meeting in Murcia on 27 and 28 September 2023. It says that, looking ahead to a further enlarged Union, both the EU and future members need to be ready, and that the EU must lay the necessary internal groundwork and reforms in parallel with aspiring members’ reforms. Spain’s government summarised the summit as agreeing to help candidates speed up their reforms and to reform the EU itself, to promote efficiency and agility in decision-making. In December 2023 the European Council recalled the declaration, called enlargement a geo-strategic investment, and said it would address internal reforms with a view to adopting conclusions on a roadmap for future work by summer 2024.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that member states’ responses to proposals for institutional reform are uncertain and currently limited to the conclusions of the declaration, which stressed that enlargement and reform should proceed in parallel. Those proposals include a Franco-German report of September 2023, which explicitly linked the EU’s deepening and widening and considered the prospect of ten new members. As in the treaty reform debates of the 1990s and 2000s, the authors say, reform proposals are tied to the enlargement prospect, and the questions left open at Amsterdam became the ‘Amsterdam leftovers’ that the Treaty of Nice was meant to settle. The slides list the reforms made in anticipation of Eastern enlargement, from the Treaty of Amsterdam and the voting weights at Nice to the rise of trilogues. The authors write that further progress stumbles against unanimous decision-making and a lack of appetite for treaty reform, and the Presidency report of December 2023 recorded that many ministers considered the current Treaties enlargement-proof.

cards.question: Dated 18 September 2023, the Franco-German Working Group’s report on EU institutional reform, titled _____: Reforming and Enlarging the EU for the 21st Century, outlined scenarios with far-reaching proposals.
cards.answerDate: Report18 September 2023Group of FriendsMay 2023
cards.abstract:
Sailing on High Seas is the title of a report of the Franco-German Working Group on EU Institutional Reform, dated Paris and Berlin, 18 September 2023, with the subtitle Reforming and Enlarging the EU for the 21st Century. The German and French governments tasked twelve experts, the Group of Twelve, with writing it in January 2023, and Olivier Costa and Daniela Schwarzer were its rapporteurs. It was expressly not an official government position, and the report itself says that its opinions are those of the authors only. The experts presented it to the General Affairs Council in Brussels on 19 September 2023, during an informal lunch of ministers. It sets three goals, which are to increase the EU’s capacity to act, to make the EU enlargement-ready and to strengthen the rule of law and democratic legitimacy.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops say the report outlined scenarios with far-reaching proposals, explicitly linked the EU’s deepening and widening, and considered the prospect of ten new members, while the report itself speaks of up to 10 new Member States. The report proposes that all remaining policy decisions move from unanimity to qualified majority voting before the next enlargement, and that the EU and candidates aim to be ready by 2030. The authors set it beside the Group of Friends of May 2023 and a European Parliament Research Service study, as initiatives showing that since 2022 enlargement has prompted serious reflection on institutional reform. Member states’ responses are, they say, uncertain and limited to the Granada Declaration, though in December 2023 the European Council said it would address internal reforms with a view to adopting a roadmap by summer 2024. The authors note that attempts to initiate treaty change for enlargement have faced the high threshold of unanimity, and Marie Beyrich calls the report one of the most notable recent responses to reform pressure.
questions: A Franco-German report of September 2023, titled _____, explicitly linked the EU’s deepening and widening and suggested comprehensive reform options for the institutions, with ten new members in prospect.

cards.question: In June 2022 the European _____ called on the European Council to start revising the EU treaties, proposing among other things a switch from unanimity to qualified majority voting.
cards.answerDate: ResolutionJune 2022Borrell text27 June 2022
cards.abstract:
The European Parliament’s treaty-change resolution is the text adopted on 9 June 2022 that called on the European Council to agree to start the process of revising the EU treaties. It followed the Conference on the Future of Europe, whose more than 320 recommendations might require changes to the treaties. Article 48 of the Treaty on European Union lets the government of any member state, the European Parliament or the Commission propose amendments, which the Council submits to the European Council. If the European Council decides by a simple majority to examine them, its President convenes a Convention, and amendments enter into force only after ratification by all member states. A simplified route in Article 48(7) lets the European Council, acting unanimously with the Parliament’s consent, authorise the Council to use qualified majority voting where the treaties require unanimity, but not for military or defence decisions.

The resolution asked for reform of the Council’s voting procedures, including a switch from unanimity to qualified majority voting in areas such as sanctions, in emergencies and through the so-called passerelle clauses. It passed with 355 votes in favour, 154 against and 48 abstentions, and it fell to the heads of state or government to decide whether to set up a Convention, by simple majority. Andrew Duff wrote in March 2023 that the Council had so far refused to submit Parliament’s request to the European Council, which he called a breach of its treaty obligations. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops call the Parliament one of the first institutions to join the debate that framing enlargement as a geopolitical necessity revived, and they cite a text of 27 June 2022 by High Representative Josep Borrell. They write that progress stumbles against unanimity and a lack of appetite for treaty reform, and the slides list the passerelle clause in Article 31(3) among the options for foreign policy, which excludes military and defence matters.
questions: Among the first institutions to join the reform debate revived by enlargement as a geopolitical necessity was the European _____ of June 2022, which proposed use of passerelle clauses.

cards.question: As a reaction to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Denmark’s government called the _____ of June 2022, which produced a resounding “yes” to abolishing a 30-year-old opt-out from EU defence policy.
cards.answerDate: ReferendumJune 2022
cards.abstract:
The Danish defence opt-out referendum of 1 June 2022 was a vote on abolishing Denmark’s exemption from the Common Security and Defence Policy, the CSDP, and about 67% of voters said yes. The exemption dated from 1992, when Danish voters narrowly rejected the Maastricht Treaty, and Denmark then negotiated opt-outs from the euro, defence, justice and home affairs, and union citizenship. The defence opt-out sits in Article 5 of Protocol No 22 on the position of Denmark, which recalls the Edinburgh decision of 12 December 1992 and kept Denmark out of Union decisions with defence implications and out of their operational costs. Pedersen and colleagues note that defence cooperation is intergovernmental, with unanimity and voluntary participation, so voters did not see a major transfer of sovereignty. The government announced the vote on 6 March 2022, and Frederiksen said that ‘Historic events call for historic decisions’.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that the vote produced a resounding yes to abolishing the 30-year-old opt-out, which the Danish government had called as a reaction to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The vote paved the way, they write, for Denmark to join the CSDP and to take part in EU military missions, and they cite a Guardian report headed Denmark Votes Overwhelmingly to Join EU’s Common Defence Policy. They call the change significant because security and defence have always been highly intergovernmental and rely on the member states for their effectiveness. The High Representative called the result historic and said the EU would act quickly once Denmark formally notified the member states, Denmark joined EU defence cooperation on 1 July 2022, and it became the 26th member of PESCO, the EU’s Permanent Structured Cooperation in defence, in May 2023. The authors count the Danish opt-in among the policy innovations since 2022, beside stronger sanctions and financing and a new Commissioner for Defence, yet find that unanimity rules still prevail and that Ireland, Austria and Malta keep their neutral stance.
questions: A resounding “yes” in the _____ paved the way in June 2022 for Denmark to join the Common Security and Defence Policy and to take part in EU military missions.
Because security and defence have always been highly intergovernmental, the change of position that Denmark made in the _____ of June 2022 was significant for EU defence policy.

cards.question: Unlike earlier EU training missions deployed in countries such as Mali, Somalia and Niger, _____ trains Ukrainian forces inside EU member states and includes lethal training.
cards.answerDate: Civilian mission2014MPCC created2017
cards.abstract:
EUMAM Ukraine, the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine, is a military training mission that the Council set up on 17 October 2022 and launched on 15 November 2022. It trains the Ukrainian Armed Forces at multiple locations in EU member states, with up to 15,000 personnel to be trained and an initial duration of two years. The Military Planning and Conduct Capability, the MPCC, is its operations headquarters, and the MPCC Director, Vice Admiral Hervé Bléjean at the launch, is the mission commander. Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/971 of 8 June 2017 created the MPCC as the static command structure at the military strategic level for non-executive military missions, within the EU Military Staff. Its first missions were training missions in Somalia, Mali and the Central African Republic, and the Mali decision of 2013 shows their type, military advice and training with no involvement in combat operations.

The lecture slides describe the MPCC as a permanent command and control structure within the EU Military Staff, established in June 2017, and the only EU military permanent strategic headquarters. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that with EUMAM the Council created, for the first time, a military training mission carried out within EU member states rather than outside the EU, whereas earlier missions in Mozambique, Mali, Somalia and Niger trained military staff in non-lethal aspects. EUMAM is decidedly different, they say, because it includes lethal training and trains Ukrainian staff in EU countries, and Matisek, Ostanina and Reno call it the first EU training mission organised on EU territories. Training runs through a Combined Arms Training Command in Poland and a Special Training Command in Germany, and the authors add that the MPCC Director coordinates it, which might lead to an EU operations headquarters for executive operations. Before 2022, the authors write, member states rejected a Ukrainian request for an EU military operation after Crimea and approved only a civilian advisory mission in 2014 that excluded military training.
questions: Coordinated and run by the Military Planning and Conduct Capability, _____ has trained the Armed Forces of Ukraine, including the Territorial Defence Forces, in Poland and Germany.
After 2014, member states settled for a civilian advisory mission in Ukraine, but the war later led the Council to approve _____, the first military training mission carried out within EU states.
