cards.question: Created in March 2024 under the European Peace Facility, the _____ provides an additional 5 billion euros for lethal and non-lethal military aid to Ukraine and is legally embedded within the CFSP.
cards.answerDate: Council decision18 March 2024EPF establishedMarch 2021
cards.abstract:
The Ukraine Assistance Fund is a €5 billion fund that the Council created on 18 March 2024 inside the European Peace Facility, the EPF, to pay for military support to Ukraine. The EPF was created in March 2021 as an instrument outside the EU budget, financed by the member states according to their gross national income, and its ceiling now exceeds €17 billion for 2021–2027. The Council said the new fund would finance lethal and non-lethal military equipment and training for Ukraine’s armed forces, and the European Parliamentary Research Service calls it the third top-up of the EPF. The Council also revised the EPF’s governance, with joint procurement from European and Norwegian industry as the aim, some flexibility for producers outside the EU and Norway, and limited reimbursement of member states’ donations after a transition period. The research service records that Hungary reportedly blocked the mobilisation of the fund’s money in May 2024.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops describe the fund as a further enhancement of the EPF, cite Council Decision CFSP 2024/890 of 18 March 2024, and call it a more predictable, dedicated financing tool legally embedded within the Common Foreign and Security Policy. The fund is linked to a “buy European” clause that, the authors write, nudges member states to accelerate their own defence industrial base, in line with the recently adopted European Defence Industrial Strategy. That strategy invites member states to buy at least half of their defence equipment within the EU by 2030 and 60% by 2035, since more than three-quarters of purchases since the invasion came from outside the EU. Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley report that France and others argued for “buy European”, whereas Sweden, Germany and Poland lobbied for UK and other non-EU firms to receive EU-mobilised funding. The authors set the fund apart from the Ukraine Facility, €50 billion of long-term support for 2024 to 2027, and say accession funding is committed separately from defence.
questions: A “buy European” clause linked to the European Defence Industrial Strategy comes with the _____, a dedicated and more predictable financing tool for Ukraine adopted by the Council in March 2024.

Whereas the Ukraine Facility gives 50 billion euros of long-term support, the _____ adds 5 billion euros of military aid under the Peace Facility and nudges members towards their own defence industry.

cards.question: In the stairway of change, constitutional level rules can be modified within the existing treaties through trilogues or the extended use of emergency powers under _____, rather than through formal treaty amendment.
cards.answerDate: Regulation27 May 2025
cards.abstract:
Article 122 TFEU is the emergency provision of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, under which the Council can adopt measures on a proposal from the Commission without involving the European Parliament. Its first paragraph lets the Council decide measures appropriate to the economic situation in a spirit of solidarity between member states, especially if serious supply problems arise, as with energy. Its second paragraph lets the Council grant Union financial assistance to a member state in difficulties from natural disasters or exceptional occurrences beyond its control, and the Council President then informs Parliament. The provision descends from the Treaty of Rome of 1957, the Lisbon Treaty then adding the reference to solidarity. Since 2010 it has served for migration emergency support, the SURE scheme against pandemic unemployment, Next Generation EU and the energy crisis measures of 2022.

In the stairway of change of Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops, Article 122 TFEU is the basis of the emergency powers whose extended use, beside trilogues, is an example of constitutional level rules being modified within the existing treaty frameworks. They argue that a critical juncture needs constitutional level change, whether codified in treaty change or modified within existing frameworks, because otherwise changes remain reversible, and find that neither enlargement nor security and defence has yet seen it. They name Article 122 again for the Security Action for Europe, SAFE, which the Council adopted on 27 May 2025 as up to €150 billion in loans for member states’ joint defence procurement. Their note says the Commission used Article 122 as the legal basis and that the Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs unanimously rejected fast-tracking the SAFE loan, which Eunews reports as a non-binding recommendation against that basis. The procedure bypassed the Parliament’s involvement, the authors say, and the Parliament opposes the legal basis and not the content, while Leson argues that Article 122 cannot give a policy shift of this size democratic legitimacy.
questions: The Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs unanimously rejected fast-tracking the SAFE loan because the Commission had used _____ as the legal basis, which bypassed Parliament’s involvement in decision-making.
Adopted in May 2025 with up to 150 billion euros in loans, the Security Action for Europe rested on _____, a legal basis the European Parliament opposed although not the Regulation’s content.

cards.question: Although the Eastern enlargement of 12 new member states was viewed as a success, the Union already showed signs of _____, with increased labour mobility affecting public opinion in older member states.
cards.answerDate: Perspective2003Croatia joined2013Revised approach2020
cards.abstract:
Enlargement fatigue names the shift among the Union’s governments and citizens from seeing enlargement as a success story to doubting further enlargement, which Devrim and Schulz date to after the last round ended in 2007. That fifth round brought in eight central and eastern European states plus Cyprus and Malta on 1 May 2004, and Bulgaria and Romania on 1 January 2007, making 12 new members. Szolucha argues that the idea is not new, because the Union has shown symptoms of fatigue at several points in its history. Economides describes it as a worry about the Union’s waning ‘absorption capacity’ in governance and administration, which he says showed itself most powerfully after the ‘Big Bang’ enlargement of 2004. Fihel and colleagues add that in 2004 only Ireland, Sweden and the United Kingdom opened their labour markets, while most other older members kept transitional restrictions.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that signs of the fatigue appeared even before the Eastern enlargement was complete, although it was viewed as a success despite the complexity of preparing 12 new members, most of them not market economies at the start of negotiations. They say the societal effects were significant, with increased labour mobility affecting public opinion in older member states, and that the politicisation of enlargement debates became a major constraint on further enlargement. Despite the European perspective for the Western Balkans in 2003 and Croatia’s accession in 2013, they find no significant progress in the last decade. The Commission’s Communication of 5 February 2020 proposed grouping negotiating chapters into thematic clusters opened as a whole, yet the authors say the increased funding proposed with it was rejected, partly because Covid-19 redirected funds, so the method did not break the deadlock. The lecture slides likewise present enlargement as deadlocked for the last 13 years, as politicised and questioned by domestic publics, and list geopolitical enlargement versus domestic politicisation among the dilemmas of enlargement.

cards.question: A 2007 speech at Harvard held that, because of the Union’s _____, the EU was not well placed to respond to something that might look like great power politics.
cards.answerDate: Speech2007Georgia war2008Crimea annexed2014Global Strategy2016
cards.abstract:
Post-modern DNA is a phrase from a 2007 speech by Javier Solana, the EU’s first High Representative, which Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops quote as showing a security discourse rooted in a rejection of power politics. Robert Cooper used ‘post-modern’ in an essay of 2002 for states that no longer think of security mainly in terms of conquest, and called the EU the most developed example of such a system. He listed its features as the rejection of force in disputes, mutual interference and surveillance, and security based on transparency and interdependence. Solana presented the European Security Strategy in June 2003, and the European Council adopted it on 12 December 2003. It said the Union should work for closer relations with Russia, and that respect for common values would reinforce progress towards a strategic partnership.

Solana says in the quoted passage that because of this DNA the EU is not well placed to respond to something that might look like ‘great power politics’, and that cooperation with Russia is best done through agreed rules. The authors note that the Strategy of 2003 referred to Russia as a ‘strategic partner’, and that neither the war with Georgia in 2008 nor the annexation of Crimea in 2014 immediately led to a major shift in policies. After the Georgian war the European Council of 1 September 2008 called Russia’s reaction disproportionate, but it saw no desirable alternative to a strong relationship and postponed the partnership talks. The authors call the shift in discourse since 2014 very slow and gradual, since even after Crimea Catherine Ashton struggled to have ‘Russia’s invasion’ accepted over ‘Russia’s aggression’, and only after 2022 is Russia named an ‘existential’ challenge. The lecture slides say the Global Strategy of 2016 added ‘hard’ power to ‘soft’, and the Strategy itself says that soft and hard power go hand in hand while it calls managing the relationship with Russia a key strategic challenge.
questions: When Russia went to war against Georgia in 2008, the EU’s security discourse still rejected power politics, as a 2007 speech showed with its phrase _____ and its call for agreed rules.

cards.question: In 2008 the Union criticised Russia over Georgia while relying on Russian military transport aircraft to move its troops for _____, a CSDP military operation, and even invited Russia to take part.
cards.answerDate: Georgia war2008Council decision13 October 2008Crimea annexed2014
cards.abstract:
EUFOR Tchad/RCA was a military operation of the European Union in eastern Chad and the north-east of the Central African Republic, which ran from 28 January 2008 to 15 March 2009 under the European Security and Defence Policy. It rested on UN Security Council Resolution 1778 of 25 September 2007 and aimed to protect civilians in danger, especially refugees and displaced persons, and to help humanitarian aid reach them. The Council adopted the joint action on 15 October 2007, and at full strength the force numbered as many as 3,700 troops from 26 states, three of them outside the EU: Albania, Croatia and Russia. Tull of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs wrote in February 2008 that delays in generating troops and equipment, including helicopters, reflected the unease of many member states. Seibert of the Royal United Services Institute noted in January 2008 that European shortfalls in strategic mobility meant leasing carriers, and that moving the 400 Irish troops alone reportedly needed 30 sorties of the Russian Antonov AN-124-100.

Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops use the operation to show that in 2008 the Union depended on military assets from outside, which led to the absurd situation that it criticised Russia diplomatically over Georgia while relying on Russian military transport aircraft to move EU troops. The European Council of 1 September 2008 called Russia’s reaction in Georgia disproportionate and postponed partnership talks, yet it also saw no desirable alternative to a strong relationship with Russia. On 13 October 2008 the Council approved the agreement on Russian participation in the operation, in Decision 2008/868/CFSP, published on 18 November 2008. The Council’s factsheet records that the presence of Russian helicopters from December 2008 increased the mobility of the force. As a result, the authors add, the EU even officially invited Russia to take part, so that its reaction to Russia’s aggression against Georgia paradoxically coincided with enhanced cooperation in the CSDP realm.

cards.question: In March 2022 the Union decisively adapted its financing so that, for the very first time, it paid for _____ to a country in an ongoing conflict, crossing red lines of defence-policy financing.
cards.answerDate: EPF introduced2021AbstentionFebruary 2022AdaptationMarch 2022
cards.abstract:
Lethal aid through the EPF is the supply of weapons to Ukraine financed by the European Peace Facility, the EPF, since the Council adopted Decision 2022/338 on 28 February 2022 for equipment designed to deliver lethal force. The EPF is an instrument outside the EU budget, operational since 1 July 2021 and funded by the member states according to their gross national income. The first package had €450 million for lethal equipment and €50 million, under Decision 2022/339, for fuel, protective equipment and medical items. The European Parliamentary Research Service wrote in March 2022 that for the first time the EU was using a dedicated tool, though an off-budget one, to finance lethal equipment for a third country. It puts the military support for Ukraine approved under the EPF at about €10.6 billion, while Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report €11.1 billion mobilised between 2022 and 2024.

They write that in March 2022 the financing mechanisms were decisively adapted to allow, for the very first time, lethal equipment for a country in an ongoing conflict, whereas the EPF of 2021 had been set up only for non-lethal aid. The change crossed the red lines of EU financing for the Common Security and Defence Policy and also national laws, such as Germany’s armament export laws. The authors present the negotiations as constructive abstention, in which Austria, Malta and Ireland, who saw the adaptation as a step too far but did not want to stop the process, invoked Article 31 of the Treaty on European Union in February 2022. Article 31 lets an abstaining state attach a formal declaration, so that it need not apply the decision but accepts that it binds the Union, and Council records of April 2023 recall Ireland’s declaration of 27 February 2022. Michaels and Sus describe the EPF as overnight transformed from a conflict prevention tool into a powerful instrument for giving Ukraine lethal weapons, a broken taboo they count among signs of a more capable EU.

cards.question: Applied to the Union’s security and defence policy since 1998, _____ is a staged and non-linear process that allows signs of regression and ends with the Union shaping its own environment.
cards.answerDate: Discovery1998 – mid-2013Second phaseFrom late 2013Split24 February 2022
cards.abstract:
Maturation is the lens through which Maurer, Raube and Whitman ask, in the introduction to a special issue of European Security, whether the Union has come of age as a foreign and security actor. They borrow the idea from political psychology, where maturity means the ability to deal effectively and resiliently with experience and to perform satisfactorily in developmental tasks. From this they derive four processes of a mature actor: reflecting on its own journey, making informed decisions, holding a stable identity and building increasingly salient relations with others. The policy that Michaels and Sus trace took off after the British change of attitude that led to Saint-Malo in December 1998, and a 2001 compilation of core texts called its first two years almost revolutionary in political commitments. The European Council of 19 and 20 December 2013 held its first thematic debate on defence since the Lisbon Treaty took effect, and its conclusions use the words strategic autonomy once, in a passage on the defence industry.

Michaels and Sus follow the proposition that maturation occurs in different stages and is non-linear, so that signs of regression are possible. In their theory the Union has matured into a serious actor, meaning one that is prominent, respectable and recognised, only once it shows high reflexivity, adjusts to changed realities and seeks to shape its environment according to its own identity and worldview. They identify two phases so far, discovery from late 1998 to mid-2013 and definition and experimentation since late 2013, and they divide the second phase at 24 February 2022. That date marks Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine, which prompted a rethinking of cooperation across member states, and the Strategic Compass of March 2022 introduction notes that war had returned to Europe. The third phase, in which the Union would shape its environment and draw on past experience, has not been reached, they argue, because there is no EU-wide acceptability for a more serious security and defence role.

cards.question: Measuring whether a proposed EU security measure is acceptable in member states’ capitals, _____ is the underexplored aspect that a study based on 20 interviews in seven countries brings to the fore.
cards.answerDate: InterviewsSeptember – December 2023
cards.abstract:
National acceptability asks whether a proposed EU policy measure can be accepted in member states’ capitals, an idea Michaels and Kissack developed in a 2021 working paper for the ENGAGE project. They treat acceptability as a process that starts with a political initiative and continues after the decision, because national actors can still help, hinder or block implementation. A measure can also be accepted out of indifference, but acceptance of that kind is unlikely to bring a substantial commitment. The Treaty on European Union gives the idea force, because security and defence decisions need the Council’s unanimity and a common defence would need adoption by member states under their constitutional requirements. A study of more than 40,000 respondents in 24 member states and the United Kingdom found that perceived foreign threats go with more favourable views of security and defence integration, even among Eurosceptics.

Michaels and Sus call national acceptability an underexplored aspect of EU external action and link it to the Union’s maturation as a security and defence actor. Their evidence is 20 interviews, held between September and December 2023, with policymakers and experts in Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Poland and Spain, asked about beliefs, perceptions, goals and red lines. They offer only a snapshot, yet believe that the variation among the seven countries makes the study sufficiently representative of the mood music across member states. The European Council on Foreign Relations took a wider approach in 2019, when researchers in all 28 member states interviewed more than 100 policymakers and analysts and found a picture of uncertainty and confusion. Michaels and Sus argue that asking what is acceptable gives a more nuanced account of change than the claim that outside shocks lead to real turning points.

cards.question: Defined respectively as a mental state of conviction, an understanding formed after processing information and a desired policy outcome, _____ together decide whether an EU measure is acceptable in a national capital.
cards.answerDate: French paper1994
cards.abstract:
Political beliefs, perceptions and goals are the three ideas that, in Michaels and Kissack’s framework, together decide whether an EU measure is acceptable in a national capital. A belief is a mental state of acceptance or conviction held without needing evidence, and it tends to be deep-seated and stable. A perception is a way of understanding something after processing information and depends more on context than a belief does, while a goal is the aim towards which efforts are directed, here a desired policy outcome. Threat perception shows context at work, since a survey of 24 member states and the United Kingdom found that perceived foreign threats go with more favourable views of security and defence integration. Official texts accept such differences: Saint-Malo said the different situations of countries in relation to NATO must be respected, and Article 42 of the treaty respects states that see their common defence realised in NATO.

Michaels and Sus asked interviewees about beliefs, perceptions, goals and red lines, and conclude that national differences in them have hampered the Union’s maturation. France is their example of stability, since a French desire for independence and a concern to guarantee strategic autonomy, set out in the 1994 White Paper on Defence, informed ideas that have stayed relatively stable in Paris. The European Council on Foreign Relations adds that this white paper’s concept replaced the earlier notion of strategic independence, and that for Paris autonomy is about choosing its level of dependence on the United States, not about independence from it. Michaels and Sus report that eastern flank countries kept seeing the United States as their key ally because they share a threat perception of Russia, while perceptions of Russia differ among EU countries, most notably Germany. They argue that maturation can only occur if most members converge in these ideas, which could inform a shared identity and worldview and make more ambitious policy measures easier to adopt.

cards.question: Added to the Union’s quest for strategic autonomy from 2020 with close attention to economic aspects, _____ became in 2023 the base of the Spanish presidency’s Resilient EU2030 strategy.
cards.answerDate: Term widenedAfter 2016Open addedFrom 2020Spanish lead2023
cards.abstract:
Open strategic autonomy is the form in which EU actors have reiterated their quest for strategic autonomy since 2020, adding the qualifier ‘open’ with close attention to economic aspects, according to Michaels and Sus. The lecture slides define strategic autonomy as the capacity of the EU to act autonomously in strategically important areas, a wording they credit to the European Parliament’s research service. That service says the first official use of the term appears to be in the European Council conclusions of December 2013 and links the ‘open’ version to a debate in 2020, including a joint Spanish and Dutch non-paper. The term became central to the Commission’s trade policy review of 18 February 2021, which Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said emphasised the EU’s ability to make its own choices and shape the world around it. Schmitz and Seidl argue that the Commission used open strategic autonomy as a coalition magnet to mobilise support for a doctrine of qualified openness after trade became geopoliticised.

The 2023 Spanish presidency made it the base of Resilient EU2030, which Michaels and Sus call a strategy but which describes itself as a non-paper, and which calls for greater EU capacity in energy, digital technology, health and food. That paper says nearly all member states accept open strategic autonomy as an imperfect yet useful reference and quotes the Council’s loose definition, the capacity to act autonomously when and where necessary and with partners wherever possible. The slides list the Critical Raw Materials regulation among the measures to strengthen the Union’s open strategic autonomy, under the heading of the geopolitical Commission. Michaels and Sus add that the notion shifted away from traditional security and defence, a trend that seemed counterintuitive given changing US priorities, hybrid threats and instability in the neighbourhood. One interviewee called this a hijacking of the concept, and the authors note that related terms such as strategic sovereignty, capacity to act and resilience made the notion increasingly blurred.
questions: Greater EU capacity in energy, digital technology, health and food was demanded under the banner of _____ by the 2023 Spanish presidency, while the concept drifted away from traditional security and defence.

cards.question: At the 1998 Saint-Malo negotiations, an interviewee told the authors, the wording _____ was carefully chosen, yet members have struggled to agree on its basic meaning.
cards.answerDate: French paper1994Saint-Malo1998RevivedLate 2013
cards.abstract:
Autonomy rather than independence is the wording that, according to an interviewee quoted by Michaels and Sus, was carefully chosen in the Saint-Malo negotiations of 1998. The Franco-British summit of 3 and 4 December 1998 followed a major change in British attitude towards an EU defence role, and its declaration was the first official document to set out the new orientation. Its second paragraph says the Union must have the capacity for autonomous action, backed up by credible military forces, the means to decide to use them and a readiness to do so, in order to respond to international crises. The declaration never uses the word independence and says that collective defence commitments under the Washington Treaty must be maintained. The wording had French roots, since the European Council on Foreign Relations reports that France’s 1994 white paper brought in the concept of strategic autonomy and that it replaced the earlier notion of strategic independence.

Michaels and Sus rest the claim on a single interview, which their appendix lists as an Irish senior policy expert. The lecture slides say that the European Security and Defence Policy had a new start in 1998 with the Saint-Malo initiative of France and the United Kingdom. The European Parliament’s research service adds that calls for more autonomy were made at Saint-Malo, yet the first official EU document with the words strategic autonomy appears to be the European Council conclusions of December 2013. Members have struggled to agree on basic meaning, such as autonomy from whom or for what purpose, and they could live with a deliberately ambiguous concept because paying lip service was acceptable while committing to implementation was, except for France, not. Michaels and Sus say France remains most interested in long-term independence from the United States, which many members on NATO’s eastern flank dispute, whereas the European Council on Foreign Relations reports that for Paris autonomy means choosing its level of dependence.

cards.question: Adopted in 2002 after Turkey lifted its opposition to EU–NATO cooperation, _____ carried the suggestion that the Union would have access to NATO planning, assets and capabilities, which proved impracticable.
cards.answerDate: Adopted2002Artemis2003
cards.abstract:
Berlin Plus is the set of arrangements under which the EU can use NATO planning and assets, named after a Berlin meeting of NATO foreign ministers in 1996. The package has four elements: assured EU access to NATO operational planning, availability of NATO capabilities and common assets, European command options for EU-led operations, and adaptation of NATO defence planning. Talks stalled because Turkey wanted a right to block autonomous EU operations in an area of strategic importance to it, and after Ankara accepted assurances in December 2001 Greece rejected the deal. The EU-NATO declaration of 16 December 2002 then gave the Union assured access to NATO’s planning capabilities, and a report on Turkey counts it among the steps after which Ankara lifted its veto. The package was agreed on 17 March 2003, and Concordia in Macedonia, the first EU military operation, began on 31 March with recourse to NATO assets, although most of the arrangements remain classified.

Michaels and Sus date the adoption of Berlin Plus to 2002, after Turkey lifted its opposition, which fits the declaration of December 2002 rather than the package of March 2003. They write that the suggestion of EU access to NATO planning, assets and capabilities, and unwritten rules such as NATO’s right of first refusal, proved impracticable. The Bush administration assumed that NATO held a right of first refusal on EU peacekeeping missions and was surprised when EU governments sent soldiers to Bunia in June 2003 without discussing plans in NATO. Chirac and Blair fine-tuned their commitment at Le Touquet on 4 February 2003, agreeing that the EU should examine how to contribute to peacekeeping in Africa, including through autonomous operations. Operation Artemis, launched on 12 June 2003, was the first autonomous EU military operation, the slides pair it with Concordia, and the authors add that France saw it as a chance to emancipate itself from NATO.
questions: NATO’s unwritten ‘right of first refusal’ was among the rules of _____, adopted in 2002 and, like the access to NATO planning it suggested, found impracticable.
After Turkey lifted its opposition, the arrangements called _____ were adopted in 2002, before Chirac and Blair fine-tuned their commitment in early 2003 with a geographical focus on Africa.

cards.question: Envisaging up to 60,000 troops at 60-day notice, sustained for a year, the _____ of 1999 was a force catalogue that soon became an unrealistic scenario without ever being formally abandoned.
cards.answerDate: Goal set1999EDA oversight2004Declaration2008Next goal2010
cards.abstract:
The Helsinki Headline Goal was set by the European Council in Helsinki on 10 and 11 December 1999, which asked member states to be able by 2003 to deploy forces of up to 15 brigades, or 50,000 to 60,000 people. Those forces had to be deployable in full within 60 days, with smaller rapid response elements at very high readiness, and sustainable for at least one year. A 2013 brief from the European Union Institute for Security Studies calls it the first Headline Goal, quickly following the Saint-Malo call for credible military forces. The goal did not match the higher-end equipment goals that NATO had set in April 1999, and some Americans doubted that Europeans would spend their lower budgets on lower-end peacekeeping priorities. The European Defence Agency, created by a Joint Action of 12 July 2004 after the Thessaloniki European Council of June 2003, later oversaw capability development.

Michaels and Sus describe the goal as a force catalogue that envisaged up to 60,000 troops at 60-day notice, sustained for a year, and list it among new formal objectives that would underpin the Union as an autonomous security actor. The slides say that the 1999 Helsinki European Council built on the Saint-Malo initiative and that, on the military side, headline goals were defined. The authors write that the goal was never formally abandoned but soon became an unrealistic scenario, and a declaration of December 2008 still spoke of deploying 60,000 troops within 60 days for a major operation. From 2004 the Union focused on Headline Goal 2010, endorsed by the European Council in June 2004, and on the Battlegroup concept, which the authors call Anglo-French although the paper of 10 February 2004 came from France, Britain and Germany. Battlegroups reached full operational capability on 1 January 2007, yet the authors say member states never agreed to use them, and the 2013 brief links their non-use to resource constraints and a lack of political will.
questions: Never formally abandoned yet soon unrealistic, the _____ was followed by a Headline Goal 2010 and the Battlegroup concept once the European Defence Agency oversaw capability development from 2004.

cards.question: While the UK vetoed initiatives for an Operational Headquarters on the military side, the Union adopted the _____ 2010 in 2007 and, in the same year, established its Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability.
cards.answerDate: Adopted2007Compact signed2018
cards.abstract:
The Civilian Headline Goal 2010 is a target for the civilian side of crisis management, launched at the end of 2007 as the successor to the Civilian Headline Goal 2008 of December 2004. Its roots lie in the Feira European Council of June 2000, which named police the first priority area, with up to 5,000 officers by 2003, and added the rule of law, civilian administration and civil protection. The Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability was set up in August 2007 under a Civilian Operations Commander, responsible for the operational planning, command and control of civilian missions. A 2009 volume from the European Union Institute for Security Studies found supply of civilian capabilities outpaced by demand, as the Union ran eleven civilian operations against three in 2004. A Civilian CSDP Compact, adopted by the Foreign Affairs Council on 19 November 2018, later set 10 strategic guidelines and 22 commitments to make civilian missions more capable, more effective and more joined up.

Michaels and Sus place both steps in 2007, when the Franco-British consensus had weakened, the policy had become increasingly leaderless and enthusiasm for cooperation had waned. They add that similar progress on military operational planning was not possible because the United Kingdom vetoed initiatives for an Operational Headquarters, which the 2009 volume dates to December 2008. The slides give the civilian dimension proposed at Helsinki in 1999 as police cooperation, the rule of law, civilian administration and protection, but the four priority areas appear in the Feira text of 2000. The slides list the Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability beside its military counterpart among the bodies of the European External Action Service, and say the Compact was signed under the Finnish presidency, which the Council text of 19 November 2018 does not mention. The Compact aimed for seconded staff to make up at least 70 per cent of international personnel, yet their share fell from 66 per cent in 2018 to 60 per cent in 2022.
questions: Adopted in 2007, the _____ 2010 came when the Franco-British consensus had grown weaker, the common security and defence policy had become leaderless and enthusiasm for cooperation had waned.
Overseeing all civilian operations since its creation in 2007, the Civilian Planning and Conduct Capability was joined that year by the _____ 2010, which the Union adopted.

cards.question: Heralding the second phase of the Union’s maturation, the _____ adopted a broad range of security and defence conclusions and called for intensified action in three areas.
cards.answerDate: Phase one1998 – mid-2013CouncilDecember 2013Phase twoFrom late 2013
cards.abstract:
The December 2013 European Council met in Brussels on 19 and 20 December and, for the first time since the Lisbon Treaty took effect, held a thematic debate on defence, after meeting the NATO Secretary-General. Its conclusions set priority actions built around three axes: increasing the effectiveness, visibility and impact of the common security and defence policy, enhancing the development of capabilities and strengthening Europe’s defence industry. They noted that the Union deployed more than 7,000 staff in 12 civilian missions and four military operations, and that defence budgets were constrained and defence markets fragmented. On the defence industry they wrote that a more integrated and competitive industrial base can also enhance the Union’s strategic autonomy and its ability to act with partners. They welcomed the Commission’s communication of July 2013, which argued that Europe must be able to decide and to act without depending on the capabilities of third parties.

Michaels and Sus say that the conclusions heralded the second phase of the Union’s maturation as an autonomous security and defence actor. Before 2013, they write, the struggle with the economic and financial crisis had diverted attention from security and defence, but a deteriorating security environment put the policy back on the agenda. The conclusions invited the High Representative to report in 2015 on the challenges of a changing global environment, and the Global Strategy of June 2016 states the ambition of strategic autonomy. The authors set this against a first phase of discovery from 1998 to mid-2013 and note that the second phase was initially marked by a prevailing lack of consensus about strategic autonomy. The slides date the first period of strategic autonomy to 2013 to 2016 as an approach to security and defence, and the research service of Parliament agrees on that period and on these conclusions as the apparent first official use.
questions: In three areas, namely the effectiveness, visibility and impact of the common security and defence policy, capability development and the defence industry, the _____ called for intensified action.
Strategic autonomy was revived in late 2013 for enhanced security cooperation, and one article treats the conclusions of the _____ as the herald of the Union’s second phase of maturation.

cards.question: Chosen partly for their varied stances on the _____, the seven states include France, which sees strategic autonomy as long-term independence from the United States, and Ireland, which could avoid taking either side.
cards.abstract:
The Atlanticist–Europeanist spectrum runs between governments that put NATO and the United States at the centre of European security and those that favour a more independent European coordination of security and defence. Pieper and Lak trace the divide back to the failure of the European Defence Community in the 1950s and find that it has not abated and still hampers more ambitious policy planning. Treaty law makes room for both camps: the defence policy must not prejudice the specific character of some members’ policies and must respect those that see their common defence realised in NATO. For members of NATO the Alliance remains the foundation of their collective defence, and the treaty makes the Union’s mutual assistance clause consistent with commitments under the North Atlantic Treaty. The Saint-Malo declaration of 1998 had already said that the different situations of countries in relation to NATO must be respected.

Michaels and Sus chose Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Poland and Spain partly for their varied stances on this spectrum, alongside size, exposure to crises in the neighbourhood, strategic culture and geopolitical interests. They write that the vagueness of strategic autonomy let members pay lip service to it wherever they stood, and that Ireland as a neutral state could, in an interviewee’s words, hide quite effectively without having to jump on either side. France remains most interested in long-term independence from the United States, to the disagreement of many members on NATO’s eastern flank, for whom the United States stayed an essential partner given a shared threat perception of Russia. Spain, Germany, Finland and increasingly Poland do not seek independence from the United States, the authors say, and Finland joined NATO on 4 April 2023. The European Council on Foreign Relations found in 2019 that French-style autonomy was divisive in Estonia, that Poland saw the push as some members’ wish to end dependence on the United States, and that Ireland found a nuclear element highly problematic.

cards.question: When the Union revived strategic autonomy in late 2013, its institutions chose _____ about the concept’s meaning, which let members voice support while avoiding any commitment to implement it.
cards.answerDate: Saint-Malo1998Revivedlate 2013
cards.abstract:
The deliberate ambiguity that Michaels and Sus describe attaches to a term with no universally accepted and concretely defined meaning. The Franco-British summit at Saint-Malo in December 1998 declared that the Union must have the capacity for autonomous action, and the Clinton administration warned against de-linking from NATO, duplication and discrimination. The debate returned in the 2010s, and the European Council of December 2013, its first thematic defence debate since the Lisbon Treaty, said a stronger defence industry could enhance the Union’s strategic autonomy without defining it. An SWP study found in 2019 that differing priorities within the Franco-German core had left the concept vague for decades. Helwig and Sinkkonen conclude that no one will ever conclusively define the notion and advise members to embrace the ambiguity.

Michaels and Sus report, citing an interviewee, that when the EU’s institutions revived strategic autonomy in late 2013 they kept it ambiguous on purpose. Members could live with this, because supportive words about a vague concept were acceptable to them, whereas committing to put it into practice was, France apart, more than they would accept. The word autonomy was chosen with care over independence at Saint-Malo, yet members struggle to agree on autonomy from whom or for what purpose, so states anywhere on the Atlanticist-Europeanist spectrum, even neutral Ireland, could pay lip service. The lecture slides define strategic autonomy as the EU’s capacity to act autonomously in strategically important areas, attributing this to the European Parliament’s research service, and note, citing Helwig 2023, that it has stretched to health, industrial policy and cyber. After Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine some experts declared strategic autonomy in security and defence dead, while others expected it to bounce back if Europeans discussed it more honestly and got rid of the ambiguity.
questions: Because the EU’s institutions practised _____ over autonomy from whom and for what purpose, states anywhere on the Atlanticist-Europeanist spectrum, even neutral Ireland, could pay lip service to the idea.

cards.question: The agreement between Chirac and Blair at Saint-Malo in 1998 on autonomous EU action became the _____ that shaped Operation Artemis in 2003 and the later Battlegroup concept.
cards.answerDate: Saint-Malo1998Declarationearly 2003Artemis2003Weakenedmid-2000s
cards.abstract:
The Anglo-French consensus grew out of the Saint-Malo summit of December 1998, where France and the United Kingdom declared that the Union must have the capacity for autonomous action, backed up by credible military forces. Maartje Rutten, who compiled the core documents, describes a ‘sea change’ in British attitude, yet the declaration kept NATO’s collective defence commitments in place. At Le Touquet on 4 February 2003 the two countries proposed that the EU examine how it can contribute to peacekeeping in Africa, including through autonomous operations in close cooperation with the United Nations. On 12 June 2003, at the request of the UN Security Council, the EU launched Operation Artemis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, its first EU-only military mission, led by France. In February 2004 France, Germany and the UK presented the battle group concept after a Franco-British initiative, and ministers approved groups of 1,500 troops in April.

The slides date the new start of the European security and defence policy to the 1998 initiative of France and the UK, and call Operation Artemis the first autonomous EU-led military operation. Michaels and Sus call the consensus an ideational shift above all for the UK, where an autonomous EU role had been close to unthinkable for most of the 1990s. They argue that although autonomy was not formally written into EU security documents, the consensus shaped the launch of Artemis, which they count as the EU’s second military intervention and its first overseas. From a French perspective, Artemis was an opportunity for emancipation from NATO, and the Battlegroup concept also traces to an Anglo-French initiative, though members never agreed to use the Battlegroups. The consensus grew weaker in the mid-2000s, they write, when the Common Security and Defence Policy became leaderless and the UK vetoed initiatives for an Operational Headquarters, and in April 2003 Britain had already objected that the Tervuren proposal for an EU-only planning cell breached the spirit of Saint-Malo.
questions: In the mid-2000s the _____ behind autonomous EU crisis management grew weaker, as the Common Security and Defence Policy became leaderless and the UK vetoed plans for an Operational Headquarters.

Chirac and Blair agreed in early 2003 that the EU should help manage crises through autonomous operations in close cooperation with the United Nations, focused on Africa, a _____ that shaped Operation Artemis.

cards.question: Under the _____, Irish troops may deploy on peacekeeping missions overseas only with United Nations Security Council authorisation, a rule now under review as policymakers press for legal changes to remove it.
cards.abstract:
The Irish triple lock requires that a contingent of twelve or more Irish troops serve abroad with an international force only with Government approval, a resolution of Dáil Éireann and a United Nations mandate. It rests on two Acts of the Oireachtas, passed in 1960 and 2006, that amend the Defence Act 1954. The 2006 Act counts as a qualifying force one established, mandated, authorised or otherwise sanctioned by a resolution of the Security Council or the General Assembly of the United Nations. Supporters of change note that any of the five permanent members can veto a Security Council mandate, while the General Assembly route needs a two-thirds vote and a Council majority and is rarely used. At Seville in June 2002 Ireland declared that overseas operations, including those under European defence policy, need UN authorisation, Government agreement and Dáil approval.

Michaels and Sus describe the rule as stipulating Security Council authorisation for Irish troops on peacekeeping missions overseas, and report that policymakers are pressing for legal changes to remove it. They report anxiety in Ireland about greater EU-NATO cooperation, where any NATO reference should be matched by a UN one, and more willingness to talk if cooperation entails nothing legal. They count Ireland among members with clear red lines, such as a European nuclear deterrent, yet say even neutral Ireland was willing to support strategic autonomy, and they quote an interviewee who said Ireland had kept a toe in the water at official level without ever jumping in. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write that Austria, Malta and Ireland invoked Article 31 of the Treaty on European Union in February 2022 to express reservations about financing lethal equipment for a country in an ongoing conflict, but let the change go ahead. The Government’s Bill, published in general scheme in May 2025, would drop the UN mandate, and in September 2026 the Irish Times called ending the triple lock a clear dividing line between Government and Opposition.

cards.question: After February 2022 a division of labour emerged between the EU and NATO, read as a sign of _____ and of EU defence capabilities strengthening the European pillar of NATO.
cards.answerDate: Turning pointFebruary 2022
cards.abstract:
The principle of complementarity with NATO has framed EU defence policy for years, and in December 2013 the European Council said that the Common Security and Defence Policy would continue to develop in full complementarity with NATO. NATO describes itself and the EU as playing complementary, coherent and mutually reinforcing roles and says that Allies developing capabilities must avoid unnecessary duplication. The Strategic Compass of 2022 repeats that a stronger and more capable EU in security and defence is complementary to NATO, which remains the foundation of collective defence for its members. An SWP study of 2019 called security and defence the Achilles heel of strategic autonomy, because Europe prioritises NATO over the EU in this sector, almost unrestrictedly for collective defence. When Permanent Structured Cooperation was launched in December 2017, its founding text said that stronger capabilities of member states would also benefit NATO and strengthen the European pillar within the Alliance.

After February 2022, Michaels and Sus report, a certain division of labour has emerged between the EU and NATO, indicating complementarity and a perception that stronger EU defence capabilities strengthen the European pillar of NATO. The authors say the EU’s response to the war confirmed that NATO remains in the lead on European security, and that increased defence spending strains national budgets and must be channelled into a core defence structure. NATO provides a stronger and more established framework for defence planning than the EU, helped by the UK and Norway, so it is the preferred arena for advancing European defence capabilities, and this is particularly evident in Germany. In their conclusion, members see the EU’s comparative advantage in budgetary instruments and industrial policy, and the Alliance’s in a highly developed framework for military cooperation, though it is too early to tell how sustainable this is given a potential Trump victory. The lecture slides add that the capability targets of Permanent Structured Cooperation serve both EU and NATO requirements.
questions: Because NATO has a stronger and more established framework for defence planning, member states increasingly view the EU’s role through _____, treating NATO as the preferred arena for developing European capabilities.

Member states see the EU’s strength in budgetary instruments and industrial policy and NATO’s in military cooperation, a division of roles read as _____ and linked to a stronger European pillar within NATO.

cards.question: Because of the _____, cooperation between the EU and NATO still largely relies on informal contacts and ad hoc formats, even though a network of institutionalised mechanisms exists between them.
cards.answerDate: Berlin Plus2002Declarations2016, 2023
cards.abstract:
The Turkey–Cyprus stalemate is a double veto, in which Turkey has blocked Cyprus from EU-NATO cooperation and Cyprus has blocked Turkey from EU defence arrangements. It dates from 1 May 2004, when Cyprus joined the EU, because Berlin Plus admitted non-NATO states to the cooperation only if they belonged to the Partnership for Peace, which Cyprus did not. The Berlin Plus arrangements, agreed on 17 March 2003, let the Alliance support EU-led operations in which NATO as a whole is not engaged, and Operation Concordia in North Macedonia was the first to use them. Turkey had vetoed a formal EU-NATO framework until its key demands were met by the 2003 Berlin Plus arrangements, which let non-EU NATO members take part in EU missions that used NATO assets. By 2014 only two EU missions could call on Berlin Plus, and Cyprus can block any EU proposal to use it while Turkey can block the provision of NATO assets.

Michaels and Sus write that, despite an existing network of institutionalised mechanisms, EU-NATO cooperation still largely relies on informal contacts and ad hoc formats because of the stalemate. They date the Berlin Plus deal to 2002, after Turkey lifted its opposition to the Common Security and Defence Policy, whereas NATO’s chronology places the joint declaration in December 2002 and the framework in March 2003. The suggestion that the EU would have access to NATO planning, assets and capabilities, along with unwritten rules such as NATO’s right of first refusal, proved impracticable, they say. They cite joint declarations of 2016 and 2023, yet in 2026 the Centre for European Reform still reported that Turkey forces EU and NATO civil servants to cooperate informally, unable to exchange classified information. The slides call a Council body the Political and security group and say it prepares the Political and Security Committee’s meetings, implementation and partnership with NATO, whereas the European External Action Service names the Politico-Military Group as the body with particular responsibility for EU-NATO relations.
questions: Although the 2002 Berlin Plus arrangements suggested the EU would have access to NATO planning, assets and capabilities, a _____ now limits EU-NATO cooperation largely to informal contacts and ad hoc formats.

cards.question: Countries on NATO’s _____ kept regarding the United States as an essential partner and key ally, sharing its threat perception of Russia even through the setbacks of Donald Trump’s presidency.
cards.abstract:
The Eastern Flank of NATO is the belt of member states facing Russia, running from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the Black Sea in the south. At the Warsaw Summit of July 2016 NATO decided on an enhanced Forward Presence in the north-east, and by August 2017 four multinational battlegroups were operating in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. After Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 Allies agreed to scale the battlegroups up to brigade size where required. A 2021 analysis by the Center for European Policy Analysis said these states face a more clear and present danger from Russia than their Western allies, so NATO is central to their defence. An SWP study of 2019 added that Central and Eastern European NATO states had greater faith in Washington’s bilateral guarantees than in the EU’s solidarity.

Michaels and Sus report that for countries on NATO’s Eastern Flank the United States remained an essential partner, with a common threat perception of Russia, even through the setbacks of Donald Trump’s presidency. They say this was in particular because threat perceptions of Russia differed among EU countries, most notably Germany, and that the cracks in US commitments brought no substantial convergence on strategic autonomy. After February 2022, they write, France remained most interested in independence from the US, to the disagreement of many Eastern Flank states, particularly the small ones, which think Europe can defend itself against Russia in the mid-term only with US cooperation. Germany has tried to restore its credibility with the Eastern Flank and the US by raising defence spending and sending a battalion to Lithuania, and in December 2023 Berlin and Vilnius agreed to station a whole brigade there, inaugurated in May 2025. Burilkov and Wolff write that for countries on the eastern flank most exposed to Russia, and those with substantial gaps even in the basic components of deterrence, a substantial increase in defence spending might be realistic politically.
questions: Many states on the _____ disagree with France, which remains most interested in independence from the United States, because they think Europe can defend itself in the mid-term only with US cooperation.
Germany has tried to restore its credibility as a reliable ally in the eyes of the US and of countries on the _____, raising defence spending and sending a battalion to Lithuania.

cards.question: Experts speak of a _____ in the period after 2016, as the Implementation Plan on Security and Defence set off the rapid development of new instruments in the fastest-growing field of European cooperation.
cards.answerDate: Global StrategyJune 2016PESCO2017Peace FacilityMarch 2021CompassMarch 2022
cards.abstract:
The security momentum is the burst of EU defence initiatives that followed the Global Strategy of June 2016. On 14 November 2016 the Council welcomed the Implementation Plan on Security and Defence and set a level of ambition that included the capacity to act autonomously when and where necessary and with partners wherever possible. The same conclusions agreed to explore an inclusive Permanent Structured Cooperation, and that framework was launched in December 2017. The Coordinated Annual Review on Defence began in 2017, and the European Defence Fund has nearly €7.3 billion for 2021 to 2027. The European Peace Facility has since 2021 been an off-budget fund for military and defence actions, set at €5.7 billion for seven years and later raised to €17 billion.

Michaels and Sus write that experts mention a security momentum, citing a 2019 European Parliament source, in particular for the period after 2016. The authors present it as the translation into material terms of strategic reflection that produced the Global Strategy of June 2016 and the Strategic Compass of March 2022, and as the start of the fastest-growing field of European cooperation. They say the European Defence Fund and the Coordinated Annual Review improved defence-industrial cooperation, Permanent Structured Cooperation enhanced interoperability, and the European Peace Facility provided a funding mechanism for actions with military and defence implications. Nonetheless, they add, implementation was cumbersome until February 2022, because members differed on long-term objectives and national defence funding was insufficient, so strategic autonomy remained an aspiration rather than a political reality. The slides list the Review, the Peace Facility, established in March 2021, and Permanent Structured Cooperation, established in 2017, as implementing the Global Strategy, and count 17 projects adopted in 2018 and more than 70 ongoing, while the European Defence Agency counts 83 from 2018 to 2025, 75 still ongoing.
questions: After the Union’s 2016 strategy, new instruments such as Permanent Structured Cooperation and the European Peace Facility fed what experts call a _____, though implementation stayed cumbersome until February 2022.

cards.question: On the EU’s likely security and defence role, a 2023 article says it is set to become that of a _____ to the United States and NATO.
cards.answerDate: Helwig article2023
cards.abstract:
Michaels and Sus quote Niklas Helwig’s 2023 article for the view that the EU’s security and defence role is set to become that of a muscled-up junior partner to the United States and NATO. A Helwig working paper of 2020 separates a conventional view of strategic autonomy, focused narrowly on the EU’s dependence on the US as a security provider, from a global view about advancing values and interests abroad. In its table the conventional view asks for autonomy from the United States and autonomy to act militarily in Europe’s neighbourhood. NATO says the development of European defence capabilities contributes to transatlantic burden-sharing, and SWP argued in 2019 that a larger European contribution could make the transatlantic relationship more symmetrical. The Strategic Compass of 2022 says a stronger and more capable EU in security and defence is complementary to NATO, and that the EU will act with partners whenever possible and alone when necessary.

The authors report Helwig’s argument that, while the shortcomings in EU security and defence policy were obvious, the Union has displayed autonomous agency within transatlantic security and global economic interdependencies and has shaped global responses to Russia’s war. They set beside it Hoffmeister’s point that the EU, rather than NATO, gave the immediate political response to the attack, among other things by activating the European Peace Facility, which the European External Action Service says has mobilised €6.1 billion for Ukraine. Juncos and Vanhoonacker, they add, conclude that most EU members are comfortable with NATO overseeing European security, and they themselves say the EU’s response confirmed that NATO remains in the lead. They say their emphasis on acceptability complements approaches such as Helwig’s that move from negative understandings of strategic autonomy, meaning decoupling or autonomy from, to positive ones, meaning enhancing capacity or autonomy to. The slides, citing Helwig 2023, likewise distinguish strategic autonomy from, which means acting without interference, from strategic autonomy to, which means having the capacity to act in a competitive global arena.
questions: Having shown autonomous agency within transatlantic security and shaped global responses to the war, the EU is set to become, one 2023 view holds, a _____ to the United States and NATO.
Although the EU, rather than NATO, gave the immediate political response to Russia’s attack, one view sees its likely security role as that of a _____ to the United States and NATO.

cards.question: After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, some suggested that EU actors should embrace _____ instead of strategic autonomy, an idea put forward in a 2023 policy brief for the European Council on Foreign Relations.
cards.answerDate: InvasionFebruary 2022Policy brief2023
cards.abstract:
The idea of strategic interdependence holds that the EU has a myriad of interdependencies with other powers, will never be totally self-sufficient, and needs a foreign policy that acknowledges this. It was set out in policy brief ECFR/513 of October 2023, written for the European Council on Foreign Relations by eight authors including Aslı Aydıntaşbaş and Mark Leonard. The brief calls it a middle way between strategic autonomy, which it says threatens to divide the EU and alienate the rest of the world, and full alignment with the US in an anti-China bloc. The Strategic Compass of March 2022 had already observed that after three decades of strong economic interdependence the return to power politics made interdependence increasingly conflictual, and it promised to reduce strategic dependencies. In March 2023 Commission President Ursula von der Leyen likewise called for de-risking instead of decoupling in EU relations with China, saying that decoupling was neither viable nor in Europe’s interest.

Michaels and Sus write that after Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine it seemed at first that the responses of the EU and its members had set aside calls for strategic autonomy for good. This led to suggestions that EU actors should embrace strategic interdependence instead, and the authors cite the 2023 policy brief by Aydıntaşbaş and colleagues, titled Strategic interdependence: Europe’s new approach in a world of middle powers. At the same time, they say, some experts declared strategic autonomy in security and defence dead, while others figured it would bounce back, especially if Europeans discussed the notion more honestly and got rid of ambiguity. Helwig and Sinkkonen, writing as the invasion began, held instead that members should embrace the ambiguity of strategic autonomy and move to implementation. Michaels and Sus add that studying which ideas about strategic autonomy members find acceptable lets them discuss how the EU manages its interdependencies with the US, NATO and others, after a post-2016 shift to global economic interdependencies had pushed the notion off the EU’s radar.
questions: Initially it seemed that the EU’s responses to the invasion had ended calls for strategic autonomy for good, which led to the suggestion of _____ as an alternative approach.
Europe’s new approach in a world of middle powers, as a 2023 policy brief put it, was _____, an alternative to strategic autonomy after the invasion.

cards.question: In June 2026 about 2,600 soldiers from 13 nations took part in _____, a live exercise near Zaragoza in which the Union tested its Rapid Deployment Capacity in the fictional state of Seglia.
cards.answerDate: Seglia crisissummer 2025ExerciseJune 2026Earlier MILEX2024
cards.abstract:
The MILEX26 exercise was a live drill of the Union’s Rapid Deployment Capacity, held in June 2026 at the San Gregorio training area near Zaragoza in Spain. Eurocorps, the multinational army corps that supplied the deployed force headquarters, calls it the fourth live exercise the Union has held in support of the Capacity. The first was MILEX23 in October 2023 near Cádiz, which the External Action Service counts as the Union’s first ever live military exercise, with 2,800 personnel from member states. Its predecessor, MILEX25, sent forces from across Europe to Hungary in March 2025 for a field phase set in a fictional country named Seglia. The Strategic Compass of March 2022 had already asked for frequent live exercises with the progressive involvement of the Military Planning and Conduct Capability, which it said would shape the Capacity.

Soler reports that 2,600 soldiers from 13 nations took part in what she calls one of the EU’s largest live exercises yet, while the Spanish Defence Staff and Eurocorps both count about 2,500. Its scenario centred on Seglia, a fictional state where security had deteriorated since the summer of 2025 after a self-declared autonomous administration emerged with the backing of an armed insurgent group. After the president of Seglia appealed for European military assistance the Union activated its Capacity, and an insurgent ambush on a battalion convoy triggered a combined-arms response in which commanders had to improvise when one of four tanks failed to exit as scheduled. Soler names Lieutenant General Michiel van der Laan, director of the Brussels-based Military Planning and Conduct Capability, as commander, and the Spanish Defence Staff says the Capacity was tested at strategic, operational and tactical level. Soler presents the exercise as a test of whether the EU can move fast enough to matter in a real crisis, and the lecture slides add that in 2024 the Capability acted as Operation Headquarters for the MILEX exercise.

cards.question: Evolving out of the battlegroups, the _____ is designed to deploy within 10 days with at least 5,000 troops and can act across land, air, maritime and cyber domains.
cards.answerDate: Deploys within10 daysEPF foundedMarch 2021ExerciseJune 2026
cards.abstract:
The Rapid Deployment Capacity is the force that the Strategic Compass of March 2022 promised, a modular force of up to 5,000 troops with land, air and maritime components. The Compass said it should work in a non-permissive, meaning hostile, environment as initial entry, reinforcement or a reserve to secure an exit, with scenarios first focused on rescue and evacuation. It was to consist of substantially modified EU Battlegroups together with pre-identified forces and capabilities that member states keep ready. The External Action Service announced on 20 May 2025 that the Capacity was operational, adding that its use needs a unanimous decision of the member states. Meyer, Van Osch and Reykers list what differs from the battlegroups: a joint design, earmarked enablers, about 5,000 troops against 1,500 and a proposed standby of 12 months.

Soler describes the force the battlegroups evolved into as having at least 5,000 troops, whereas the Compass and the External Action Service say up to 5,000. She adds that it is designed to deploy within 10 days across land, air, maritime and cyber domains, with a standby period of one year and the Brussels-based Military Planning and Conduct Capability as its operational headquarters. The lecture slides list the European Peace Facility as established in March 2021, and Soler says members can draw on its €17 billion for a significant share of training and deployment costs, though the Parliament’s research service estimates it covers only 5% to 10% of mission costs. The force was tested at MILEX26 in June 2026, where the scenario began with the Union activating it, and Eurocorps says the Spanish-led battlegroup was validated there for a standby from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027. Soler says the biggest obstacle may also be the oldest, since sending the force in still needs the unanimous approval of all 27 member states, and Yf Reykers of Maastricht University sees up to 5,000 troops as only a limited quantitative improvement.

cards.question: Created in 2004 and fully operational from 2007, the _____ were multinational formations of around 1,500 troops, mostly for land operations, with willing member states rotating through six-month standby periods.
cards.answerDate: Created2004Operational2007
cards.abstract:
The EU Battlegroups were rapid-reaction units of around 1,500 troops, proposed by France and Britain with German support on 10 February 2004 as part of the Union’s capability target, the Headline Goal 2010. They built on Operation Artemis, the first autonomous EU-led military operation, launched in June 2003 under a United Nations mandate in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A battlegroup was meant to be deployable within 10 days of a Council decision and to sustain operations for 30 days. The concept was launched on 22 November 2004 and the groups reached full operational capability on 1 January 2007, each standing by for six months at a time. Michaels and Sus add that the concept became a key element of the EU’s capability efforts from 2004, based on an Anglo-French initiative and the Artemis experience, but that member states never agreed to use the groups.

Soler writes that participation was voluntary and that the EU assembled 18 regional groups, among them the Swedish-led Nordic Battlegroup, the Spanish-Italian Amphibious Battlegroup and the Polish-led Visegrad Battlegroup. In two decades they were never deployed, not even during the chaotic evacuation from Afghanistan in 2021, and on 29 August 2021 Josep Borrell said the EU has battlegroups that have never been mobilized. Critics saw them as victims of the EU’s decision-making process, a force that existed on paper without the political consensus needed to deploy, while others blamed the lack of an agile command structure and NATO’s competing claims on the same troops. Meyer, Van Osch and Reykers find that the main obstacle was political disincentive, as states lost interest after the financial crisis of 2008 to 2009, while the cost of standby and deployment fell on the contributing nations. The lecture slides list the battlegroups among the tools for strengthening rapid response in the Implementation Plan on Security and Defence of 2016, and Soler says they evolved into the Rapid Deployment Capacity after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

cards.question: The EU remains dependent on NATO and national militaries for _____ such as airlift, satellite intelligence and integrated air defence, a gap that the European Defence Fund only partly narrows.
cards.answerDate: Bruegel analysis21 February 2025Soler article29 June 2026
cards.abstract:
Strategic enablers are the supporting assets that make a deployment possible, and the Strategic Compass lists strategic transport, force protection, medical assets, cyber defence, satellite communication and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities. It also names strategic airlift, space-based communication, amphibious capabilities and remotely piloted aircraft among the critical shortfalls that it promised to mitigate. The External Action Service factsheet of March 2024 counts enablers among the building blocks of the Rapid Deployment Capacity, beside the planning headquarters, common funding and secure communications. The Parliament’s research service named intelligence and strategic reconnaissance, strategic transport and air-to-air refuelling as key gaps in 2023 and reported that experts doubted they would be made up by 2025. In its resolution on Afghanistan of 16 September 2021 the European Parliament said that the EU must invest in surveillance and reconnaissance, intelligence and strategic airlift.

Soler gives airlift, satellite intelligence and integrated air defence as examples, and writes that the EU remains dependent on NATO and national militaries for them, a challenge raised by Javi López, a vice president of the European Parliament. López says that the nearly €8 billion European Defence Fund and the €1.5 billion European Defence Industrial Programme narrow the gap but remain modest for the challenge, while the Commission’s page gives the Fund nearly €7.3 billion for 2021 to 2027. Yf Reykers of Maastricht University adds that the balance of land, air, maritime and special operations forces, alongside strategic enablers, would vary significantly from one operation to another, so the key question is whether the Capacity can assemble different force packages. Burilkov and Wolff write that Ukraine and the EU rely on some critical US strategic enablers, including intelligence and satellite communications, which are difficult to replace in the short term but have substitutes if necessary. They add that US troops are backed by the full might of American strategic enablers, including strategic aviation and space assets, which European militaries lack.

cards.question: Earlier in 2026 the Union’s defence commissioner proposed a standing pan-European force of at least 100,000 troops, separate from national armies, reviving the long-debated idea of a _____ to complement US forces in Europe.
cards.answerDate: Proposal2026Force sizeat least 100,000
cards.abstract:
The idea of a European army dates to October 1950, when the French prime minister René Pleven proposed a European Army under supranational authority and funded by a common budget. Six states signed the treaty creating a European Defence Community in May 1952, but the French National Assembly rejected it in August 1954, refusing even to discuss it. Defence cooperation then took place mainly inside NATO, as the Western European Union of 1954 played only a small role. Article 42 of the Treaty on European Union says that the common security and defence policy will lead to a common defence only when the European Council, acting unanimously, so decides. Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker called for a common army in March 2015, and Angela Merkel told the European Parliament in November 2018 that she backed Emmanuel Macron’s call for a ‘real, true’ army.

Soler says the idea is back on the political agenda as anxieties grow over a reduced US military presence in Europe, and that Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain calls a European army under a single flag the only way to guarantee lasting peace. On 11 January 2026 Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius asked who would replace the 100,000 American troops that form Europe’s backbone force, and set 27 ‘bonsai armies’ against a powerful, standing European military force of 100,000 troops. Soler describes his proposal as a force of at least 100,000 troops separate from national armies, and Defence24 reports that Sweden’s defence minister Pål Jonson rejected an EU army and pointed to NATO. Soler writes that the idea of the Rapid Deployment Capacity as the nucleus of a future European army remains largely theoretical, and General Seán Clancy, chairman of the EU Military Committee, called the matter ultimately a political question. Christoph Meyer of King’s College London says the EU must walk before it can run, and that for tasks beyond crisis management Europe already has a dedicated organisation in NATO.

cards.question: Critics called the EU battlegroups a force that existed on paper, and they were never deployed in two decades, not even during the chaotic _____ of 2021.
cards.answerDate: Created2004Operational2007Evacuation2021
cards.abstract:
The Kabul evacuation was the airlift from Hamid Karzai International Airport that began on 15 August 2021 after the rapid fall of the Afghan capital. By 24 August the US military alone had airlifted about 64,000 people since July, and on 22 August the US and its allies flew 94 flights from Kabul. On 29 August 2021 Josep Borrell said that Europe had not been able to send 6,000 soldiers to secure the area around Kabul airport. The European Parliament’s resolution of 16 September 2021, adopted by 536 votes to 96, said that no cooperation or coordination among member states took place during the rescue operation, which caught most embassies by surprise. The Strategic Compass later stated that the crisis in Afghanistan underscored the importance of an increased ability to rescue and evacuate EU citizens at risk beyond the Union’s borders.

Soler brings the evacuation in through the battlegroups, which she says were never deployed in two decades, not even during the chaotic evacuation from Afghanistan in 2021, and she does not name Kabul. The battlegroups, created in 2004 and operational from 2007, had around 1,500 troops, and critics saw them as a force that existed on paper without the political consensus needed to deploy. In the same interview Borrell noted that the EU has battlegroups but that they have never been mobilized, and he proposed a permanent Initial Entry Force of 5,000 soldiers able to mobilise at short notice. The Rapid Deployment Capacity that evolved from them is designed to deploy within 10 days and to field troops for evacuation, and Maślanka notes that its first planned scenario was inspired by the Afghanistan evacuation of 2021. Michaels and Sus list the rapid fall of Kabul among the violent conflicts affecting European security that caught the EU and its members off guard, and add that Europeans were criticised for over-reliance on US intelligence and policymaking.

cards.question: One expert argued that keeping 5,000 troops on high alert year-round needs a considerably higher pool of personnel, since units standing by, rotating in and recovering all count towards _____ for a rapid force.
cards.abstract:
Force generation is the work of matching the forces that member states offer to what an operation needs, as participants did at a Rapid Deployment Capacity conference in Brussels on 8 and 9 April 2025. The Strategic Compass promised to incentivise force generation for military missions and operations, for example by making the rotation of troops more transparent and predictable and by widening the common costs under the European Peace Facility. The External Action Service expects pre-identified national modules to make force sensing and force generation in a crisis much quicker. For the battlegroups, Meyer, Van Osch and Reykers report, standby rotations lasted six months and gaps in the roster appeared from 2012. For the Capacity they note proposed revisions such as a default standby of 12 months and staggered readiness, and Maślanka adds that it is up to 5,000 soldiers instead of two battlegroups of 1,500 each.

Soler’s article makes the point behind force generation without using the term, saying that keeping a 5,000-troop force package on high alert year-round would require a considerably higher pool of personnel. The point comes from Yf Reykers, associate professor of International Relations at Maastricht University, who explains that while some units remain on standby, others would be preparing to rotate in and others would be recovering from previous deployments and training cycles. He sees the expansion to up to 5,000 personnel as only a limited quantitative improvement, and says the key question is whether the Capacity can assemble different force packages depending on mission and geography. A study cited by the Parliament’s research service suggests 7,000 to 10,000 troops including enablers as a rough indication of what the envisaged scenarios require, since 5,000 would not cover all of them. Soler herself describes the Capacity as expanding to at least 5,000 troops, whereas the Compass speaks of up to 5,000, and she notes that its standby period has been extended to one year against six months for the battlegroups.
