cards.question: Published jointly by Bruegel and the Kiel Institute on 21 February 2025, _____ offered initial estimates of the weapons and troops Europe would need to defend itself if the United States effectively withdrew.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
Defending Europe without the US: first estimates of what is needed is Bruegel Analysis 05/2025, published on 21 February 2025 by Alexandr Burilkov and Guntram B. Wolff jointly with the Kiel Institute for the World Economy. Both authors had worked on a Kiel Institute report of September 2024, which found Russian military industrial capacity rising strongly while ‘peace dividend’ cuts had left German forces short of mass. SIPRI counted $454 billion of military spending by the European members of NATO in 2024, and 18 of the 32 members spent at least 2.0 per cent of GDP. Since 2022 the United States has kept between about 75,000 and 105,000 military personnel in Europe, and in May 2026 the Pentagon announced a withdrawal of 5,000 troops from Germany. Sophia Besch wrote in June 2025 that Europe’s dependence on the United States for strategic enablers, war-ready troops and ammunition was long known, and that Europeans should assume the US backstop may not hold.

Burilkov and Wolff write that Europe needs to be able to defend itself against Russia, with or without the United States, and they estimate the extra weapons and troops it would need. They focus on land warfare because they judge that invasion by Russia will remain the main security challenge to Europe, and they leave nuclear deterrence and hybrid warfare aside. Five headed sections cover the Russian threat, Europe’s needs, military coordination, equipment and production, and the fiscal aspect, under a subtitle of 300,000 more troops and at least €250 billion more a year. They call continued support for Ukraine Europe’s first priority and say replacing US military support to Ukraine would cost the EU only another 0.12 per cent of its GDP. The lecture slides cite the analysis twice: ‘What is needed in defense - an example’ sets out replacing 300,000 US troops, and ‘What is needed - 2’ the Baltic equipment and the spending increase.

cards.question: The combat power of 300,000 US troops is substantially greater than that of an equal number of European troops spread across _____, which lack a unified command.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
The 29 national armies are the European forces, the UK included, over which Burilkov and Wolff say a force of 300,000 European troops would be spread. NATO’s Command Structure is headed by the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, while its Force Structure brings together the forces that member countries place at the Alliance’s disposal. On the eastern flank, NATO’s Forward Land Forces are nine multinational battlegroups, provided by framework nations and other contributing Allies on a voluntary, rotational basis. Sophia Besch wrote in 2025 that Europe’s command and control infrastructure is still underpinned by US personnel and systems, and that the United States ensures interoperability between European forces. A 2023 CSIS brief found that European NATO allies still lacked sufficient air enabling capabilities, such as air-to-air refuelling and airborne intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

The analysis says the combat power of 300,000 US troops is substantially greater than that of the same number of European troops distributed over 29 national armies. US troops, the authors write, would come in large, cohesive, corps-sized units with a unified command tighter than NATO joint command, backed by strategic aviation and space assets that European militaries lack. They cite SIPRI’s figure of 1.47 million active-duty personnel in Europe, but say effectiveness is hampered by the lack of a unified command, since NATO assumes a top US general as Supreme Allied Commander Europe. Europe therefore faces a choice: add more than 300,000 troops to make up for fragmented national militaries, or find ways to rapidly enhance coordination, because failure to coordinate means much higher costs. The lecture slides give the same figures, with 300,000 US troops replaced by a similar number of European troops lacking strong coordination, while the analysis says more than 300,000 would be needed unless coordination improves.
questions: Although Europe, including the UK, has 1.47 million active-duty military personnel, effectiveness is hampered by the lack of a unified command among its _____, unlike the corps-sized units of the US.
Europe must either add more than 300,000 troops or rapidly improve coordination, because its forces are fragmented across _____ without a unified command, according to the analysis.

cards.question: To replace the fighting capacity of 300,000 US troops, with a focus on mechanised and armoured forces to stand in for US heavy units, Europe needs roughly _____, the analysis estimates.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
The estimate of roughly 50 new European brigades translates the US reinforcement that NATO planners assume into a European equivalent. A brigade groups several battalions, and the US Army’s Spartan Brigade, converted to an armoured brigade in 2016, was to receive 87 Abrams tanks and 138 Bradley fighting vehicles for a force of about 4,200 soldiers. The Council on Foreign Relations puts the number of US military personnel in Europe since 2022 between about 75,000 and 105,000, so the 100,000 that the planners assume sits inside that range. At Madrid in 2022, NATO leaders agreed to raise the number of high-readiness forces to well over 300,000. Sophia Besch noted that Europe lacks war-ready troops, and that even its nominally deployable forces remain heavily dependent on the United States for strategic enablers.

Burilkov and Wolff cite the assumption of NATO military planners, taken from RAND in 2024, that 100,000 US troops in Europe would be rapidly joined by up to 200,000 more if Russia attacked a European NATO country. They add that these extra US troops would be concentrated in armoured units best suited to the East European battlefield. A realistic estimate may therefore be a European increase equal to the fighting capacity of 300,000 US troops, focused on mechanised and armoured forces to replace US army heavy units, which translates to roughly 50 new brigades. The authors add that 300,000 new personnel would have to be recruited and trained, and recall that West Germany under Chancellor Schmidt rapidly modernised the Bundeswehr between 1974 and 1982. The lecture slides put it more briefly, saying that replacing 300,000 US troops would require a similar number of European troops, ready to be deployed, whereas the analysis expresses the need as fighting capacity.

cards.question: Measured against the US Army III Corps, at least 1,400 tanks, 2,000 infantry fighting vehicles and 700 artillery pieces form the _____ needed to prevent a rapid Russian breakthrough in the Baltics.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
The minimum deterrence package is the equipment that Burilkov and Wolff say credible European deterrence would require, for instance to prevent a rapid Russian breakthrough in the Baltics. They take the US Army III Corps as a reference point, a corps whose official page lists three divisions under it: the 1st Cavalry, the 1st Armored and the 1st Infantry Division. A Kiel Institute report found that in 2021 Germany had only 339 tanks and 121 howitzers, against around 4,200 Leopard tanks in 1992, with French and British stocks comparable to the German ones. NATO’s Forward Land Forces include battlegroups in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which framework nations and other contributing Allies provide on a voluntary, rotational basis. The Commission’s SAFE instrument offers €150 billion in long-maturity loans for defence investment and encourages joint procurement to support economies of scale.

The package comes to a minimum of 1,400 tanks, 2,000 infantry fighting vehicles and 700 artillery pieces, the artillery meaning 155mm howitzers and multiple rocket launchers. The authors say this is more combat power than currently exists in the French, German, Italian and British land forces combined. They add that these forces need sufficient munitions beyond the barebones stockpiles now available, and that Europe would also need aviation, transport, missile, drone warfare, communication and intelligence capacities. To reach the targets production across Europe would need to surge and equipment spending, now about 0.7 per cent of GDP, would need to rise substantially, with very large orders under a single European standard cutting costs. The lecture slides give the same three figures on ‘What is needed - 2’ but more cautiously, saying they ‘may be needed’ to deter Russia in the Baltics, and add that single European standards would have to be agreed.

Beyond the tanks, vehicles and artillery of the _____, Europe would also need aviation and transport, missile, drone warfare, communication and intelligence capacities, and sufficient munitions.

cards.question: From about 2 per cent of GDP now, an initial assessment suggests European defence spending should rise in the short term to around _____, though the computation is not straightforward.
cards.answer: Three and a half per cent of GDP
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
A defence budget of 3.5 per cent of GDP is the level that Burilkov and Wolff reach in the short term by adding about €250 billion a year to Europe’s present spending. SIPRI recorded military spending of 1.9 per cent of GDP for Germany and 4.2 per cent for Poland in 2024, with European NATO members spending $454 billion in total. In June 2025 NATO allies agreed to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP a year on core defence by 2035, within a 5 per cent total. The Commission’s White Paper of March 2025 proposed letting Member States raise defence spending by up to 1.5 per cent of GDP outside the EU’s fiscal rules. In March 2025 Germany amended its Basic Law to exempt defence spending above 1 per cent of GDP from its constitutional debt brake.

Burilkov and Wolff write that European defence spending will have to rise substantially from about 2 per cent of GDP, and that an increase of about €250 billion a year, to around 3.5 per cent, is warranted in the short term. They add that the computation is not straightforward, since larger orders should bring down unit prices while a rapid rise in demand will certainly push prices up in the short term. German leadership and commitment, they say, will be critical, with national defence spending rising from €80 billion to €140 billion a year, approximately 3.5 per cent of GDP, and topped up with joint EU funding. Military equipment spending, now about 0.7 per cent of GDP, would need to rise substantially, and by their calculation Poland put 70 per cent of its additional funds into equipment, while Germany’s Sondervermögen debt fund went only to equipment. The lecture slides repeat the point that spending needs to rise to about 3.5 per cent of GDP, funded through debt but also increasing permanently.
cards.answerText: Three and a half per cent of GDP

cards.question: An initial assessment suggests that European defence spending should rise in the short term by about _____, though larger orders should cut unit prices while rapid demand growth will lift them.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025German pledge2022
cards.abstract:
An increase of about €250 billion a year is the short-term rise in European defence spending that Burilkov and Wolff’s initial assessment suggests, and their subtitle speaks of a hike of at least that sum. SIPRI calculated that European NATO members would have needed to spend $33.7 billion more in 2024 to reach 2.0 per cent of GDP, and $663 billion more to reach 5.0 per cent. The Commission’s White Paper of March 2025 said defence investment could reach at least €800 billion over four years, including €150 billion from the SAFE loan instrument. SAFE is financed by EU borrowing on capital markets and aims to reduce fragmentation between national defence markets through joint procurement. The authors expect larger orders to bring down unit prices, though a rapid rise in demand will certainly push them up in the short term, and a Kiel Institute report found German 155mm ammunition cost less per shell in larger orders.

The authors illustrate the cost with the Leopard II tank: Germany has ordered 105 since February 2022 at €28 million each, which could add up to €40 billion for 1,400 tanks, though unit prices should fall substantially. They suggest splitting the €250 billion equally between EU and national funding, with countries not spending more nationally getting less from the common pot to address moral hazard. Such hikes should be funded through debt in the short run for political and economic reasons, they say, but funding must rise permanently, and one solution would raise €125 billion a year for five years at EU level. Germany would have to raise at least half of that €125 billion itself, lifting national defence spending from €80 billion to €140 billion, and its contribution would be close to an additional 100,000 troops. The lecture slides state the funding point briefly: spending should be funded through debt but also needs to increase permanently.

cards.question: Providing the required tanks, vehicles and artillery with enough munitions means going beyond today’s barebones stockpiles to a _____ of one million, the minimum for 90 days of high-intensity combat.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
A 155mm shell stockpile of one million shells would be the minimum for 90 days of high-intensity combat, according to Burilkov and Wolff. Camille Grand wrote in 2023 that the West collectively lacked both the stockpiles and the production capacity to meet the demands of high-intensity warfare, and he called NATO’s stockpile guidance too vague. The EU’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production is the third, industrial track of the three-track ammunition plan agreed by the Council, and aims to raise production capacity across Europe. A Kiel Institute report cited Commission claims that Europe’s annual 155mm capacity would reach 1 million in 2024 and 2 million by the end of 2025, but judged the estimates most likely too optimistic. A 2024 investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty found that the EU had given Ukraine about half as many shells as it promised, and an industry source put real capacity at about a third of the official figure.

The figure comes in the section on equipment and production, where the authors set a minimum of 1,400 tanks, 2,000 infantry fighting vehicles and 700 artillery pieces, meaning 155mm howitzers and multiple rocket launchers. Providing these forces with sufficient munitions will be essential, they write, beyond the barebones stockpiles currently available. The Kiel report names a baseline firing rate of 10,000 shells a day for Russian forces in Ukraine, while one million shells over 90 days works out at roughly 11,000 a day. To reach the targets production across Europe would need to surge, equipment spending of about 0.7 per cent of GDP would have to rise substantially, and bundled procurement with more competition could cut costs. The Commission’s White Paper of 2025 likewise lists ammunition and missiles as a priority, calling for a strategic stockpile backed by enough industrial capacity to ensure timely replenishment.

cards.question: The quadrennial _____ in Belarus in summer 2025 would, the analysis says, demonstrate Russia’s ability to manage military exercises at scale even during a war.
cards.answerDate: ExercisesSummer 2025Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
The quadrennial Zapad exercises belong to a cycle in which Russia’s strategic exercises rotate through its western, southern, central and eastern military districts, so that each district hosts one every four years. Russia notified the OSCE that Zapad 2017 involved 12,700 people, 300 fewer than the 13,000 at which the Vienna Document requires observation. Before it, US General Ben Hodges feared a ‘Trojan Horse’ that would leave Russian forces in Belarus, and ECFR noted that Russia’s 2008 war in Georgia and 2014 annexation of Crimea were both preceded by exercises. Zapad 2021 involved 200,000 personnel, and RUSI judged it Russia’s first preparation for operations on a scale comparable to those undertaken in Ukraine a year later. Zapad 2025 was held in September 2025, and RUSI found it more compact than its predecessors, spread over several training areas and designed to stay below the Vienna Document thresholds.

Burilkov and Wolff wrote in February 2025 that the exercises would take place in Belarus in summer 2025 and would demonstrate Russia’s ability to manage military exercises at scale even during a war. They raise the exercises when asking how soon Russia could attack, noting that assessments by NATO, Germany, Poland, Denmark and the Baltic states put Russia as ready within three to ten years and that it could be sooner. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service gave timelines of about six months for a local war, two years for a regional war around the Baltic Sea and five years for a large-scale war in Europe. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service judged in 2025 that Russia was rebuilding its mass army, aiming for 1.5 million soldiers by 2026, and would station more units along Estonia’s borders if the war ended favourably for Russia. The authors call an attack on an EU country conceivable because Russia’s military is larger, more experienced and better equipped than in 2022, with roughly 700,000 troops in Ukraine at the end of 2024.

cards.question: Estimates cited in the analysis say Ukraine would need around _____ to deter Russia effectively, but such troops would need to be ready to deploy rapidly wherever Russia might attack the EU.
cards.answerDate: Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
A force of 150,000 European troops is the size that estimates cited by Burilkov and Wolff say Ukraine would need to deter Russia, and they footnote it to a New York Times report of 11 February 2025. Leo Litra noted in April 2025 that Zelensky had floated a need for 200,000 foreign troops to enforce a peace deal, while the debates then involved far smaller numbers, usually 10,000 to 30,000 to begin with. The Paris Declaration of January 2026 sets out a European-led Multinational Force for Ukraine from the Coalition of the Willing, to act at Ukraine’s request once a credible cessation of hostilities has taken place. Michael Carpenter wrote in August 2025 that a senior European defence official put the proposed force at roughly 5,000 troops, most likely in rear areas, too few to deter renewed Russian attacks. The declaration also says the Armed Forces of Ukraine will remain the first line of defence and deterrence, supported by long-term military assistance.

Burilkov and Wolff call a peace deal accepted by Ukraine unlikely but far harder for Europe, because Russia would probably continue its build-up and pose a formidable challenge to the whole EU in a very short period. In that case, they write, the EU and allies including the UK and Norway would need to accelerate their military build-ups immediately and massively. They call the question of what capacities would secure a peace deal in Ukraine at some level secondary, since the troops estimated for Ukraine would need to be ready to deploy rapidly wherever Russia might attack the EU. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service judged in 2025 that if the war ended favourably for Russia or froze, Russian units would almost certainly be stationed along Estonia’s borders in greater numbers than before 2022. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service judged in September 2026 that a Russian invasion of a NATO country was highly unlikely, since Russia would need at least six months to prepare and build up the necessary forces.

cards.question: In 2024 alone Russia produced and refurbished an estimated 1,550 tanks, 5,700 armoured vehicles and 450 artillery pieces, figures the analysis uses to show the _____ compared with 2022.
cards.answerDate: Output2024Baseline2022Published21 February 2025
cards.abstract:
The Russian production surge is the rapid ramp-up of Russian defence production since 2022, which Burilkov and Wolff document alongside the Kremlin’s broad mobilisation of society and industry. SIPRI estimated Russian military spending at $149 billion in 2024, a rise of 38 per cent that took it to 7.1 per cent of GDP. A Kiel Institute report found tank production up 215 per cent between the last quarter of 2022 and the second quarter of 2024, with about 80 per cent of production still drawing on retrofits of older vehicles. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service judged in 2026 that the Russian economy was on the brink of a major crisis driven by military expenditure, sanctions and Ukrainian strikes. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported that Russia had used over 8,000 Shahed, Geran and Garpiya drones in Ukraine by December 2024, and that its armed forces were growing despite the heaviest losses since the Second World War.

Burilkov and Wolff estimate that in 2024 alone Russia produced and refurbished 1,550 tanks, 5,700 armoured vehicles and 450 artillery pieces of all types, and deployed 1,800 long-range Lancet loitering munitions. Compared with 2022, they say, this is a 220 per cent increase in tank production, 150 per cent in armoured vehicles and artillery, and 435 per cent in long-range loitering munitions. Most of it is modernised Soviet equipment, but production will continue, albeit at a reduced tempo, once Soviet stockpiles are exhausted, and the reduction will be felt less if it comes after hostilities in Ukraine have ended. Russia has also made substantial advances in drones after previously relying on Iran, and the Kiel report expects the surge in Lancet production to continue beyond the end of hostilities in Ukraine. The authors therefore call an attack on an EU country conceivable, since Russia’s military is now considerably larger and more experienced than in 2022, with roughly 700,000 troops in Ukraine at the end of 2024.
questions: In Russia, output of tanks rose 220 per cent and of long-range loitering munitions 435 per cent between 2022 and 2024, the _____ that the analysis describes as a rapid ramp-up of production.

cards.question: A web of interactions between governments, firms, sources of finance and innovation, and supranational institutions in European defence production is conceptualised as the _____, which is contested and negotiated on multiple levels.
cards.answerDate: JunctureFebruary 2022Analysis endsMarch 2025
cards.abstract:
The European Iron Network is the term Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley use for a web of interactions between governments, firms, sources of finance and innovation, and supranational institutions in European defence production. In 2010 Mérand, Hofmann and Irondelle surveyed 73 defence officials in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and Brussels and found weak transgovernmentalism, with cross-border links but formal state actors in the strategic positions. Weiss and Biermann argue that defence integration is often demanded but rarely supplied because of sovereignty concerns, and they trace the exception of the firm EADS to national and transnational networks. Håkansson shows the Commission arguing since 1996 that European defence markets are fragmented and moving from market integration towards security integration. Bruegel’s Mejino-López and Wolff describe national preferences and little joint procurement, and the Parliament’s research service notes 27 sovereign buyers.

The course reading calls this web contested and negotiated on multiple levels, unlike the more static military-industrial complex models of the US-centric literature. They analyse three types of actor on three levels, namely the EU and NATO, national governments, and defence firms, and say NATO has most influence over what members procure whereas the EU plays a much more important role in financing and industrial policy. Unlike the hierarchical Iron Triangle of the United States, it rests on strong many to many organic connections, with nodes coordinating shared objectives through multiple lateral and vertical links, and its states form a core, a semi-periphery and a periphery. The authors take Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 as a critical juncture, meaning a turning point, after which the nodes and relationships are being reconstituted, and their analysis of EU policy documents ends in March 2025. Permanent contestation over whether and how to reconstitute the network is a source of dynamism, and the authors conclude that it will probably never attain the economies of scale or secure long-term financing of its US counterpart, though its structure gives it adaptive resilience.

Comprising three types of actor on three levels, namely supranational institutions, national governments and defence firms, the _____ has a core, a semi-periphery and a periphery of European states.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: Coined during the Cold War, the _____ model identifies legislators, bureaucrats and defence firms as the most influential nodes in the political economy of US defence production.
cards.answerDate: Earlier work1973Model1981Extended2001Similar view2003
cards.abstract:
The Iron Triangle is an image of the policy process in which a limited number of participants keep stable relations in a relatively closed policy area. In 1981 A. Grant Jordan set it beside issue networks, which are fragmented, open and extraordinarily complex, and argued that the United States had moved to some degree from the triangle towards a looser pattern. The worry about defence industry and government is older than the model, since Dwight Eisenhower’s farewell address of 17 January 1961 warned against a ‘military-industrial complex’. In the United States the Department of Defense is effectively the sole customer of the defence industrial base, a monopsony, meaning a market with one dominant buyer, and the sector keeps close ties to government through lobbying and the employment of former defence officials. Five firms, Lockheed Martin, RTX, General Dynamics, Boeing and Northrop Grumman, hold around a third of Department of Defense contract obligations.

In the political economy of defence production, Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley write, the key relationships of the Cold War were coined in Adams’ 1981 model, which identifies legislators, bureaucrats and defence firms as the most influential nodes. They say that Adams builds upon earlier analysis of the US military-industrial complex and give the work of Rosen in 1973 as an example. Subsequently, scholars pointed out that internationalisation had added new actors beyond the triangle, so Cerny, in a 2001 article on globalising the policy process, proposed adding multinational firms and international frameworks, and Lavallee argued in 2003 for public and private international links. The authors judge that these models are both static and less well suited to Europe, where they cite the remark that there are 27 military industrial complexes, not just one, and the EU has 27 sovereign buyers. They set the hierarchical, US-based triangle against their European Iron Network, in which a variety of actors at multiple levels constantly negotiate influence and resources.
questions: Held to be hierarchical and static, the _____ of US defence production links legislators, bureaucrats and defence firms and builds on earlier analysis of the military-industrial complex.

Scholars proposed extending the _____ with multinational firms and international frameworks because internationalisation had added actors beyond its three nodes, though such models were judged static and less well suited to Europe.

cards.question: Adding multinational firms and international frameworks to a Cold War model of US defence production produced what a 2001 proposal dubbed flexible _____, judged static and less well suited to Europe.
cards.answerDate: Proposed2001Similar case2003
cards.abstract:
Golden pentangles is the image Cerny set against ‘iron triangles’ in a 2001 article in Global Governance asking whether triangles of policy-making give way to pentangles as the policy process is globalised. The triangle he started from is the image of stable relations among a limited number of participants in a relatively closed policy area, as A. Grant Jordan described it in 1981. Jordan found that the United States had moved to some degree from that pattern towards a looser, more complex one resembling issue networks. In the SIPRI ranking for 2024 the three Trans-European firms Airbus, MBDA and KNDS, whose ownership and control span more than one European country, have combined arms revenues of $22.7 billion. Bruegel adds that the missile maker MBDA is owned by BAE Systems and Airbus at 37.5 per cent each and by Leonardo for the rest.

Cerny proposed in 2001 adding two categories, multinational firms and the international frameworks, to form what he dubs flexible golden pentangles, Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley report, and they use the idea for defence although Cerny’s own title speaks of the policy process in general. The Iron Triangle’s three nodes are legislators, bureaucrats and defence firms, so the two additions bring the model to five categories. The authors report that scholars have pointed out that internationalisation has added new actors and relationships to the political economy of US defence production, and the US industry is international too, with 43 per cent of global arms exports in 2020 to 2024 and major arms supplied to 107 states. They add that Lavallee in 2003 similarly argues for the inclusion in analytical models of public and private international links. The authors judge that these models are both static and less well suited to the European context, and against them they set the European Iron Network, in which influence and resources are constantly negotiated at multiple levels.

cards.question: Under _____, national governments were left the production of arms, ammunition and war material so long as they did not prejudice competition in non-military sectors.
cards.abstract:
Article 346 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, known as the TFEU, is the treaty’s security exception for arms, numbered Article 296 in the earlier EC Treaty. Its paragraph 1(b) lets any Member State take such measures as it considers necessary to protect the essential interests of its security connected with the production of or trade in arms, munitions and war material. Such measures must not adversely affect the conditions of competition in the internal market for products not intended for specifically military purposes. Paragraph 2 lets the Council, acting unanimously on a Commission proposal, change the list of products drawn up on 15 April 1958. The Commission’s guidance on the Defence Procurement Directive calls it the most relevant treaty derogation in defence and says the Court of Justice limits it to exceptional and clearly defined cases.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley summarise it as leaving the production of arms, ammunition and war material to national governments so long as they did not prejudice competition in non-military sectors, which compresses the treaty’s wording. They give it as an example of why integration in defence production has progressed more slowly than in other policy sectors, since for decades the area was seen as one of national competence. Håkansson shows the Commission pressing from 1996 against fragmentation, yet the Parliament’s research service notes Member States still invoke Article 346 to circumvent procurement rules. The authors add that the EU extended its competence into defence industrial policy in the 1990s, and that the Defence Industrial Strategy of 2024 proposed an unprecedented role, with powers to impel defence firms to share information about capacities and to force civilian firms to produce defence equipment. A study for the Parliament adds that the defence industry programme would let the Commission, in exceptional circumstances, impose priorities on defence companies, while the authors note that the literature assumed national security concerns no longer apply, which since 2022 has proved wrong.

cards.question: Network centrality, based on the depth of political and industrial integration, sorts the states of the European Iron Network into the _____, with Serbia and Switzerland placed in the last.
cards.answerDate: UK withdrawalearly 2020EU–UK pactMay 2025
cards.abstract:
The core, semi-periphery and periphery are the three zones into which Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley sort the states of the European Iron Network by network centrality, the depth of political and industrial integration. A node’s weight depends on the size of its firms and its procurement spending. The core is made of states that belong to both the EU and NATO, and the four EU members outside NATO are Ireland, Malta, Austria and Cyprus. Links beyond the Union are formal but thin, since the European Defence Agency has administrative arrangements with Norway, Serbia, Switzerland and Ukraine, and the Commission lets Ukraine and EEA-EFTA countries join SAFE procurements. Up until 2020, the authors say, the core held the states with the largest defence industries, and the UK’s withdrawal raised whether extra-EU states should be full members or kept at arm’s length.

The core members with the greatest power include France, Germany, Italy, Sweden, Spain, Poland and Czechia, all with a firm in SIPRI’s ranking of the 100 largest defence companies, as the 2024 table shows. Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, Romania and Finland are other core members, assessed by SIPRI as having exported more than $100 million worth of newly produced arms during 2000 to 2024. The authors place the United Kingdom in the semi-periphery on the assumption that the May 2025 defence pact with the EU lets its firms receive EU funding, although OSW analysts call it largely a declaration of intent and Britain said in November 2025 that its SAFE talks had broken down. They also place Ukraine there, because EU initiatives integrate it into the network, and Norway, because it has sought as close defence industry integration with the EU as possible without becoming a member state. Serbia and Switzerland, neither a member of the EU and NATO, lack integration on several levels and so are on the periphery, and Switzerland’s refusal to allow Swiss-made ammunition to go to Ukraine led European governments to avoid its firms.

cards.question: France and others argued for a _____ policy, whereas Sweden, Germany and Poland lobbied for UK and other extra-EU firms to be able to receive defence funding mobilised by the EU.
cards.answerDate: Ukraine fundMarch 2024Industry heads2024CompromiseMarch 2025EU–UK pactMay 2025
cards.abstract:
Buy European is a preference for European-made equipment in EU defence spending, summed up by Ursula von der Leyen as spending ‘more, better and European’. Bruegel’s Mejino-López and Wolff reject a Europe-only approach for risking slower, inferior or dearer systems and favour an ‘intelligent European preference’. The preference answers fragmentation, since collaborative procurement was only 18 per cent of equipment procurement in 2020, far below the 35 per cent benchmark agreed in 2007. Parliament’s committees backed a buy European rule of at least 70 per cent Union or associated content for the defence industry programme, but the October 2025 agreement caps components from other third countries at 35 per cent of cost. In a Carnegie panel of March 2025, Anna Wieslander wanted new money kept for buy European purchases, open to the UK or Turkey only after agreements with the EU, while Gesine Weber urged extending the preference to the UK on conditions.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley explain that the debate is about whether defence firms in extra-EU states could benefit from EU spending, made apparent by the UK’s withdrawal in early 2020. France and others argued for a buy European policy, whereas Sweden, Germany and Poland lobbied for UK and other extra-EU firms to receive EU-mobilised defence funding. European defence firms played a key part, with the heads of MBDA and Saab arguing in 2024 for including UK firms, although prioritising Iron Network firms would be dearer and might bring less advanced equipment later. A compromise of March 2025 let extra-EU firms receive funding if their governments signed a defence pact with the EU, as the EU and UK did in May 2025, though Britain said in November 2025 that its SAFE talks had broken down. Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops report that the Ukraine Assistance Fund, added to the European Peace Facility in March 2024 with an extra €5 billion, is explicitly linked to a buy European clause nudging member states to develop their own defence industrial base.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: Adopted by the Council in May 2025, the _____ instrument offers up to 150 billion in loans to member states raising investment in defence industrial production through joint procurement.
cards.answerDate: Ukraine fundMarch 2024Regulation27 May 2025
cards.abstract:
SAFE, short for Security Action for Europe, is a financial instrument that the Council adopted in May 2025, with up to €150 billion in loans, to support member states seeking to increase their investments in defence industrial production through joint procurement. It belongs to the ReArm Europe plan of March 2025, which aims to leverage over €800 billion in defence spending with SAFE as its loan instrument. The Commission proposed SAFE on 19 March 2025 as a regulation under Article 122 TFEU, giving member states loans backed by the EU budget. Article 122 lets the Council act on a Commission proposal without involving the European Parliament, a route praised for speed but seen as limiting democratic legitimacy. The Commission says projects generally rest on common procurement by at least two countries, with at least 65 per cent of component costs originating in the EU, Ukraine or eligible EEA-EFTA countries.

Before it, Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops write, the EU mobilised €11.1 billion under the European Peace Facility between 2022 and 2024 to support the Ukrainian armed forces, and a Ukraine Assistance Fund of March 2024 added €5 billion, which they call a substantial shift in EU security policy financing. The act is Council Regulation (EU) 2025/1106 of 27 May 2025, and the same authors name extended use of Article 122 TFEU emergency powers among the ways rules can change without treaty change. They report that the Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs, JURI, unanimously rejected fast-tracking the SAFE loan because Article 122 bypassed the Parliament, which opposes the legal basis and not the content. The Parliament then brought an action to annul the Regulation, arguing that it should have rested on Article 173 TFEU on industrial policy and that the Council gave inadequate reasons. Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley list the SAFE Regulation, with ReArm Europe and the White Paper, as outlining an EU ambition for a far greater future role that introduces new elements to the Iron Network.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: An analysis that treats the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine as a critical juncture ends in March 2025 with the launch of the _____ programme and the White Paper for European Defence.
cards.answerDate: Period beginsFebruary 2022LaunchedMarch 2025
cards.abstract:
The ReArm Europe plan is a package of financing measures that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen presented on 4 March 2025, aiming to enable €800 billion of defence investment. It rests on five pillars: a new loan instrument, national fiscal flexibility, more flexible EU budget instruments, European Investment Bank lending and private capital. The second pillar lets a state raise defence spending by up to 1.5% of its gross domestic product a year, for up to four years, by activating the national escape clause of the EU’s fiscal rules. On 6 March 2025 the European Council took note of the Commission’s plan for loans of up to €150 billion backed by the EU budget. Three economists writing for Bruegel estimated up to €650 billion of extra capabilities over four years, but warned that most would be financed nationally and that fiscally weaker states might not follow.

The plan was later rebranded ReArm Europe Plan/Readiness 2030 after a backlash from the prime ministers of Italy and Spain, and the White Paper for European Defence followed on 19 March 2025. The law professor Paul Dermine called it a significant first step but not a transformative shift, because it stays focused on national spending. Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley name the ReArm Europe programme, with the SAFE Regulation and the White Paper, as outlining the EU’s ambition to play a far greater future role, which they say adds new elements to the Iron Network. Their analysis takes the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine as a critical juncture and ends with the launch of ReArm Europe and the White Paper in March 2025, after evaluating the key EU documents adopted since 2022, from the Strategic Compass onward. They add that rearmament requires complex decisions about public and private finance, regulatory authority and political accountability, and they expect further policy developments after March 2025.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: Launched in March 2025, the _____ outlines spending worth up to EUR 800 billion, through EU loans backed by the EU budget and relaxed macroeconomic constraints on member states’ borrowing.
cards.answerDate: LaunchedMarch 2025
cards.abstract:
The White Paper for European Defence, subtitled ‘Readiness 2030’, is a strategy that the Commission and the High Representative for foreign affairs presented on 19 March 2025, the first of its kind. EU leaders asked for it at a special European Council on 6 March 2025, wanting options to boost defence financing and strengthen the industrial base. It describes a defence industry that is too fragmented, with dominant national players serving mostly domestic markets, and unable to produce at the speed member states need. Its financing chapter lists loans of up to €150 billion, national flexibility of up to 1.5% of gross domestic product and a projected €800 billion or more of defence investment over four years. Marianne Paire of the ICDS research centre in Tallinn calls it a short roadmap in which the EU mainly facilitates, while member states bear primary responsibility.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley call it the most significant EU action as of spring 2025, with more financing for arms procurement, encouragement of collaborative procurement and research investment, and a call for a unified, integrated defence market. They say it envisages six means of financing higher spending, most prominently an EU instrument of loans backed by the EU budget, with relaxed macroeconomic constraints on borrowing, collectively worth up to €800 billion. It also encourages private capital, which they say brings trade-offs because private finance has its own interests and may be less reliable than EU or state money. On extra-EU states they say €150 billion of new EU-financed spending can go to Ukraine and to members of the European Free Trade Association and European Economic Area, in practice Switzerland and Norway, and that Ukrainian industry may join collaborative procurements on the same footing as EU industry. They place it after earlier initiatives on industrial strategy, innovation and ammunition, and Dimitrova, Gürkan and Koops give the same up to €150 billion in loans for the Council’s SAFE instrument of May 2025, aimed at joint procurement.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: Among the new mechanisms fostering EU industrial cooperation launched after February 2022, the _____ is described as the most tangible example by interviewees in a study of strategic autonomy.
cards.answer: Act in Support of Ammunition Production
cards.abstract:
The Act in Support of Ammunition Production, known as ASAP, is Regulation (EU) 2023/1525, an emergency law that mobilised €500 million from the EU budget to raise European output of ammunition and missiles. It was the third track of a plan the Council agreed on 20 March 2023, after Ukraine asked for 155-millimetre artillery rounds: states would send ammunition from stocks, jointly buy 1 million rounds and expand industrial capacity. The Commission proposed it on 3 May 2023, Parliament and Council agreed on 6 July, and it was published on 24 July 2023. It paid grants of up to 35% of the eligible costs of new production capacity between 25 July 2023 and 30 June 2025, to firms in the Union or an associated country that were not controlled by a non-associated third country. The Parliament’s research service noted that European firms were geared to peacetime and built to order, so new plants took large investment and years.

The Commission reported that on 13 March 2024 a committee of member states and Norway backed 31 proposals, with €248 million for powder and €124 million for explosives, the bottlenecks for shell production. The EU Institute for Security Studies later put the total at €513 million shared by 31 projects, and noted that official evaluations were not yet available. Michaels and Sus write that after February 2022 a number of new mechanisms fostering EU industrial cooperation were launched, with ASAP the most tangible example according to their interviewees, though many stressed the importance of national decisions to raise defence spending. Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley list ASAP among the key documents they evaluated, and report that Norway, the only non-member in the European Defence Fund, also takes part in it and in EDIRPA, the EU programme promoting joint procurement. They add that ammunition firms are fragmented across national borders and were criticised for prioritising extra-European exports when the EU missed its target for supplying ammunition to Ukraine.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: In a remark cited to show how different Europe’s political economy of defence production is from that of the United States, Europe is said to have _____, not just one.
cards.answerDate: Cited piece22 May 2024EU push1990s
cards.abstract:
The remark that Europe has 27 military-industrial complexes, not just one, uses a phrase that President Dwight D. Eisenhower made famous in his farewell address of 17 January 1961. Eisenhower warned against the unwarranted influence of the military-industrial complex and called an immense military paired with a large arms industry new in the American experience. In Europe, Article 346 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union lets any member state take measures it considers necessary to protect its essential security interests connected with arms, munitions and war material. Such measures must not distort competition for non-military products, and the Commission says much defence spending still falls outside the EU’s 2009 procurement directive. The Parliament’s research service adds that demand comes almost exclusively from national governments, and that Europe builds 17 types of main battle tank where the United States builds one.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley quote the remark, from Bergmann as cited by Cohen and Alderman in the New York Times of 22 May 2024, to show that European defence production differs greatly from American. They say integration here has progressed more slowly than in other sectors because for decades the area was seen as one of national competence, and they give Article 346 as an example. Against the static models of the American literature they argue that the Iron Network is contested and negotiated on several levels, and cite Caverley that the war shows multiple defence industries with different dynamics, routines and characteristics. They say the EU has pushed since the 1990s for consolidation around a few prime contractors, to the benefit of Western European firms, while Central and Eastern European states now appear to push back, since Ukraine has shown the value of a national defence industry. Jan Joel Andersson of the EU Institute for Security Studies notes that member states spent an estimated €326 billion on defence in 2024, against about €11–12 billion in the EU’s common defence budget for 2021–2027.

cards.sub: Reading 8 · Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley (2025)

cards.question: Largely self-sufficient and developed under the auspices of ministries, private companies and even individual hobbyists, _____ had by March 2024 the capacity to produce 150,000 combat drones a month.
cards.answerDate: Drone capacityMarch 2024EU strategy2024White Paper2025
cards.abstract:
Ukraine’s drone industry produced about 2.2 million drones of various types in 2024, according to a Polish think tank’s estimate, and more than 4.5 million were expected in 2025. The state is the main buyer, with 775 billion hryvnias set aside from the budget for domestic drones, though much of the procurement is classified and the figures are estimates. Volunteer networks ran public fundraising campaigns that partly filled equipment gaps and fed a surge of private assembly, often in home workshops. The government launched the Brave1 defence-tech cluster in spring 2023 to coordinate the private sector, government, the military and investors, and it has since supported more than 2,300 companies. In 2024 Defence Minister Rustem Umerov put annual capacity at up to 3 million drones, and Brave1 counted more than 500 innovators working on unmanned aircraft.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley call it the world’s largest combat drone industry, with by March 2024 the capacity to produce 150,000 drones a month, a figure they take from a report quoting a deputy minister. They say the industry was largely self-sufficient, with drones developed under the auspices of ministries, by private companies and even by individual hobbyists, and that its innovation came from outside the traditional defence industry in an ecosystem of entrepreneurs, risk capital, government, corporations and universities. European governments want to mass produce such technologies, they add, but national procurement frameworks often put off the small high-tech firms that mattered so much in Ukraine. The EU’s 2024 industrial strategy promised joint drone production and an Innovation Office in Kyiv, which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen inaugurated on 20 September 2024 to connect EU start-ups with Ukraine’s defence industry and armed forces. The 2025 White Paper added direct procurement from Ukrainian firms, and the authors place Ukraine in the semi-periphery of the Iron Network, saying its integration shows the network can add new nodes.

cards.question: Signed in May 2025, the _____ satisfied the March 2025 compromise under which firms in extra-EU states could receive EU defence funding if their governments signed a defence pact with the EU.
cards.answerDate: UK leaves EUearly 2020AnnouncedMarch 2025Pact signedMay 2025
cards.abstract:
The EU–UK defence pact is the Security and Defence Partnership that the European Union and the United Kingdom concluded at their first summit in London on 19 May 2025. The European External Action Service calls it a structured political framework with six-monthly foreign policy dialogues between the High Representative and UK ministers and an annual defence dialogue. It says the partnership may allow UK participation in selected EU defence programmes such as the proposed SAFE loan instrument, but only where both agree. The Council’s SAFE regulation of 27 May 2025 lets countries with such a partnership join common procurements, caps components from outside the EU, the EFTA states of the European Economic Area and Ukraine at 35% of cost, and allows a further agreement to open them. Łukasz Maślanka notes that such further agreements need unanimity among member states, and the White Paper ties eligibility to terms on finance and security of supply.

Marsh, Oliveira Martins and Mawdsley report that a March 2025 compromise let firms in extra-EU states receive funding if their governments signed a defence pact with the EU, which the EU and UK signed in May 2025, so they assume the UK will join the Iron Network’s semi-periphery. They say the UK has by far the largest defence industry among extra-EU states, with an estimate that British companies make up 38% of the European sector and own 10.2% of the largest EU defence firms. Among European firms in the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s top 100 for 2022, the seven UK firms made 35% of defence revenue, the largest national share. The UK’s role provoked prolonged contestation, with France and others arguing for ‘buy European’ while Sweden, Germany and Poland lobbied for UK and other extra-EU firms to receive EU-mobilised funding. The pact did not settle access in practice, because talks on UK participation in SAFE broke down in November 2025 over the fee, leaving British firms to take part on third-country terms.
